They know because they obeyed — they filled the jars, they drew the water, they carried it to the headwaiter. Their knowledge comes from their participation in Jesus's command. The pattern mirrors what will develop through the document: those who do what Jesus says come to know who he is (7:17: "If anyone is willing to do His will, he will know of the teaching, whether it is of God or whether I speak from Myself").

"Every man serves the good wine first." The headwaiter's observation operates on two levels. On the surface, it is a comment about the social convention of serving better wine early when guests can appreciate it, and lesser wine later when their palates are dulled. The bridegroom has apparently reversed the convention, saving the best for last.

On a deeper level, the statement articulates a principle that the author may intend to apply beyond the wedding. The "good wine" that has been kept "until now" (heos arti) corresponds to the messianic reality that is now appearing. What came first — the water of purification, the old system of ritual cleansing, the existing structures of Jewish religious practice — was good but not the best. What comes now, through Jesus, surpasses it. The principle echoes the prologue: "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (1:17). The relationship is not opposition but escalation — the best has been kept for now.

The word arti ("now, at this moment") will appear at significant points in the document (9:19, 25; 13:7, 19, 33, 37; 16:12, 31). It marks the present moment as the moment when something decisive is happening.

div.title: Verse 11: The Author's Interpretation of the Sign
div.p: "This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him."
This verse is the author's own commentary on the event, and it introduces three terms that will structure the rest of the document.

"Beginning of his signs" (archen ton semeion). The word semeion ("sign") is this author's preferred term for Jesus's extraordinary acts. The other accounts use dynamis ("mighty work, power") as their primary term; this author never uses dynamis for Jesus's miracles. Instead, he uses semeion — a word that means an indicator, a pointer, something that signifies a reality beyond itself. A sign is not merely an act of power; it is an act that communicates meaning. The signs in this document are not random displays of ability; each one reveals something specific about Jesus's identity and mission. The author will use the term approximately seventeen times, and at the document's conclusion will state his purpose explicitly: "Many other signs Jesus also performed in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book; but these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name" (20:30-31). The signs exist to produce belief, and belief produces life.

The term semeion also connects to the LXX, where it is used for the acts of God in Israel's history, particularly the plagues in Egypt. Exodus 7:3 (LXX): "I will multiply My signs (ta semeia mou) and wonders in the land of Egypt." Deuteronomy 4:34: "Has a god tried to go to take for himself a nation... by signs (semeiois) and wonders?" The signs of the Exodus were acts that identified YHWH as the one true God and secured Israel's liberation. For a first-century reader, calling Jesus's acts "signs" places them in the category of God's acts in Israel's defining story.

The word arche ("beginning") recalls the document's opening: "In the beginning" (en arche). The beginning of creation was through the Word (1:1-3); the beginning of signs is through the Word-made-flesh. The signs are a new creative activity, the incarnate Word acting within the creation he made.

"Manifested his glory" (ephanerosen ten doxan autou). The verb phaneroo ("to make visible, to reveal, to manifest") and the noun doxa ("glory") connect directly to the prologue: "we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father" (1:14). The glory that the community beheld in the incarnate Word is now made visible through a specific act. In Israel's experience, God's glory was manifested in particular moments: the glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35), the glory filled the temple (1 Kings 8:11), the glory appeared to the people at specific moments of divine intervention (Exodus 16:7, 10; Numbers 14:10, 22; 16:19, 42). The author's claim is that the transformation of water into wine is a manifestation of the same kind of glory — the glory of God's presence and power, now visible in the person of Jesus.

"His disciples believed in him" (episteusan eis auton hoi mathetai autou). The verb pisteuo ("to believe") with the preposition eis ("into") is this author's characteristic construction for the act of believing. It appears approximately thirty-six times in the document and carries more weight than simple intellectual assent. To believe "into" someone is to place one's trust in that person, to commit oneself to that person, to rely on that person as one's foundation. The disciples' belief here is genuine — the author does not qualify it as he will qualify the belief of the Jerusalem crowds in 2:23-25. The sign has accomplished its purpose: it has made Jesus's glory visible and has produced committed trust among those who are following him.

div.title: Verse 12: Transition to Capernaum
div.p: "After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples; and they stayed there a few days."

The mention of Jesus's "brothers" (adelphoi) is the first reference to them in this document. They will reappear in 7:3-10, where they urge Jesus to go to Judea and the author notes that "not even his brothers were believing in him" (7:5). The detail here is transitional — Capernaum is on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, and the narrative is about to shift from Galilee to Jerusalem. The phrase "went down" (katebe) reflects the geography: Cana is in the hills, Capernaum is below, at the level of the lake. The author regularly notes geographical movements with precision (2:13: "went up to Jerusalem" — Jerusalem is elevated; one always "goes up" to Jerusalem and "goes down" from it).

div.title: Verses 13-14: Jesus Goes to Jerusalem for Passover
div.p: "The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. And he found in the temple those who were selling oxen and sheep and doves, and the money changers seated at their tables."

"The Passover of the Jews" (to pascha ton Ioudaion). This is the first of three Passovers mentioned in the document (2:13, 6:4, 11:55/12:1/13:1). The other three accounts of Jesus's life mention only one Passover — the final one. This author structures the entire narrative around the Passover cycle, and Jesus's ministry spans at least three years. The designation "of the Jews" (ton Ioudaion) is again explanatory, suggesting the author's audience may include those unfamiliar with the festival's identity. But the phrase also creates a subtle distance: this is the Passover as the Jews observe it, the existing institutional celebration — and what is about to happen in the temple will challenge the institutional arrangements surrounding it.

Passover itself commemorated Israel's liberation from Egypt — the night when the blood of the lamb on the doorposts protected Israel's firstborn from the destroying angel (Exodus 12). It was the foundational act of redemption in Israel's history, the event that constituted Israel as a people. Every year, Jewish families reenacted the Passover meal and retold the story of the Exodus. The Passover setting places what follows in the context of Israel's primal liberation narrative and connects to John the Baptist's identification of Jesus as "the Lamb of God" (1:29, 36).

"He found in the temple." The word hieron ("temple") refers to the entire temple complex — the courts, porticoes, and surrounding structures — not the inner sanctuary (naos), which will appear in verse 19 with different significance. The selling of oxen, sheep, and doves took place in the outer courts (the Court of the Gentiles), where pilgrims coming from distant regions could purchase animals for sacrifice rather than bringing them on the journey. The money changers (kermatistas) exchanged foreign currency for the Tyrian shekel, the only coinage accepted for the temple tax (Exodus 30:13-16), since Roman and other coins bore images considered idolatrous. These commercial activities were technically in service of the sacrificial system — they enabled pilgrims to fulfill their obligations. But their presence in the temple precincts had turned the house of God into a marketplace.

div.title: Verses 15-17: Jesus Drives Out the Merchants
div.p: "And he made a whip of cords, and drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables; and to those who were selling the doves he said, 'Take these things away; stop making my Father's house a house of trade.' His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for Your house will consume me.'"

"He made a whip of cords" (phragellion ek schoinion). The detail is unique to this document. The other accounts of the temple action (Matthew 21:12-13, Mark 11:15-17, Luke 19:45-46) do not mention a whip. The word phragellion is a Latin loanword (flagellum), indicating the author writes in a context where Latin terms are familiar — consistent with a community in contact with Roman culture. The whip is made of cords (schoinion), likely the ropes used to tie animals in the market area. The act is physical and forceful: Jesus drives out (exebalen) the animals and their sellers, pours out (execheen) the coins, and overturns (anetrepsen) the tables. The verbs convey decisive, authoritative action.

The act has precedent in Israel's prophetic tradition. The prophets challenged the temple establishment when its practices violated God's purposes. Jeremiah 7:11: "Has this house, which is called by My name, become a den of robbers in your sight?" Malachi 3:1-3: "The Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to His temple... and He will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, so that they may present to the LORD offerings in righteousness." Malachi's prophecy describes the Lord himself coming to his own temple to purify its worship — a direct parallel to what Jesus enacts here.

"Stop making my Father's house a house of trade" (me poieite ton oikon tou patros mou oikon emporiou). The phrase "my Father's house" (ton oikon tou patros mou) is a claim of unique relationship. Jesus calls the temple "my Father's house" — claiming a filial relationship with God that identifies the temple as his own family's dwelling. This echoes his first recorded words in Luke's account: "Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?" (Luke 2:49). In this document, the claim is even more potent because the prologue has already identified Jesus as the unique one "in the bosom of the Father" (1:18). The one who was with God from the beginning now enters the temple — the place on earth that was designated as God's dwelling — and claims it as his Father's house.

The phrase "house of trade" (oikon emporiou) draws on Zechariah 14:21: "And there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of hosts in that day." The word "Canaanite" (kena'ani) in Hebrew also means "trader" or "merchant." The LXX renders Zechariah 14:21b: "there shall no longer be a trader (Chananios) in the house of the Lord Almighty in that day." Zechariah's prophecy describes the eschatological day when all trading activity will be removed from the temple. Jesus's action enacts this prophecy: the messianic purification of the temple that Zechariah foretold is now taking place.

"His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for Your house will consume me.'" The quotation is from Psalm 69:9 (68:10 LXX): "For zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach You have fallen on me" (ho zelos tou oikou sou katephagen me). The author changes the tense from past ("has consumed me," katephagen, aorist) to future ("will consume me," kataphagetai, future) — a significant shift. The psalmist in Psalm 69 speaks of zeal that has already consumed him; the author's quotation points to a zeal that will consume Jesus in the future. The implication is that Jesus's zeal for God's house will ultimately lead to his death. Psalm 69 is a psalm of the righteous sufferer who endures reproach, opposition, and betrayal for God's sake (69:4: "those who hate me without a cause"; 69:8: "I have become estranged from my brothers"; 69:21: "for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" — a detail fulfilled at the crucifixion in 19:28-30). The disciples' remembrance of this psalm places the temple action not merely as a prophetic protest but as the beginning of a path that will lead to Jesus's death. His zeal will consume him — it will cost him his life.

div.title: Verses 18-19: The Demand for a Sign and Jesus's Answer
div.p: "The Jews then said to him, 'What sign do you show us as your authority for doing these things?' Jesus answered them, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.'"

"What sign do you show us?" (ti semeion deiknueis hemin). "The Jews" (hoi Ioudaioi) — here meaning the temple authorities, the religious establishment — demand authorization. The question is not unreasonable in its context: a man has just disrupted the temple's commercial operations, and the authorities ask what sign validates his authority to do so. The prophets of Israel authenticated their messages with signs (1 Kings 18:36-38: Elijah's fire from heaven; Isaiah 7:11-14: the sign of Immanuel). Moses performed signs before Pharaoh (Exodus 4:1-9). The demand for a sign as validation of prophetic authority has deep roots.

But in this document, the demand for signs will become a recurring point of tension. In 4:48, Jesus says, "Unless you people see signs and wonders, you simply will not believe." In 6:30, after the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd asks, "What then do You do for a sign, so that we may see, and believe You?" The pattern is that those who demand signs as prerequisites for belief are operating from a posture that the author views as deficient. The signs exist to reveal glory (2:11), but demanding signs as proof reveals a hardness that signs alone cannot overcome.

"Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (lysate ton naon touton, kai en trisin hemerais egero auton). The word naos — not hieron — is critical. Hieron is the temple complex; naos is the inner sanctuary, the dwelling place of God's presence, the holy of holies. Jesus uses the more intimate term, the one that designates where God actually dwells. The imperative lysate ("destroy") is not a command but a conditional challenge: "If you destroy this naos, I will raise it in three days." The verb egero ("I will raise") is the standard resurrection verb in early Christian usage (the same word used in 1 Corinthians 15:4: "he was raised on the third day").

On the surface, the statement sounds like a claim about the physical temple building. "The Jews" will understand it that way (verse 20). But the author will clarify in verse 21 that Jesus was speaking about his own body. The statement contains, in compressed form, the entire trajectory of the document: the destruction of Jesus's body (the crucifixion) and its raising in three days (the resurrection). The temple is not merely a building; it is the place where God's presence dwells. If Jesus's body is the true temple — the true dwelling of God's presence among human beings — then the prologue's claim that the Word "tabernacled among us" (1:14) receives its full force. The tabernacle/temple was where God dwelt; Jesus's body is where God now dwells. The destruction and raising of this temple will be the decisive sign the authorities demanded.

div.title: Verses 20-22: Misunderstanding and Later Understanding
div.p: "The Jews then said, 'It took forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?' But he was speaking of the temple of his body. So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this; and they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken."

"Forty-six years." Herod the Great began the reconstruction and expansion of the Second Temple around 20/19 BCE. If this Passover falls around 27/28 CE, approximately forty-six years have elapsed. The detail grounds the narrative in a specific historical moment. But it also highlights the absurdity of the misunderstanding from the authorities' perspective: a construction project spanning nearly half a century cannot be replicated in three days. Their response is literalistic — they hear a claim about the stone-and-mortar building and reject it as impossible.

"But he was speaking of the temple of his body" (ekeinos de elegen peri tou naou tou somatos autou). The author breaks the narrative to provide the reader with the correct interpretation. Jesus's body is the naos — the sanctuary, the holy of holies, the place of God's indwelling. This is the most direct articulation of what the prologue declared in metaphor: "the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us" (1:14). The tabernacle was the naos in portable form; Jesus's body is the naos in human form. God's glory, which once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the temple (1 Kings 8:11), now fills a human body. The physical temple in Jerusalem, with its forty-six years of construction, is a copy and shadow of the true dwelling of God — the body of the incarnate Word.

This identification also shifts the meaning of the temple action in verses 14-16. Jesus did not merely cleanse the temple to restore proper worship; he acted as one who has authority over the temple because something greater than the temple is here — his own body, the true locus of God's presence. The old temple system — with its animal sales, its money changing, its ritual purification (the six stone jars of verse 6 are filled with water for Jewish purification rites) — is being superseded by the one whose body is the meeting place of God and humanity. This is the meaning of the promise to Nathanael: "You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man" (1:51). The Son of Man — in his own body — is the place where heaven and earth meet.

"When he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered." The author notes that the disciples did not understand the statement at the time. Understanding came only after the resurrection. The verb emnesthesen ("remembered") parallels the disciples' remembrance of Psalm 69:9 in verse 17, but here the remembrance is post-resurrection. The author is transparent about the gap between event and understanding: the disciples lived through things they could not interpret until later. This retrospective understanding is a feature of the entire document (12:16: "His disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written of Him and that they had done these things to Him"; 13:7: "What I do you do not realize now, but you will understand hereafter").

"They believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken" (episteusan te graphe kai to logo hon eipen ho Iesous). The post-resurrection belief has two objects: "the Scripture" (te graphe — the singular likely refers to a specific scriptural text, perhaps Psalm 16:10 LXX: "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor allow Your Holy One to undergo decay," or possibly Hosea 6:2) and "the word which Jesus had spoken" (the temple saying of verse 19). The Scripture and Jesus's word are placed on the same level of authority — both are objects of belief, both are confirmed by the resurrection. This pairing anticipates the way the document will consistently present Jesus's words as carrying divine authority: "the word which you hear is not mine, but the Father's who sent me" (14:24).

div.title: Verses 23-25: Belief Based on Signs and Jesus's Knowledge
div.p: "Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he was doing. But Jesus, on his part, was not entrusting himself to them, for he knew all men, and because he had no need for anyone to testify concerning man, for he himself knew what was in man."

"Many believed in his name, observing his signs" (polloi episteusan eis to onoma autou, theorountes autou ta semeia ha epoiei). The verb pisteuo eis ("believed in/into") is the same construction used in verse 11 for the disciples' belief. The content is belief "in his name" (eis to onoma autou) — the same phrase from the prologue: "to those who believe in his name, he gave the right to become children of God" (1:12). On the surface, this looks like the same belief the disciples exercised at Cana.

"But Jesus was not entrusting himself to them" (autos de Iesous ouk episteuen auton autois). The wordplay is sharp and deliberate. The same verb pisteuo is used in both directions: the crowds "believed" (episteusan) in Jesus, but Jesus did not "believe" (episteuen) — did not "entrust himself to" — them. The verb pisteuo, when followed by a direct object in the dative or accusative, carries the sense of entrusting, committing, placing confidence in. The crowds placed their trust in Jesus's name based on signs; Jesus did not place his trust in them. The asymmetry reveals a problem with sign-based belief: it may be genuine recognition of Jesus's power, but it is not yet the kind of belief that Jesus can rely on. These believers are impressed but uncommitted. Their faith is responsive to spectacle but has not yet been tested by the demands Jesus will make.

This section introduces a critical distinction that the author will develop throughout the document. Not all belief is the same. The disciples at Cana believed and are never criticized for it (2:11). The crowds in Jerusalem believe and are treated with reserve (2:23-24). Nicodemus will come in the next chapter having seen the signs and drawn a conclusion (3:2: "we know that You have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that You do unless God is with him"), but Jesus will press him beyond that conclusion to the necessity of being "born from above" (3:3). Later, crowds who saw the feeding of the five thousand will "believe" but will abandon Jesus when he makes demands they find intolerable (6:66). The document traces a spectrum of responses to Jesus, and this passage is the first explicit signal that some responses that look like belief are inadequate.

"For he knew all men" (autos gar eginosken pantas). The verb ginosko ("to know") is used in the imperfect tense, indicating continuous, habitual knowledge. Jesus's knowledge of people is not acquired through investigation; it is inherent and comprehensive. This echoes the supernatural knowledge already displayed in chapter 1: Jesus knew Simon's name and parentage before being told (1:42); he knew Nathanael's character and location before meeting him (1:47-48). The pattern will continue: Jesus will know the Samaritan woman's marital history (4:17-18), will know who will betray him "from the beginning" (6:64), will know Lazarus is dead before being told (11:11-14).

"He had no need for anyone to testify concerning man, for he himself knew what was in man" (autos gar eginosken ti en en to anthropo). The phrase "what was in man" (ti en en to anthropo) is comprehensive and unsparing. Jesus knows the interior of human beings — their motives, their commitments, their capacity for defection. The word anthropos ("man, human being") is singular but generic: it refers to human nature itself. This knowledge is not cynicism but discernment. The author is not saying that Jesus suspected everyone of bad faith; he is saying that Jesus understood the depth of the human heart and knew that sign-based belief, however sincere in the moment, could not be relied upon as final commitment.

The statement sets up the next chapter. The phrase "what was in man" leads directly into "Now there was a man (anthropos) of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus" (3:1). Nicodemus is the immediate example of "what was in man" — a sincere, interested, impressed inquirer who nevertheless does not yet understand what Jesus requires. The transition from 2:25 to 3:1 is seamless: Jesus knew what was in man; here is a man; and Jesus will show him what he needs.

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument
div.p: The author constructs chapter 2 as the first demonstration of the identity declared in chapter 1. Two scenes — the wedding at Cana and the temple in Jerusalem — reveal who Jesus is through what he does, and both scenes carry meaning at multiple levels simultaneously.

list.item: The wedding at Cana reveals Jesus as the one who brings the messianic abundance. The water of Jewish purification is transformed into wine of extraordinary quality. The prophets promised that the messianic age would be marked by overflowing wine (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18, Isaiah 25:6). The six stone jars — one short of seven, the number of completeness — represent a system that is good but incomplete. Jesus fills and transforms them, producing something that surpasses what came before. The headwaiter's observation — "you have kept the good wine until now" — articulates the chapter's principle: the best has been reserved for this moment. What the existing system of purification and ritual could not provide, the incarnate Word provides in abundance.

The temple action reveals Jesus as the one whose body replaces the temple. Jesus enters the temple with the authority of the one whose Father's house it is and drives out the commercial activities that have turned it into a marketplace. When challenged, he does not point to the stone building but to his own body: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The naos — the inner sanctuary where God dwells — is now the body of the incarnate Word. The tabernacle imagery of the prologue (1:14: "tabernacled among us") is made explicit: Jesus's body is the place of God's dwelling, the meeting point of heaven and earth, the reality to which the Jerusalem temple pointed. The destruction and raising of this temple-body will be the definitive sign.

The chapter introduces the "hour" that governs the entire narrative. Jesus's statement "my hour has not yet come" (2:4) establishes a temporal framework that will run through the document until it reaches its fulfillment in 12:23 ("the hour has come") and 13:1 ("knowing that His hour had come to depart out of this world"). Everything between Cana and the cross is the time before the hour — the period of signs, teachings, and confrontations that point toward the decisive moment. The signs are real manifestations of glory, but they are not the glory itself; the glory reaches its fullness at the hour.

The chapter begins to distinguish between types of belief. The disciples at Cana believe upon seeing Jesus's glory revealed through a sign (2:11), and their belief is presented without qualification. The crowds in Jerusalem believe upon seeing signs (2:23), but Jesus does not entrust himself to them (2:24). The difference is not explained in terms of the signs themselves but in terms of what is "in man" — the interior disposition that determines whether sign-based belief will deepen into committed trust or remain superficial. This distinction will become a major theme: the feeding of the five thousand will produce a crowd that wants to make Jesus king by force (6:15) and then abandons him when his teaching proves too demanding (6:66). The signs point to glory, but glory demands a response that goes beyond being impressed.

The two scenes are connected by the theme of replacement and fulfillment. At Cana, the water of purification becomes the wine of the messianic feast. At the temple, the stone building gives way to the body of the incarnate Word. Both transformations follow the same pattern established in the prologue: the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (1:17). What Moses mediated — the purification system, the temple, the sacrificial order — was real and given by God. But what Jesus brings is the reality to which those institutions pointed. The water jars are filled to the brim and transformed; the temple is claimed by its owner's son and identified with his body. In both cases, the old is not destroyed but fulfilled — filled up and brought to its intended purpose.

Jesus's supernatural knowledge of people is established as a narrative pattern. The knowledge displayed in chapter 1 (knowing Simon's name, knowing Nathanael under the fig tree) expands here into a comprehensive knowledge of "what was in man" (2:25). This knowledge will function throughout the document as evidence of Jesus's divine identity — the God of Israel who "searches the heart and tests the mind" (Jeremiah 17:10), who "knows the secrets of the heart" (Psalm 44:21/43:22 LXX), is now present in human flesh, knowing human beings from the inside. It is also the basis for the document's distinction between genuine and superficial belief: Jesus can distinguish them because he knows what is within each person.

The chapter moves from private revelation to public confrontation. At Cana, the sign is witnessed by a small group — the disciples and the servants. At the temple, the confrontation is public and provokes the authorities' demand for authorization. This movement from private to public mirrors the larger structure of the document: the early chapters involve relatively contained encounters (Cana, Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman), while the later chapters involve increasingly intense public confrontation (the healing at Bethesda in chapter 5, the bread of life discourse in chapter 6, the conflicts at the Feast of Tabernacles in chapters 7-8, the healing of the blind man in chapter 9, the raising of Lazarus in chapter 11). The trajectory leads to the cross, where the most public event — a Roman execution — becomes the supreme private revelation: "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He" (8:28).

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 2): John 2 narrates two events connected by location, timing, and theological weight. First, at a wedding in Cana of Galilee, Jesus turns water into wine — described as "the beginning of his signs" (archen ton semeion), which "revealed his glory" (ephanerosen ten doxan autou) and produced belief among his disciples (2:11). The water was contained in six stone jars set aside "for the Jewish rites of purification" (kata ton katharismon ton Ioudaion, 2:6). Jesus transforms the water of Jewish purification into wine, and the master of the feast notes that the best wine has been kept until now (2:10). The sign communicates that something superior has arrived to replace what came before — a theme the prologue established with "grace upon grace" (1:16) and "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (1:17).

Second, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for Passover and drives the merchants from the temple, declaring "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (2:19). The author notes that "he was speaking of the temple of his body" (2:21). The one who "tabernacled among us" (1:14) confronts the existing temple because he himself is its replacement — the true locus of God's presence.

The chapter then closes with a passage that is the direct antecedent to chapter 3: "Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he was doing. But Jesus himself was not entrusting himself to them, because he knew all people, and because he had no need for anyone to testify concerning man, for he himself knew what was in man" (2:23-25). This passage creates a category of belief that Jesus does not trust — belief based on observing signs without deeper understanding. The phrase "he knew what was in man" (autos eginosken ti en to anthropo) is the hinge on which the door to chapter 3 swings open.

What the author argues immediately after (John 4): Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee and "had to" (edei) pass through Samaria, where he encounters a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. The conversation moves from physical water to "living water" (hydor zon, 4:10), just as the chapter 3 conversation moved from physical birth to birth "from above." Jesus tells the woman that "the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father" (4:21) — continuing the temple-replacement theme from 2:19-21. The woman's misunderstanding of Jesus's offer parallels Nicodemus's misunderstanding of birth from above: both interlocutors hear physical language and miss the spiritual reality. But unlike Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman moves from confusion to testimony, bringing her whole town to encounter Jesus. The Samaritans declare Jesus "the Savior of the world" (4:42) — a title that extends beyond Israel and fulfills 3:16-17's declaration that God sent the Son not to judge the world but to save it. The chapter ends with Jesus returning to Cana and performing his "second sign" (deuteron semeion, 4:54) — healing a royal official's son from a distance, producing belief in the official and "his whole household" (4:53).

How chapter 3 connects these: John 2 ended by establishing that Jesus knows "what is in man." Chapter 3 immediately presents a specific man — "Now there was a man of the Pharisees" (en de anthropos ek ton Pharisaion, 3:1) — who comes to Jesus and receives a diagnosis of what that man lacks. The word anthropos ("man") in 3:1 directly echoes the anthropos of 2:25. Nicodemus is the test case, the specific instance of the general category the author has just introduced. He is one who has seen the signs and concluded something about Jesus, but Jesus knows what is in him — and what is in him is not yet sufficient. What follows in chapter 3 is the author's exposition of what is actually required: not merely observing signs and drawing correct conclusions, but being born from above by water and Spirit, believing in the lifted-up Son of Man, and coming to the light. Chapter 4 will then demonstrate this pattern in action through the Samaritan woman's encounter, extending the scope of the offer from a teacher of Israel (Nicodemus) to a Samaritan outsider, and from there to the whole world.

The chapter also continues the purification/replacement theme. In chapter 2, Jesus replaced purification water with wine and the physical temple with his body. In chapter 3, a dispute arises between John's disciples and a Jew "about purification" (peri katharismou, 3:25), directly echoing the purification jars of 2:6. The old categories of purification are being superseded by what Jesus brings. And the chapter as a whole presents the transition from John's ministry to Jesus's ministry — from the baptism of water to the baptism of Spirit — completing the subordination of the forerunner that chapter 1 began.

div.title: Verses 1-2: Nicodemus Comes at Night
div.p: "Now there was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to him at night and said to him, 'Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.'"

The conjunction de ("now, and") links this passage directly to the preceding statement about Jesus knowing "what was in man" (2:25). The author does not begin a new topic; he provides the first illustration of it. "There was a man" (en de anthropos) — the same word anthropos from 2:25 — signals that Nicodemus is the concrete example of the general principle just stated.

Nicodemus's identity. He is identified three ways: he is "of the Pharisees" (ek ton Pharisaion), his name is Nicodemus (a Greek name, Nikodemos, meaning "conqueror of the people" — common among Hellenized Jews), and he is "a ruler of the Jews" (archon ton Ioudaion). The word archon designates a member of the ruling council, the Sanhedrin. In this document, "the Jews" (hoi Ioudaioi) typically refers to the Jerusalem religious establishment. Nicodemus is therefore not an ordinary inquirer but a man of authority, education, and status within Israel's leadership. He will appear twice more in the document: in 7:50-51, where he challenges the council's condemnation of Jesus by asking "Does our law judge a man without first hearing him?", and in 19:39, where he brings an enormous quantity of myrrh and aloes for Jesus's burial. His trajectory through the document — from nighttime inquiry, to partial defense, to burial devotion — traces its own narrative arc.

"He came to him at night" (elten pros auton nyktos). The detail "at night" (nyktos) carries both practical and symbolic weight. Practically, a member of the Sanhedrin visiting a controversial Galilean teacher might prefer discretion. But for the author of this document, "night" is never merely a clock reading. The prologue declared that "the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it" (1:5). Later, when Judas leaves the last supper to betray Jesus, the author notes: "it was night" (en de nyx, 13:30). Nicodemus comes out of the darkness toward the light — but as the conversation will reveal, he does not yet fully enter the light. He is between the two realms.

"Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher." Nicodemus addresses Jesus as "Rabbi" (the same title the first disciples used in 1:38, 49), acknowledging him as a teacher. The plural "we know" (oidamen) may indicate that Nicodemus speaks for a group — perhaps other Pharisees or council members who have observed Jesus's signs — or it may be a communal expression of what the Jerusalem audience generally recognized. His conclusion is that Jesus "has come from God" (apo theou elelythas), because "no one can do these signs unless God is with him" (ean me e ho theos met' autou). The reasoning is straightforward: miraculous signs require divine backing. This echoes the logic of 2:23, where "many believed in his name, observing his signs." Nicodemus's assessment is accurate as far as it goes — Jesus has indeed come from God — but the conversation will expose how far short of full understanding this assessment falls. Nicodemus has drawn the right inference from the signs but has not yet grasped what the signs point to.

The phrase "God is with him" (ho theos met' autou) appears in the LXX as a marker of divine favor and empowerment. Genesis 21:22: Abimelech says to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do." Genesis 39:2-3: "The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man." 1 Samuel 3:19: "The LORD was with Samuel." Isaiah 7:14 (LXX): the child shall be called "Immanuel" — "God with us." Nicodemus places Jesus in the category of one whom God accompanies and empowers. What he does not yet understand is the prologue's claim: this is not merely a man accompanied by God but the Word who was God and has become flesh.

div.title: Verses 3-8: Born from Above
div.p: "Jesus answered and said to him, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.'"

Jesus does not respond to Nicodemus's statement by accepting, qualifying, or correcting the compliment. He bypasses it entirely and addresses what Nicodemus actually needs. The double "amen" (amen amen lego soi), characteristic of this author (appearing twenty-five times in the document), introduces a solemn pronouncement.
"Born from above" (gennethe anothen). The word anothen is the crux of the passage. It has two established meanings in Greek:

list.item: "From above." This is the spatial/directional meaning — from a higher place. This is how the author uses the word elsewhere in this document: in 3:31, "The one who comes from above (anothen) is above all"; in 19:11, "You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above (anothen)"; in 19:23, Jesus's tunic was "woven from the top (anothen)." The author's consistent usage of anothen as "from above" strongly indicates this is the primary meaning intended here.

"Again, anew." This is the temporal meaning — a second time, once more. This is the meaning Nicodemus hears, as his response in verse 4 makes clear: "How can a man be born when he is old? He cannot enter his mother's womb a second time (deuteron) and be born, can he?"

div.p: The ambiguity is not accidental. The author constructs the conversation so that Nicodemus hears one meaning (again) while the reader, who has read the prologue, hears the other (from above). The prologue already established this concept: those who become children of God are "born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God" (1:13). Birth "from above" is birth "of God" — the same reality, stated now to Nicodemus in language he should recognize but does not.

"Cannot see the kingdom of God" (ou dynatai idein ten basileian tou theou). The phrase "the kingdom of God" (he basileia tou theou) appears in this document only here and in verse 5. This is remarkable because the kingdom of God is a dominant theme in the other three accounts of Jesus's life. This author virtually never uses the phrase, preferring instead "eternal life" (zoe aionios) as the equivalent concept. The use of "kingdom of God" here, in conversation with a Pharisee, suggests Jesus is using the language Nicodemus would recognize from Israel's prophetic tradition. The kingdom of God is what the prophets promised — the time when God's sovereign rule would be fully established on earth, when the promises to Abraham and David would be fulfilled, when Israel would be restored and the nations would acknowledge Israel's God. Daniel 2:44: "The God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed." Daniel 7:14: the Son of Man receives "dominion and glory and a kingdom." Obadiah 1:21: "the kingdom will be the LORD's."

The verb "see" (idein) here means more than visual perception; it means to experience, to enter into, to participate in (as confirmed by the parallel in v. 5, where "see" is replaced by "enter into"). Nicodemus cannot access, cannot participate in, cannot experience the kingdom of God without being born from above. His Pharisaic learning, his position on the council, his acknowledgment that Jesus comes from God — none of these grant entry. Something radically different is required.
Verse 4: Nicodemus's misunderstanding. "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can a man be born when he is old? He cannot enter his mother's womb a second time and be born, can he?'"

The misunderstanding follows a pattern this author uses repeatedly throughout the document: Jesus makes a statement with layered meaning; the interlocutor takes it at the most literal, physical level; Jesus then explains the deeper meaning. The same pattern occurs with the Samaritan woman and "living water" (4:10-15), with the crowd and "the bread of God" (6:32-34), with the disciples and "Lazarus has fallen asleep" (11:11-14). Each time, the misunderstanding creates the opening for Jesus to unfold what he actually means.

Nicodemus hears "born again" (a second physical birth) and objects that this is impossible. His objection is correct on its own terms — physical rebirth is indeed impossible. But his inability to hear the other meaning ("from above") is itself diagnostic. He is "the teacher of Israel" (ho didaskalos tou Israel, v. 10) and should know the prophetic texts that describe God giving new life, new hearts, new beginnings to his people.
Verse 5: "Born of water and the Spirit." "Jesus answered, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.'"

Jesus restates the requirement with greater specificity. The single birth "from above" is now described as birth "of water and the Spirit" (ex hydatos kai pneumatos). The kai ("and") links water and Spirit as components of a single birth, not two separate births. What does "water and Spirit" mean?

The most direct background is Ezekiel 36:25-27, a passage any teacher of Israel would know: "Then I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean; I will cleanse you from all your filthiness and from all your idols. Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes." In this prophetic text, water (cleansing) and Spirit (new inner life) are joined in God's promise of restoration. God would cleanse his people with water and renew them with his Spirit. This was a promise for the future — for the time when God would act decisively to restore Israel. Jesus is telling Nicodemus that this promised time has arrived, that the Ezekiel 36 renewal is now operative, and that without it, one cannot enter the kingdom.

Isaiah 44:3 similarly joins water and Spirit: "For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants." Joel 2:28-29 (LXX 3:1-2) promises the outpouring of the Spirit on "all flesh." These prophetic promises form the interpretive background that Nicodemus, as a teacher of Israel, should have recognized.

The water component may also connect to the baptismal practice that John has been performing — a baptism in water as a sign of repentance and preparation for the one who would "baptize in the Holy Spirit" (1:33). Water baptism and Spirit baptism, already distinguished in John the Baptist's testimony, are here joined as the twin elements of the new birth. The reader who has heard 1:33 ("He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit") now learns what that Spirit-baptism accomplishes: it constitutes the birth from above without which no one enters the kingdom.

Verse 6: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." Jesus draws a categorical distinction. Flesh (sarx) produces flesh; Spirit (pneuma) produces spirit. These are two different orders of existence. Physical birth produces physical life; birth from the Spirit produces spiritual life. The categories do not overlap. No amount of fleshly birth — no genealogy, no ethnic identity, no human effort — can produce what only the Spirit can produce. This restates the prologue's declaration about the children of God being born "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God" (1:13). The three excluded sources in 1:13 all belong to the category of "flesh." The one sufficient source — God — operates through the Spirit.

Verse 7: "Do not be amazed that I said to you, 'You must be born from above.'" The verb thaumases ("be amazed, marvel") indicates that Nicodemus is visibly astonished. Jesus's response is: do not marvel at this. The requirement of new birth should not surprise a teacher of Israel. The prophets taught it. Ezekiel promised it. The dei ("must" — implied in the necessity of the requirement) is the divine necessity that runs through this document and this author's argument.

The pronoun shift in verse 7 is significant. In verse 3, Jesus said "unless one is born from above" (third person singular, ean me tis gennethe anothen). In verse 7, he says "you must be born from above" (hymas dei gennethenai anothen) — second person plural. The "you" (hymas) extends the requirement beyond Nicodemus as an individual. Jesus is not saying that Nicodemus personally has an unusual deficiency; he is saying that everyone — "you all" — must be born from above. The plural includes Nicodemus, his fellow Pharisees, the rulers, all of Israel, and by extension every human being. No one is exempt from this requirement.

Verse 8: "The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from and where it is going; so is everyone who is born of the Spirit." The word pneuma means both "wind" and "spirit" in Greek (as ruach does in Hebrew). Jesus exploits the double meaning: the wind/spirit blows (pnei) where it wills (thelei), you hear its sound (phonen) but cannot track its origin or destination. So it is with the Spirit-born person. The point is not that the new birth is arbitrary or random but that it operates beyond human control and comprehension. You cannot manufacture it, schedule it, or constrain it. You can perceive its effects (you hear the sound) but cannot master its process. This directly challenges Nicodemus's assumption that understanding God's ways is a matter of study and expertise. The Spirit is sovereign; the teacher of Israel does not command it.

div.title: Verses 9-13: Earthly and Heavenly Things
div.p: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered and said to him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and do not understand these things?'"

Nicodemus's third question — "How can these things be?" (pos dynatai tauta genesthai) — echoes Mary's question to Gabriel: "How will this be?" (pos estai touto, Luke 1:34). But where Mary asked how and received an answer, Nicodemus asks how and receives a rebuke. The difference lies in what each should already know. Nicodemus is ho didaskalos tou Israel — "THE teacher of Israel," the definite article indicating a recognized and authoritative position. The rebuke is that someone who holds this position should understand these things. The prophets — Ezekiel, Isaiah, Joel — described the new birth, the new heart, the Spirit's outpouring. A teacher of Israel should recognize what Jesus is describing. His failure to do so reveals that his knowledge of scripture, though extensive, has not penetrated to the level of comprehension that the prophetic texts demand.

Verse 11: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know and testify of what we have seen, and you do not receive our testimony." A significant pronoun shift occurs. Jesus moves from "I" to "we" (legomen, oidamen, heorakamen, martyroumen — all first person plural). Who is "we"? Several possibilities exist: Jesus and the Father who sent him, Jesus and his disciples, Jesus and the prophets who testified before him, or a plurality within Jesus's own identity (in line with the prologue's presentation of the Word who was with God and was God). Whatever the referent, the "we" places Jesus's teaching within a corporate testimony that Nicodemus and those he represents ("you" is also plural — hymeis — "you all do not receive our testimony") are rejecting. The dynamic is the prologue enacted: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him" (1:11). The testimony is offered; the reception is refused.

Verse 12: "If I told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?" Jesus distinguishes between "earthly things" (ta epigeia) and "heavenly things" (ta epourania). What are the "earthly things" he has told Nicodemus? The most natural referent is the analogy of birth from above — the wind, the flesh/spirit distinction, the observable effects of the Spirit's work. These are earthly analogies for heavenly realities, drawn from common experience and prophetic tradition. If Nicodemus cannot grasp these, how will he receive the heavenly realities themselves — the direct revelation of God's nature, purposes, and action? The progression from earthly to heavenly anticipates what Jesus is about to say in verses 13-21, where the discourse moves from analogies (the serpent lifted up) to the most extraordinary claim in the document (God's love sending the Son for the world's salvation).

Verse 13: "No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven: the Son of Man." The claim is exclusive. No one has gone up to heaven to bring back direct knowledge of heavenly things — not Moses (though later Jewish tradition speculated about Moses's ascent), not Enoch (though Genesis 5:24 says God took him), not Elijah (though 2 Kings 2:11 narrates his ascent in a whirlwind). The only one qualified to speak of heavenly things is the one who descended from heaven: the Son of Man. This connects directly to the prologue: the Word was with God (1:1-2), the Word became flesh (1:14), and therefore the Word-become-flesh is the only one who can reveal what is in heaven. The claim is the same as 1:18: "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known." The Son of Man has come from the realm of heavenly things and therefore speaks from direct knowledge.

The title "Son of Man" (ho huios tou anthropou) connects to its use in 1:51, where Jesus told Nathanael: "You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man." The Son of Man is the point of connection between heaven and earth. He descended from heaven and is therefore the one through whom heavenly realities are communicated to earthly people.

div.title: Verses 14-15: The Serpent Lifted Up
div.p: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him will have eternal life."

This passage anchors its claim in a specific event from Israel's recorded history. Numbers 21:4-9 narrates the episode: during the wilderness wandering, the people "spoke against God and against Moses" (Numbers 21:5), saying "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?" God sent fiery serpents (nachashim seraphim) among them, and the serpents bit the people, and many died. The people confessed their sin and asked Moses to intercede. God instructed Moses: "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole; and it shall be that everyone who is bitten, when he looks at it, shall live" (Numbers 21:8). Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, "and it came about, that if a serpent bit anyone, when he looked to the bronze serpent, he lived" (Numbers 21:9).
Several features of this episode are directly relevant to what Jesus claims:

list.item: The condition was looking. Survival was not automatic. Those who were bitten had to look at (hibit el in Hebrew, epeblepsen in the LXX) the bronze serpent. The looking was an act of trust in God's provision — God said "look and live," and those who looked did live. Those who refused to look, or who did not look, died. The condition was real: looking was necessary. Wisdom of Solomon 16:6-7, a first-century Jewish text, interprets this episode explicitly: "For they were troubled for a little while as a warning, and received a token of salvation to remind them of the commandment of your law. For the one who turned toward it was saved, not by the thing that was beheld, but by you, the Savior of all." The Wisdom of Solomon makes clear that the bronze serpent itself did not save; God saved. But the looking was required as the response through which salvation was received.

The lifting up was necessary. The serpent had to be placed on a pole (nes in Hebrew, semeion/semasian in the LXX) — it had to be elevated, made visible, made accessible to all who would look. If it had not been lifted up, no one could have seen it and lived.

The crisis was universal among those in the camp. Everyone who had been bitten was in danger of death. The remedy was available to everyone — "whoever looks, lives." The scope was not limited to certain tribes or families but extended to everyone in the camp who had been afflicted.

div.p: Jesus draws a direct typological parallel: "as" (kathos) Moses lifted up the serpent, "even so" (houtos) must (dei — divine necessity) the Son of Man be lifted up. The verb "lifted up" (hypsothenai) is the first of three uses in this document (3:14, 8:28, 12:32-34). In 8:28, Jesus tells the religious leaders: "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he." In 12:32-34: "'And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.' But he was saying this to indicate the kind of death by which he was about to die." The author's own gloss in 12:33 makes explicit that "lifted up" refers to crucifixion. But the word hypsoo also means "to exalt, to elevate to a position of honor" (as in the LXX of Isaiah 52:13: "Behold, my servant shall prosper, he shall be exalted [hypsothsetai] and lifted up and shall be very high"). This author appears to use the word with deliberate double meaning: the Son of Man is lifted up on the cross, and in that very act is exalted. The crucifixion is not a defeat that must be overcome by the resurrection; it is itself the moment of glorification.

"So that whoever believes in him will have eternal life" (hina pas ho pisteuon en auto eche zoen aionion). The purpose (hina, "so that") of the Son of Man's lifting up is stated: whoever believes will have eternal life. Two elements require attention:

First, "whoever believes" (pas ho pisteuon). The word pas ("every, all, whoever") echoes the scope of the serpent narrative — everyone who looked, lived. The scope is universal in availability: not limited to a particular group but open to every person (pas) who responds. The participle pisteuon is present tense — "the one believing," "the one who goes on believing" — denoting continuous, ongoing trust, not a single past act. This is consistent with the author's use of pisteuo throughout the document as an active, sustained orientation toward Jesus.

Second, "eternal life" (zoe aionios). This is the first occurrence of this phrase in the document. It will appear seventeen times, always in connection with believing in Jesus (3:15, 16, 36; 4:14, 36; 5:24, 39; 6:27, 40, 47, 54, 68; 10:28; 12:25, 50; 17:2, 3). The word aionios derives from aion ("age") and in the LXX context refers to the life of the age to come — the life that belongs to God's restored creation, the life that the prophets promised for the messianic age. Daniel 12:2 (LXX): "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake, some to everlasting life (zoen aionion), others to disgrace and everlasting contempt." The phrase does not merely mean life that lasts forever (though it includes that); it means the quality and kind of life that belongs to God's age, God's realm, God's own existence. In 17:3, the author will define it explicitly: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." Eternal life is relational knowledge of God through Christ.

The typological parallel is precise: the bitten Israelites who looked at the lifted serpent received physical life; those who believe in the lifted-up Son of Man receive eternal life. In both cases, the provision comes from God, the lifting up is necessary, and the human response (looking/believing) is the condition through which the provision is received.

div.title: Verses 16-18: The Purpose of the Son's Sending
div.p: A question of voice arises here. In the Greek text, there are no quotation marks, and scholars have debated whether verses 16-21 are a continuation of Jesus's words to Nicodemus or the author's own commentary on the dialogue. Several features suggest the author's voice: the shift from "I" to third-person references to God and the Son, the summary-like quality of the statements, and the thematic parallels with the prologue. However, the question of speaker does not change the meaning, since the author presents both Jesus's words and his own commentary as authoritative revelation. The argument is continuous regardless of who is speaking it.

p.hi: Verse 16: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish, but have eternal life."

div.p: This verse is frequently extracted from its context and treated as a freestanding summary. In context, it is the explanation (gar, "for") of why the Son of Man must be lifted up (v. 14) and why believing in him produces eternal life (v. 15). The logic flows directly: the Son of Man is lifted up because God loved the world and gave his Son for this purpose.

"God so loved" (houtos gar egapesen ho theos). The word houtos ("so, thus, in this way") does not primarily indicate the degree of God's love (how much God loved) but the manner of it (this is how God loved, this is what God's love looked like in action). God's love is demonstrated not by an emotion but by an act: he gave.

"The world" (ton kosmon). In 1:10, "the world" was the creation that came into being through the Word but did not recognize him. In 1:29, Jesus was identified as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world." The scope is the same here: the object of God's love is the entire created human order, not a select portion of it. The "world" in this author's vocabulary includes those who will reject the light (3:19-20) as well as those who will come to it (3:21). God's love is directed toward the world in its entirety; the world's response to that love varies.

"He gave his only-begotten Son" (edoken ton huion ton monogene). The verb edoken ("gave") can mean both "gave" as in "provided, sent" and "gave up, handed over." The latter sense connects to the crucifixion — God gave the Son to death. The word monogenes ("only-begotten, unique, one-of-a-kind"), as noted in the analysis of 1:14 and 1:18, echoes the LXX of Genesis 22:2, where God commands Abraham to take "your son, your only son" (ton monogene sou) — Isaac. The Aqedah (binding of Isaac) looms over this verse: as Abraham was willing to give his only son, so God gives his only Son. But where Abraham's sacrifice was halted and a substitute provided (Genesis 22:12-13), God's giving of the Son is completed. The parallel that was foreshadowed in the Aqedah reaches its fulfillment in the cross.

"That whoever believes in him shall not perish, but have eternal life" (hina pas ho pisteuon eis auton me apoletai all' eche zoen aionion). The purpose of the giving is salvation, not judgment. Two outcomes are set in contrast: perishing (apoletai, from apollymi — "to be destroyed, to be lost, to perish") and having eternal life. Between these two outcomes stands the condition: believing (pisteuon, present tense participle — again, ongoing trust and commitment, not a single moment of assent). The one who goes on believing does not perish but has (present tense, eche) eternal life. The present tense of "has" is striking — eternal life is not only a future hope but a present possession for the one who believes.

p.hi: Verse 17: "For God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him."

div.p: The verb krinein ("to judge") will become central later in the document. In 5:22, "the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son." In 5:27, "he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man." In 8:15-16, Jesus says "I judge no one. But even if I do judge, my judgment is true." In 12:47-48, "If anyone hears my sayings and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world. The one who rejects me and does not receive my sayings has a judge; the word that I spoke will judge him at the last day." The picture across the document is complex: the Son has authority to judge (5:22, 27), but his purpose in coming was not judgment but salvation (3:17, 12:47). Nevertheless, judgment occurs as a consequence of the response to the Son — those who refuse the light judge themselves (3:18-19).

The verb sothe ("might be saved") echoes the LXX's soteria ("salvation"), the comprehensive term for God's rescue of his people. Isaiah 45:22: "Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth." Isaiah 49:6: "I will make you a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth." The scope again is "the world" — God's intent in sending the Son was the salvation of the whole world, not its condemnation.

p.hi: Verse 18: "He who believes in him is not judged; he who does not believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God."

div.p: Two present realities are stated. The one who believes (ho pisteuon — present participle, ongoing belief) is not judged (ou krinetai — present tense, "is not being judged, does not come under judgment"). The one who does not believe (ho me pisteuon) has been judged already (ede kekritai — perfect tense, "has already been judged, stands in a state of judgment"). The perfect tense indicates a completed state with ongoing effect. The person who does not believe is not awaiting a future judgment; the judgment is already operative. The refusal to believe constitutes the judgment itself.

The reason is stated: "because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God" (hoti me pepisteuken eis to onoma tou monogenous huiou tou theou). The verb pepisteuken is also perfect tense — "he has not come to believe and does not stand in a state of belief." The name (onoma) of the Son carries the full reality of the Son's identity. To believe "in the name" is to commit to the person the name identifies — the only-begotten Son of God, the one the prologue described as the Word who was God and became flesh.

The logic is stark: the sending of the Son creates a dividing line. Before the Son's coming, the world existed in a general condition of darkness. The Son's coming introduces light, and light forces a decision. To believe is to step into the light and escape judgment. To refuse to believe is to remain in darkness, and the darkness is itself the judgment.

div.title: Verses 19-21: Light, Darkness, and the Verdict
div.p: "This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their deeds were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his deeds be exposed. But he who practices the truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be manifested as having been wrought in God."

"This is the judgment" (haute de estin he krisis). The word krisis ("judgment, verdict, separation") defines what judgment means in this context. It is not a future tribunal but a present reality: the light has entered the world (the incarnation described in 1:9-14 and everything that flows from it), and human beings have responded by preferring darkness. The judgment consists of the choice itself. The light does not need to condemn; the preference for darkness is self-condemning.

"Men loved the darkness rather than the light" (egapesan hoi anthropoi mallon to skotos e to phos). The verb egapesan ("they loved") is aorist, describing the characteristic human response. It echoes the prologue's "the world did not know him... his own did not receive him" (1:10-11). The love of darkness is not presented as a philosophical position but as a moral preference: "for their deeds were evil" (en gar auton ponera ta erga). The word ponera ("evil, wicked, worthless") describes actions, not merely thoughts. People love the darkness because they are doing things that the light would expose. The flight from the light is a flight from exposure.

Verse 20: "Everyone who does evil hates the light." The verb phaula prasson ("doing worthless/base things") intensifies the description. Such a person "does not come to the light" (ouk erchetai pros to phos) — the same directional language used of Nicodemus in verse 2 (elthe pros auton, "came to him"). Coming to the light or remaining in the darkness is the fundamental human choice this passage describes. The reason for avoiding the light is "lest his deeds be exposed" (hina me elegchthe ta erga autou). The verb elegcho means "to expose, convict, reprove, bring to light." It does not merely mean "criticized" but "shown for what they truly are." The light functions as revelation — it makes visible what darkness conceals.

Verse 21: "But he who practices the truth comes to the light." The phrase "practices the truth" (poion ten aletheian) is arresting. Truth (aletheia) is not merely spoken or believed; it is done, practiced, performed. This is an Hebraic idiom. In the LXX and Jewish literature, "doing truth" (Hebrew: 'asah emet) means acting faithfully, living with integrity. Genesis 47:29 (LXX): Jacob asks Joseph to "deal with me in kindness and truth" (poieseis met' emou eleemosyne kai aletheian). Nehemiah 9:33: "You are just in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt truthfully" (aletheian epoiesas). Tobit 4:6 and 13:6: "If you do what is true, your ways will prosper." Truth in this framework is not an abstraction to be grasped intellectually but a way of living to be enacted.

The one who does truth comes to the light "so that his deeds may be manifested as having been wrought in God" (hina phanerothe autou ta erga hoti en theo estin eirgasmena). The phrase "wrought in God" (en theo eirgasmena) means that the person's deeds have been done in communion with God, in dependence on God, in alignment with God. The person who practices truth does not fear the light because the light will reveal that their deeds have their source in God. The contrast is not between perfect people and sinful people but between those who live in openness to God's revelation and those who hide from it.

This passage completes the Nicodemus scene by explaining why Nicodemus came "at night." He came in the darkness, drawn toward the light but not yet fully entering it. His position between night and light mirrors the position described in these verses: the light has come, and the question is whether a person will come to it or remain in the darkness. The author leaves Nicodemus's response unresolved at this point, allowing the reader to track his trajectory through the rest of the document (7:50-51, 19:39).

div.title: Verses 22-24: Jesus and John Baptizing
div.p: "After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and there he was spending time with them and baptizing. John also was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and people were coming and were being baptized. For John had not yet been thrown into prison."

The scene shifts from Jerusalem (where the Nicodemus conversation took place) to the Judean countryside. Jesus and his disciples are baptizing — though 4:2 will clarify that "Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were." The detail is significant: Jesus's ministry involves baptism, an activity parallel to John's and inevitably inviting comparison.

"Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there." Aenon (from the Hebrew/Aramaic 'ayin, "spring") is a location with abundant water. The geographical detail serves the narrative but also carries symbolic weight in a document that will repeatedly use water as a sign of what Jesus offers (4:10-14, 7:37-39). The juxtaposition of two baptizing ministries — John's and Jesus's — sets the stage for the discussion that follows about who is greater and what each baptism means.

"For John had not yet been thrown into prison." This chronological note distinguishes this document's timeline from those of the other three accounts, where John's imprisonment precedes the bulk of Jesus's public ministry (Matthew 4:12, Mark 1:14). This author places the early phase of Jesus's ministry as overlapping with John's, allowing for the comparison and contrast that follows.

div.title: Verses 25-30: John's Final Testimony and the Bridegroom
div.p: "Therefore there arose a discussion on the part of John's disciples with a Jew about purification. And they came to John and said to him, 'Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified — behold, he is baptizing, and all are coming to him.'"

"A discussion... about purification" (zetesis... peri katharismou). The word katharismos ("purification, cleansing") directly echoes 2:6, where the water jars at Cana were set aside "for the Jewish rites of purification." The dispute about purification provides the context for the question about Jesus's baptizing activity. The connection is deliberate: the old purification system (represented by the water jars and by John's water baptism) is being superseded by what Jesus brings. The dispute about purification leads to the question about Jesus, because Jesus is the answer to the purification question.

"He is baptizing, and all are coming to him." John's disciples report what they perceive as a competitive threat. The one to whom John testified is now attracting everyone. Their tone implies concern: John's prominence is declining. The word pantes ("all") may be hyperbolic, but it captures the shift in momentum.

Verse 27: "John answered and said, 'A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.'" John's response reframes the situation. No one takes a role for himself; every role is assigned from heaven. John's ministry was given to him by God; Jesus's ministry was given to him by God. There is no competition because neither one chose his position.

Verse 28: "You yourselves are my witnesses that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.'" John recalls his own prior testimony (see 1:20: "He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, 'I am not the Christ'"). He explicitly reaffirms his subordinate role. He is not the Christ but the one sent before the Christ. His role is preparatory, not ultimate.

p.hi: Verses 29-30: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice. So this joy of mine has been made full. He must increase, but I must decrease."

div.p: John employs the bridegroom-friend metaphor. In first-century Jewish wedding custom, the "friend of the bridegroom" (ho philos tou nymphiou) was the shoshbin — the best man who arranged the wedding, facilitated the match, and presented the bride to the groom. The shoshbin's role was essential but temporary; once the groom and bride were united, his work was complete. His joy was not diminished by the wedding's consummation but fulfilled by it.

The bridegroom imagery carries deep scriptural resonance. In Israel's prophetic tradition, God is consistently portrayed as the bridegroom of Israel. Hosea 2:16 (LXX 2:18): "In that day, declares the LORD, you will call me 'My husband.'" Isaiah 54:5: "For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name." Isaiah 62:5: "As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you." Jeremiah 2:2: "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride." Ezekiel 16 portrays the entire history of Jerusalem as a marriage between God and his people. By calling Jesus the bridegroom, John places him in the role that the prophets assigned to God himself. The bridegroom of Israel has arrived, and the shoshbin's work is finished.

"He must increase, but I must decrease" (ekeinon dei auxanein, eme de elattousthai). The dei ("must") again invokes divine necessity. This is not John's personal preference or resignation; it is the ordained pattern. The forerunner's diminishment and the bridegroom's exaltation are both necessary, both planned, both part of God's design. John's ministry is not failing; it is completing its purpose.

div.title: Verses 31-36: The One from Above
div.p: As with verses 16-21, the question of speaker arises. Are these words John the Baptist's continued speech, or the author's own theological commentary? The content shifts from John's concrete, first-person testimony (vv. 27-30) to sweeping declarations about the one from above, the one from earth, testimony, the Spirit, the Father's love for the Son, and the wrath that remains on the disobedient. The style and vocabulary are closer to the author's own voice (especially the prologue and vv. 16-21) than to John the Baptist's typical speech in this document. But again, whether John or the author speaks, the argument is continuous with everything that precedes it.

Verse 31: "He who comes from above is above all; he who is of the earth is from the earth and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all." This restates the categorical distinction of verse 6 (flesh/Spirit) and verse 13 (the one who descended from heaven). Two origins produce two kinds of speech. The one "of the earth" (ek tes ges) speaks "of the earth" (ek tes ges lalei) — earthly speech, limited by earthly perspective. The one "from above" (anothen — the same word from verse 3) is "above all" (epano panton estin). The word anothen links this verse directly to the earlier dialogue: to be born anothen is to be born from the realm of the one who comes anothen. The birth from above connects the believer to the one who is himself from above.

Verse 32: "What he has seen and heard, of that he testifies; and no one receives his testimony." The one from above testifies based on direct observation — he has seen (heoraken) and heard (ekousen) heavenly realities. This echoes verse 11: "We speak of what we know and testify of what we have seen." The lament "no one receives his testimony" (oudeis lambanei autou ten martyrian) restates the prologue's theme of rejection (1:10-11) and echoes the experience described in verses 11-12, where Nicodemus and those he represents do not receive the testimony. The "no one" (oudeis) is hyperbolic — verse 33 immediately names an exception — but it captures the prevailing response.

Verse 33: "He who has received his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true." The person who does receive the testimony thereby confirms (esphragisen, "has set a seal on") a fundamental truth: God is truthful (ho theos alethes estin). The act of believing the Son's testimony is simultaneously an affirmation of God's truthfulness, because the Son speaks God's words (v. 34). To believe the Son is to trust God; to reject the Son is to call God a liar. This logic will recur in 5:37-38: "The Father who sent me has himself testified about me... you do not have his word remaining in you, because you do not believe the one he sent."

Verse 34: "For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for he gives the Spirit without measure." The one God sent (hon gar apesteilen ho theos) speaks "the words of God" (ta rhemata tou theou) — not his own words but God's. The authority of the Son's speech derives from the Father's commissioning. The phrase "he gives the Spirit without measure" (ou gar ek metrou didosin to pneuma) indicates that the Spirit is given to the Son without limitation. In the LXX and Jewish tradition, the Spirit was given to prophets for specific tasks and in limited measure — the Spirit came upon Saul and departed (1 Samuel 16:14); the Spirit rested on the seventy elders temporarily (Numbers 11:25). The Spirit descended on Jesus and "remained" (emeinen, 1:33) — the permanence was already established. Now the author adds that the Spirit is given "without measure" — without the limitation that characterized every prior gift of the Spirit in Israel's history. The fullness of the Spirit on the Son corresponds to the fullness of grace and truth (1:14) that the prologue attributed to the Word-made-flesh.

Verse 35: "The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand." The verb agapa ("loves") describes the Father's relationship to the Son — the same verb used in verse 16 for God's love for the world.
