The author traces a trajectory from minimal knowledge to full confession, and each stage is forced forward by the pressure of the investigation.

"Where is he?" "I do not know." The man does not know where Jesus is. He was sent away to the pool before the healing was complete; he returned seeing but without Jesus present. He has received the benefit of Jesus's action without yet knowing where Jesus is or, in a deeper sense, who Jesus is. This mirrors 5:13, where the man healed at Bethesda "did not know who it was" because Jesus had slipped away. But the two men will take opposite trajectories: the Bethesda man, upon learning who Jesus was, reported him to the authorities (5:15); this man, under increasing pressure from the authorities, will move toward deeper and deeper confession.

div.title: Verses 13-17: The Pharisees' First Investigation
div.p: "They brought to the Pharisees the man who was formerly blind. Now it was a Sabbath on the day when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Then the Pharisees also were asking him how he received his sight. And he said to them, 'He applied clay to my eyes, and I washed, and I see.' Therefore some of the Pharisees were saying, 'This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.' But others were saying, 'How can a man who is a sinner perform such signs?' And there was a division among them. So they said to the blind man again, 'What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?' And he said, 'He is a prophet.'"

"They brought to the Pharisees the man who was formerly blind." The neighbors take the man to the Pharisees. The verb agousin ("they bring, they lead") may indicate coercion or simply that the community's instinct is to bring unusual events to the religious authorities for adjudication. The Pharisees function as judges and interpreters — the ones who determine what events mean within the framework of the law.

"Now it was a Sabbath on the day when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes." As in 5:9b, the Sabbath detail is revealed after the healing has been narrated, so that the reader evaluates the healing first and the controversy second. This is the third Sabbath healing in the document (after 5:1-18 and possibly implied in 7:23). The author's specification that Jesus "made the clay" (ton pelon epoiesen) highlights the deliberate nature of the violation: making clay involves kneading, a prohibited Sabbath activity. Jesus could have healed by a word alone, as he did at Bethesda. Instead, he chose a method that involved an act classifiable as work. The Sabbath violation is not incidental but integral to the sign's meaning.

"He applied clay to my eyes, and I washed, and I see." The man's testimony is direct and factual. He reports three things: what was done to him (clay applied), what he did (washed), and the result (he sees). The simplicity of the testimony contrasts with the complexity of the interrogation that surrounds it. The man has no theology, no explanation, no defense strategy. He has facts: I was blind; a man put clay on my eyes; I washed; I see.

"This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath." The first group of Pharisees reasons deductively: a man from God would keep the Sabbath; this man does not keep the Sabbath; therefore this man is not from God. The reasoning is formally valid but depends on the premise that no legitimate divine agent would ever act in apparent violation of the Sabbath. Jesus has already challenged this premise in 5:17 ("My Father is working until now, and I am working") and in 7:22-23 (the circumcision argument). The Pharisees operate from the assumption that the Sabbath regulation as they interpret it is the definitive test of a person's relationship to God. Jesus has been arguing that the works themselves — specifically, the giving of life and wholeness — are the definitive evidence of the Father's authorization.

"How can a man who is a sinner perform such signs?" The second group reasons inductively from the evidence: the sign is real, and signs of this magnitude require divine power. A sinner — one alienated from God — could not perform such works. The reasoning echoes Nicodemus's initial approach: "Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher; for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2). The same logic that drew Nicodemus to Jesus at night now creates dissent within the Pharisaic council.

"And there was a division among them" (kai schisma en en autois). The word schisma ("division, split") appeared in 7:43 for the division among the crowd and will appear in 10:19 for the division caused by the shepherd discourse. Jesus produces division wherever the light encounters the darkness. The division is not between believers and random opponents but within the religious establishment itself. Some Pharisees can see the evidence; others cannot. The light is separating those who will acknowledge what they see from those who will not.

"What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?" Unable to resolve the division among themselves, the Pharisees turn back to the man. The question is remarkable: they ask the formerly blind beggar for his theological assessment. The one with the least formal education is asked for his opinion because the ones with the most formal education cannot agree. The irony echoes 7:15, where the authorities marveled at Jesus's learning "having never been educated," and 7:49, where the Pharisees dismissed the believing crowd as "accursed" because they "do not know the Law." Here, the unlearned man is consulted because the learned cannot resolve their dispute.

"He is a prophet" (prophetes estin). The man's second identification of Jesus advances from "the man called Jesus" (v. 11) to "a prophet." The step is significant. A prophet in Israel's understanding was one through whom God spoke and acted — one authorized by God, empowered by God's Spirit, doing God's work. The identification of Jesus as a prophet connects to the same conclusion the crowd reached after the feeding of the multitude ("This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world," 6:14) and to the declaration of some at the Feast of Tabernacles ("This certainly is the Prophet," 7:40). The man has moved from knowing only a name to making a theological judgment: this man acts with divine authorization.

div.title: Verses 18-23: The Interrogation of the Parents
div.p: "The Jews then did not believe it about him, that he had been blind and had received sight, until they called the parents of the very one who had received his sight, and questioned them, saying, 'Is this your son, who you say was born blind? Then how does he now see?' His parents answered them and said, 'We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; but how he now sees, we do not know; or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him; he is of age, he will speak for himself.' His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. For this reason his parents said, 'He is of age; ask him.'"

"The Jews then did not believe it about him." The term "the Jews" (hoi Ioudaioi) here, as throughout this document, refers to the religious authorities — the leadership establishment in Jerusalem. Their initial response to the healing is not investigation but disbelief: they do not believe that the man was actually blind and actually received sight. Their strategy is to disprove the miracle rather than to explain it. If the man was not really blind from birth, the entire controversy evaporates. The shift from "some of the Pharisees" (v. 16) to "the Jews" (v. 18) signals that the investigation has moved from an informal Pharisaic inquiry to an official proceeding.

"They called the parents." The parents are summoned as witnesses to establish the foundational fact: was this man born blind? Two questions are put to them: (1) Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? (2) How does he now see? The first question challenges the identity and the condition; the second demands an explanation of the change.

"We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind." The parents confirm both facts under questioning: identity (this is our son) and condition (he was born blind). Their testimony eliminates any possibility that the man is an imposter or that his blindness was acquired rather than congenital. The facts are established by witnesses who have no motive to fabricate.

"But how he now sees, we do not know; or who opened his eyes, we do not know." The parents' refusal to explain the healing is not based on ignorance — their son could have told them what happened — but on fear, as the author immediately explains. They deflect the question to their son: "He is of age" (helikian echei, literally "he has age," meaning he is a legal adult capable of giving testimony). The deflection is self-protective.

"His parents said these things because they feared the Jews." The author provides an explicit motive for the parents' evasiveness: fear. The verb ephobountho ("they were fearing," imperfect tense) indicates an ongoing, established fear, not a momentary fright. The parents are afraid of the religious authorities.

"For the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue." This is one of the most significant statements in the chapter. The author reveals that a formal decision has been made: anyone who confesses (homologese, from homologeo, "to confess, to acknowledge publicly, to say the same thing") Jesus as the Christ will be expelled from the synagogue. The term aposynagogos ("put out of the synagogue, excommunicated") appears only in this document (9:22, 12:42, 16:2). Its severity in a first-century Jewish context cannot be overstated. The synagogue was not merely a place of worship; it was the center of communal life — economic, social, educational, and religious. Expulsion from the synagogue meant exclusion from the community, loss of social standing, disruption of commercial relationships, and effective banishment from Jewish life. For a family whose livelihood depended on community participation, the threat was existential.

The word homologese ("should confess") is the aorist subjunctive of homologeo, a word the author uses with precision. In 1:20, John the Baptist "confessed and did not deny, but confessed, 'I am not the Christ.'" In 12:42, "many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they were not confessing him, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue." Confession (homologia) is the public, vocal acknowledgment of what one believes to be true. The threat is specifically directed against public confession, not private belief. The authorities cannot control what people think, but they can punish what people say. The result is a system that separates belief from confession — that allows people to believe privately while forbidding them to acknowledge publicly. The parents embody this separation: they may believe or at least suspect, but they will not confess.

"For this reason his parents said, 'He is of age; ask him.'" The author repeats the parents' deflection and states the reason a second time, ensuring the reader understands: the parents' caution is not about not knowing but about not risking. Their testimony confirms the miracle (he was born blind; he now sees) but refuses to interpret it (who did it; what it means). They will testify to facts but not to theology, because theology — specifically, confession of Jesus as Christ — carries a cost they are unwilling to pay.

The parents stand in contrast to their son, who will shortly demonstrate the opposite posture: he will interpret the healing, identify its theological significance, and accept the consequences. The chapter sets up a choice between the parents' fear-driven silence and the son's courage-driven speech.

div.title: Verses 24-34: The Second Interrogation and the Man's Expulsion
div.p: "So a second time they called the man who had been blind, and said to him, 'Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner.' He then answered, 'Whether he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.' So they said to him, 'What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?' He answered them, 'I told you already and you did not listen; why do you want to hear it again? You do not want to become his disciples too, do you?' They reviled him and said, 'You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.' The man answered and said to them, 'Well, this is an amazing thing, that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is God-fearing and does his will, he hears him. Since the beginning of the world it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one who was born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.' They answered him, 'You were born entirely in sins, and are you teaching us?' And they put him out."

"Give glory to God" (dos doxan to theo). This phrase is not an invitation to praise. It is a solemn adjuration, a formula used to place someone under oath to tell the truth. The identical phrase appears in Joshua 7:19 (LXX), where Joshua says to Achan before his confession: "My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and give confession to him; and tell me what you have done. Do not hide it from me." The phrase functions as: "Swear before God to tell the truth." The Pharisees are placing the man under a solemn obligation.

"We know that this man is a sinner" (hemeis oidamen hoti houtos ho anthropos hamartolos estin). The authorities state their conclusion as established fact. The pronoun hemeis ("we") is emphatic — we, the authorized interpreters, we who know the Law, we who have the credentials to determine such things. The verdict is pre-established: Jesus is a sinner because he violated the Sabbath. The investigation has been conducted backward — the conclusion was determined first, and the evidence is being forced into conformity with it. The authorities are not investigating; they are building a case.

"Whether he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see" (hen oida hoti typhlos on arti blepo). The man's response is one of the most rhetorically effective statements in the document. He refuses to engage on the authorities' terrain — the question of Jesus's sinfulness — and plants himself on the ground of his own experience: I was blind. Now I see. This is not a theological argument but an empirical fact that no authority can overturn. The man has separated what he does not know (whether Jesus is a sinner by the Pharisees' criteria) from what he does know (the incontestable fact of his own transformation). The contrast between the authorities' confident hemeis oidamen ("we know") and the man's simple hen oida ("one thing I know") exposes the difference between institutional certainty and personal knowledge.

"I told you already and you did not listen; why do you want to hear it again?" The man's patience is wearing thin. He has answered the question about how his eyes were opened (v. 15), and the authorities are asking again — not because they want information but because they want a different answer. The man perceives this: "you did not listen" (ouk ekousate) implies not deafness but refusal.

"You do not want to become his disciples too, do you?" (me kai hymeis thelete autou mathetai genesthai). The question, introduced by me (expecting a negative answer), is sarcastic or pointed. The word "too" (kai) is telling — it implies that the man himself is already, at least functionally, a disciple. Whether he intends this or it slips out under pressure, the effect is the same: he has positioned himself on Jesus's side against the authorities. This is remarkable for a man who, twenty verses earlier, knew nothing about Jesus beyond his name.

"You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses." The Pharisees' response draws a line: Jesus's disciples stand on one side; Moses's disciples stand on the other. The pronoun sy ("you") is contemptuous — you, a blind beggar, are his follower; we, the trained interpreters, follow Moses. The claim to be "disciples of Moses" is not merely sectarian identity; it is an appeal to the foundational authority of the Torah. Moses is the lawgiver, the one through whom God spoke at Sinai, the one whose books are the basis of Israel's entire religious system.

But the author has already undermined this claim. In 5:45-47, Jesus told these same authorities: "Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father; the one who accuses you is Moses, in whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" The claim to follow Moses while rejecting the one Moses wrote about is, by Jesus's own argument, a contradiction. The Pharisees appeal to Moses as the authority that discredits Jesus; Jesus has already argued that Moses, properly understood, points to him.

"We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from." The contrast is between the certainty of Moses's divine authorization and the uncertainty of Jesus's origin. "We know" (oidamen) that God spoke to Moses — this is the bedrock of Jewish faith, grounded in the Sinai revelation (Exodus 19-20, 33:11). "We do not know where he is from" (touton de ouk oidamen pothen estin) — this is the same objection raised in 7:27, where the Jerusalemites said "we know where this man is from" and used that knowledge to disqualify him. But now the authorities say they do not know where he is from. The irony is that their not-knowing is closer to the truth than the Jerusalemites' knowing was: Jesus's origin is indeed unknown to them, because his true origin is the Father, and they do not know the Father (7:28, 8:19, 55).

"Well, this is an amazing thing, that you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes." The man's response is the theological center of the chapter. He finds it astonishing — thaumaston, "amazing, marvelous, worthy of wonder" — that the religious authorities, the experts in discerning God's activity, cannot identify the origin of someone who performed an unprecedented miracle. The word thaumaston echoes Psalm 118:23 (LXX 117:23): "This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous (thaumaste) in our eyes." The thing that should produce wonder and recognition in the experts produces only confusion and hostility.

"We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is God-fearing and does his will, he hears him." The man now constructs his own theological argument, and it is remarkably competent. He appeals to a principle the Pharisees themselves would accept: God does not answer the prayers or empower the works of sinners; God hears those who fear him and do his will. The principle is rooted in scripture. Psalm 66:18 (LXX 65:18): "If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened." Proverbs 15:29: "The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous." Isaiah 1:15: "Even though you multiply prayers, I will not listen. Your hands are full of blood." Job 27:9: "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?" Job 35:13: "Surely God will not listen to an empty cry, nor will the Almighty regard it." The man's argument is constructed from principles embedded in Israel's wisdom and prophetic tradition: God hears the righteous, not sinners. If Jesus were a sinner, God would not have enabled this miracle. Since God manifestly did enable it, Jesus is not a sinner. The argument is a qal va-homer that the Pharisees' own principles require them to accept.

"Since the beginning of the world it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one who was born blind" (ek tou aionos ouk ekousthe hoti enoixen tis ophthalmous typhlou gegennemenou). The man escalates his argument by identifying the unprecedented nature of the sign. Opening the eyes of one born blind has no precedent in Israel's history. Elijah raised the dead (1 Kings 17:17-24); Elisha healed leprosy (2 Kings 5:1-14); Moses performed signs that affected nature (Exodus 7-12). But none of Israel's prophets gave sight to a person born without it. The absence of precedent raises the theological stakes: this is not merely a remarkable healing but an act without parallel in the entire scriptural record. The only category adequate to explain it is the creative work of God himself — the God who said "Let there be light" is the only one who can bring light where there has never been light.

The connection to Isaiah's messianic promises is also in view. Isaiah 29:18: "On that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see." Isaiah 35:5: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped." Isaiah 42:7: "To open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness." These are promises attached to God's end-time deliverance — the coming age of salvation. The opening of blind eyes was a marker of the messianic age. The man's argument, though he may not fully grasp its implications, is pointing toward a messianic conclusion: the one who does what only God promised to do in the age to come must be from God.

"If this man were not from God, he could do nothing" (ei me en houtos para theou, ouk edynato poiein ouden). The man's conclusion is stated with the force of logical necessity: if not from God, then incapable of doing anything. The phrase para theou ("from God") is the same language Jesus used of himself: "I am from him" (par' autou eimi, 7:29). The man has arrived, through reasoning from evidence, at a conclusion that echoes Jesus's own self-identification.

"You were born entirely in sins, and are you teaching us?" The Pharisees' response abandons argument for insult. They return to the framework Jesus explicitly rejected in verse 3: the man's blindness was caused by sin. "You were born entirely in sins" (en hamartiais sy egenneths holos) reasserts the very assumption Jesus denied. The word holos ("entirely, completely") intensifies the contempt: you are sin from head to foot, from birth to the present. The question "are you teaching us?" (kai sy didaskeis hemas) is an outraged assertion of hierarchy: you, the blind beggar born in sin, presume to instruct us, the authorized teachers of Israel?

The irony, which the reader perceives and the Pharisees do not, is that the man born blind is in fact seeing more clearly than the teachers of Israel. The one they dismiss as unqualified to speak is the one whose argument they cannot answer. They respond to his reasoning not with counter-reasoning but with expulsion.

"And they put him out" (kai exebalon auton exo). The verb ekballo ("to cast out, throw out, expel") is strong. It is the same verb used in 6:37, where Jesus promised "the one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out (ou me ekbalo exo)." The Pharisees do what Jesus will not do: they cast out the one who confesses. The expulsion fulfills the threat of 9:22 — the man is made aposynagogos, expelled from the synagogue community. He has paid the cost that his parents were unwilling to pay. His confession has resulted in his exclusion from the community of Israel as defined by its current leadership.

The expelled man is now outside — outside the synagogue, outside the community, outside the social and religious structure that has defined Jewish life. This is the condition of the sheep whom the shepherd will find. The thief and robber of 10:1 climb over the wall to control the sheep; the shepherd calls his own by name and leads them out (10:3). The man has been put out by the thieves; he is about to be found by the shepherd.

div.title: Verses 35-38: Jesus Finds the Man
div.p: "Jesus heard that they had put him out, and finding him, he said, 'Do you believe in the Son of Man?' He answered, 'Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?' Jesus said to him, 'You have both seen him, and he is the one who is talking with you.' And he said, 'Lord, I believe.' And he worshiped him."

"Jesus heard that they had put him out, and finding him" (ekousen Iesous hoti exebalon auton exo, kai heuron auton). Jesus seeks out the expelled man. The verb heuron ("finding, having found") indicates that Jesus looked for him. The pattern is the same as 5:14 ("Jesus found him in the temple") but with opposite dynamics. In chapter 5, Jesus found the healed man and warned him; the man then reported Jesus to the authorities. Here, Jesus finds the expelled man and offers him something far greater than physical sight: the opportunity to believe.

The narrative structure is deliberately chiastic with the opening of the chapter. In verse 1, Jesus "saw" the blind man and initiated the healing. In verse 35, Jesus "found" the healed man and initiates the encounter of faith. Both times, Jesus takes the initiative. The man did not seek Jesus for healing; the man does not seek Jesus for faith. Jesus comes to him both times.

"Do you believe in the Son of Man?" (sy pisteueis eis ton huion tou anthropou). The question is personal and direct. The pronoun sy ("you") is emphatic: you yourself, having gone through what you have just endured — do you believe? The title "Son of Man" (ho huios tou anthropou) connects to Daniel 7:13-14, where "one like a son of man" comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom. It is the title Jesus has used throughout this document for himself (1:51, 3:13-14, 5:27, 6:27, 53, 62, 8:28). The question is whether the man will take the final step — beyond "a man called Jesus," beyond "a prophet," beyond "from God" — to believing in the figure who has cosmic authority.

"Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" The man's response reveals both his willingness and his ignorance. He does not know who the Son of Man is — he has never seen Jesus, since Jesus sent him to the pool before his eyes were opened, and he has not seen Jesus since. The word kyrie ("Lord, sir") could be either respectful address or something more; at this stage, the man is using it as a form of respect toward the stranger who is questioning him. But the hina clause — "that I may believe in him" (hina pisteuso eis auton) — reveals his disposition: he is ready to believe. He asks not "why should I believe?" but "who is he?" The willingness is established; only the object needs to be identified.

"You have both seen him, and he is the one who is talking with you." Jesus's self-identification echoes the pattern of 4:26, where Jesus told the Samaritan woman, "I who speak to you am he" (ego eimi, ho lalon soi). In both cases, the revelation comes to someone who has been on a journey of progressive understanding: the Samaritan woman moved from "a Jew" to "Sir" to "a prophet" to "could this be the Christ" before Jesus declared himself; the blind man has moved from "the man called Jesus" to "a prophet" to "from God" before Jesus declares himself.

The phrase "you have seen him" (kai heorakas auton) carries extraordinary weight in context. The man has "seen" — and this is the first person in his entire life that he has seen with the eyes Jesus gave him. The verb horao ("to see") in the perfect tense (heorakas) indicates completed action with ongoing result: you have seen him and are seeing him now. The eyes that Jesus created are now looking at their creator.

"Lord, I believe" (pisteuo, kyrie). The man's confession is brief and absolute. The word kyrie now carries its full weight: not merely "sir" but "Lord" — the same address used by Peter in 6:68 ("Lord, to whom shall we go?") and Thomas in 20:28 ("My Lord and my God!"). The verb pisteuo ("I believe") stands without qualification. There is no "I believe, but..." or "I believe if..." The confession is whole.

"And he worshiped him" (kai prosekynesin auto). The verb proskyneo ("to worship, to bow down before") is the most significant action in the chapter. In Israel's scriptures, proskyneo is directed to God alone. Exodus 20:5 (LXX): "You shall not worship (proskynesis) them nor serve them." Deuteronomy 6:13: "You shall fear the LORD your God and worship (proskynesis) him." When Cornelius falls at Peter's feet in Acts 10:25-26, Peter says, "Stand up; I too am just a man." When the seer in Revelation 19:10 falls at the angel's feet to worship, the angel says, "Do not do that; I am a fellow servant of yours." But when the man born blind worships Jesus, there is no correction, no rebuke, no redirection. Jesus accepts the worship. In the theology of this document, this acceptance is consistent: the Word who was God (1:1), the only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father (1:18), the one who claims "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), properly receives worship.

The man's trajectory is now complete. He moved from blindness to sight, from "the man called Jesus" to "Lord," from ignorance to worship. Every step of his progression was forced forward by opposition: the neighbors' inquiry prompted him to identify Jesus; the Pharisees' investigation prompted him to call Jesus a prophet; the second interrogation prompted him to argue that Jesus is from God; the expulsion prompted nothing — but Jesus came to him, and the encounter prompted worship. The man grew not in spite of the pressure but through it. Each confrontation with the authorities drove him deeper into understanding.

div.title: Verses 39-41: Judgment, Sight, and Blindness
div.p: "And Jesus said, 'For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind.' Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, 'We are not blind too, are we?' Jesus said to them, 'If you were blind, you would have no sin; but since you say, "We see," your sin remains.'"

"For judgment I came into this world" (eis krima ego eis ton kosmon touton elthon). The word krima ("judgment") appears here rather than krisis (which appears in 3:19, 5:22, 24, 27, 29, 30). The two words are related but not identical: krisis is the process of judging; krima is the result, the verdict, the enacted judgment. Jesus's coming into the world enacts a judgment — not a future forensic proceeding but a present sorting that occurs through the encounter with him.

This statement must be reconciled with 3:17: "God did not send the Son into the world to judge (krine) the world, but that the world might be saved through him." And with 8:15: "I judge (krino) no one." And with 12:47: "I did not come to judge (krino) the world but to save the world." The reconciliation lies in the author's understanding of how judgment works: Jesus does not come with the explicit purpose of condemning, but his presence creates a crisis that separates people by their response. The judgment is not imposed from outside; it is produced by the encounter. The light does not intend to expose the darkness — it intends to illuminate — but its illumination necessarily exposes what the darkness conceals. The judgment in 9:39 is this kind of separating effect: the light reveals who will receive it and who will not. The same principle was stated in 3:19: "This is the judgment (krisis), that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light."

"So that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind." The double purpose clause (hina ... kai hina ...) describes a reversal. Those who do not see (hoi me blepontes) will receive sight. Those who see (hoi blepontes) will become blind. The reversal echoes the pattern of Israel's prophetic tradition. Isaiah 6:9-10 (LXX): "Go, and say to this people: 'You will keep on hearing, but will not understand; you will keep on seeing, but will not perceive.' Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed." This passage is the most frequently quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament documents (Mark 4:12, Matthew 13:14-15, Luke 8:10, Acts 28:26-27, Romans 11:8). Its function is to explain why the revelation of God produces blindness in those who should be most prepared to receive it: the teachers of Israel, the custodians of the scriptures, the ones who claim to see.

The chapter has just enacted this reversal. The man born blind — the one who literally could not see — has received both physical and spiritual sight. The Pharisees — the ones who claim to see, who claim to know the Law, who claim to discern God's activity — have become blind to what is in front of them. The man who began the chapter in total physical darkness ends it in worship. The authorities who began the chapter confident of their theological vision end it unable to recognize what God has done.

The reversal also echoes Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2:4-8 (LXX): "The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble gird on strength... The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low, he also exalts. He raises the poor from the dust." And Mary's song in Luke 1:51-53 (though outside this document): "He has scattered those who were proud in the thoughts of their heart. He has brought down rulers from their thrones, and has exalted those who were humble." The pattern of divine reversal — the humbled are exalted, the exalted are brought low — is a consistent theme in Israel's scriptures and is now being demonstrated in the contrast between the blind beggar and the Pharisees.

"We are not blind too, are we?" (me kai hemeis typhloi esmen). The question, introduced by me, expects a negative answer: "Surely we are not blind?" The Pharisees perceive that Jesus's statement about the seeing becoming blind might apply to them, and they push back. The emphatic hemeis ("we") echoes their earlier assertions: "we know that this man is a sinner" (v. 24), "we are disciples of Moses" (v. 28), "we know that God has spoken to Moses" (v. 29). Each use of "we" has been a claim to authoritative knowledge. Now Jesus is suggesting that their knowledge is blindness.

"If you were blind, you would have no sin; but since you say, 'We see,' your sin remains." Jesus's response is the chapter's final statement and its theological climax. It establishes a paradox with two parts:

First: if you were blind — if you genuinely did not know, if you were in the condition of innocent ignorance — you would have no sin (hamartian ouk eichete). Ignorance mitigates guilt. The man born blind began in ignorance and progressed toward knowledge. His movement was from not-seeing to seeing, and each step brought him closer to the truth. The Pharisees do not have the excuse of ignorance.

Second: since you say "we see" (hoti legete hoti blepomen) — since you claim to possess knowledge, since you present yourselves as the ones who can see clearly — your sin remains (he hamartia hymon menei). The verb menei ("remains, abides") is from meno, the same verb that runs throughout this document for the abiding that characterizes the life of the believer (1:33, 38-39; 3:36; 6:56; 8:31; 15:4-10). But here meno describes something that abides to the detriment of those in whom it remains: their sin. The claim to see, when coupled with the refusal to acknowledge what is visible, transforms ignorance into culpability. The Pharisees are not blind in the sense of being unable to see; they are blind in the sense of refusing to see while claiming that they do see. Their sin is not ignorance but the pretense of knowledge that shields them from the truth.

The phrase "your sin remains" carries the weight of a verdict. It is the counterpart to the promise of 8:31-32, where Jesus told those who had believed: "If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." The opposite is also true: if you refuse the word while claiming to know the truth, the sin that enslaves you remains. The Pharisees' condition is not a temporary misunderstanding that will naturally resolve; it is a settled posture — they say "we see" — and as long as that posture is maintained, their sin is not removed but remains.

list.item: The chapter is the dramatic enactment of "I am the light of the world" (8:12). The claim that was verbal in chapter 8 is demonstrated in chapter 9. The light of the world encounters a man who has never seen light and gives him sight. The sign does not merely illustrate the claim; it enacts it. The light enters the darkness — the lifelong, congenital, absolute darkness of a man born blind — and the darkness gives way. But the sign also enacts the other half of the light's effect: it exposes the darkness in those who claim to see. The Pharisees, confronted with an undeniable work of God, refuse to acknowledge it because it contradicts their theological framework. The light reveals both the man's capacity for sight and the authorities' incapacity for recognition. The same act that opens blind eyes closes seeing eyes.

The chapter structures itself as a legal proceeding with four rounds of testimony, and the evidence progressively overwhelms the verdict. The neighbors establish the man's identity and condition (vv. 8-12). The Pharisees establish the Sabbath violation and produce a division among themselves (vv. 13-17). The parents confirm the congenital blindness and the reality of the healing (vv. 18-23). The man himself delivers an argument the authorities cannot refute (vv. 24-34). At each stage, the evidence for the divine origin of the healing grows stronger. At each stage, the authorities' resistance becomes more desperate. By the end, they have abandoned argument for insult ("you were born entirely in sins") and abandoned persuasion for coercion ("they put him out"). The legal form of the chapter serves the author's theological point: the evidence for Jesus is not lacking; what is lacking is the willingness to follow the evidence where it leads.

The man born blind undergoes a progressive transformation that is the opposite of the authorities' progressive hardening. The man moves from "the man called Jesus" (v. 11) to "a prophet" (v. 17) to "from God" (v. 33) to "Lord, I believe" with worship (v. 38). At each stage, his understanding of Jesus deepens. The Pharisees move in the opposite direction: from a division among themselves (v. 16) to a unified verdict that Jesus is a sinner (v. 24) to a contemptuous dismissal of both the evidence and the witness (v. 34). The two trajectories cross: the man begins in darkness and ends in worship; the authorities begin in confidence and end in blindness. The chapter dramatizes the principle of 3:20-21: "Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds will not be exposed. But he who practices the truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be manifested as having been worked in God."

The chapter deliberately parallels and contrasts with the healing of chapter 5. Both chapters narrate a Sabbath healing in Jerusalem. Both involve a man with a long-standing condition. Both produce confrontation with the religious authorities. But the healed men respond in opposite ways. The man at Bethesda did not know who healed him (5:13) and, once told, reported Jesus to the authorities (5:15); the chapter does not record any further spiritual development. The man born blind begins not knowing who healed him but, under pressure from the authorities, moves steadily toward deeper confession until he worships Jesus as Lord (9:38). The man at Bethesda became the instrument of escalation against Jesus; the man born blind became a witness for Jesus against the authorities. The contrast suggests that the same miraculous encounter can produce opposite trajectories depending on the response of the one who is healed. The healing itself does not determine the outcome; the recipient's response does.

The synagogue expulsion (aposynagogos) introduces the cost of confession and the separation between institutional Judaism and those who confess Jesus. The formal agreement to expel anyone who confesses Jesus as Christ (v. 22) creates a binary: confess and be expelled, or be silent and remain. The parents choose silence and security; the son chooses speech and expulsion. The cost is real — loss of community, social standing, economic relationships, religious participation. The chapter does not present the cost as trivial or the choice as easy. It presents the choice as a test that reveals what a person values most. The parents value their place in the community; the son values the truth of what has happened to him. The chapter's trajectory suggests that what is lost through expulsion — communal belonging as defined by the current authorities — is surpassed by what is gained through encounter with Jesus: a new community defined by the shepherd who calls his own by name (10:3) and who never casts out the one who comes to him (6:37).

The question of Jesus's origin ("where he is from") continues from chapters 7 and 8 and reaches a new resolution. In 7:27, the Jerusalemites said "we know where this man is from" and used that knowledge to disqualify him. In 7:28, Jesus responded that they do not know the one who sent him. In 9:29, the Pharisees say "we do not know where he is from" and use that ignorance to disqualify him. The irony is complete: whether they claim to know or claim not to know his origin, the result is the same — rejection. The man born blind provides the answer the authorities will not accept: "If this man were not from God, he could do nothing" (v. 33). He has arrived at the truth about Jesus's origin through reasoning from evidence, while the authorities, who have access to the same evidence and far more scriptural training, refuse to follow the argument to its conclusion.

The creation imagery pervading the healing connects Jesus's work to the work of God in Genesis. The making of clay from the ground (v. 6) echoes the forming of man from the dust in Genesis 2:7. The giving of sight to one who has never seen echoes the giving of light to a dark creation in Genesis 1:3. The method Jesus chose — clay, water, the command to go and wash — is not arbitrary but symbolic: it recapitulates the creative acts that only God performs. The sign does not merely demonstrate Jesus's power; it identifies the kind of power at work. This is not therapeutic skill but creative authority — the authority of the Word through whom "all things came into being, and apart from him nothing came into being that has come into being" (1:3).

The Pool of Siloam ties the healing to the Tabernacles context and to Jesus's identity as the sent one. The author's deliberate translation of the pool's name as "Sent" (apestalmenos) connects the healing to the document's central christological claim: Jesus is the one sent by the Father. The pool from which the Tabernacles water was drawn — the water Jesus claimed to fulfill in 7:37-38 — is now the instrument through which a blind man receives sight. Water and light converge: the living water of chapter 7 and the light of the world of chapter 8 meet in chapter 9 at the pool whose name means "Sent."

Jesus's statement "your sin remains" (9:41) functions as a verdict that inverts the authorities' verdict against him. The Pharisees pronounced Jesus a sinner (v. 24). Jesus pronounces that their sin remains. They cast out the man born blind; Jesus will describe them as thieves and robbers who do not enter by the door (10:1). They claimed the authority to determine who is from God and who is not; Jesus declares that their claim to see is the very thing that keeps their sin in place. The judgment of 9:39 is enacted in 9:41: those who claimed to see have become blind, and their blindness is culpable because it is chosen.

The present-tense language of believing continues from earlier chapters. In verse 35, Jesus asks "Do you believe (pisteueis, present tense) in the Son of Man?" In verse 38, the man responds "I believe (pisteuo, present tense)." The question and the answer are in the present: do you now, at this moment, place your trust? The man's answer is an act in the present moment. His ongoing discipleship will be tested by the ongoing encounter with Jesus. The chapter does not treat belief as a past event to which one looks back; it treats belief as a present posture to which one commits. The worship that follows the confession — "and he worshiped him" (v. 38) — is the first act of that ongoing posture.

The chapter demonstrates that encounter with Jesus produces not consensus but separation. The neighbors are confused (vv. 8-9). The Pharisees are divided (v. 16). The parents are fearful and evasive (vv. 20-23). The man himself moves toward confession and worship, while the authorities move toward hardened rejection. The same event — a blind man receiving sight — produces opposite responses in those who witness it. The chapter does not present the evidence as ambiguous; it presents the responses as revealing. The evidence is clear; what differs is the willingness to follow it. This is the enacted form of 7:17: "If anyone is willing to do his will, he will know of the teaching, whether it is of God." The man was willing; the authorities were not. The same light illuminated both, and the same light divided them.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 9): Chapter 9 narrates the healing of a man born blind — a healing that Jesus performs on the Sabbath by making clay, anointing the man's eyes, and sending him to wash in the pool of Siloam (9:6-7). The chapter's primary concern is not the miracle itself but the escalating confrontation between the healed man and the Pharisees, a confrontation that reveals who is truly blind and who truly sees. The Pharisees interrogate the healed man repeatedly, refuse to accept the evidence of the sign, and finally cast him out of the synagogue (9:34). They are unable to recognize God's work because it does not fit their Sabbath framework: "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath" (9:16). The healed man, by contrast, progresses from ignorance to confession: he calls Jesus "a man" (9:11), then "a prophet" (9:17), then reasons that Jesus must be "from God" (9:33), and finally, when Jesus finds him after his expulsion, worships him as "Lord" (9:38). The chapter ends with Jesus pronouncing judgment on the Pharisees: "For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind" (9:39). When some Pharisees ask, "We are not blind too, are we?" Jesus responds: "If you were blind, you would have no sin; but since you say, 'We see,' your sin remains" (9:40-41).

This is the immediate audience and occasion for what follows in chapter 10. There is no scene break between 9:41 and 10:1. The "Truly, truly, I say to you" of 10:1 is addressed to the same Pharisees who have just expelled the healed man from the synagogue and been told that their sin remains.

What the author argues immediately after (John 11): The narrative moves to the illness and death of Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus raises from the dead after four days in the tomb (11:1-44). The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and climactic sign in this document, and it demonstrates in the most dramatic possible terms the claim Jesus has been making since chapter 5: that the Son gives life to the dead (5:21, 25-26). When Martha meets Jesus, she confesses: "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" (11:24). Jesus responds: "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me will live even if he dies, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (11:25-26). The declaration is the sixth "I am" statement with a predicate (after bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life). The raising of Lazarus directly precipitates the decision by the chief priests and Pharisees to kill Jesus (11:47-53), fulfilling the pattern established in chapter 10: the shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11, 15, 17-18), and that laying down now approaches. Caiaphas's prophecy that "one man should die for the people" (11:50) is glossed by the author as extending beyond Israel: "not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad" (11:52) — language that directly echoes the "other sheep that are not of this fold" whom Jesus must bring so that there will be "one flock, one shepherd" (10:16).

How chapter 10 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 9 ended with a concrete demonstration of failed shepherding: the Pharisees expelled a man whom God had healed, punishing the sheep rather than caring for it. Chapter 10 opens by interpreting what the reader has just witnessed. The Pharisees are not the true shepherds of Israel. They are the thieves and robbers who climb in by another way (10:1), the hired hands who flee when the wolf comes (10:12-13), the strangers whose voice the sheep do not recognize (10:5). Jesus is the true shepherd — the one who enters by the door, who calls his own sheep by name, who leads them out, who lays down his life for them. The shepherd discourse is not a free-standing allegory; it is Jesus's interpretive commentary on the events of chapter 9.

The chapter then moves forward in time to the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), where the same confrontation continues. The authorities demand a plain declaration: "If you are the Christ, tell us plainly" (10:24). Jesus responds by pointing to his works (10:25) and to the relationship between himself and the Father (10:30), which provokes another attempt to stone him (10:31). The chapter concludes with Jesus withdrawing beyond the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing (10:40), closing a geographic and thematic circle back to the beginning of the document (1:28). The narrative moves from the beginning of Jesus's public ministry (John's baptism) to the threshold of its conclusion (the raising of Lazarus and the decision to kill him).

The chapter also completes a major movement in the document's argument about Israel's leadership. The confrontation with the religious authorities began at the pool of Bethesda in chapter 5, where the Sabbath healing provoked the charge of blasphemy. It continued through the bread-of-life discourse in chapter 6 (grumbling, departure of disciples), the Tabernacles disputes of chapters 7-8 (origin, Abraham, "before Abraham was, I am"), and the blind-man controversy of chapter 9. In chapter 10, Jesus gathers all of this into a single image: Israel's leaders are not shepherds but hired hands, and Israel's true shepherd — the one Ezekiel prophesied God would send — is standing before them.

div.title: The Shepherd Tradition in Israel's Scriptures: Background Essential for Hearing the Chapter
div.p: Before proceeding verse by verse, the scriptural background of the shepherd image must be established, because the author assumes the reader hears it and builds the entire first half of the chapter on it.

The shepherd was not merely a literary metaphor in Israel's tradition. It was the primary image for leadership — political, military, and spiritual. The patriarchs were shepherds (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob). Moses was tending sheep when God called him at the burning bush (Exodus 3:1). David was taken from following the sheep to shepherd Israel (2 Samuel 7:8, Psalm 78:70-72). The image of shepherd-as-leader is so deeply embedded in Israel's language that "shepherd" and "ruler" are nearly interchangeable.
Several scriptural texts are directly relevant to what the author presents in this chapter:

list.item: Ezekiel 34. This is the foundational text. God delivers a comprehensive indictment of Israel's shepherds (the leaders — kings, priests, elders) for their failure to care for the flock: "Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been feeding themselves! Should not the shepherds feed the flock? You eat the fat and clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones without feeding the flock. Those who are sickly you have not strengthened, the diseased you have not healed, the broken you have not bound up, the scattered you have not brought back, nor have you sought for the lost; but with force and with severity you have ruled them. They were scattered for lack of a shepherd, and they became food for every beast of the field" (Ezekiel 34:2-5, LXX). God then pronounces judgment on the shepherds and declares that he will take over the shepherding himself: "Behold, I myself will search for my sheep and seek them out... I will deliver them from all the places to which they were scattered... I will feed them on the mountains of Israel... I will feed my flock and I will lead them to rest... I will seek the lost, bring back the scattered, bind up the broken and strengthen the sick" (Ezekiel 34:11-16). After announcing his own direct shepherding, God promises to appoint one shepherd: "I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them; he shall feed them and be their shepherd. And I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David shall be prince among them" (Ezekiel 34:23-24).

div.p: The double claim in Ezekiel 34 is essential: God will shepherd Israel himself AND will raise up a Davidic shepherd. The two are not alternatives but a single program. When Jesus claims in chapter 10 to be the good shepherd and then declares "I and the Father are one" (10:30), the claim is that both halves of Ezekiel's promise are being fulfilled simultaneously: God shepherds Israel through the Davidic shepherd who is one with him.

list.item: Jeremiah 23:1-4. "Woe to the shepherds who are destroying and scattering the sheep of my pasture... You have scattered my flock and driven them away, and have not attended to them... I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them and bring them back to their fold, and they will be fruitful and multiply. I will also raise up shepherds over them and they will tend them; and they will not be afraid any longer, nor be terrified, nor will any be missing."

Zechariah 11. The prophet enacts a parable of two shepherds: the good shepherd whose labor is rejected by the flock, whose wages are set at thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12-13), and the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock. The passage interweaves judgment on the flock with judgment on its failed leaders, and the thirty-pieces-of-silver detail will resonate with this document's betrayal narrative.

Psalm 23 (LXX 22). "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters; he restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for you are with me." The psalm establishes that shepherding is God's own activity. When Jesus claims to be the good shepherd, he claims to perform the activity that Psalm 23 attributes to the LORD himself.

Numbers 27:15-17. Moses, at the end of his life, asks God to "appoint a man over the congregation, who will go out and come in before them, and who will lead them out and bring them in, so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep which have no shepherd." The language of "going out and coming in" and "leading out" matches the language of John 10:3-4 precisely: the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name and leads them out" (exagei auta). The shepherd of Numbers 27 is Joshua (Yeshua in Hebrew — the same name as Jesus in Greek, Iesous). Moses asks for a shepherd; God provides Joshua/Jesus.

Micah 2:12-13. "I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob, I will surely gather the remnant of Israel. I will put them together like sheep in the fold; like a flock in the midst of its pasture they will be noisy with people. The breaker goes up before them; they break out, pass through the gate and go out by it. So their king goes on before them, and the LORD at their head." The image of the king going before the flock, breaking out through the gate, is strikingly close to the language of John 10:4: "When he puts forth all his own, he goes ahead of them."

div.p: A first-century Jewish hearer encountering Jesus's shepherd discourse would have these texts resonating simultaneously. The shepherd image was not optional or decorative; it was the definitive image for Israel's relationship with God and for the role of Israel's leaders. A claim to be "the good shepherd" was a claim laden with scriptural authority and political force.

div.title: Verses 1-6: The Figure of Speech About the Sheepfold
div.p: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs up some other way, he is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is a shepherd of the sheep. To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he puts forth all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice. A stranger they simply will not follow, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers. This figure of speech Jesus spoke to them, but they did not understand what those things were which he had been saying to them."

"Truly, truly, I say to you" (amen amen lego hymin). The double amen is this author's characteristic marker for a statement of particular authority (used twenty-five times in the document: 1:51, 3:3, 3:5, 3:11, 5:19, 5:24, 5:25, 6:26, 6:32, 6:47, 6:53, 8:34, 8:51, 8:58, 10:1, 10:7, 12:24, 13:16, 13:20, 13:21, 13:38, 14:12, 16:20, 16:23, 21:18). The addressees are the Pharisees from 9:40-41. There is no scene change, no new audience introduction, no geographic transition. What follows is directed at the leaders who have just demonstrated their treatment of the sheep by expelling the man born blind.

"He who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs up some other way, he is a thief and a robber" (ho me eiserchomenos dia tes thyras eis ten aulen ton probaton alla anabainon allachothen ekeinos kleptes estin kai lestes). The sheepfold (aule, "courtyard, enclosed space") is the protected enclosure where the flock is kept. In Palestinian practice, a stone-walled enclosure with a single entrance was used to pen sheep at night. The single entrance was the legitimate point of access. Anyone who bypasses the entrance and climbs over the wall is identified by their method of entry: a thief (kleptes, one who steals by stealth) and a robber (lestes, one who uses violence or banditry). The two words are not synonymous — kleptes suggests cunning, lestes suggests force — but together they describe illegitimate access by any means.

The immediate referent is the Pharisees who have just been addressed. They have claimed authority over Israel's flock — the authority to determine who belongs and who is expelled (9:34: "You were born entirely in sins, and are you teaching us?" followed by expulsion). Jesus declares that their authority is illegitimate. They did not enter through the proper door; they climbed in by another way.

"He who enters by the door is a shepherd of the sheep" (ho de eiserchomenos dia tes thyras poimen estin ton probaton). The contrast is between the legitimate shepherd and the illegitimate intruders. The door distinguishes the two. The shepherd uses the door because he has the right to enter; the thieves bypass it because they do not.

"To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice." The doorkeeper (ho thyroros) is the attendant who guards the entrance and admits the rightful shepherd. The sheep respond not to the shepherd's appearance but to his voice (phone). This is the critical distinguishing mark: the sheep know their shepherd by sound. In Palestinian shepherding, multiple flocks might share a common fold overnight, each belonging to a different shepherd. When morning came, each shepherd would call his own sheep, and they would respond only to his call, not to the calls of other shepherds. The practice was well known in the first century and is attested by ancient sources. The sheep's recognition is based on habitual relationship — they have heard this voice before, they know it, they respond to it.

The word "voice" (phone) connects to a sustained theme in this document. In 5:25: "An hour is coming and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live." In 5:28: "All who are in the tombs will hear his voice." In 8:43: "Why do you not understand what I am saying? Because you cannot hear my word." In 8:47: "He who is of God hears the words of God; for this reason you do not hear them, because you are not of God." In 18:37: "Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice." The capacity to hear Jesus's voice is the marker that distinguishes those who belong to him from those who do not. And chapter 9 has just enacted this: the man born blind heard Jesus's voice and followed; the Pharisees heard the same voice and rejected it.

"He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out" (ta idia probata phonei kat' onoma kai exagei auta). Two details are significant. First, "by name" (kat' onoma) — the shepherd knows each sheep individually. This is not an impersonal, mass operation but an individual relationship. Second, "leads them out" (exagei auta) — the verb exago means "to lead out, bring out." In the LXX, exago is repeatedly used for God leading Israel out of Egypt: Exodus 3:10: "I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may bring my people, the sons of Israel, out of (exagages) Egypt." Exodus 6:6-7: "I will bring you out (exaxo hymas) from under the burdens of the Egyptians." Exodus 12:51: "On that very day the LORD brought the sons of Israel out of (exegagen) the land of Egypt." The shepherd "leading out" the sheep uses the exodus verb. The sheep are being led out of one condition into another — out of the fold and into pasture, out of confinement and into life. For the man born blind, this has just occurred literally: he was expelled from the synagogue (the fold controlled by the illegitimate shepherds), and Jesus found him and led him into the light (9:35-38). What the Pharisees intended as punishment, Jesus transforms into deliverance.

"When he puts forth all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice." The phrase "goes ahead of them" (emprosthen auton poreuetai) describes the Palestinian practice: the shepherd walks in front and the sheep follow behind. This contrasts with Western herding, where the shepherd drives from behind. The Eastern shepherd leads; the sheep follow voluntarily because they recognize the voice. The follow-from-recognition pattern is exactly what the author has depicted throughout the document. The first disciples followed after hearing Jesus's voice (1:37-43). The Samaritan woman and her townspeople responded to what they heard (4:39-42). The blind man followed after hearing and recognizing (9:35-38). Following is always a response to hearing, and hearing is always a response to voice.

"A stranger they simply will not follow, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers." The negative counterpart confirms the principle: recognition of voice determines response. The sheep's refusal to follow a stranger (allotrios, "belonging to another, foreign") is not a command but a description of behavior that follows from relationship. They flee because the voice is unfamiliar. The Pharisees' voice is the stranger's voice: the man born blind did not follow their reasoning, did not accept their conclusions, and ultimately stood against them despite the cost (9:25, 27, 30-33). He fled from the strangers' voice and recognized the shepherd's.

"This figure of speech Jesus spoke to them, but they did not understand what those things were which he had been saying to them" (tauten ten paroimian eipen autois ho Iesous; ekeinoi de ouk egnoson tina en ha elalei autois). The word paroimia ("figure of speech, proverb, dark saying") is used instead of the Synoptic authors' parabole. This author uses paroimia again in 16:25, 29, where Jesus promises to stop speaking in "figures" and speak plainly about the Father. The Pharisees' failure to understand is consistent with the pattern the author has traced: those who reject the light cannot perceive what the light reveals (9:39-41). Their claim to see ("We see," 9:41) blinds them to the meaning of what Jesus is saying. The incomprehension is not intellectual but moral — they cannot perceive because they are the very figures being described, and self-recognition is precisely what their pride prevents.

div.title: Verses 7-10: "I Am the Door"
div.p: "So Jesus said to them again, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them. I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.'"

"I am the door of the sheep" (ego eimi he thyra ton probaton). This is the third "I am" statement with a predicate in the document (after "I am the bread of life," 6:35, and "I am the light of the world," 8:12). Jesus has just described the door in the figure of speech as the legitimate point of entry to the fold. Now he identifies himself as that door. The image carries a double function: the door provides access for the legitimate shepherd and protection against the illegitimate intruders. In ancient Palestinian practice, the shepherd himself would often lie across the entrance to the fold at night, his body forming the barrier between the sheep and predators. The shepherd was, physically, the door. Jesus claims to be the point of access to the flock and the point of protection for it.

"All who came before me are thieves and robbers" (pantes hosoi elthon pro emou kleptai eisin kai lestai). The phrase "all who came before me" has been debated. It cannot mean all of Israel's leaders without exception — Moses, Joshua, David, the prophets were not thieves and robbers. The phrase must be understood in context: those who came claiming shepherd-authority over Israel but without entering through the legitimate door — that is, without divine authorization, without doing the Father's will, without caring for the sheep. The immediate referent remains the current religious leadership, the Pharisees who claim to shepherd Israel but who expel and abuse the sheep. But the indictment also extends backward to the long history of failed leadership that Ezekiel 34 condemned: the kings who exploited, the priests who profited, the rulers who fed themselves rather than the flock. The phrase "came before me" (elthon pro emou) may mean "came before me in time" or "came instead of me" — those who put themselves forward as shepherds in place of the one God was sending.

"But the sheep did not hear them" (all' ouk ekousan auton ta probata). Despite the illegitimate leaders' claims, the true sheep did not listen. The verb akouo ("hear, listen to, obey") in this document consistently describes the response of those who belong to Jesus (5:25, 8:47, 10:3, 16, 27, 18:37). The sheep's refusal to hear the false shepherds is the same refusal described in verse 5: they will not follow a stranger's voice. In the chapter 9 narrative, the man born blind refused to hear the Pharisees' conclusion that Jesus was a sinner (9:24-25). He could not be made to deny what he knew.

"I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture" (ego eimi he thyra; di' emou ean tis eiselthe sothesetai kai eiseleusetai kai exeleusetai kai nomen heurese). The repetition "I am the door" reinforces the identification. The promise has three elements:

list.item: "He will be saved" (sothesetai). The verb sozo ("to save, rescue, deliver") echoes the name Jesus itself (Iesous = Yeshua = "the LORD saves") and the Samaritans' confession: "This is truly the Savior of the world" (4:42). Salvation is deliverance from the danger the thieves and robbers represent — the danger of being exploited, scattered, destroyed.

"Will go in and out" (eiseleusetai kai exeleusetai). The phrase "going in and going out" is an idiom in Israel's scriptures for the full range of daily life, unhindered movement, and free activity. Numbers 27:17: Moses asks for a leader "who will go out and come in before them, and who will lead them out and bring them in." Deuteronomy 28:6: "Blessed shall you be when you come in, and blessed shall you be when you go out." Psalm 121:8: "The LORD will guard your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forever." The image is of complete freedom of movement under divine protection — the opposite of the confinement the Pharisees imposed through their synagogue expulsion (9:22, 34).

"Find pasture" (nomen heurese). The word nome ("pasture, grazing land") appears in the LXX in Ezekiel 34:14: "I will feed them in good pasture (nome agathe), and their grazing ground (nome) will be on the mountain heights of Israel." The finding of pasture is the fulfillment of the Ezekiel 34 promise: God himself providing what the failed shepherds did not. Psalm 23:2: "He makes me lie down in green pastures."

div.p: "The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy" (ho kleptes ouk erchetai ei me hina klepse kai thyse kai apolese). Three verbs define the thief's purpose: to steal (klepto, to take what is not his), to kill (thyo, literally "to sacrifice, slaughter" — the word carries sacrificial overtones, suggesting that the thief kills the sheep for his own consumption), and to destroy (apollymi, "to destroy, ruin, lose"). The verb apollymi is the same word used throughout the document for perishing (3:16, "should not perish"; 6:12, "that nothing will be lost"; 6:39, "that I lose nothing"). The thief's purpose is the opposite of the shepherd's: the shepherd gives life, the thief takes it. The Pharisees' treatment of the man born blind — using him, interrogating him, expelling him — illustrates the pattern of exploitation that "steal, kill, destroy" describes.

"I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly" (ego elthon hina zoen echosin kai perisson echosin). The contrast between the thief's purpose and Jesus's purpose could not be sharper. The word perisson ("abundantly, more than enough, overflowing") indicates not merely survival but superabundance. This echoes the pattern of Jesus's provision throughout the document: the wine at Cana was abundant (six stone jars, twenty to thirty gallons each, 2:6-7), the bread in chapter 6 left twelve baskets of surplus (6:13), the living water will become "a spring of water springing up to eternal life" (4:14) and "rivers of living water" (7:38). The shepherd does not bring the sheep to a meager existence but to overflowing life. The "life" (zoe) Jesus came to give is the same life that was in the Word from the beginning (1:4), the life the Father has in himself and has granted the Son to have in himself (5:26), the eternal life that is the document's central promise (3:16, 36; 5:24; 6:40, 47, 54).

div.title: Verses 11-18: "I Am the Good Shepherd"
div.p: "I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who is not the owner of the sheep, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them. He flees because he is a hired hand and is not concerned about the sheep. I am the good shepherd, and I know my own and my own know me, even as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and they will become one flock with one shepherd. For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life so that I may take it again. No one has taken it away from me, but I lay it down on my own initiative. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This commandment I received from my Father."

"I am the good shepherd" (ego eimi ho poimen ho kalos). The fourth "I am" statement with a predicate. The adjective kalos means not merely "good" in the sense of competent or adequate but "good" in the sense of noble, beautiful, excellent, ideal — the shepherd who fulfills what a shepherd is supposed to be. The LXX uses kalos to describe what is fitting, right, and pleasing (Genesis 1:31: God saw all that he had made, and it was "very good," kalon lian). The "good shepherd" is the true shepherd, the one who embodies the shepherd-ideal that all others have failed to meet.

The claim, set against the background of Ezekiel 34, is staggering. God declared: "I myself will search for my sheep... I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep" (Ezekiel 34:11, 15). And then: "I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David" (34:23). Jesus claims to be the good shepherd, enacting what God promised to do personally and what God promised to accomplish through the Davidic shepherd-king. The dual claim — shepherd and one with the Father — will become explicit in verse 30.

"The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (ho poimen ho kalos ten psychen autou tithesi hyper ton probaton). The phrase "lays down his life" (ten psychen tithesi) is distinctive. The verb tithemi means "to place, set down, put." It is a deliberate, intentional act — not having life taken but placing it down. The preposition hyper ("for, on behalf of") indicates substitutionary or representative action, the same preposition used in 6:51 ("the bread which I will give for [hyper] the life of the world is my flesh"). The good shepherd does not merely risk his life for the sheep; he lays it down — voluntarily, deliberately, in their place. This is the first explicit statement in the document that Jesus will die for others, though the language has been building: John the Baptist identified him as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (1:29); Jesus spoke of his flesh given "for the life of the world" (6:51); the "lifting up" of 3:14 and 8:28 pointed to the cross. Now the act is described in shepherd terms: the shepherd puts his life between the wolf and the sheep.

"He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who is not the owner of the sheep." The hired hand (misthotos, "one who works for wages") is distinguished from the shepherd by ownership and motivation. The shepherd's sheep are "his own" (idia, vv. 3-4); the hired hand's are not. The hired hand works for pay, not for love of the sheep. This figure directly targets the religious leaders of chapter 9, who treated the flock as a source of their own authority and status, not as a charge entrusted to them by God. The hired hand is not identical to the thief — the thief intends to destroy; the hired hand merely does not care enough to protect. Both fail the sheep, but for different reasons.

"Sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them." The wolf (lykos) is the natural predator of the flock. In Israel's prophetic literature, wolves represent foreign oppressors and corrupt rulers. Ezekiel 22:27: "Her princes within her are like wolves tearing the prey, by shedding blood and destroying lives in order to get dishonest gain." Zephaniah 3:3: "Her judges are wolves of the evening; they leave nothing for the morning." The wolf's two actions — snatching (harpazei) and scattering (skorpizei) — are precisely the actions the Pharisees have performed in chapter 9. They snatched the healed man from Jesus's influence by interrogating and threatening him, and they scattered the flock by making an example of anyone who confessed Jesus (9:22: "the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue"). The hired hand's response — leaving and fleeing — is the abdication of protective responsibility.

The verb harpazei ("snatches") will return in verse 28 ("no one will snatch them out of my hand") and verse 29 ("no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand"). The same verb used for the wolf's predatory action is then used to describe what cannot be done to the sheep under the good shepherd's protection. The wolf snatches; but no one — no wolf, no thief, no robber — can snatch the sheep from the shepherd who has laid down his life for them.

"I am the good shepherd, and I know my own and my own know me, even as the Father knows me and I know the Father." The mutual knowledge between shepherd and sheep is modeled on the mutual knowledge between Father and Son. This is an extraordinary analogy. The intimacy between Jesus and his sheep is compared to the intimacy between Jesus and the Father — the most profound relationship in the document (1:1, "the Word was with God"; 1:18, "the only begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father"). The verb ginosko ("to know") in this document carries the weight of relational, experiential knowledge — not abstract awareness but intimate acquaintance. The knowledge is reciprocal: the shepherd knows the sheep, the sheep know the shepherd. This reciprocity was established in verses 3-5 (the shepherd calls by name; the sheep hear his voice) and is now grounded in the deepest possible reality: the Father-Son relationship.

"I lay down my life for the sheep." The phrase is repeated from verse 11, now in the first person. The emphasis on voluntary self-sacrifice intensifies: the shepherd does not merely protect the sheep while alive; he gives his life as the act of protection itself. The laying down of life is not a regrettable consequence of shepherding but its defining act.

"I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and they will become one flock with one shepherd" (kai alla probata echo ha ouk estin ek tes aules tautes; kakeina dei me agagein, kai tes phones mou akousousin, kai genesontai mia poimne heis poimen). The "other sheep" (alla probata) are distinguished from "this fold" (tes aules tautes). "This fold" is the current enclosure — Israel, specifically the community of Jewish followers. The "other sheep" are those outside this fold who will also hear Jesus's voice and be gathered in. The most natural first-century referent is the Gentile nations. This interpretation is confirmed by the document's own trajectory: in 4:42, Jesus was confessed as "the Savior of the world" (not only of Israel); in 11:52, the author will gloss Caiaphas's prophecy as meaning that Jesus would die "not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad"; in 12:20-24, Greeks come seeking Jesus, and Jesus responds by speaking of his death as the means of bearing "much fruit."
