The verb "I must bring" (dei me agagein) uses the word dei ("it is necessary"), which in this document indicates divine necessity — what the Father's plan requires (3:7, "you must be born again/from above"; 3:14, "the Son of Man must be lifted up"; 4:4, "he had to pass through Samaria"; 9:4, "we must work the works of him who sent me"; 12:34, "the Son of Man must be lifted up"). The gathering of the other sheep is not optional but is part of the Father's determined plan.

The promise is: "they will hear my voice" (tes phones mou akousousin) — future tense, a certainty, not merely a hope. And the result: "one flock, one shepherd" (mia poimne, heis poimen). The background is Ezekiel 37:24: "My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd (poimen heis)." The LXX of Ezekiel 37:24 uses the same phrase. The "one flock" also recalls Ezekiel 37:15-23, where God promises to unite the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah into one nation with one king: "I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king shall be king for all of them; and they will no longer be two nations and no longer be divided into two kingdoms" (37:22). The scope is now broader than the reunion of Israel's divided kingdoms; it encompasses the gathering of all God's scattered children — Jewish and Gentile — into one flock under one shepherd.

"For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life so that I may take it again" (dia touto me ho pater agapai hoti ego tithemi ten psychen mou, hina palin labo auten). The Father's love for the Son is not caused by the act of self-sacrifice (the Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world, 17:24), but the voluntary laying down of life is identified as a reason for the Father's love. The phrase "so that I may take it again" (hina palin labo auten) introduces the resurrection: the purpose of laying down life is not extinction but recovery — death is the means of obtaining life again. The death is purposeful, not tragic. It serves the "taking again" — the resurrection — which is the gateway to the glorification the author will develop in chapters 12-17.

"No one has taken it away from me, but I lay it down on my own initiative" (oudeis eirei auten ap' emou, all' ego tithemi auten ap' emautou). The verb airo ("to take, take away, remove") is present tense: "no one takes it from me." Even in the events of his arrest and execution, no one is the effective agent of Jesus's death except Jesus himself. The soldiers, the high priest, Pilate — none of them can take his life. He places it down on his own initiative (ap' emautou, "from myself"). This statement will govern the reader's understanding of the passion narrative: when Jesus is arrested in the garden and the soldiers fall back at his "I am" (18:6), when he tells Pilate "You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above" (19:11), when he declares "It is finished" and "gives up" his spirit (19:30) — at every point, the passion is Jesus's deliberate act, not his defeat.

"I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again" (exousian echo theinai auten, kai exousian echo palin labein auten). The word exousia ("authority, right, power") establishes that both the dying and the rising are within Jesus's legitimate power. The authority to lay down life echoes 5:26-27: "He gave to the Son also to have life in himself; and he gave him authority (exousian) to execute judgment." The authority to take it up again is the authority over death that 5:21 claimed: "For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he wishes." Both authorities — over death and over resurrection — are exercised in the single act of the shepherd laying down his life for the sheep and taking it up again.

"This commandment I received from my Father" (tauten ten entolen elabon para tou patros mou). The word entole ("commandment") grounds the entire self-sacrifice in the Father's will, not in Jesus's independent decision. The death is voluntary (Jesus lays it down of his own initiative) and commanded (the Father has given this commandment). The two are not contradictory: Jesus's initiative and the Father's command are perfectly aligned because the Son does only what the Father wills (5:19, 30; 6:38; 8:29). The commandment to die and rise is the mission itself — the reason the Father sent the Son (3:16-17). The shepherd's death is not a tragic accident or a human overreach; it is the Father's plan, executed by the Son in perfect freedom.

div.title: Verses 19-21: Division Again
div.p: "A division occurred again among the Jews because of these words. Many of them were saying, 'He has a demon and is insane. Why do you listen to him?' Others were saying, 'These are not the sayings of one demon-possessed. A demon cannot open the eyes of the blind, can he?'"

"A division occurred again" (schisma palin egeneto en tois Ioudaiois). The word schisma ("division, split") appeared previously in 7:43 (at the Feast of Tabernacles) and 9:16 (among the Pharisees over the blind man's healing). The pattern is consistent throughout the document: Jesus's words and works produce division, not consensus. The light separates those who come to it from those who flee (3:19-21). The shepherd's voice distinguishes those who hear from those who do not (10:3-5).

"He has a demon and is insane" (daimonion echei kai mainetai). The charge of demonic possession appeared in 7:20 ("You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?") and 8:48 ("Do we not say rightly that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?") and 8:52 ("Now we know that you have a demon"). The accusation is the opponents' explanation for speech they cannot comprehend: if Jesus's words are beyond their categories, the source must be demonic. The addition of "insane" (mainetai, "he is mad, raving") intensifies the dismissal — not merely deceived but deranged. The irony is thick: the one through whom all things were made (1:3), who carries life in himself (1:4), who speaks the Father's words (3:34), is accused of madness and demonic influence.

"These are not the sayings of one demon-possessed. A demon cannot open the eyes of the blind, can he?" The defense comes not from Jesus but from the crowd itself. Their reasoning is empirical: the signs — specifically the healing of the man born blind from chapter 9 — are evidence that Jesus is not demonized. A demon destroys; it does not heal. The question "A demon cannot open the eyes of the blind, can he?" (me daimonion dynatai typhlon ophthalmous anoixai) expects a negative answer. The sign carries its own testimonial force: the work testifies to the worker's identity, as Jesus argued in 5:36 ("the works which the Father has given me to accomplish — the very works that I do — testify about me, that the Father has sent me"). The healing of the blind was understood in Israel's prophetic tradition as a sign of the messianic age: Isaiah 29:18, "On that day the deaf will hear words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind will see." Isaiah 35:5, "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped." Isaiah 42:7, describing the servant of the LORD: "to open blind eyes, to bring out prisoners from the dungeon." The opening of blind eyes was God's own promised work, and no demon performs God's work.

div.title: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah): Background for Verses 22-39
div.p: The narrative now advances to a new setting: the Feast of Dedication in winter. The background of this festival is essential for hearing what follows.

The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah, from the Hebrew chanukah, "dedication") commemorated the rededication of the temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BCE, after Antiochus IV Epiphanes had desecrated it by erecting an altar to Zeus in the holy place and sacrificing swine on the altar (1 Maccabees 1:54-59, 4:36-59; 2 Maccabees 10:1-8). The Maccabean revolt restored Jewish worship and political independence. The festival lasted eight days and was celebrated with lights (Josephus calls it "the festival of lights," Antiquities 12.325), singing the Hallel psalms, and communal rejoicing.
Several features of Hanukkah are relevant to the confrontation in verses 22-39:

list.item: The temple is central. Hanukkah celebrates the temple's purification and rededication. Jesus is in the temple during this festival (v. 23), and the question put to him — whether he is the Christ — is asked in the space whose dedication the festival celebrates. Jesus has already claimed that his body is the true temple (2:19-21). The festival celebrates the dedication of a building; Jesus claims to be the reality that the building represented.

The question of legitimate authority. The Maccabees fought against foreign rulers who had profaned God's house and installed false worship. The festival thus celebrated the overthrow of illegitimate authority and the restoration of legitimate worship. Jesus has just been discussing legitimate and illegitimate shepherds. The Pharisees and chief priests claim legitimate authority over Israel's worship; Jesus's discourse has declared them thieves and hired hands.

The concept of consecration/dedication. The Hebrew root chanakh and the Greek verb egkainizo ("to dedicate, renew, consecrate") describe the setting apart of something for God's use. Jesus will use related language in verse 36: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated (hegiasen) and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming'?" The verb hagiazo ("to consecrate, make holy, sanctify") applies to Jesus what Hanukkah celebrates for the temple: Jesus is the one the Father has consecrated. The festival celebrates the dedication of a temple; Jesus claims to be the one whom God himself has dedicated.

div.title: Verses 22-30: "My Sheep Hear My Voice" and "I and the Father Are One"
div.p: "At that time the Feast of the Dedication took place at Jerusalem; it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple in the portico of Solomon. The Jews then gathered around him, and were saying to him, 'How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.' Jesus answered them, 'I told you, and you do not believe; the works that I do in my Father's name, these testify of me. But you do not believe because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all; and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand. I and the Father are one.'"

"It was winter" (cheimōn en). The detail is unusual for this author, who typically marks time by festivals rather than seasons. The mention of winter may be atmospheric — the cold, inhospitable season contrasting with the hostility Jesus faces — or it may be chronological, indicating that several months have elapsed since the Tabernacles setting of chapters 7-8 (Tabernacles falls in September-October; Hanukkah falls in November-December). The narrative has jumped forward in time; the shepherd discourse of verses 1-18 (which continued the chapter 9 confrontation at Tabernacles) is now followed by a scene set at a later festival.

"Jesus was walking in the temple in the portico of Solomon" (periepatei ho Iesous en to hiero en te stoa tou Solomonos). Solomon's Colonnade was a covered portico along the eastern side of the temple mount, believed to be a remnant of Solomon's original temple. It was a natural gathering place for teaching and discussion (Acts 3:11, 5:12). Jesus walks in the place associated with the king who built the first temple — the king who was David's son and shepherd of Israel. The setting places Jesus in the space of the Davidic shepherd-king during the festival that celebrates the temple's rededication.

"How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly" (heos pote ten psychen hemon aireis; ei sy ei ho Christos, eipe hemin parresia). The demand for a plain declaration (parresia, "openly, boldly, without figures") echoes the frustration of 7:26 ("The rulers do not really know that this is the Christ, do they?") and 8:25 ("Who are you?"). The question sounds reasonable: just tell us directly. But Jesus's response reveals why a plain answer would not accomplish what they expect. The problem is not that Jesus has been unclear; the problem is that they have not believed what he has already said and done.

"I told you, and you do not believe; the works that I do in my Father's name, these testify of me." Jesus's answer is: the declaration has already been made — through his works. The works (erga) testify (martyrousin). This is the same argument from 5:36: "the very works that I do testify about me, that the Father has sent me." The healing at the pool, the feeding of the multitude, the opening of the blind man's eyes — each is a declaration made in the Father's name. The authorities' demand for a plain verbal statement ignores the testimony of the works, which is the testimony of the Father himself (5:37). The demand for more words is an evasion: they have not believed the evidence already given.

"But you do not believe because you are not of my sheep" (alla hymeis ou pisteuete, hoti ouk este ek ton probaton ton emon). This is a diagnostic statement, not a prescriptive one. Jesus does not say "you cannot become my sheep" or "you are excluded from ever becoming my sheep." He says that their current unbelief is explained by the fact that they are not, at this moment, acting as his sheep — hearing his voice, following him. The phrase "not of my sheep" (ouk este ek ton probaton ton emon) describes their present condition and identifies it as the reason for their unbelief. In the same way, 8:47 said: "He who is of God hears the words of God; for this reason you do not hear them, because you are not of God." The diagnosis works from the symptom (you do not believe) to the condition (you are not of my sheep). Their failure to hear and follow is what makes them not-sheep, and their not-being-sheep is what explains their failure to believe. The two are mutually defining: sheep hear; these do not hear; therefore they are not sheep.

This must be read alongside the author's earlier statements about how one becomes "of God" or becomes one of Jesus's sheep. In 6:45, the mechanism is hearing and learning from the Father: "Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father, comes to me." In 7:17, the prerequisite is willingness: "If anyone is willing to do his will, he will know of the teaching." In 8:47, the condition is being "of God" — oriented toward God. The Pharisees' exclusion from the sheep is not an arbitrary divine decree but the consequence of their own refusal to hear, learn, and follow. The man born blind demonstrated that a person can move from outside to inside — from not knowing Jesus (9:12, "I do not know") to worshiping him (9:38). The Pharisees' present condition is self-imposed: they claim to see but refuse to look (9:41).

"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me" (ta probata ta ema tes phones mou akouousin, kago ginosko auta, kai akolouthousin moi). Three present-tense verbs describe the sheep: they hear (akouousin), they are known by the shepherd (ginosko), and they follow (akolouthousin). The present tense is consistent and significant. These are not past-tense accomplishments but ongoing activities. The sheep are defined by what they are currently doing: hearing, being known, following. This matches the present-tense pattern throughout the document: "the one believing" (ho pisteuon, 3:16, 18, 36; 6:35, 40, 47), "the one coming" (ho erchomenos, 6:35), "the one eating" (ho trogon, 6:54, 56, 57, 58). The condition described is an ongoing state, not a completed transaction. The sheep's identity is constituted by their continuous activity of hearing and following.

"And I give them eternal life, and they will never perish" (kago didomi autois zoen aionion, kai ou me apolontai eis ton aiona). The verb "give" (didomi) is present tense — "I am giving" them eternal life. This is the life the document has been describing since the prologue: the life that was in the Word (1:4), the eternal life promised to those who believe (3:16, 36; 5:24; 6:40, 47, 54). The promise "they will never perish" (ou me apolontai) uses the double negative ou me (the strongest negation in Greek) with the verb apollymi ("to perish, be destroyed, be lost"). This is the same verb used in 3:16 ("should not perish but have eternal life") and in 6:39 ("that I lose nothing"). The promise is emphatic: these sheep will not perish.

But the identity of "these sheep" must be determined by the preceding verse: they are the ones hearing, being known, and following. The promise of not perishing is made to the sheep in their capacity as hearing-and-following sheep. The text does not address what happens if a sheep stops hearing and following — it describes the condition and promise for those who are currently in the described state. This is parallel to 3:16: "everyone who believes [present tense, ho pisteuon] will not perish but have eternal life." The promise is for the one who is believing. The question of whether a person can stop believing — and what happens if they do — is addressed elsewhere in the document (6:66, where disciples who had been following ceased to follow; 15:2, 6, where branches that do not abide are removed).

"And no one will snatch them out of my hand" (kai ouch harpasei tis auta ek tes cheiros mou). The verb harpazo ("to snatch, seize, take by force") returns from verse 12, where the wolf "snatches" the sheep, and from 6:15, where the crowd tried to "take Jesus by force" to make him king. The statement addresses external threats: no thief, no wolf, no hired hand, no hostile authority can forcibly remove the sheep from the shepherd's grasp. The hand (cheir) represents power and protective authority. In the LXX, "the hand of the LORD" is the standard idiom for God's saving power: Deuteronomy 33:3, "Indeed, all your holy ones are in your hand" (en te cheiri sou); Isaiah 49:16, "Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands"; Psalm 95:7 (LXX 94:7), "For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand" — a text that combines the shepherd-sheep image with the hand image in the same verse.

The promise concerns external predation. The wolf snatches (v. 12), but no one can snatch from Jesus's hand. The thieves steal, kill, and destroy (v. 10), but they cannot overcome the shepherd who has laid down his life. The assurance is that no outside force can separate the sheep from the shepherd's protection. What the text does not address is the sheep's own choice to leave — to stop hearing, stop following, walk away. The document has already demonstrated that disciples can do precisely this (6:66: "many of his disciples withdrew and were not walking with him anymore"). The departure in 6:66 was not a snatching by a wolf but a voluntary turning back. The promise of verse 28 protects against the wolf; it does not address the sheep that wanders. This is consistent with the Ezekiel 34 background, which distinguishes between threats from outside the flock (wolves, bears, lions) and judgment within the flock itself (Ezekiel 34:17-22: God judges "between sheep and sheep, between the rams and the male goats").

"My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all; and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand" (ho pater mou ho dedoken moi panton meizon estin, kai oudeis dynatai harpazein ek tes cheiros tou patros). The protective assurance is now doubled: the sheep are in Jesus's hand (v. 28) and in the Father's hand (v. 29). The Father "who has given them to me" echoes the giving language of 6:37 ("All that the Father gives me will come to me") and 6:39 ("of all that he has given me I lose nothing"). The Father's role is the giving; the Son's role is the receiving and keeping. The Father is "greater than all" (panton meizon) — no force in the universe exceeds the Father's power. If the sheep are in the Father's hand, no external agent can extract them. The double assurance — Jesus's hand and the Father's hand — prepares for the next statement, which explains why these two hands provide a single, unified protection.
"I and the Father are one" (ego kai ho pater hen esmen). This is the climactic declaration of the passage, and its meaning must be determined by the author's own usage and by the immediate context.

The word "one" (hen) is neuter, not masculine (heis). If Jesus had said ego kai ho pater heis esmen ("I and the Father are one person"), it would be a claim to be the same individual as the Father. But hen (neuter) means "one thing" — one in nature, purpose, will, and action. The distinction between Father and Son is maintained throughout the document: the Son is sent by the Father (3:17, 5:36, 6:57, 7:29, 8:42, 10:36), does the Father's will (4:34, 5:30, 6:38), speaks the Father's words (3:34, 7:16, 8:28, 12:49-50), and returns to the Father (13:1, 14:12, 16:28, 20:17). The Father and Son are not interchangeable; they are one in the shared purpose, authority, and protective power that the shepherd discourse has been describing. What the Father does, the Son does (5:19). The Father's hand and the Son's hand are not two separate protections but one unified custody, because the Father and the Son are one in their shepherding of the flock.

The Ezekiel 34 background provides the scriptural foundation: God promised both that "I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep" (34:15) and that "I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David" (34:23). The two promises are not in tension because the Davidic shepherd exercises God's own shepherding. Jesus's declaration "I and the Father are one" is the fulfillment of both promises simultaneously: the shepherd is the Davidic king, and the Davidic king is one with God in the act of shepherding. This is not a philosophical assertion about the metaphysics of the divine nature but a functional declaration about the unity of purpose and power between Father and Son in the act of protecting and giving life to the sheep.

div.title: Verses 31-39: The Stoning Attempt and the Argument from Psalm 82
div.p: "The Jews picked up stones again to stone him. Jesus answered them, 'I showed you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you stoning me?' The Jews answered him, 'For a good work we do not stone you, but for blasphemy; and because you, being a man, make yourself God.' Jesus answered them, 'Has it not been written in your Law, "I said, you are gods"? If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture cannot be broken), do you say of him, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, "You are blaspheming," because I said, "I am the Son of God"? If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, though you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.' Therefore they were seeking again to seize him, and he eluded their grasp."

"The Jews picked up stones again to stone him." The word "again" (palin) connects this to 8:59, where the authorities took up stones after Jesus's declaration "Before Abraham was, I am." The escalation is consistent: the claims Jesus makes produce the charge of blasphemy, which under Jewish law warranted stoning (Leviticus 24:16: "whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him"). The pattern is the same in both cases: Jesus makes a statement that the authorities hear as a claim to divinity; they respond with lethal force.

"I showed you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you stoning me?" Jesus's response redirects the conversation from the verbal claim ("I and the Father are one") to the visible evidence (the works). The adjective "good" (kala) uses the same word as "good shepherd" (kalos) — these are noble, excellent, beautiful works. They are "from the Father" (ek tou patros) — their origin is divine. Jesus's question forces the opponents to evaluate what they have seen rather than react to what they have heard.

"For a good work we do not stone you, but for blasphemy; and because you, being a man, make yourself God." The authorities articulate their understanding of the offense: Jesus, a human being, claims to be God. They heard "I and the Father are one" as a claim to deity. Their reading is not incorrect — Jesus has been claiming functions that belong to God alone (giving life, judging, forgiving sins, receiving worship) — but their response assumes that no human being could legitimately bear these functions. They separate "being a man" from "being God" as mutually exclusive categories. The entire thrust of the prologue ("the Word became flesh," 1:14) challenges this assumption: the Word was God (1:1) and became flesh (1:14). The categories the authorities treat as exclusive are, in this author's presentation, united in a single person.

"Has it not been written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'?" Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6 (LXX 81:6). The psalm depicts God standing in the divine assembly (en synagoge theon, "in the assembly of the gods") and judging those who judge Israel unjustly. God addresses these judges: "I said, 'You are gods (theoi este), and all of you are sons of the Most High (huioi hypsistou pantes).' Nevertheless you will die like men and fall like one of the princes" (Psalm 82:6-7). The "gods" (theoi/elohim) of Psalm 82 are human rulers or judges of Israel who have been entrusted with God's authority to administer justice. They are called "gods" because they exercise a divine function — judging — on God's behalf. But they will die like men because they have exercised this function corruptly.

The phrase "your Law" (en to nomo hymon) extends the term "Law" beyond the Pentateuch to include the Psalms, which is consistent with broader first-century usage where "the Law" could designate the entire scriptures (cf. 12:34, 15:25, where Jesus cites Psalms as "the Law").

"If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture cannot be broken)." The argument is qal va-homer — from the lesser to the greater, the same form of reasoning Jesus used in 7:23 (the circumcision-versus-healing argument). The lesser case: the scriptures applied the title "gods" (theoi) to human judges who received God's word. If the scripture itself calls mere humans "gods" in a limited, derivative sense — humans to whom the word of God came — then the greater case: how can it be blasphemy for the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world to say "I am the Son of God"?

The parenthetical "the Scripture cannot be broken" (ou dynatai lythenai he graphe) is a striking affirmation of scriptural authority. The verb lyo ("to loose, break, dissolve") means that scripture's declarations cannot be nullified or set aside. If Psalm 82 called human judges "gods," that verdict stands and cannot be overturned. Jesus's argument builds on his opponents' own authority — the inviolability of scripture — to establish that his claim is, at the very least, consistent with scriptural precedent.
"Do you say of him, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?" Two elements require attention:

list.item: "Whom the Father sanctified" (hon ho pater hegiasen). The verb hagiazo ("to sanctify, consecrate, set apart, dedicate") connects directly to the festival context. The Feast of Dedication celebrates the consecration (chanukah) of the temple. Jesus claims that the Father has consecrated him. He is the dedicated one — not a building but a person, set apart by God for God's purpose. The temple was dedicated for God's presence to dwell there; Jesus, in whom "all the fullness of deity" tabernacles (to use later apostolic language, though this document makes the point in its own way: "the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us," 1:14), is the reality the temple anticipated.

"I am the Son of God" (huios tou theou eimi). Jesus frames his claim not as "I am God" but as "I am the Son of God." The title "Son of God" (huios tou theou) has appeared throughout the document: the Baptist's testimony (1:34), Nathanael's confession (1:49), Jesus's own self-reference through the discourse of chapter 5 (5:19-26), and Martha's coming confession (11:27). The title, in its scriptural background, applies to the Davidic king. 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me." Psalm 2:7: "He said to me, 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you.'" Psalm 89:26-27: "He will cry to me, 'You are my Father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.' I also shall make him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth." The title "Son of God" carries royal-messianic significance: the Davidic king is God's son in a special, covenantal sense. Jesus's argument is that if human judges can be called "gods" by scripture, how much more can the one whom God consecrated and sent claim the title "Son of God."

div.p: The argument does not retreat from the earlier claim ("I and the Father are one"); it reframes it in terms the opponents should be able to accept. If scripture's own usage permits calling human judges "gods," the threshold for blasphemy is higher than the opponents assume. And the one making the claim is not a mere human judge but the one uniquely consecrated and sent by the Father.

"If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, though you do not believe me, believe the works." Jesus offers an empirical test: judge by the works. This is the same argument from 5:36 and 10:25. If the works do not match the Father's character, reject the claim. But if they do — if the healing of the paralyzed, the feeding of the hungry, the opening of the blind — match what God himself promised to do (Isaiah 35:5-6, Ezekiel 34:16), then let the works settle the question, even if the verbal claim seems incredible.

"So that you may know and understand that the Father is in me, and I in the Father" (hina gnote kai ginoskete hoti en emoi ho pater kago en to patri). The mutual indwelling — "the Father in me, I in the Father" — restates "I and the Father are one" in relational rather than numerical terms. The preposition en ("in") describes interpenetration, mutual presence: the Father's presence in Jesus and Jesus's presence in the Father. This is not the language of identity (they are the same person) but of inseparability (each is present in the other). The same mutual-indwelling language will be extended to the relationship between Jesus and believers in 14:20 ("You will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you") and 15:4 ("Abide in me, and I in you"). The intimacy that defines the Father-Son relationship is the model and basis for the shepherd-sheep relationship.

"Therefore they were seeking again to seize him, and he eluded their grasp." The verb ezercheto ("he went out") indicates departure; the phrase exelthen ek tes cheiros auton ("he eluded their grasp," literally "he went out from their hand") is rich in irony. The opponents cannot even keep hold of Jesus's physical person, let alone snatch his sheep from his hand (v. 28). Their hand cannot hold him; his hand cannot be overcome. The divine sovereignty over the "hour" continues to operate: they cannot arrest him because the time has not yet arrived (as in 7:30, 44; 8:20, 59).

div.title: Verses 40-42: Beyond the Jordan
div.p: "And he went away again beyond the Jordan to the place where John was first baptizing, and he was staying there. Many came to him and were saying, 'While John performed no sign, yet everything John said about this man was true.' Many believed in him there."

"Beyond the Jordan to the place where John was first baptizing." The geographic detail creates an inclusio — a literary bracket. The document began with John's testimony at this same location: "These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing" (1:28). The public ministry that began at the Jordan now pauses at the Jordan. The circle is closing. From here, the narrative will move to Bethany near Jerusalem for the raising of Lazarus (chapter 11), and from Lazarus's raising to the final Passover.

The return to the baptismal site recalls the testimony John gave there: "Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (1:29), "I have seen the Spirit descending as a dove out of heaven, and he remained upon him" (1:32), "This is the Son of God" (1:34). These declarations — lamb, Spirit-bearer, Son of God — have now been filled with content through ten chapters of narrative. The reader who returns to the Jordan with Jesus hears John's earlier words with the depth the intervening narrative has provided.

"John performed no sign, yet everything John said about this man was true." The crowd's observation is significant for the author's theology of witness. John's role was testimony, not signs (1:7: "He came as a witness, to testify about the light"). He was the voice, not the light (1:8, 1:23). Yet his testimony is vindicated by the signs Jesus has performed. The crowd recognizes the alignment: what John said (testimony) matches what Jesus has done (works). The two forms of witness — verbal and visible — converge. John's words were true; Jesus's works confirm them. The author's careful presentation of John as a witness rather than a rival (1:8, 1:15, 1:20, 1:27, 3:28-30) reaches its conclusion here: the witness's testimony has been validated by the one he testified about.

"Many believed in him there" (kai polloi episteusan eis auton ekei). The aorist episteusan ("believed") records the response at that location. Beyond the Jordan, away from the hostile Jerusalem authorities, in the place where John first testified, many come to belief. The pattern is consistent with the document's geography: belief flourishes away from the center of institutional power. The Samaritans believed (4:39-41), the Galilean crowd initially followed (6:2), and now the Transjordanians believe. Jerusalem remains the place of confrontation and rejection. The contrast reinforces Ezekiel 34's indictment: the failure is in the shepherds, not in the sheep. When the sheep hear the shepherd's voice without the interference of the hired hands and thieves, many respond.

list.item: The chapter is an interpretive commentary on the events of chapter 9, cast in the language of Ezekiel 34. There is no scene break between 9:41 and 10:1. Jesus addresses the Pharisees who have just expelled the healed man and tells them what their action reveals: they are not shepherds but thieves and hired hands. The shepherd discourse is not an abstract teaching about pastoral ministry; it is a prophetic indictment of Israel's current leaders, drawing on Ezekiel's indictment of Israel's historical leaders. The Pharisees have "scattered the sheep" (by expelling the believing man), "not healed the sick" (by refusing to acknowledge the sign), and "fed themselves" (by preserving their authority at the expense of the flock). God's response in Ezekiel was to declare: "I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep." Jesus now enacts that declaration.

The chapter contains two "I am" statements with predicates — the door (vv. 7, 9) and the good shepherd (vv. 11, 14) — both drawn from the same image. As the door, Jesus is the point of legitimate access to the flock and the barrier against illegitimate entry. As the good shepherd, Jesus is the one who calls, knows, leads, protects, and dies for the sheep. The two identifications are complementary: Jesus is both the means of entry and the one who enters. The dual imagery ensures that no aspect of the flock's protection and provision falls outside his role.

The chapter's central claim is that Jesus is the fulfillment of Ezekiel 34's double promise: God shepherding Israel himself and raising up a Davidic shepherd-king. The declaration "I and the Father are one" (v. 30) is the claim that these two promises converge in a single person. The Father's hand and the Son's hand are one protective custody because the Father and the Son are one in purpose, authority, and action. This does not erase the distinction between Father and Son (the Son is sent, the Son obeys, the Son does the Father's will) but declares their operational unity in the work of shepherding.

The "no one will snatch them" promise (vv. 28-29) addresses external threats, not the sheep's own capacity to depart. The language of "snatching" (harpazo) comes from the wolf's predatory action in verse 12 and from the thieves and robbers of verses 1 and 10. No external force — no wolf, no thief, no hostile authority — can forcibly remove the sheep from the shepherd's protective hand. The document has already shown that followers can voluntarily depart (6:66, "many of his disciples withdrew and were not walking with him anymore"), and this chapter's own imagery depends on the sheep's voluntary activity of hearing and following (vv. 4-5, 27). The promise protects against predation; it does not eliminate the sheep's own agency. The Ezekiel 34 background itself includes judgment between sheep within the flock (34:17-22), indicating that not all within the flock remain faithful.

The present-tense grammar of believing, hearing, and following continues the pattern established throughout the document. In verse 27, "my sheep hear" (akouousin, present), "I know them" (ginosko, present), "they follow" (akolouthousin, present). In verse 28, "I give them" (didomi, present) eternal life. The sheep are defined by their ongoing activity, not by a past-tense credential. This matches "the one believing" (ho pisteuon, 3:16, 36; 6:35, 40, 47), "the one coming" (ho erchomenos, 6:35), "the one eating" (ho trogon, 6:54, 56-58). The promises attach to persons in the continuous state of hearing, following, and believing. The chapter does not describe a category of persons who heard once, followed once, and are now guaranteed safety regardless of their ongoing relationship to the shepherd. It describes persons whose identity is constituted by their current posture of responsiveness to the shepherd's voice.

The Psalm 82 argument (vv. 34-36) is a qal va-homer from within the opponents' own scriptures. If scripture calls human judges "gods" because they received God's word and exercised God's delegated authority, then the one whom the Father uniquely consecrated and sent into the world has a stronger claim to the title "Son of God" than those judges had to the title "gods." The argument does not retreat from the "I and the Father are one" claim but establishes that the claim is consistent with scriptural precedent and should be evaluated by the evidence of the works, not dismissed reflexively as blasphemy.

The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) provides the theological backdrop for the second half of the chapter. The festival celebrates the consecration of the temple; Jesus claims to be the one the Father has consecrated (v. 36, hegiasen). The temple was the place of God's dwelling; Jesus is the one in whom the Father dwells ("the Father is in me, and I in the Father," v. 38; "the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us," 1:14). The festival celebrates the overthrow of illegitimate rulers who profaned God's house; the shepherd discourse has just declared that Israel's current leaders are thieves and hired hands who exploit the flock. The convergence of the festival's themes and Jesus's claims is deliberate: the true dedication is not a building but a person, and the true restoration of Israel is not a military victory over Seleucids but the arrival of the shepherd God promised through Ezekiel.

The "other sheep" of verse 16 extends the scope of Jesus's mission beyond Israel to the Gentile nations. The promise of "one flock, one shepherd" fulfills Ezekiel 37:24 and anticipates the document's later statements about gathering "the children of God who are scattered abroad" (11:52) and drawing "all people" to himself through his lifting up (12:32). The shepherd's death is not only for "this fold" (Israel) but for the other sheep as well. The scope of the good shepherd's sacrifice is universal, consistent with the Samaritans' confession ("the Savior of the world," 4:42) and the prologue's declaration ("the true light which, coming into the world, enlightens every man," 1:9).

The chapter's argument about Jesus's death as voluntary and commanded culminates in verses 17-18. The shepherd does not die because he is overpowered but because he chooses to lay down his life. No one takes it; he places it down. He has authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This authority comes from the Father's commandment. The death is simultaneously Jesus's free act and the Father's plan. This establishes the interpretive framework for the passion narrative: when Jesus is arrested, tried, and crucified, the reader knows that none of these events escape Jesus's own initiative and authority. The cross is the shepherd's deliberate self-placement between the wolf and the sheep.

The geographic return to the Jordan (vv. 40-42) creates an inclusio with the beginning of the document. The ministry that began with John's testimony at the Jordan reaches a resting point at the same location. The crowd's observation — "everything John said about this man was true" — validates the entire testimony arc of the document. John testified to the Lamb of God, the Spirit-bearer, the Son of God. The intervening narrative has demonstrated each of these identities through signs, discourses, and confrontations. The return to the beginning is also a preparation for the end: from the Jordan, the narrative will move to Bethany, to the raising of Lazarus, to the final Passover, and to the death that the good shepherd has been announcing throughout this chapter. The shepherd who has declared his authority to lay down his life and take it up again is about to exercise that authority.

The chapter completes the confrontation between Jesus and the religious authorities that has been building since chapter 5. The healing at Bethesda (ch. 5) produced the charge of Sabbath-breaking and the intention to kill. The bread-of-life discourse (ch. 6) produced grumbling and mass departure. The Tabernacles confrontation (chs. 7-8) produced attempted stonings and the accusation of demonic possession. The healing of the man born blind (ch. 9) produced expulsion from the synagogue. Now, in chapter 10, Jesus gathers all of this into a single image: the religious leaders are not shepherds but thieves, and the sheep do not recognize their voice. The confrontation will not be resolved by argument but by the events that follow — the raising of Lazarus (ch. 11), which will trigger the decision to kill Jesus (11:47-53), and the passion narrative (chs. 18-19), where the shepherd will lay down his life as he has promised.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 10): Chapter 10 presented Jesus as the good shepherd of Ezekiel 34 — the one whom God promised to raise over Israel after indicting the nation's failed leaders. The chapter opened without a scene break from chapter 9, interpreting the Pharisees' expulsion of the healed blind man as evidence that they are thieves and hired hands, not true shepherds. Jesus declared himself the door of the sheep (10:7, 9) and the good shepherd (10:11, 14), the one who calls his own sheep by name, whose sheep hear his voice and follow him. He announced that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep — voluntarily, deliberately, on his own initiative, with authority both to lay it down and to take it up again (10:17-18). He declared that his sheep will never perish, that no one can snatch them from his hand or from the Father's hand, and that "I and the Father are one" (10:30). The chapter also extended the scope of the shepherd's mission beyond Israel: "I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and they will become one flock with one shepherd" (10:16). At the Feast of Dedication, the authorities demanded a plain declaration of his messiahship, provoked by Jesus's response to attempt stoning a second time (after 8:59), and then attempted to seize him. Jesus withdrew beyond the Jordan to where John had baptized, creating a geographic inclusio with the beginning of his public ministry (1:28). Many believed in him there. The chapter's final word was belief; its sustained argument was that the shepherd's death is not defeat but the deliberate act of the one who has authority over life and death.

What the author argues immediately after (John 12): Chapter 12 opens with Jesus returning to Bethany six days before Passover, where Mary anoints his feet with expensive perfume — an act Jesus interprets as preparation for his burial (12:7). Lazarus is present at the table, a living witness to the power just demonstrated, and the chief priests make plans to kill Lazarus as well because "on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus" (12:10-11). Jesus enters Jerusalem to the acclaim of crowds who specifically cite the raising of Lazarus as the reason for their coming out (12:17-18). The Pharisees say to one another, "You see that you are not doing any good; look, the world has gone after him" (12:19) — a statement immediately followed by Greeks coming to seek Jesus (12:20-21), which fulfills the "other sheep not of this fold" promise of 10:16 and the "gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad" of 11:52. Jesus responds to the Greeks' arrival by declaring that "the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (12:23) and employs the grain-of-wheat image: "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (12:24). The one who raised Lazarus from the dead now announces that he himself must die in order to give life on the largest scale. Chapter 12 thus translates the events of chapter 11 into their consequences: the sign that demonstrated Jesus's power over death precipitates the events that will bring about his own death, which will in turn bring about the universal gathering of life.

How chapter 11 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 10 ended with the shepherd declaring his authority to lay down his life and take it up again. Chapter 11 now demonstrates, in the most dramatic sign yet, that this authority is real: the one who claims power over death raises a man who has been dead four days. The claim is no longer abstract. The shepherd who says he can give life to the dead now does so — publicly, before witnesses, in a village two miles from Jerusalem where the authorities will inevitably hear of it. And the result of this supreme demonstration of life-giving power is the decision to kill Jesus (11:47-53). The chapter thus functions as the hinge of the entire document: it is the climactic sign that proves who Jesus is, and it is the event that sets in motion the passion narrative that will prove what the shepherd meant by "I lay down my life for the sheep." The one who gives life to the dead will be put to death by those who refuse to believe, and that death will itself become the means of giving life to the world.

The chapter also completes a series of sign-and-discourse pairings that have structured the document. In chapter 5, Jesus healed a paralytic and then discoursed on the Son's authority to give life and raise the dead (5:21-29). In chapter 6, Jesus fed the multitude and then discoursed on himself as the bread of life (6:35-58). In chapter 9, Jesus gave sight to the blind man and then discoursed on the good shepherd (10:1-18). Now in chapter 11, the discourse comes first — Martha and Jesus exchange words about resurrection and life (11:21-27) — and then the sign follows (11:38-44). The pattern is inverted: the theological declaration ("I am the resurrection and the life") precedes and governs the interpretation of the act. The reader is told what the sign means before the sign is performed.

div.title: The Lazarus Narrative in Israel's Scriptural Tradition
div.p: Before proceeding to the text, several scriptural precedents must be established, because the author's first-century audience would have heard them resonating throughout the chapter.

list.item: Elijah raises the son of the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:17-24). The child became ill and "there was no breath left in him" (17:17). The widow accused the prophet: "What do I have to do with you, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my iniquity to remembrance and to put my son to death!" (17:18). Elijah stretched himself upon the child three times and cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, I pray you, let this child's life return to him" (17:21). The LORD heard, and "the life of the child returned to him and he revived" (17:22). The widow responded: "Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth" (17:24). The pattern is: death of a loved one, an accusation or reproach directed at the prophet, the prophet's prayer, the raising, and a confession of the prophet's identity. John 11 follows this pattern precisely: Lazarus dies, Martha reproaches Jesus ("if you had been here, my brother would not have died"), Jesus prays to the Father, Lazarus is raised, and the witnesses respond.

Elisha raises the son of the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4:18-37). The child died, and the mother went to the prophet at Mount Carmel and said, "Did I ask for a son from my lord? Did I not say, 'Do not deceive me'?" (4:28). Elisha came to the house, found the child dead, shut the door on the two of them, and prayed to the LORD (4:33). He stretched himself upon the child, and the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (4:35). As with the widow of Zarephath, the elements include: death, the mother's confrontation of the prophet, prayer, and the raising.

Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1-14). God set Ezekiel in a valley full of dry bones and asked, "Son of man, can these bones live?" (37:3). God commanded Ezekiel to prophesy to the bones: "Thus says the Lord GOD to these bones: 'Behold, I will cause breath to enter you that you may come to life'" (37:5). The bones came together, sinews and flesh grew, skin covered them, breath entered, and they stood on their feet as a vast army (37:10). God interpreted the vision: "These bones are the whole house of Israel... Behold, I will open your graves and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD" (37:11-13). The parallels with John 11 are striking: the question of whether the dead can live, the command to the dead to come forth, the response of recognition ("you will know that I am the LORD"), and the connection between raising the dead and the identity of the one who raises them.

Daniel 12:2. "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake, these to everlasting life, but the others to disgrace and everlasting contempt." Martha's statement in 11:24 — "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" — reflects precisely this expectation of a general resurrection at the end of the age. Jesus does not deny this expectation but redefines it: the resurrection is not only a future event but a present person.

Isaiah 25:8 and 26:19. "He will swallow up death for all time, and the Lord GOD will wipe tears from all faces" (25:8). "Your dead will live; their corpses will rise. You who lie in the dust, awake and shout for joy" (26:19). The defeat of death and the raising of the dead are marks of God's own eschatological action. When Jesus raises Lazarus, he performs what Isaiah attributed to God himself.

div.title: Verses 1-4: The Setting and the Purpose Statement
div.p: "Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was the Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick. So the sisters sent word to him, saying, 'Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.' But when Jesus heard this, he said, 'This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified by it.'"

"A certain man was sick, Lazarus of Bethany." The name Lazarus is the Greek form of the Hebrew Eleazar (El'azar), meaning "God has helped" or "God is my help." The name is significant: the man whose name means "God helps" will receive the ultimate divine help — restoration from death. Bethany is identified as "the village of Mary and her sister Martha." This Bethany is near Jerusalem (11:18, "about fifteen stadia," approximately two miles), distinct from the Bethany beyond the Jordan where John baptized (1:28, 10:40). The proximity to Jerusalem is essential to the narrative: the sign will occur close enough to the center of religious authority that its consequences will be immediate and unavoidable.

"It was the Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair." The author identifies Mary by an event that has not yet been narrated in the document — the anointing will occur in 12:1-8. This anticipatory identification suggests that the audience already knows the story, either from oral tradition or from other accounts (a similar anointing appears in the Synoptic traditions, though the details differ). The author uses the anointing as a marker of identity: this Mary is known for this act. The detail that she wiped Jesus's feet with her hair will be narrated in full in 12:3 and connects to the foot-washing of 13:1-17, where Jesus performs the servant's act for his disciples. The anointing foreshadows death and burial; by introducing it here, the author places the entire Lazarus narrative under the shadow of Jesus's own approaching death.

"Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick" (kyrie, ide hon phileis asthenei). The sisters' message does not contain a request. They report a fact: the one you love is sick. The word for love here is phileo ("to love, to have affection for, to be fond of"), denoting personal friendship and attachment. The sisters assume that this information alone — that the one Jesus loves is in danger — will be sufficient. The message appeals to the relationship, not to Jesus's power. It is a statement of confidence: you love him; therefore you will act. The verb asthenei ("is sick, is weak") comes from asthenes ("without strength"), which in the LXX describes both physical illness and broader human frailty.

"This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified by it" (haute he astheneia ouk estin pros thanaton all' hyper tes doxes tou theou, hina doxasthe ho huios tou theou di' autes). Jesus's response echoes his statement in 9:3 about the man born blind: the blindness existed "so that the works of God might be displayed in him." Here the sickness exists "for the glory of God." In both cases, human suffering is interpreted not as punishment but as occasion for divine self-revelation.

The phrase "not to death" (ouk estin pros thanaton) is paradoxical: Lazarus will in fact die. The statement is true at a deeper level — the sickness is not aimed at death as its final destination. Death will occur but will not be the outcome. The outcome is glory. The word doxa ("glory") in this document refers to the visible manifestation of God's character and power. It was used in 2:11 for the sign at Cana: "This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory" (ephanerosen ten doxan autou). The glory Jesus manifested through the signs is the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (17:5). Each sign is a partial unveiling of that glory; the raising of Lazarus will be the most complete unveiling yet.

The phrase "so that the Son of God may be glorified" (hina doxasthe ho huios tou theou) introduces a double meaning. The Son will be glorified through the raising of Lazarus — the sign will reveal his identity and power. But the Son will also be glorified through his own death, which the raising of Lazarus will precipitate. In this author's usage, "glory" and "glorification" consistently point toward the cross as the supreme revelation of God's character: 12:23 ("The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified"), 12:28 ("Father, glorify your name"), 13:31 ("Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him"), 17:1 ("Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that the Son may glorify you"). The glory revealed in raising Lazarus and the glory revealed in Jesus's death are not two different glories but two aspects of the same reality: the life-giving power of the one who lays down his life.

div.title: Verses 5-6: The Deliberate Delay
div.p: "Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So when he heard that he was sick, he then stayed two days longer in the place where he was."

"Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus" (egapa de ho Iesous ten Marthan kai ten adelphen autes kai ton Lazaron). The verb here is agapao, the other Greek word for love, distinct from the phileo used in the sisters' message (v. 3). Whether the author intends a meaningful distinction between the two verbs is debated; in this document, the two seem largely interchangeable (cf. 21:15-17, where both are used in the same exchange between Jesus and Peter). The statement's function in context is to establish a causal connection — or more precisely, to expose the paradox of what follows. Jesus loves this family. And therefore (oun, "so, therefore, accordingly") he stayed two days longer.

"He then stayed two days longer in the place where he was" (tote men emeinen en ho en topo dyo hemeras). The conjunction oun ("so, therefore") connecting Jesus's love to his delay is one of the most jarring transitions in the document. The reader expects: "Jesus loved them, so he immediately went to them." Instead: "Jesus loved them, so he stayed where he was." The delay is deliberate, not accidental. The author presents it as flowing from Jesus's love, not contradicting it. The two-day delay will mean that by the time Jesus arrives, Lazarus will have been in the tomb four days (v. 17). The four-day detail matters: a widespread first-century Jewish belief held that the soul lingered near the body for three days, hoping to return, but departed permanently on the fourth day when the body began to decompose (this belief is attested in later rabbinic sources, including Genesis Rabbah, though the tradition may reflect first-century popular understanding). The delay ensures that no one can claim Lazarus was merely in a coma, merely sleeping, merely revivable by ordinary means. By the fourth day, decomposition has begun (Martha says so explicitly in v. 39: "Lord, by this time there will be a stench"). The delay ensures that the sign will be unambiguous.

The pattern of deliberate delay is established throughout the document. Jesus delays his departure for Galilee (1:43, 2:1-4, where his mother says "they have no wine" and he responds "my hour has not yet come"). He arrives at the pool of Bethesda long after the paralytic has been waiting (5:5, "thirty-eight years"). He delays his departure for the Feast of Tabernacles (7:6-10, "my time is not yet here"). In each case, the delay is not negligence but sovereign timing — Jesus acts at the moment the Father's purpose requires, not at the moment human urgency demands. The delay is itself part of the sign.

div.title: Verses 7-10: The Decision to Return to Judea
div.p: "Then after this he said to the disciples, 'Let us go to Judea again.' The disciples said to him, 'Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?' Jesus answered, 'Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.'"

"Let us go to Judea again." After the two-day delay, Jesus initiates the return. The disciples' reaction — "the Jews were just now seeking to stone you" (10:31, 39) — reveals the danger. The word "again" (palin) recalls the violence of the recent visit. The disciples' protest is reasonable by any human calculation: returning to Judea means returning to lethal hostility.

"Are there not twelve hours in the day?" Jesus's response reframes the question. The issue is not safety but timing. The twelve-hour day is a fixed period; the one who walks during it does not stumble because the light is present. The metaphor operates on two levels. On the surface, it addresses the practical concern: while it is "day" — while Jesus's appointed time of ministry has not ended — he cannot be cut short. The hour of his death is determined by the Father, not by the intentions of the authorities. On the deeper level, the light-darkness language continues the sustained theme from chapters 1, 3, 8, and 9. Jesus is the light of the world (8:12, 9:5), and while the light is in the world, those who walk with it do not stumble. The disciples' fear assumes that the darkness can overcome the light; Jesus's answer states that it cannot (cf. 1:5: "the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it").

"But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him." The warning applies to those who walk without the light — not merely those who walk at nighttime but those who are not oriented toward the light. The phrase "the light is not in him" (to phos ouk estin en auto) distinguishes between the one who carries the light within (who walks without stumbling) and the one who does not (who stumbles). This connects to the judgment language of 3:19-21: those who love darkness rather than light do evil, and those who practice truth come to the light. The disciples are being told: follow me into Judea, because walking with me is walking in the light, regardless of the external danger.

div.title: Verses 11-16: "Lazarus Has Fallen Asleep"
div.p: "This he said, and after that he said to them, 'Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep; but I go, so that I may awaken him out of sleep.' The disciples then said to him, 'Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.' Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he was speaking of literal sleep. So Jesus then said to them plainly, 'Lazarus is dead, and I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe; but let us go to him.' Therefore Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, 'Let us also go, so that we may die with him.'"

"Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep" (Lazaros ho philos hemon kekoimetal). Jesus uses the verb koimaomai ("to fall asleep, to sleep"), a well-attested euphemism for death in both Jewish and Greek usage. In the LXX, the phrase "slept with his fathers" describes the death of kings (1 Kings 2:10, David; 1 Kings 11:43, Solomon; 2 Kings 14:22, Azariah). Daniel 12:2: "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake." The metaphor of sleep for death implies the possibility of waking — which is precisely Jesus's point. He calls Lazarus "our friend" (ho philos hemon), using philos, the noun form of the same verb (phileo) the sisters used in their message. The relationship is personal, not professional. Jesus is going to raise a friend, not perform a clinical demonstration.

"I go, so that I may awaken him out of sleep" (poreuomai hina exypniso auton). The verb exypnizo ("to awaken from sleep") appears only here in the New Testament. The prefix ex- ("out of") combined with hypnos ("sleep") creates a vivid image: to pull someone out of sleep. If death is sleep, then what Jesus intends is to wake Lazarus from death. The confidence of the statement is remarkable: not "I will try to wake him" or "perhaps God will wake him through me" but "I go so that I may wake him." The purpose of the journey is stated as a fact.

"Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover." The disciples' misunderstanding is characteristic of this author's technique. Throughout the document, Jesus speaks on one level and his interlocutors hear on another: Nicodemus misunderstands "born again/from above" as re-entering the womb (3:4), the Samaritan woman misunderstands "living water" as flowing well water (4:11-12), the crowd misunderstands "eat my flesh" as literal cannibalism (6:52). The misunderstandings serve a literary function: they force Jesus to make explicit what was implicit, thereby advancing the reader's understanding. Here the disciples hear "sleep" and think of natural rest that will restore health. Their misunderstanding forces Jesus to speak plainly.
"Lazarus is dead" (Lazaros apethanen). The aorist verb apethanen ("he died") is unambiguous. The euphemism is dropped. The plain statement confirms what "sleep" meant: death.

"And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe" (kai chairo di' hymas, hina pisteusete, hoti ouk emen ekei). Jesus's gladness is not about Lazarus's death but about what the death will make possible. Had Jesus been present, presumably he would have healed Lazarus before death, as the sisters themselves will suggest (vv. 21, 32). A healing would have been a sign, but it would have been the same kind of sign already performed in chapters 4, 5, and 9 — healing the sick. The death of Lazarus creates the occasion for a greater sign: raising the dead. And this greater sign serves a greater purpose: "so that you may believe" (hina pisteusete). The subjunctive pisteusete could be translated "so that you may come to believe" (if they do not yet believe) or "so that you may believe more deeply" (if they already have some level of belief). Given that the disciples have been following Jesus throughout the document, the latter seems more likely: the sign is intended to deepen and solidify their belief, especially in preparation for the crisis that the passion will bring.

"Therefore Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, 'Let us also go, so that we may die with him'" (agomen kai hemeis hina apothanomen met' autou). Thomas (Aramaic for "twin"; Didymus is the Greek equivalent) speaks for the first time in the document. His statement is ambiguous: "die with him" could mean "die with Jesus" (who is walking into lethal danger) or "die with Lazarus" (who is already dead). The more natural reading is "die with Jesus" — Thomas recognizes the danger of returning to Judea and expresses a willingness to share Jesus's fate, even if that fate is death. The statement has a quality of resigned courage — not faith that all will be well, but loyalty that does not demand safety. Thomas's willingness to die with Jesus anticipates the language of the good shepherd discourse: the shepherd lays down his life, and the sheep follow. Thomas follows, even into danger. His statement also carries dramatic irony: when the time for dying with Jesus actually arrives, the disciples will scatter (16:32), and Thomas himself will not believe the resurrection until he sees the wounds (20:24-29). The courage expressed here will not hold.

div.title: Verses 17-20: Arrival at Bethany
div.p: "So when Jesus came, he found that he had already been in the tomb four days. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia off; and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother. Martha therefore, when she heard that Jesus was coming, went to meet him, but Mary stayed at the house."

"He had already been in the tomb four days" (tessaras ede hemeras echonta en to mnemelo). The four-day detail is stated with precision. Combined with the two-day delay (v. 6), the travel time from beyond the Jordan to Bethany (approximately a day's journey), and the time for the message to reach Jesus (approximately a day), the chronology suggests that Lazarus may have died around the time the message was sent — or even before it reached Jesus. If so, Jesus's declaration "this sickness is not to death" (v. 4) was spoken when Lazarus was already dead or dying, making it not a prognosis but a prophetic interpretation: death is not the destination; glory is.

The four days also place the raising beyond any natural explanation. As noted above, the popular belief that the soul departed after three days means that at four days, the death is considered final and irreversible by the standards of the time. Martha's statement in verse 39 — "by this time there will be a stench" — confirms that decomposition is expected to have begun. The sign that follows will not be a resuscitation of the recently dead but a reversal of advanced death.

"About fifteen stadia." Approximately 1.7 miles (2.8 kilometers). The proximity to Jerusalem means that many from the city have come to mourn. These mourners will become witnesses to the sign, and their reports will reach the authorities in Jerusalem almost immediately.

"Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary, to console them." The "Jews" (Ioudaioi) here appear in a neutral or sympathetic role — mourners fulfilling the obligation of consolation. This is one of many instances where the author's use of "the Jews" does not denote hostility but describes the Jewish community of Jerusalem. The practice of communal mourning was well established: visitors would come to the house of the bereaved during the period of sitting shiva (seven days of mourning), to weep with the mourners and offer comfort. The presence of these mourners is essential to the narrative: they provide witnesses for the sign and messengers who will carry the report back to the Pharisees (v. 46).

"Martha therefore, when she heard that Jesus was coming, went to meet him, but Mary stayed at the house." The two sisters respond differently. Martha goes out; Mary stays. The author distinguishes the sisters' temperaments without evaluating either response. Martha's initiative parallels the portrait of her in Luke 10:38-42 as the active, practical one. Mary's remaining at the house is consistent with the custom of mourning — the bereaved sat in the house and received visitors rather than going out. Martha's going out to meet Jesus is an act of initiative that breaks from mourning convention.

div.title: Verses 21-27: Martha's Confession
div.p: "Martha then said to Jesus, 'Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.' Jesus said to her, 'Your brother will rise again.' Martha said to him, 'I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.' Jesus said to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me will live even if he dies, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?' She said to him, 'Yes, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, even he who comes into the world.'"

"Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died" (kyrie, ei es hode ouk an apethanen ho adelphos mou). Martha's statement is a reproach and a confession simultaneously. The reproach: you were absent, and your absence cost my brother his life. The confession: your presence would have been sufficient to prevent death. She believes Jesus could have healed Lazarus had he been there. The conditional sentence (a contrary-to-fact condition using ei with the imperfect and the aorist with an) implies: "you were not here, and therefore he died." The statement limits Jesus's power to physical proximity — a limitation the sign will demolish. Martha does not yet understand that the one who gives life does not need to be physically present to do so (cf. 4:46-54, where Jesus healed the royal official's son from a distance, saying "Go; your son lives," and the child recovered at the moment Jesus spoke).

"Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you" (alla kai nyn oida hoti hosa an aitese ton theon dosei soi ho theos). This statement is harder to interpret. It appears to express an open-ended confidence in Jesus's petition: whatever you ask, God will grant. But does Martha mean that Jesus could ask God to raise Lazarus from the dead? Her subsequent response in verse 24 suggests she does not expect an immediate raising — she deflects to the general resurrection at the last day. The statement may express a hopeful but unfocused faith: I know you have a special relationship with God, and I believe God responds to you, but I do not know what to expect in this specific situation. The faith is real but its object is unclear.

"Your brother will rise again" (anastesetai ho adelphos sou). Jesus's response is deliberately ambiguous. The verb anistemi ("to raise up, to rise again") is used in the LXX and in Jewish discourse for both ordinary rising and eschatological resurrection. Martha hears the familiar theological category: the resurrection on the last day.

"I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" (oida hoti anastesetai en te anastasei en te eschate hemera). Martha's response is theologically correct. She holds the Pharisaic belief in a general, future resurrection of the dead (cf. Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7:9, 14, 23; Acts 23:8, where the Pharisees affirm the resurrection while the Sadducees deny it). Her statement reflects the mainstream of first-century Jewish eschatological expectation: God will raise the dead at the end of the age. She understands resurrection as a doctrine about the future. Jesus is about to redefine it.

"I am the resurrection and the life" (ego eimi he anastasis kai he zoe). This is the fifth "I am" declaration with a predicate in the document (after "bread of life" in 6:35, "light of the world" in 8:12, "the door" in 10:7/9, and "the good shepherd" in 10:11/14). The statement does not deny the future resurrection that Martha confessed. It redefines resurrection from an event to a person. Martha said: "He will rise at the last day" — a statement about a future happening. Jesus says: "I am the resurrection" — a statement about a present reality embodied in a person. The resurrection is not merely something that will happen; it is someone who is here. The future event has entered the present in the person of the one speaking.

The pairing of "the resurrection and the life" (he anastasis kai he zoe) joins two concepts that this document has been developing. Resurrection (anastasis) addresses death — it is the reversal of death, the raising of the dead. Life (zoe) addresses the ongoing condition after death is overcome — not merely resuscitation but the quality of existence that characterizes God himself. In 5:26, "the Father has life in himself, and has granted the Son also to have life in himself." In 1:4, "in him was life, and the life was the light of men." The two terms cover the entire scope of Jesus's claim: he is both the act of overcoming death and the ongoing reality of the life that follows.

"He who believes in me will live even if he dies" (ho pisteuon eis eme kan apotheane zesetai). The first half of the promise addresses physical death. The person who believes in Jesus will die physically (kan apotheane, "even if he dies") but will live (zesetai, future tense). This is the resurrection promise: physical death does not end the life of the one who believes. Lazarus is about to demonstrate this visibly — he died, and he will live again.

"And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (kai pas ho zon kai pisteuon eis eme ou me apotheane eis ton aiona). The second half addresses spiritual reality. The one who "lives and believes" — that is, the one who is presently alive in the sense this document gives to "life" (zoe, the life that comes from God, the eternal life of 3:16, 5:24, 6:47) and who is presently believing — will never die (ou me apotheane, using the emphatic double negative). The phrase eis ton aiona ("into the age, forever") intensifies the negation: such a person will not experience the ultimate death, the death that is separation from God. Physical death is acknowledged (the first clause says "even if he dies"); ultimate death is denied (the second clause says "will never die"). The two clauses are not contradictory but complementary: the believer may die physically but will not die ultimately, because the resurrection and the life is not a future event but a present relationship with the person standing before Martha.

The two present participles — "the one living" (ho zon) and "the one believing" (ho pisteuon) — describe ongoing states, consistent with the present-tense pattern throughout the document. The promise is for the one who is living and believing, not for one who once believed and then stopped. This matches the grammar of 3:16 (ho pisteuon, "the one believing"), 6:35 (ho pisteuon eis eme, "the one believing in me"), 6:54 (ho trogon mou ten sarka kai pinon mou to haima, "the one eating my flesh and drinking my blood"), and 10:27 (ta probata ta ema tes phones mou akouousin, "my sheep hear my voice"). The condition described is continuous.

"Do you believe this?" (pisteueis touto;). Jesus asks Martha directly. The question is not rhetorical; it demands a personal response. The theological discussion about resurrection becomes a personal confrontation: do you believe that I am what I have just claimed to be?

"Yes, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, even he who comes into the world" (nai, kyrie; ego pepisteuka hoti sy ei ho Christos ho huios tou theou ho eis ton kosmon erchomenos). Martha's confession is the fullest christological declaration in the document thus far, rivaling Peter's confession in the Synoptic accounts (Matthew 16:16, Mark 8:29, Luke 9:20) and paralleling Peter's confession within this document itself (6:68-69: "You are the Holy One of God"). Martha's confession contains three titles:

list.item: "The Christ" (ho Christos). The Messiah, the anointed one, the king of David's line whom Israel expected (1:41, 4:25-26, 7:26-27, 31, 41-42).

"The Son of God" (ho huios tou theou). The title that carries both royal-messianic significance (2 Samuel 7:14, Psalm 2:7) and the deeper meaning this document has been developing: the Son who shares the Father's nature, authority, and life-giving power (5:19-26, 10:30, 36).

"He who comes into the world" (ho eis ton kosmon erchomenos). The "coming one" is a messianic designation drawn from Psalm 118:26 (LXX 117:26): "Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD." The phrase "into the world" (eis ton kosmon) connects to the prologue's declaration that the true light "was coming into the world" (1:9) and to Jesus's self-description as the one "whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world" (10:36).

div.p: Martha's confession uses the perfect tense pepisteuka ("I have believed and continue to believe"), indicating a settled, established conviction rather than a spontaneous reaction to the present conversation. Her faith was not generated by Jesus's "I am the resurrection" statement; it preceded it. What she expresses is not new belief but existing belief that has now been given a deeper object. She believed Jesus was the Christ; she is now learning what that means.

div.title: Verses 28-32: Mary Comes to Jesus
