div.p: "When she had said this, she went away and called Mary her sister, saying secretly, 'The Teacher is here and is calling for you.' And when she heard it, she got up quickly and was coming to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha met him. Then the Jews who were with her in the house, and consoling her, when they saw that Mary got up quickly and went out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Therefore, when Mary came where Jesus was, she saw him, and fell at his feet, saying to him, 'Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.'"

"The Teacher is here and is calling for you" (ho didaskalos parestin kai phonei se). Martha calls Jesus "the Teacher" (ho didaskalos), the same title used by the disciples (1:38, where Rabbi is translated "Teacher," and 13:13-14, "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right"). The verb phonei ("calls") echoes the shepherd's calling: in 10:3, the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name" (phonei kat' onoma). Mary is called by name, as a sheep is called by the shepherd.
"She got up quickly and was coming to him." Mary's response is immediate. The adverb tachy ("quickly") conveys urgency.

"Now Jesus had not yet come into the village." Jesus remains outside the village at the point where Martha met him. This geographic detail creates a sequence: Martha went out to meet Jesus, returned to call Mary, and Mary now goes out to the same location. Jesus does not come to the house; the sisters come to him. The one who summons must be sought out.

"The Jews who were with her in the house, and consoling her... followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there." The mourners' assumption is natural: a bereaved woman leaving the house suddenly would be going to the tomb. Their following ensures that they will be present to witness what happens next. The author carefully positions witnesses for the sign.

"Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." Mary repeats Martha's words almost exactly (cf. v. 21). The identical wording suggests either a shared family conviction ("if only he had come sooner") or a set phrase that both sisters had been repeating during the days of mourning. The repetition also invites comparison between the two encounters: Martha's confession led to a theological exchange; Mary's identical words lead in a different direction — to Jesus's emotional response.

div.title: Verses 33-37: Jesus's Response to Grief
div.p: "When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews who came with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in spirit and was troubled, and said, 'Where have you laid him?' They said to him, 'Lord, come and see.' Jesus wept. So the Jews were saying, 'See how he loved him!' But some of them said, 'Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have kept this man also from dying?'"

"He was deeply moved in spirit and was troubled" (enebrimesato to pneumati kai etaraxen heauton). The verb embrimaomai is difficult to translate. In its other uses (Mark 1:43, 14:5; Matthew 9:30), it carries the sense of stern warning or indignation. It is used in the LXX to describe the snorting of horses (a sound associated with anger or agitation). The word does not primarily denote grief or sadness; it denotes agitation, anger, or deep disturbance. Jesus does not merely feel sad; he is stirred to the point of visible turmoil. The question is: at what is this agitation directed?

Several possibilities present themselves from the immediate context. Jesus may be moved by the power of death itself — its hold on the creation, its capacity to break human lives, its domination of the world he came to liberate. He may be responding to the grief of Mary and the mourners — not merely sympathizing with it but being angered by the reality that causes it. He may be responding to the unbelief implied in the mourning: these people weep as though death is final, as though the one who gives life is not standing among them. The text does not specify a single object for the emotion; the breadth of the verb allows all of these to be in play.

"And was troubled" (kai etaraxen heauton). The verb tarasso ("to trouble, agitate, disturb") is used of Jesus in 12:27 ("Now my soul is troubled") and 13:21 ("he was troubled in spirit" when he announced the betrayal). The reflexive heauton ("himself") makes the action deliberate: "he troubled himself." This is consistent with the author's portrait of Jesus as sovereign over his own emotional states, just as he is sovereign over his own death (10:18, "I lay it down on my own initiative"). Even Jesus's grief is a chosen entry into the human condition, not an involuntary reaction.

"Where have you laid him?" The question is not for information — the one who knew Lazarus was dead before the message arrived (v. 4, if the chronology is read this way), who knew Lazarus had "fallen asleep" (v. 11), does not need to ask where the tomb is. The question serves the narrative: it invites the mourners to lead him to the site, making them participants in what is about to happen.

"Jesus wept" (edakrysen ho Iesous). The verb dakryo ("to shed tears") appears only here in the New Testament. It differs from klaio ("to wail, weep loudly"), the verb used for Mary's weeping (v. 33) and the mourners' weeping. Klaio is demonstrative, vocal lamentation; dakryo is the quiet shedding of tears. The shortest verse in many English translations, it is among the most theologically dense. The one who is about to demonstrate absolute authority over death first weeps at its devastation. The one who has declared "I am the resurrection and the life" stands before a tomb and sheds tears. The tears are not evidence that Jesus doubts his power to raise Lazarus; they are evidence that the one who has life in himself enters fully into the grief of those who do not yet see what he sees.

In Israel's scriptures, God's grief over death and suffering is not absent. Isaiah 63:9: "In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them." Judges 10:16: "He could bear the misery of Israel no longer." The God of Israel is not impassive in the face of human suffering. Jesus's tears at the tomb of Lazarus place him in continuity with the God who weeps over the affliction of his people.

"See how he loved him!" The mourners interpret the tears as evidence of love — phileo love, personal attachment, friendship. Their interpretation is correct as far as it goes: Jesus loved Lazarus. But the tears carry more than personal grief; they carry the weight of the one who has life confronting the domain of death.

"Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have kept this man also from dying?" Some of the mourners voice the same question Martha and Mary expressed: if Jesus has power (evidenced by the healing of the blind man, chapter 9), why did he not use it in time? The question assumes that prevention would have been better than cure — that healing Lazarus before death would have been preferable to raising him after death. Jesus's deliberate delay (v. 6) has already answered this question from the reader's perspective: the greater sign requires the greater extremity. But the mourners do not know this yet.

div.title: Verses 38-44: The Raising of Lazarus
div.p: "So Jesus, again being deeply moved within, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone was lying against it. Jesus said, 'Remove the stone.' Martha, the sister of the deceased, said to him, 'Lord, by this time there will be a stench, for he has been dead four days.' Jesus said to her, 'Did I not say to you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?' So they removed the stone. Then Jesus raised his eyes, and said, 'Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me.' When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come forth.' The man who had died came forth, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, 'Unbind him, and let him go.'"

"Again being deeply moved within" (palin embrimomenos en heauto). The same intense emotion from verse 33 recurs as Jesus approaches the tomb. The repetition underscores that what Jesus is about to do is not a dispassionate exercise of power but an act performed in the midst of profound emotional engagement.

"Now it was a cave, and a stone was lying against it." The tomb is described as a cave (spelaion) with a stone placed against the entrance, a common first-century Judean burial arrangement. Rock-cut tombs with rolling stones or blocking stones have been extensively documented in the Jerusalem area. The detail establishes the physical reality of the burial: this is a real tomb, with a real stone, containing a real body.

"Remove the stone" (arate ton lithon). Jesus commands the bystanders to remove the stone. He does not remove it himself. The pattern is consistent with the document: human participation is involved in the divine act. In chapter 2, the servants filled the water jars. In chapter 6, the disciples distributed the bread. In chapter 9, the blind man went and washed. Here, the mourners remove the stone. The human action does not produce the miracle, but the miracle incorporates human cooperation.

"Lord, by this time there will be a stench, for he has been dead four days" (kyrie, ede ozei, tetartaios gar estin). Martha's protest is both practical and theological. Practically: the body has been decomposing for four days; opening the tomb will expose the mourners to the odor of decay. Theologically: the four-day detail confirms that Lazarus is beyond the point of natural recovery. Martha, who had just confessed Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of God" (v. 27), now objects to the very action that will fulfill that confession. Her faith, though genuine, encounters a practical limit when confronted with the reality of decomposition. The gap between theological confession and practical trust is one of the most realistic psychological details in the narrative.

"Did I not say to you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?" Jesus's response recalls verse 4 ("this sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God") and the broader theme of the relationship between believing and seeing in this document. In 2:11, the disciples saw the glory at Cana. In 1:14, the community testified: "We saw his glory." In 12:41, the author will say that Isaiah "saw his glory." The pattern throughout is that the glory of God is visible to those who believe — not that belief produces the glory, but that belief enables the perception of it. Martha is being told: believe, and you will see what God is about to reveal.

"Then Jesus raised his eyes" (eren oun ho Iesous tous ophthalmous ano). The upward gaze is the posture of prayer, directing attention toward God. The gesture is public and visible — the bystanders can see that Jesus is addressing the Father.

"Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me." The prayer is remarkable for what it reveals about the relationship between Jesus and the Father. Several elements deserve attention:

list.item: "I thank you that you have heard me" (eucharisto soi hoti ekousas mou). The aorist ekousas ("you heard") indicates that the hearing has already occurred. Jesus is not making a request; he is thanking the Father for having already heard. This implies that the prayer — whatever its specific content — was offered at some earlier point, perhaps during the two-day delay (v. 6) or in the silent communion between Father and Son that this document presupposes as continuous (5:19-20, 8:29, "He who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him").

"I knew that you always hear me" (ego de edein hoti pantote mou akoueis). The statement goes beyond this single occasion to establish a general principle: the Father always hears the Son. The verb akouo carries the same weight it has carried throughout the shepherd discourse — hearing that leads to response. The Father hears the Son as the sheep hear the shepherd's voice. The relationship of hearing is reciprocal: the Son hears the Father (5:30, "I can do nothing on my own initiative; as I hear, I judge"), and the Father hears the Son. The "always" (pantote) excludes the possibility of refusal or inattention. This distinguishes Jesus from every prophet who preceded him: Elijah prayed and God heard (1 Kings 17:22); Elisha prayed and God heard (2 Kings 4:33); but Jesus declares that God always hears him — not as a special grace but as a permanent condition of their relationship.

"Because of the people standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me" (dia ton ochlon ton periestota eipon, hina pisteusosin hoti sy me apesteilas). The prayer is spoken aloud for the sake of the witnesses. The purpose is not to inform God but to inform the crowd. They need to understand that what is about to happen comes from the Father, through the Son. The sign is not an independent display of Jesus's power but a work performed by the one the Father sent. The phrase "that you sent me" (hoti sy me apesteilas) is the document's central claim about Jesus's identity: he is the sent one, the apostle of the Father (3:17, 34; 5:36, 38; 6:29, 57; 7:29; 8:42; 10:36). The purpose of the sign is to produce belief in this specific claim: Jesus acts on behalf of the Father who sent him.

div.p: "He cried out with a loud voice, 'Lazarus, come forth'" (phone megale ekraugasen, Lazare, deuro exo). The command is issued with a "great voice" (phone megale), a loud cry audible to all present. The volume is deliberate — this is a public act, not a whispered incantation. The command to Lazarus echoes 5:25: "Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live." What was announced in chapter 5 as a coming reality is now enacted: a dead man hears the voice of the Son of God and lives. The "hour that is coming and now is" has arrived at this tomb.

The command also echoes 5:28-29: "Do not marvel at this; for an hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and will come forth" (ekporeusontai). The raising of Lazarus is a preview of the general resurrection. One man in one tomb hears one command and comes out; at the last day, all who are in the tombs will hear the same voice and come out. Lazarus's raising is not the final resurrection but a sign pointing to it — a demonstration, in a single instance, of the power that will eventually operate universally.

The fact that Jesus calls Lazarus by name connects to the shepherd discourse: "He calls his own sheep by name" (10:3). The shepherd's voice, heard and recognized, is what brings life. The dead man, who cannot hear naturally, hears the shepherd's call and responds. The power of the voice overcomes death itself.

"The man who had died came forth, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth" (exelthen ho tethnekos dedemenos tous podas kai tas cheiras keiriais, kai he opsis autou soudario periededeto). The description emphasizes both the reality of the death and the reality of the raising. The man who had died (ho tethnekos, perfect participle, indicating a completed state of death) came forth (exelthen) still bound in burial cloths. The wrappings (keiriai, strips of linen) and the face cloth (soudarion, a cloth for wiping sweat, used to cover the face of the dead) are the physical evidence of death and burial. Lazarus emerges from the tomb in the condition of a corpse — wrapped for burial, bound hand and foot. The raising does not undo the burial procedure; it overcomes the death while leaving the physical evidence of death's reality in place. The wrappings must be removed by human hands; the life was restored by the divine voice.

The face cloth (soudarion) will appear again in 20:7, at the empty tomb of Jesus, where Peter sees "the face-cloth which had been on his head, not lying with the linen wrappings, but rolled up in a place by itself." The contrast is deliberate: Lazarus came out still bound; Jesus's tomb shows the wrappings left behind, neatly arranged. Lazarus was raised to resume mortal life (he would die again); Jesus rose to immortal life and left the trappings of death behind permanently.

"Unbind him, and let him go" (lysate auton kai aphete auton hypagein). Again, Jesus involves human action: the bystanders must unwrap the burial cloths. The raising is Jesus's work; the unbinding is the community's work. The verb lyo ("to loose, unbind, release") is the same verb used in 5:18, where Jesus was accused of "loosing" (breaking) the Sabbath, and in 10:35, where Jesus said "the Scripture cannot be broken" (lythenai). The dead are bound by death; Jesus commands their release. The community participates in the liberation that the shepherd's voice has made possible.

div.title: Verses 45-46: The Division Among Witnesses
div.p: "Therefore many of the Jews who came to Mary, and saw what he had done, believed in him. But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them the things which Jesus had done."

"Many of the Jews... believed in him." The sign produces belief, fulfilling the purpose stated in verse 15 ("so that you may believe") and verse 42 ("so that they may believe that you sent me"). The witnesses saw (theasamenoi, from theaomai, "to behold, to observe carefully" — this is attentive seeing, not a casual glance) what Jesus had done, and they believed. The sign functions as the author stated in 20:30-31: "These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name." The seventh and greatest sign produces faith in those who see it rightly.

"But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them." Not all who witnessed the sign believed. Some became informants. The same event — the raising of a dead man — produces faith in some and hostility-by-proxy in others. The division is consistent with the pattern throughout the document: the light illuminates some and blinds others (9:39); the shepherd's voice is heard by some and not by others (10:26-27). The sign does not compel universal belief; it reveals the existing orientation of the heart. Those who are disposed toward the light come to it; those who are not carry the report to those who oppose the light.

div.title: Verses 47-53: The Council's Decision
div.p: "Therefore the chief priests and the Pharisees convened a council, and were saying, 'What are we doing? For this man is performing many signs. If we let him go on like this, all men will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.' But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, 'You know nothing at all, nor do you take into account that it is expedient for you that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish.' Now he did not say this on his own initiative, but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad. So from that day on they planned together to kill him."

"The chief priests and the Pharisees convened a council" (synegagon oun hoi archiereis kai hoi Pharisaioi synedrion). The two groups that have opposed Jesus throughout the document — the chief priests (Sadducean aristocracy associated with the temple) and the Pharisees (Torah-interpreters associated with the synagogue) — now unite in formal deliberation. The word synedrion ("council, Sanhedrin") refers to the supreme judicial body of the Jewish nation. The raising of Lazarus has escalated the confrontation beyond individual encounters and street-level disputes. The authorities now gather in an official capacity.

"What are we doing? For this man is performing many signs." The question is not about the reality of the signs. The council does not deny that Jesus performs signs; they acknowledge it openly ("this man is performing many signs," polla poiei semeia). The issue is not whether the signs are genuine but what consequences they will have. The authorities' problem is not insufficient evidence but an unwillingness to follow the evidence where it leads. Their concern is political, not theological.

"If we let him go on like this, all men will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." The fear is concrete: popular enthusiasm for Jesus will provoke Roman intervention. "Our place" (hemon ton topon) likely refers to the temple (the "place" par excellence in Jewish usage; cf. Acts 6:13-14, 21:28, where "this place" means the temple, and 2 Maccabees 5:19: "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place, but the place for the sake of the nation"). "Our nation" (to ethnos) refers to the political entity of Judea under Roman tolerance. The authorities fear that a messianic movement — and the signs are generating exactly the kind of popular excitement that Rome watched for — will trigger a military response. Rome had little patience for messianic agitation in the provinces. The fear is not irrational; the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE proved that Roman patience with Jewish agitation had limits. The council's reasoning is political pragmatism: better to suppress one man than to risk the entire nation.

The irony is profound: the authorities fear losing the temple and the nation. Within a generation of this decision, both will be lost. The temple will be destroyed in 70 CE, and the nation will be devastated. The very catastrophe they sought to prevent by eliminating Jesus will occur regardless — not because they killed Jesus but because they rejected the shepherd God sent and continued on the path that led to confrontation with Rome.

"But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year." Caiaphas (Joseph bar Caiaphas) served as high priest from approximately 18-36 CE, the longest tenure of any first-century high priest. The phrase "that year" (tou eniautou ekeinou) does not mean Caiaphas was high priest for only one year (the author repeats the phrase in vv. 51 and 18:13); it identifies the specific year — the year in which these events occurred, the year of Jesus's death. The author marks the year by its high priest, as one might mark a year by a consulate or a kingship.

"You know nothing at all" (hymeis ouk oidate ouden). Caiaphas's contempt for his colleagues is blunt. They are deliberating, weighing options, agonizing over strategy. Caiaphas cuts through the discussion with pragmatic decisiveness.

"It is expedient for you that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish" (sympherei hymin hina heis anthropos apotheane hyper tou laou kai me holon to ethnos apoletai). Caiaphas's statement is pure political calculation: it is better (sympherei, "it is advantageous, profitable, expedient") for one man to die than for the whole nation to be destroyed. The logic is utilitarian: sacrifice the individual to save the collective. The preposition hyper ("for, on behalf of") is the same preposition Jesus used in the good shepherd discourse: "I lay down my life for [hyper] the sheep" (10:11, 15) and in the bread of life discourse: "the bread which I will give for [hyper] the life of the world is my flesh" (6:51). Caiaphas speaks the word hyper in the sense of political expediency; the author hears it in the sense of sacrificial substitution. The high priest says more than he knows.

"Now he did not say this on his own initiative, but being high priest that year, he prophesied" (touto de aph' heautou ouk eipen, alla archiereus on tou eniautou ekeinou epropheteuse). The author's editorial comment is extraordinary. Caiaphas did not speak "from himself" (aph' heautou) — the same phrase used in 10:18, where Jesus said "I lay it [my life] down from myself" (ap' emautou). Jesus acts from his own sovereign initiative; Caiaphas speaks from a source beyond himself, unwittingly. The high priest, by virtue of his office (archiereus on, "being high priest"), prophesied. The role of the high priest in Israel included, in certain traditions, an oracular function — the high priest bore the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:30) and could inquire of the LORD. The author sees in Caiaphas's cynical political calculation a genuine prophetic utterance: Jesus was going to die for the nation.

"And not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad" (kai ouch hyper tou ethnous monon, all' hina kai ta tekna tou theou ta dieskorpismena synagage eis hen). The author extends Caiaphas's prophecy far beyond what the high priest intended. Jesus would die not only for the Jewish nation but to gather God's scattered children into unity. Several phrases require attention:

list.item: "The children of God who are scattered abroad" (ta tekna tou theou ta dieskorpismena). The phrase "children of God" (tekna tou theou) connects to the prologue: "to those who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God" (1:12). The "scattered" children are those who will come to belief but are currently dispersed among the nations — the "other sheep" of 10:16 who are "not of this fold." The verb diaskorpizo ("to scatter, disperse") is used in the LXX for the scattering of Israel among the nations (Deuteronomy 30:3, Ezekiel 34:5-6, Jeremiah 10:21), but here the scope is broader than ethnic Israel. The scattered children include all who will be gathered by the shepherd's voice.

"Gather together into one" (synagage eis hen). The verb synago ("to gather together, to assemble") is the root of "synagogue" (synagoge, "assembly, gathering"). The gathering of the scattered is a central promise of the prophets: Ezekiel 34:13, "I will bring them out from the peoples and gather them from the countries"; Isaiah 43:5-6, "I will bring your offspring from the east, and gather you from the west. I will say to the north, 'Give them up!' and to the south, 'Do not hold them back.' Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the ends of the earth"; Micah 2:12, "I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob, I will surely gather the remnant of Israel." Jesus's death accomplishes the gathering that the prophets promised God would perform. The "one flock, one shepherd" of 10:16 is achieved through the shepherd's death.

div.p: The entire passage is the document's clearest statement of the purpose of Jesus's death. The shepherd does not lay down his life merely as an act of love or courage; he dies to gather the scattered children of God into unity. The death is the mechanism of the gathering. How the death accomplishes the gathering is not explained here in abstract terms; the document will develop it through the foot-washing (13:1-17), the farewell discourse (14-17), and the passion narrative (18-19). But the fact is stated: the death is for gathering.

"So from that day on they planned together to kill him" (ap' ekeines oun tes hemeras ebouleusanto hina apokteinosin auton). The verb bouleuo ("to plan, to take counsel, to resolve") indicates a formal decision, not merely hostile intention. The council has resolved on Jesus's death. The supreme demonstration of life-giving power — raising a dead man — has produced the decision to kill the life-giver. The irony is the deepest in the document: the one who gives life to the dead will be put to death by those who fear the consequences of his life-giving. And the death they plan will itself become the means by which life is given to the world.

div.title: Verses 54-57: Withdrawal and the Approaching Passover
div.p: "Therefore Jesus no longer continued to walk publicly among the Jews, but went away from there to the country near the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim; and there he stayed with the disciples. Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up to Jerusalem out of the country before the Passover to purify themselves. So they were seeking for Jesus, and were saying to one another as they stood in the temple, 'What do you think; that he will not come to the feast at all?' Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he was to report it, so that they might seize him."

"Jesus no longer continued to walk publicly among the Jews." The withdrawal from public activity echoes earlier strategic retreats: 6:15, when the crowd tried to make him king; 7:1, when he remained in Galilee because "the Jews were seeking to kill him"; 10:40, when he withdrew beyond the Jordan. Each retreat is temporary, and each precedes a return at the divinely appointed moment.

"To the country near the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim." Ephraim is identified as near the wilderness (eremos), likely the Judean wilderness northeast of Jerusalem. The name Ephraim carries scriptural associations: Ephraim was the name of one of Joseph's sons (Genesis 41:52) and one of the northern tribes of Israel. Hosea's prophecy addressed Ephraim extensively as a wayward child God nevertheless loved: "How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel?" (Hosea 11:8). Whether the author intends these associations is uncertain, but the withdrawal to a place named Ephraim, near the wilderness, creates a sense of liminal existence — between the public ministry and the final Passover, between the signs and the passion.

"Now the Passover of the Jews was near." This is the third Passover in the document (the first in 2:13, the second in 6:4, and now the third in 11:55). If the unnamed feast of 5:1 was also a Passover, it is the fourth. The Passover — the feast that commemorates God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt through the death of the firstborn and the blood of the lamb — is the festival at which Jesus will die. The author has identified Jesus as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (1:29). The lamb of the first Passover was slaughtered so that the firstborn might live; the Lamb of God will be slaughtered so that the scattered children might be gathered and given life.

"Many went up to Jerusalem out of the country before the Passover to purify themselves." Ritual purification before the feast was required for those who had become ceremonially unclean (Numbers 9:6-10 describes provisions for those unable to observe Passover due to corpse contamination). The pilgrims gather in Jerusalem, creating the enormous crowd that will be present for the final events.

"What do you think; that he will not come to the feast at all?" The question among the pilgrims reveals that Jesus's presence is the subject of public speculation. The tension is palpable: will the one who raised the dead come to the feast where the authorities plan to kill him? The question parallels the one in 7:11 at the Feast of Tabernacles: "Where is he?" The crowd senses that the confrontation between Jesus and the authorities has reached a decisive point.

"The chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he was to report it." The authorities have issued a warrant. Information about Jesus's whereabouts is to be reported so that they can arrest him. The shepherd who laid down his life "on his own initiative" (10:18) is now the object of a coordinated search. But the arrest, when it comes, will happen on Jesus's terms, at Jesus's chosen moment, at the Passover feast where the lamb is slain.

list.item: The chapter is the climactic sign of the document — the seventh and greatest. It demonstrates, in the most extreme possible terms, the claim Jesus has been making since chapter 5: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he wishes" (5:21). The claim has been progressive: healing a paralytic (ch. 5), feeding a multitude (ch. 6), giving sight to the blind (ch. 9), and now raising a man dead four days. Each sign escalates the demonstration. The feeding showed Jesus as the bread of life; the sight-giving showed him as the light of the world; the raising shows him as the resurrection and the life. The signs are not disconnected wonders; they are an escalating argument, each building on the one before.

The "I am the resurrection and the life" declaration (v. 25) redefines resurrection from a future event to a present person. Martha's theology was correct but incomplete: she believed in the resurrection on the last day (v. 24). Jesus does not deny the future resurrection but relocates its source: the resurrection is not an impersonal event scheduled for the end of the age; it is a person standing before her. The future tense of eschatological hope is not abolished but grounded in the present reality of relationship with the one who has life in himself (5:26). The last day is not merely something that will come; its power has already arrived in the person of the Son.

The deliberate delay (vv. 5-6) demonstrates that Jesus's love operates according to the Father's timing, not human urgency. The author presents the delay as flowing from love, not contradicting it. Human expectation says: if you love, you act immediately. The narrative says: if you love, you act at the moment that will produce the greatest revelation of glory and the deepest foundation for faith. The delay ensures that the sign will be unambiguous — a four-day-dead man raised, not a coma patient revived. The delay is an act of love because it serves the purpose that love intends: "so that you may believe" (v. 15).

Martha's confession (v. 27) is the fullest christological declaration in the document up to this point. She confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, and the one who comes into the world — three titles that encompass the royal-messianic, the divine-filial, and the prophetic dimensions of Jesus's identity. Her confession precedes the sign; she does not need to see the raising in order to confess. Her faith is tested by the reality of decomposition (v. 39) and strengthened by Jesus's reminder (v. 40), but it was established before the sign occurred. The sign confirms her faith; it does not create it.

Jesus's prayer at the tomb (vv. 41-42) reveals the nature of his relationship with the Father. The prayer is thanksgiving, not petition — the Father has already heard. The relationship is one of permanent mutual hearing: "I knew that you always hear me." The prayer is spoken aloud not for God's benefit but for the witnesses', so that they may understand the sign as the work of the one the Father sent. The sign is not an autonomous display of Jesus's power; it is the Father's work through the Son, demonstrating the unity of purpose and action that "I and the Father are one" (10:30) declared.

The raising of Lazarus directly precipitates the decision to kill Jesus (vv. 47-53). The supreme demonstration of life is met with the decision to impose death. The pattern is the document's central paradox: the life-giver must die so that life can be given on the widest possible scale. The council's political calculation — one man must die for the nation — is reinterpreted by the author as unwitting prophecy: Jesus's death will accomplish the gathering of God's scattered children into unity (v. 52). The death that the authorities intend as the suppression of a threat becomes the mechanism of universal salvation.

Caiaphas's prophecy (vv. 49-52) provides the document's clearest statement of the purpose of Jesus's death. The shepherd lays down his life not only for "this fold" (Israel) but for "the children of God who are scattered abroad." The death accomplishes what 10:16 promised: the other sheep, not of this fold, will be brought in, and there will be one flock and one shepherd. The gathering into unity is the purpose; the death is the means. The document does not yet explain the mechanism — how one death gathers many — but it states the fact. The explanation will unfold in the farewell discourse and the passion narrative.

The chapter completes the sign-sequence that structures the first half of the document. The document has been organized around seven signs: water to wine (2:1-11), healing the official's son (4:46-54), healing the paralytic (5:1-9), feeding the multitude (6:1-14), walking on the sea (6:16-21), healing the man born blind (9:1-7), and raising Lazarus (11:1-44). The seventh sign is the climax; it demonstrates the fullest extent of Jesus's power — authority over death itself. After this sign, there will be no more signs in the document. The remainder of the narrative (chapters 12-21) will move from signs to the reality to which the signs pointed: Jesus's own death and resurrection. The signs were previews; the cross and the empty tomb are the substance.

The connection between life-giving and death-receiving runs through the entire chapter as its structural principle. Jesus gives life to Lazarus, and this act of giving life brings about the decision that Jesus himself must die. The one who has authority to "take up" his life again (10:18) first demonstrates that authority by taking up Lazarus's life. The shepherd who declared his power over death now exercises it, and the exercise provokes the very death he promised to undergo. The chapter thus functions as the hinge between the signs and the passion: it proves that Jesus can give life, and it initiates the sequence of events in which he will lay down his life. The two acts — giving life and laying down life — are not in tension but are the two aspects of a single reality: the shepherd's self-giving love for the flock.

The present-tense grammar of believing continues as the chapter's consistent pattern. "The one believing in me will live even if he dies" (ho pisteuon eis eme, v. 25). "Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (pas ho zon kai pisteuon eis eme, v. 26). The promise is addressed to the one who is presently believing and living, not to one who believed once in the past. The continuous nature of the relationship — hearing, following, believing, living — remains the condition under which the promises operate, consistent with 3:16, 6:35, 6:54, and 10:27-28.

The chapter's emotional depth — Jesus's agitation, his tears, his troubled spirit — reveals that the one who has sovereign authority over death is not indifferent to its devastation. The life-giver weeps at the tomb. The one who will command the dead to rise first enters into the grief of those who mourn. The tears are not weakness but the fullest expression of the shepherd's love: he does not merely rescue from a distance but enters the suffering of the sheep. The sovereignty and the compassion are not opposed but united in the same person. The God of Israel who was "afflicted in all their affliction" (Isaiah 63:9) is present at the tomb of Lazarus, weeping before commanding the dead to live.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 11): Chapter 11 narrates the illness, death, and raising of Lazarus of Bethany — the seventh and climactic sign in the document. Jesus receives word that Lazarus is ill (11:3) but deliberately delays his departure for two days (11:6), stating that "this sickness is not to end in death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified by it" (11:4). By the time Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been dead four days (11:17). Martha meets Jesus and confesses her belief in a future resurrection: "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" (11:24). Jesus responds with the fifth "I am" statement with a predicate: "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me will live even if he dies, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (11:25-26). He then raises Lazarus from the tomb with the command "Lazarus, come forth!" (11:43) — the most dramatic enactment of the claim from 5:25 that "the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."

The raising produces two responses. Many of the Jews who witnessed it believed in Jesus (11:45). But others reported it to the Pharisees, and the chief priests and Pharisees convened the council (synedrion), expressing concern that "if we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation" (11:48). Caiaphas, the high priest that year, speaks: "You know nothing at all, nor do you take into account that it is expedient for you that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish" (11:49-50). The author glosses this as unwitting prophecy: Caiaphas did not speak of his own accord but prophesied "that Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad" (11:51-52). This gloss directly fulfills the "other sheep" promise of 10:16 ("they will become one flock with one shepherd") and anticipates the arrival of Greeks in chapter 12. From that day, the council plotted to kill Jesus (11:53), and Jesus withdrew to a town called Ephraim near the wilderness (11:54).

The chapter ends with the approach of Passover. Many go up to Jerusalem for purification before the festival, and in the temple they ask one another, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?" (11:56). The chief priests and Pharisees have given orders that anyone who knows where Jesus is should report it, "so that they might seize him" (11:57). The stage is set: Passover approaches, Jerusalem fills, the authorities are hunting Jesus, and the question on everyone's lips is whether he will appear.

What the author argues immediately after (John 13): Chapter 13 opens with a temporal marker that signals a fundamental transition: "Now before the Feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end" (13:1). The public ministry is over. Jesus is now with "his own" — the disciples — in a private setting. He washes their feet (13:4-12), interprets the act as a model of service ("If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet," 13:14), identifies the betrayer through the morsel given to Judas (13:26), and after Judas's departure into the night (13:30), announces the glorification of the Son of Man (13:31-32) and gives the new commandment: "Love one another, even as I have loved you" (13:34). Peter's question about where Jesus is going leads to Jesus's prediction of Peter's denial (13:36-38). The entire mood shifts: from confrontation with the crowds and authorities to intimate instruction of the inner circle. The "world" to which Jesus has been speaking since chapter 1 now recedes, and the farewell discourse begins (chapters 14-17).

How chapter 12 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 12 is the hinge of the entire document. Everything before it has been building toward this moment; everything after it flows from it. The chapter closes the public ministry that began at 1:19 with John's testimony and opens the path to the death that has been anticipated since 2:4 ("My hour has not yet come"). Between chapter 11 and chapter 13, chapter 12 performs several essential functions:

First, it connects the raising of Lazarus (the final sign) to its consequences. The anointing at Bethany occurs in the house where Lazarus reclines at table — the man death could not hold is present as a living witness (12:2). The chief priests extend their murderous intent from Jesus to Lazarus himself (12:10-11), because the sign keeps producing belief. The sign is not a self-contained episode; it reverberates, and the reverberations drive the plot toward the cross.

Second, the chapter fulfills the "other sheep" promise of 10:16 and the "scattered children" prophecy of 11:52. Greeks — Gentiles — come seeking Jesus (12:20-22), and their arrival triggers Jesus's announcement that the hour has come (12:23). The hour of the shepherd's death is precipitated by the appearance of those for whom, in part, the shepherd dies. The grain of wheat must fall and die so that it does not "remain alone" (12:24) — so that the harvest extends beyond the single fold to encompass all who will hear the shepherd's voice.

Third, the chapter provides the author's own theological interpretation of why the public ministry failed to produce widespread belief. In 12:37-43, the author steps back from narration to offer commentary, citing Isaiah 53:1 and Isaiah 6:10. The signs have been performed, the words have been spoken, and yet "they did not believe in him" (12:37). The author explains this unbelief by locating it within Isaiah's prophetic vision — a vision the author identifies as a vision of Jesus's own glory (12:41).

Fourth, the chapter delivers Jesus's final public declaration (12:44-50), a compressed summary of the themes that have pervaded the entire public ministry: light and darkness, believing and judging, the Father's commandment and the Son's obedience. After this, Jesus "departed and hid himself from them" (12:36b). The public voice falls silent. What follows will be spoken only to his own.

The chapter thus functions as both a closing and an opening. It closes the narrative of signs, public discourse, and confrontation with the authorities that has occupied chapters 1-11. It opens the movement toward the cross by declaring that the hour has come, explaining the grain-of-wheat necessity of Jesus's death, and describing the "lifting up" that will draw all people. The public ministry ends not with triumph but with a mixture of acclaim and rejection, of hosannas and hardened hearts — a pattern that Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Zechariah had all described as characteristic of Israel's response to God's shepherds and servants.

div.title: Verses 1-8: The Anointing at Bethany
div.p: "Jesus, therefore, six days before the Passover, came to Bethany where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they made him a supper there, and Martha was serving; but Lazarus was one of those reclining at the table with him. Mary then took a pound of very costly perfume of pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, who was intending to betray him, said, 'Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to poor people?' Now he said this, not because he was concerned about the poor, but because he was a thief; and as he had the money box, he used to pilfer what was put into it. Therefore Jesus said, 'Let her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.'"

"Six days before the Passover" (pro hex hemeron tou pascha). The temporal marker is precise and deliberate. The Passover is the festival at which lambs are slaughtered. John the Baptist introduced Jesus at the beginning of the document as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (1:29). Six days before the Passover, the lamb arrives at the place where he will be sacrificed. The countdown to the cross has begun, and the author marks it with chronological specificity. Each remaining event moves the narrative closer to the hour that has finally come.

"Came to Bethany where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead." The identification of Bethany by its connection to Lazarus (rather than by geographic description) keeps the preceding sign in the reader's consciousness. This is not just a village near Jerusalem; it is the place where death was reversed. The one who raised the dead now enters the household of the one he raised, and the presence of the living Lazarus at the supper table is itself a silent testimony. The sign does not need to be repeated or argued; it sits at the table.

"Martha was serving; but Lazarus was one of those reclining at the table with him." Martha's role as the one who serves (diekonei) is consistent with the brief characterization the author has given her — she is the active one, the one who went out to meet Jesus (11:20) while Mary remained seated. Lazarus reclines (anakeimenon, the posture of the dinner guest at a formal meal). The image is quiet but extraordinary: a man who was dead and buried four days ago now eats supper. The author does not comment on this; the juxtaposition speaks for itself. Death and supper, the tomb and the table, the grave-clothes and the dinner couch.

"Mary then took a pound of very costly perfume of pure nard" (he oun Mariam labousa litran myrou nardou pistikes polytelous). The detail is lavish. A litra was a Roman pound (roughly twelve ounces). Nard (nardos) was an aromatic oil extracted from the spikenard plant (Nardostachys jatamansi), which grew in the highlands of India. It was imported to the Mediterranean world at great expense. The adjective pistikes (translated "pure" or "genuine") may derive from pistis ("faithful, trustworthy"), meaning the nard is authenticated, unadulterated. The adjective polytelous ("very costly, of great price") reinforces the extravagance. The quantity and quality together indicate an offering of extraordinary value — not a token gesture but an act of reckless generosity.

"Anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair" (eleipsen tous podas tou Iesou kai exemaxen tais thrixin autes tous podas autou). Two elements are significant. First, the anointing of the feet rather than the head. Anointing the head was the customary gesture of honor and hospitality (Psalm 23:5, LXX 22:5: "You have anointed my head with oil"; 2 Kings 9:3: the prophet anoints Jehu's head to make him king; 1 Samuel 10:1: Samuel anoints Saul's head). Anointing the feet is a more extreme act of humility — feet were the lowest, most servile part of the body, associated with the work of slaves (cf. 13:5-14, where Jesus will wash the disciples' feet, performing the task of a slave). Mary's act combines royal honor (anointing) with servile humility (feet), prefiguring the foot-washing of chapter 13 where Jesus himself will unite authority with servanthood.

Second, wiping with her hair. For a Jewish woman to unbind her hair in the presence of men was an act of striking intimacy and social impropriety. Hair was associated with a woman's glory and modesty. To use it as a towel for Jesus's feet was to employ her own dignity in the service of his person — to make her glory a tool for honoring him. The extravagance is not merely financial but personal: she gives her most costly possession (the nard) and her own person (her hair) without reserve.

"The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume" (he oikia eplerosthe ek tes osmes tou myrou). The detail seems incidental but carries symbolic weight. The fragrance of the anointing fills the entire house. In Israel's worship, fragrance was associated with the presence of God: the incense altar stood before the Holy of Holies, and its smoke filled the tabernacle (Exodus 30:7-8, 34-38; Leviticus 16:12-13). Isaiah 6:4 describes the temple filling with smoke at the vision of the LORD's glory. The Song of Solomon (1:12, LXX) reads: "While the king was on his couch, my nard (nardos mou) gave forth its fragrance." The perfume that fills the house at Bethany signals that something sacred is occurring — an anointing that is more than hospitality.

"Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, who was intending to betray him." The author identifies Judas with three markers: his name, his status as a disciple (one of the twelve), and his future action (ho mellon auton paradidonai, "the one about to betray him"). The identification is proleptic — the betrayal has not yet occurred, but the author ensures the reader knows who is speaking. Every word Judas says must be heard through this lens.

"Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to poor people?" Three hundred denarii represented roughly a year's wages for a common laborer (a denarius was the standard daily wage; cf. Matthew 20:2). Judas's objection sounds reasonable, even righteous: care for the poor was a central obligation in Israel's law (Deuteronomy 15:7-11, Leviticus 25:35). The suggestion appears pious. But the author immediately strips away the appearance.

"He said this, not because he was concerned about the poor, but because he was a thief; and as he had the money box, he used to pilfer what was put into it." The word kleptes ("thief") connects Judas to the shepherd discourse of chapter 10: "he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs up some other way, he is a thief (kleptes) and a robber" (10:1). "The thief comes only to steal (klepsai) and kill and destroy" (10:10). Judas is identified by the same word used for the false shepherds who exploit the flock. He carries the common fund (glossokomon, "money box, treasury") — a position of trust within the community — and uses it for theft. He is the hired hand, or worse, the thief within the fold. His pious concern for the poor is a mask for self-interest, the same pattern the Pharisees exhibited when they expelled the man born blind while claiming to defend the law.

The verb ebastazen ("used to carry" or "used to pilfer") is ambiguous. The primary meaning of bastazo is "to carry, bear," but it can also mean "to carry off, steal" (as in Josephus, Antiquities 12.383). The author's identification of Judas as a kleptes resolves the ambiguity toward the second meaning: he was stealing from what was put in.

"Let her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial" (aphes auten, hina eis ten hemeran tou entaphiasmou mou terese auto). Jesus's response reinterprets Mary's act. Whether Mary herself understood the full significance is left unstated. But Jesus declares that her anointing anticipates his burial. The word entaphiasmos ("burial, preparation for burial") points directly ahead: Jesus's body will be prepared for burial at 19:38-42, when Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus will wrap his body with spices and linen. Mary's anointing is a premature burial preparation — she anoints the body that is about to die. The extravagance of the perfume, which scandalized Judas, is appropriate precisely because of what it signifies: the death of the one whose body she anoints.

The phrase "the day of my burial" also establishes that Jesus knows what is coming. He is not surprised by the approaching death; he interprets the anointing in light of it. The shepherd who said "I lay down my life on my own initiative" (10:18) now receives anointing for the burial that his voluntary death will require.

"For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me." Jesus echoes Deuteronomy 15:11: "For the poor will never cease to be in the land; therefore I command you, saying, 'You shall freely open your hand to your brother, to your needy and poor in your land.'" The Deuteronomy text does not dismiss care for the poor; it establishes it as a permanent obligation precisely because poverty is permanent. Jesus's point is not that the poor do not matter but that his presence is temporary and unrepeatable. The anointing is an act suited to the unique and unrepeatable occasion: the presence, in the flesh, of the one who is about to die. Care for the poor will continue after Jesus departs; the opportunity to anoint his body before his death will not.

div.title: Verses 9-11: The Response of the Crowd and the Plot Against Lazarus
div.p: "The large crowd of the Jews then learned that he was there; and they came, not for Jesus' sake only, but that they might also see Lazarus, whom he raised from the dead. But the chief priests planned to put Lazarus to death also; because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and were believing in Jesus."

"The large crowd of the Jews" (ho ochlos polys ek ton Ioudaion). The Passover pilgrims gathering in Jerusalem are aware of Jesus's presence in nearby Bethany. They come to see not only Jesus but Lazarus — the sign still speaks. The raised man is a living witness whose mere existence testifies to Jesus's power over death. He does not need to preach or argue; his breathing, eating, reclining at table is the argument.

"The chief priests planned to put Lazarus to death also" (ebouleuonto de hoi archiereis hina kai ton Lazaron apokteinosin). The murderous intent extends from Jesus to the evidence of Jesus's power. The logic is brutally clear: if the sign keeps producing belief, eliminate the sign. Kill the witness to remove the testimony. This is the definitive exposure of the authorities' motives. They are not defending the law or protecting the nation (despite Caiaphas's claim in 11:50). They are suppressing evidence. They want to kill a man whose only offense is that he was raised from the dead — that God's work was performed in him. The irony is thick: they plot to kill a man who has already been dead and whom Jesus raised. If Jesus can raise the dead once, what guarantees that killing Lazarus will end the problem?

The term "chief priests" (hoi archiereis) shifts the opposition from the Pharisees (who have been the primary antagonists since chapter 5) to the priestly aristocracy — the Sadducean party that controlled the temple and the council. The political dimension is now dominant: the chief priests' concern is institutional survival, the preservation of "our place" (the temple) and "our nation" (11:48). Their response to the sign is not theological investigation but political calculation.

"On account of him many of the Jews were going away and were believing in Jesus" (hoti polloi di' auton hypeegon ton Ioudaion kai episteuon eis ton Iesoun). The verb hypago ("to go away, depart") describes Jews who are "going away" from the authorities — departing from the sphere of the chief priests' influence and transferring their allegiance to Jesus. The present tenses (hypegon, episteuon — imperfect tense, describing ongoing action) indicate that this was not a single event but a continuing movement. The authorities are losing people. The sign is an ongoing drain on their authority, which is why they feel compelled to eliminate not only the sign-worker but the sign itself.

div.title: Verses 12-19: The Entry into Jerusalem
div.p: "On the next day the large crowd who had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him, and began to shout, 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel.' Jesus, finding a young donkey, sat on it; as it is written, 'Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your King is coming, seated on a donkey's colt.' These things his disciples did not understand at the first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things to him. So the crowd who were with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead, continued to testify. For this reason also the crowd went to meet him, because they heard that he had performed this sign. So the Pharisees said to one another, 'You see that you are not doing any good; look, the world has gone after him.'"

"Took the branches of the palm trees" (elabon ta baia ton phoinikon). Palm branches carried specific associations in Jewish memory and practice. The palm (phoinix) was a symbol of national victory and liberation. When Judas Maccabeus rededicated the temple after its profanation by Antiochus IV, the people celebrated "carrying ivy-wreathed wands and beautiful branches and also fronds of palm" (2 Maccabees 10:7). When Simon Maccabeus entered the citadel of Jerusalem after expelling the Greek garrison, "the Jews entered it with praise and palm branches, and with harps and cymbals and stringed instruments, and with hymns and songs, because a great enemy had been destroyed out of Israel" (1 Maccabees 13:51). The palm branch was the emblem stamped on coins during the periods of Jewish independence. By taking palm branches, the crowd is making a political statement: they hail Jesus as a national liberator in the mold of the Maccabees.

"Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" The crowd's shout draws from Psalm 118:25-26 (LXX 117:25-26). The Hebrew hoshia na ("save now, save please") was the cry embedded in the psalm's liturgical context. Psalm 118 was sung during the great festivals, particularly Tabernacles and Passover. In its original setting, the psalm is a processional hymn in which a victorious king or deliverer approaches the temple: "Open to me the gates of righteousness; I shall enter through them, I shall give thanks to the LORD. This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous will enter through it" (118:19-20). "Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD" (118:26) was the priests' greeting to the arriving worshiper or king.

The crowd adds a phrase not found in Psalm 118: "even the King of Israel" (ho basileus tou Israel). This addition makes explicit what the palm branches imply. The crowd is not merely welcoming a pilgrim or a prophet; they are acclaiming a king. The title "King of Israel" appeared in the document's opening chapter: Nathanael's confession in 1:49, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel." The crowd's acclamation now echoes Nathanael's early and private confession on a public and dramatic scale. But the crowd's understanding of what "King of Israel" means is about to be reframed.

"Jesus, finding a young donkey, sat on it" (heuron de ho Iesous onarion ekathisen ep' auto). While the crowd enacts a triumphal procession appropriate for a military liberator, Jesus responds by sitting on a young donkey (onarion, a diminutive — a small donkey, a colt). The action is deliberate and interpretive. The crowd offers him a warrior-king's welcome; he accepts it on a donkey.

"As it is written, 'Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your King is coming, seated on a donkey's colt'" (kathos estin gegrammenon, Me phobou, thygater Sion; idou ho basileus sou erchetai, kathemenos epi polon onou). The citation blends two prophetic texts. The primary source is Zechariah 9:9, which in the LXX reads: "Rejoice greatly (chaire sphodra), daughter of Zion! Shout aloud (keryssse), daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king comes to you; he is righteous and saving (dikaios kai sozon), lowly (prays), and riding on a beast of burden and a young colt (kai epi polon neon)." The author's version replaces "Rejoice greatly" with "Fear not" (me phobou), a phrase that echoes Zephaniah 3:14-16: "Shout for joy, O daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter of Jerusalem!... Do not fear (me phobou), Zion." The blending of the two prophetic texts is not accidental. Zephaniah 3:15 continues: "The LORD has taken away his judgments against you, he has cleared away your enemies. The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst; you will fear disaster no more." In Zephaniah, the "King of Israel" who is "in your midst" is the LORD himself. By fusing Zephaniah's "Fear not" with Zechariah's "your king is coming on a donkey's colt," the author presents Jesus as the king whose arrival fulfills both prophecies: the humble, peaceable king of Zechariah and the LORD-as-King of Zephaniah.

The Zechariah 9:9 context is critical for understanding what kind of king is being described. The full passage contrasts this king with the military empires of the surrounding nations. Zechariah 9:1-8 announces judgment on Damascus, Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia. Then verse 9 introduces a different kind of king: not a war-king riding a horse (the animal of war) but a peace-king riding a donkey (the animal of peacetime transport). Zechariah 9:10 continues: "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; and the bow of war will be cut off. And he will speak peace to the nations; and his dominion will be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth." The king who rides the donkey brings not military conquest but peace, and his dominion is universal — "to the ends of the earth." This is the king Jesus enacts.

The crowd hailing Jesus with palm branches (the emblem of military victory) and Jesus sitting on a donkey (the emblem of peaceful kingship) creates a tension. The crowd sees one kind of king; Jesus presents another. The palm-waving crowd expects a Maccabean liberator; Jesus offers the Zechariah king whose kingdom is established not through force but through his own death (as the grain-of-wheat teaching in verses 24-25 will shortly explain).

"These things his disciples did not understand at the first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things to him." The author acknowledges the disciples' incomprehension at the time. They participated in the events without grasping their scriptural significance. The understanding came later — "when Jesus was glorified" (hote edoxasthe Iesous). The verb edoxasthe ("was glorified") refers to the complex of events that this author calls "glorification": the death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus, and the giving of the Spirit (cf. 7:39: "the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified"). The glorification opened the disciples' eyes to the scriptural patterns that the events fulfilled. This is consistent with the document's teaching that the Spirit would "bring to your remembrance all that I said to you" (14:26) and "guide you into all the truth" (16:13). The disciples' subsequent understanding was not invention but recognition — they remembered what had been written and saw its correspondence with what had occurred.

"The crowd who were with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead, continued to testify." The sign of Lazarus is the engine driving the crowd's response. The witnesses to the raising are still talking about it (emartyrei, imperfect tense — they "kept testifying"). Their testimony draws others: "For this reason also the crowd went to meet him, because they heard that he had performed this sign." The sign produces testimony; testimony produces a larger crowd; the larger crowd threatens the authorities. The chain of cause and effect is clear and unbroken. The sign's power is not exhausted in the moment of its occurrence; it propagates through witness.

"The Pharisees said to one another, 'You see that you are not doing any good; look, the world has gone after him'" (theoreite hoti ouk opheleite ouden; ide ho kosmos opiso autou apelthen). The Pharisees' frustrated observation is loaded with irony the author clearly intends. The word "world" (kosmos) in their mouths means merely "everyone, the whole populace" — a hyperbolic expression of their political frustration. But in this author's vocabulary, kosmos is a theological term that has been in play since the prologue: "He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him" (1:10). "God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son" (3:16). "The Savior of the world" (4:42). "The bread of God is that which comes down out of heaven, and gives life to the world" (6:33). When the Pharisees say "the world has gone after him," they speak more truly than they know. The kosmos — the whole created order that God loves and for which Jesus dies — is indeed going after him, as the arrival of the Greeks in the next verse will immediately confirm.

div.title: Verses 20-26: Greeks Seek Jesus — The Grain of Wheat and the Hour of Glorification
div.p: "Now there were some Greeks among those who were going up to worship at the feast; these then came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and began to ask him, saying, 'Sir, we wish to see Jesus.' Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip came and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, saying, 'The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. He who loves his life loses it, and he who hates his life in this world will keep it to life eternal. If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also; if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.'"

"Some Greeks" (Hellenes tines). The word Hellenes ("Greeks") designates Gentiles — non-Jews who are, however, sufficiently attracted to Israel's God that they have come "to worship at the feast" (hina proskynesosin en te heorte). These are likely "God-fearers" (theosebeis or phoboumenoi ton theon), Gentiles who attended synagogue worship and observed aspects of the law without undergoing full conversion through circumcision. The existence of such a class of Gentile worshipers is well attested in first-century sources (Acts 10:2, 22; 13:16, 26, 50; 17:4, 17; Josephus, Antiquities 14.110; inscriptions from synagogues throughout the diaspora). They represent the first wave of the nations drawn to Israel's God — and now, to Israel's Messiah.

Their arrival at this precise moment in the narrative is the fulfillment of multiple earlier statements. In 10:16: "I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice." In 11:52: Jesus would die "not for the nation only, but in order that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad." The Pharisees have just said "the world has gone after him" (12:19). Now the world appears, in the persons of these Greek worshipers. The "other sheep" are at the door.

"Sir, we wish to see Jesus" (kyrie, thelomen ton Iesoun idein). The verb idein ("to see") in this document frequently carries the sense of perception, recognition, and spiritual understanding (1:14: "we saw his glory"; 1:46: "Come and see"; 6:40: "everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life"; 9:39: "that those who do not see may see"). The Greeks' request to "see Jesus" is more than a desire for a physical audience; it is the reaching out of the Gentile world toward the one in whom all nations will be blessed.

"Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip came and told Jesus." The two-stage relay through Philip and Andrew is noted with specificity. Both are Greek-named disciples (Philippos, Andreas), and Philip is identified as being from Bethsaida of Galilee — a city in the tetrarchy of Philip, on the border between Jewish and Gentile territory, with a mixed population. The Greeks naturally approach the disciples who are culturally and linguistically most accessible. The chain — Greeks to Philip to Andrew to Jesus — is a model of the mediation through which the nations are brought to the shepherd.

"The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (elelythen he hora hina doxasthe ho huios tou anthropou). This is the pivotal declaration of the document. Since 2:4, "my hour" (he hora mou) has been a recurring marker of the event that has not yet arrived: "My hour has not yet come" (2:4); "his hour had not yet come" (7:30, 8:20). The hour has been the unseen horizon toward which the entire narrative has been moving. Now, with the arrival of the Greeks — the first wave of the "other sheep," the world that the Father loved enough to give his Son for (3:16) — the hour has come.

The title "Son of Man" (ho huios tou anthropou) appears for the final time in this author's record of Jesus's public teaching. In Daniel 7:13-14 (LXX), "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and is presented before the Ancient of Days, receiving "dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and men of every language might serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion which will not pass away, and his kingdom is one which will not be destroyed." The "Son of Man" in Daniel is the figure who receives universal dominion. In this document, the Son of Man is the one who will be "lifted up" (3:14, 8:28, 12:32-34) — a term that embraces both crucifixion and exaltation.

The word "glorified" (doxasthe) carries particular weight. In the LXX, doxa is the standard translation of the Hebrew kavod — the weighty, luminous presence of God (Exodus 33:18-23, 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Isaiah 6:3; Ezekiel 1:28). The prologue declared: "We saw his glory (doxan), glory as of the only begotten from the Father" (1:14). The first sign "manifested his glory" (2:11). Now the hour of the definitive manifestation of glory has arrived. But the glory will be manifested through death — the grain falling into the earth. This redefines glory: it is not triumph in the conventional sense but self-giving love carried to the point of death.

"Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (amen amen lego hymin, ean me ho kokkos tou sitou peson eis ten gen apothane, autos monos menei; ean de apothane, polyn karpon pherei). The double amen introduces a statement of fundamental importance (the twenty-fifth use of this formula in the document). The agricultural image is drawn from universal experience: a seed that remains in the granary retains its individual existence but produces nothing. A seed that is buried in the soil — that "dies" to its existence as a separate grain — germinates and produces a harvest.

The application to Jesus's impending death is immediate and explicit. If Jesus does not die, he "remains alone" (autos monos menei) — the good shepherd without the flock, the single grain without the harvest. The "other sheep" of 10:16 remain ungatheered; the "children of God scattered abroad" of 11:52 remain scattered; the Greeks standing in the outer court remain outside. The death is the necessary condition for the harvest. The shepherd must lay down his life so that the sheep may be gathered. The grain must die so that the field may be filled.

The word monos ("alone") is significant. In 8:16 and 16:32, Jesus says he is "not alone" because the Father is with him. But if the grain does not fall and die, it remains monos — solitary, singular, unaccompanied by the harvest that its death would produce. The death is not merely sacrificial but generative. It produces what would not exist without it. The "much fruit" (polyn karpon) is the community that will emerge from the shepherd's self-sacrifice — the one flock gathered from many folds, the children of God assembled from among the nations.

"He who loves his life loses it, and he who hates his life in this world will keep it to life eternal" (ho philon ten psychen autou apollyei auten, kai ho mison ten psychen autou en to kosmo touto eis zoen aionion phylaxei auten). The grain-of-wheat principle now extends beyond Jesus to his followers. The pattern of dying-to-live is not unique to Jesus; it describes the condition of discipleship. The verb phileo ("to love") here describes attachment to one's own psyche — one's natural life, one's self-preservation. The one who clings to self-preservation loses (apollyei, "destroys, ruins") the very life being preserved. The one who "hates" (miseo, a Semitic idiom for "places in lower priority" — as in "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated," Malachi 1:2-3) his life in this world (en to kosmo touto) will "keep" (phylaxei, "guard, protect, preserve") it for eternal life (eis zoen aionion).

The verb apollyei is the same root used in 3:16 ("should not perish," me apoletai), 6:39 ("that I lose nothing"), and 10:10 ("the thief comes to steal and kill and destroy"). The one who clings to life in this world participates in the very destruction the thief brings. The one who releases the grip on earthly self-preservation enters the life the shepherd came to give abundantly (10:10).

This statement is the first explicit extension in this document of the self-sacrificial pattern from Jesus to his followers. The shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11, 15, 17-18); the grain falls and dies to bear fruit (12:24); and now the disciple who follows is called to the same pattern of relinquishment. This will be developed further in the farewell discourse: "Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his life for his friends" (15:13).

"If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also; if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him." The verb akoloutheo ("to follow") has been the defining activity of discipleship since the first chapter: "Follow me" (1:43), "the sheep follow him because they know his voice" (10:4, 27). The servant (diakonos, one who serves) must follow where the master goes. And where is the master going? Into death. The grain is falling into the earth. The servant who follows will be "where I am" (hopou eimi ego) — a phrase that in this document carries eschatological weight (14:3: "where I am, there you may be also"; 17:24: "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, be with me where I am"). The promise is that the one who follows Jesus through the pattern of self-giving will share his destiny.

The final phrase — "the Father will honor him" (timesei auton ho pater) — uses the verb timao ("to honor, value, esteem"). In 5:23, the Father and Son share honor: "so that all will honor the Son even as they honor the Father." The Father's honor is extended to those who serve the Son. The glory that comes from God (doxa para tou theou, cf. 5:44) is contrasted, by implication, with the glory that comes from men — a contrast that will become explicit in verses 42-43.

div.title: Verses 27-36a: The Troubled Soul, the Voice from Heaven, and the Lifting Up
div.p: "Now my soul has become troubled; and what shall I say, 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name. Then a voice came out of heaven: 'I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.' So the crowd of people who stood by and heard it were saying that it had thundered; others were saying, 'An angel has spoken to him.' Jesus answered and said, 'This voice has not come for my sake, but for your sakes. Now judgment is upon this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself.' But he was saying this to indicate the kind of death by which he was about to die. So the crowd answered him, 'We have heard out of the Law that the Christ is to remain forever; and how can you say, "The Son of Man must be lifted up"? Who is this Son of Man?' So Jesus said to them, 'For a little while longer the Light is among you. Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you; he who walks in the darkness does not know where he goes. While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of Light.'"

"Now my soul has become troubled" (nyn he psyche mou tetaraktai). The verb tarasso ("to trouble, disturb, agitate") describes inner turmoil. The same verb appears in 11:33, where Jesus was "deeply moved in spirit and was troubled" (etaraxen heauton) at Lazarus's tomb, and in 13:21, where he will be "troubled in spirit" (etarachthe to pneumati) as he identifies the betrayer.
