The pattern is consistent: Jesus is not stoic or detached from the events that approach. The prospect of his death produces genuine anguish. The verb is in the perfect tense (tetaraktai) — "has become troubled and remains troubled." The disturbance is not a momentary pang but an ongoing condition as the hour arrives.

The significance of the statement is heightened by the document's consistent presentation of Jesus as the one who acts with sovereign authority: "I lay down my life on my own initiative. No one takes it from me" (10:18). The troubling of his soul does not contradict this sovereignty; it reveals that the voluntary self-sacrifice is costly. The shepherd freely lays down his life, but the laying down is not painless or easy. The will to die for the sheep and the natural recoil from death coexist in the same person.

"What shall I say, 'Father, save me from this hour'?" The question is rhetorical. Jesus articulates the prayer he could pray — "save me from this hour" — and then explains why he will not: "But for this purpose I came to this hour" (alla dia touto elthon eis ten horan tauten). The "hour" (hora) is the very thing toward which the entire narrative has been moving. To pray for deliverance from it would be to pray for deliverance from his mission. The logic is the same as the grain-of-wheat saying: if the grain does not fall, it remains alone. If Jesus does not enter the hour, the harvest does not come. The prayer for rescue is considered and rejected — not because Jesus is unfeeling but because the purpose of his coming is the hour itself.

"Father, glorify your name" (pater, doxason sou to onoma). Instead of praying for rescue, Jesus prays for the Father's name to be glorified. The name (onoma) of God in Israel's scriptures is not a label but the full expression of God's character, power, and reputation (Exodus 3:13-15, 34:5-7; Psalm 8:1; Isaiah 42:8). To "glorify the name" is to ask that God's character be fully displayed and vindicated. In 17:6, Jesus will say, "I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world." In 17:26, "I have made your name known to them, and will make it known." The glorification of the Father's name is accomplished through the events of the hour — the cross, the resurrection, the gathering of the harvest. The death that the world will perceive as defeat will be, in reality, the supreme revelation of who God is: a God who gives his Son for the world (3:16), a shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11).

"Then a voice came out of heaven: 'I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again'" (elthen oun phone ek tou ouranou: kai edoxasa kai palin doxaso). The voice from heaven (bat qol in rabbinic terminology, "daughter of a voice" — the heavenly echo of God's speech) responds directly to Jesus's prayer. The two verbs — "I have glorified" (edoxasa, aorist) and "will glorify" (doxaso, future) — encompass both past and future. The past glorification includes the signs already performed: the water-to-wine (2:11, "manifested his glory"), the feeding, the healings, the raising of Lazarus ("for the glory of God," 11:4, 40). The future glorification will occur through the events about to unfold: the death, resurrection, and exaltation that are the content of the hour.

The voice from heaven has precedent in Israel's history. At Sinai, God spoke audibly to Moses (Exodus 19:19; 20:1-17). God spoke to Abraham at critical moments (Genesis 12:1; 15:1; 22:11-12). The bat qol was understood in later Jewish tradition as the mode of divine communication available after the cessation of prophecy. In this document, this is the only occurrence of a heavenly voice speaking directly in the hearing of a crowd.

"The crowd who stood by and heard it were saying that it had thundered; others were saying, 'An angel has spoken to him.'" The crowd's divided response mirrors the pattern of division that has characterized the entire public ministry (7:43, 9:16, 10:19-21). Some hear thunder — a natural phenomenon; others hear an angel — a supernatural intermediary. Neither group recognizes the voice for what it is: the Father's direct response to the Son's prayer. The division between the two interpretations enacts the very blindness and deafness the author is about to diagnose in verses 37-43. The voice speaks; the crowd does not hear. The light shines; the darkness does not comprehend it (1:5).

Thunder in Israel's scriptures is associated with God's self-revelation: at Sinai (Exodus 19:16, 19), in the storm theophanies of the Psalms (Psalm 29:3-9, LXX 28:3-9: "the voice of the LORD is upon the waters; the God of glory has thundered"), in Job's encounter with God (Job 37:2-5). Those who hear only thunder are hearing the form of revelation without its content — the sound without the speech.

"This voice has not come for my sake, but for your sakes." Jesus does not need the heavenly confirmation; he already knows the Father's will. The voice is for the crowd's benefit, as external confirmation of the Father-Son relationship and the Father's endorsement of what is about to happen. Whether the crowd benefits from it depends on whether they have ears to hear — the same condition that has separated sheep from non-sheep throughout the shepherd discourse (10:3-5, 27).

"Now judgment is upon this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out" (nyn krisis estin tou kosmou toutou; nyn ho archon tou kosmou toutou ekblethesetai exo). Two "now" (nyn) statements announce what the hour accomplishes. Both are declarative: the hour is not merely Jesus's death but the crisis (krisis, "judgment, decisive turning point") of the entire world-order.

The word krisis has been building throughout the document. In 3:19: "This is the judgment (krisis), that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light." In 5:22: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment (krisin) to the Son." In 5:24: "He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment (krisin)." In 5:27: the Father gave the Son "authority to execute judgment (krisin), because he is the Son of Man." In 5:30: "My judgment (krisis) is just." In 8:16: "If I do judge, my judgment (krisis) is true." The judgment has been a thread running through the entire document. Now it arrives: "now" (nyn), in the events of the hour.

"The ruler of this world" (ho archon tou kosmou toutou) is a figure mentioned only in this document, and only three times (12:31; 14:30; 16:11). The term archon ("ruler, prince, authority") in the LXX designates human rulers and leaders (Genesis 12:15; Exodus 2:14; Judges 11:6; Daniel 10:13, 20-21, where it extends to angelic/spiritual powers behind nations). In the context of this document, where "the world" (kosmos) is the order that opposes God's purposes and refuses the light (1:10, 7:7, 15:18-19), the "ruler of this world" is the power behind that opposition — the one Jesus identified in 8:44 as "the devil" who "was a murderer from the beginning and does not stand in the truth." The hour of Jesus's death, which appears to be the devil's triumph, is in reality the devil's ejection: "will be cast out" (ekblethesetai exo, future passive — cast out by God's action through the cross). The cross overturns the ruler's authority by demonstrating that the power of self-giving love is greater than the power of murderous deception.

"And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself" (kago ean hypsotho ek tes ges, pantas helkyso pros emauton). This is the third "lifting up" (hypsoo) statement in the document. In 3:14: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up; so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life." In 8:28: "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he." Now in 12:32: the lifting up will "draw all men" (pantas, "all people," without ethnic or national limitation).

The verb hypsoo carries a double meaning the author exploits throughout. It means both "to lift up physically" (as in crucifixion, where the body is lifted onto the cross) and "to exalt, elevate in honor" (as in Isaiah 52:13, LXX: "Behold, my servant shall understand, and shall be exalted [hypsothesetai] and glorified [doxasthesetai] exceedingly"). The same word describes the cross and the throne. For this author, they are one event.

The verb helkyso ("I will draw") appeared in 6:44: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws (helkyse) him." In chapter 6, it is the Father who draws; here, it is Jesus who draws. The unity of action between Father and Son — "I and the Father are one" (10:30) — is expressed in the shared act of drawing all people. And the scope has widened: in 6:44, the drawing was described without specifying its extent; here, it is pantas — all, everyone, without distinction of Jew or Gentile. The Greeks who have just arrived seeking Jesus are the first evidence of this universal drawing, which will continue through the testimony of the community after Jesus's departure.

"He was saying this to indicate the kind of death by which he was about to die." The author's editorial comment ensures the reader does not miss the referent of "lifted up." The hypsoo language is about crucifixion — the physical lifting of the body on the cross. The author wants no ambiguity: the exaltation is the cross, and the cross is the exaltation.

"We have heard out of the Law that the Christ is to remain forever; and how can you say, 'The Son of Man must be lifted up'? Who is this Son of Man?" The crowd's objection reveals their messianic expectations. "The Christ is to remain forever" (ho Christos menei eis ton aiona) draws on texts like Psalm 89:36-37 (LXX 88:37-38): "His seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before me; it shall be established forever like the moon" (cf. 2 Samuel 7:13, 16; Isaiah 9:7; Daniel 7:14: "His dominion is an everlasting dominion which will not pass away"). The crowd knows the Christ is supposed to reign permanently. A Christ who is "lifted up" — who dies — contradicts their expectation of an eternal king. Their question "Who is this Son of Man?" expresses genuine confusion: the categories Jesus uses do not fit the framework they possess.

The crowd's confusion is the same as Peter's reaction to the suffering Messiah in the Synoptic accounts (Mark 8:31-33), though this author presents it in the crowd rather than in a single disciple. The idea that the Messiah must die was, for first-century Jewish expectation broadly understood, a scandal. The expectation was for a conquering, reigning, permanent deliverer. The Messiah's death was not a category most hearers possessed. This is why the "lifting up" requires explanation: the cross is not the defeat of the messianic mission but its accomplishment, though almost no one present can see this.

"For a little while longer the Light is among you. Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you." Jesus does not answer the crowd's question directly. Instead, he returns to the light-darkness framework that has been in operation since the prologue (1:4-5, 9) and was explicitly claimed in 8:12 and 9:5. His presence — the Light — is temporary. The language echoes 7:33-34: "For a little while longer I am with you, then I go to him who sent me. You will seek me, and will not find me." The urgency is the same as 9:4: "We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming when no one can work." The window of direct access to the Light in the flesh is closing.

**"Walk while you have the Light" (peripatein hos to phos echete) — the imperative is present tense, indicating ongoing activity. Walking "in the light" throughout this document means living in response to the revelation Jesus brings (8:12: "he who follows me will not walk in the darkness"). The alternative — walking in darkness — is to "not know where he goes" (ouk oiden pou hypagei). Without the light, there is no orientation, no direction, no knowledge of destination. The language applies to the crowd standing before him and to all who encounter the choice between light and darkness.

"While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of Light" (hos to phos echete, pisteuete eis to phos, hina huioi photos genesthe). The phrase "sons of light" (huioi photos) designates those who belong to the light, whose identity is constituted by the light. The construction "son of X" (ben/huios + noun) is a Semitic idiom expressing essential character or origin: "sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17), "son of perdition" (17:12), "sons of disobedience" (LXX). To become "sons of light" is not merely to admire the light or acknowledge it but to be identified by it — to be, in one's essential character, shaped by and belonging to the light. The imperative "believe" (pisteuete, present tense) calls for ongoing, active trust in the light while it is accessible. The opportunity is temporal; the transformation it produces is permanent.

div.title: Verses 36b-43: The Author's Commentary on Israel's Unbelief
div.p: "These things Jesus spoke, and he went away and hid himself from them. But though he had performed so many signs before them, yet they were not believing in him. This was to fulfill the word of Isaiah the prophet which he spoke: 'Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' For this reason they could not believe, for Isaiah said again, 'He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes and perceive with their heart, and be converted and I heal them.' These things Isaiah said because he saw his glory, and he spoke of him. Nevertheless many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they were not confessing him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the approval of men rather than the approval of God."

"He went away and hid himself from them" (apelthen kai ekrybe ap' auton). The verb krypto ("to hide") appeared in 8:59, where Jesus "hid himself and went out of the temple." But here the hiding is not momentary evasion of a stoning attempt; it is permanent withdrawal from public ministry. Jesus's public teaching and signs, which have been the content of the document since chapter 1, are over. The Light that has been shining has now withdrawn. The remaining chapters will be addressed to "his own" (13:1) — not to the kosmos. The verb ekrybe is passive in form (was hidden, hid himself), suggesting both Jesus's own action and the Father's timing: the hour has come, and the public ministry's purpose is fulfilled.

"Though he had performed so many signs before them, yet they were not believing in him" (tosauta de autou semeia pepoiekotos emprosthen auton ouk episteuon eis auton). The "so many signs" (tosauta semeia) is the author's retrospective summary. The water-to-wine at Cana (2:1-11), the healing of the official's son (4:46-54), the healing at Bethesda (5:1-9), the feeding of the five thousand (6:1-14), the walking on water (6:16-21), the healing of the man born blind (9:1-7), and the raising of Lazarus (11:38-44) — each sign was a revelation of glory (2:11), a display of the Father's works (5:36, 10:25, 32), a witness to Jesus's identity and mission. And yet: "they were not believing" (ouk episteuon, imperfect tense — they continued in unbelief despite the accumulating evidence). The imperfect tense describes a settled condition, not a momentary lapse. The signs did not produce the response they should have produced.

"This was to fulfill the word of Isaiah the prophet" (hina ho logos Esaiou tou prophetou plerothe). The hina ("so that, in order that") clause raises the question of whether the unbelief was foreordained. The author's usage of hina throughout the document is complex. In some cases it indicates purpose ("so that"); in others it indicates result ("with the result that"); in still others it marks the content of a statement. The function here is to locate the unbelief within the prophetic framework: Isaiah already described this response, and the events of Jesus's ministry fulfill what Isaiah described. The author is not arguing that God arbitrarily prevented belief but that the pattern Isaiah described — the prophet's message being rejected, the arm of the LORD going unrecognized — is the same pattern now being enacted on a larger scale.

"Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" (kyrie, tis episteusen te akoe hemon; kai ho brachion kyriou tini apekalyphthe). The quotation is from Isaiah 53:1 (LXX). The passage is the opening verse of the fourth Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13-53:12), which describes the suffering servant of the LORD — despised, rejected, bearing the sins of many, "like a lamb that is led to slaughter" (53:7). The two questions are rhetorical and expect the answer "almost no one." The "report" (akoe, literally "hearing") is the prophetic message; the "arm of the LORD" (brachion kyriou) is God's saving power in action. The arm of the LORD is a standard scriptural idiom for God's mighty acts of deliverance: Exodus 6:6, "I will redeem you with an outstretched arm (brachiōn)"; Deuteronomy 4:34, 5:15, 7:19, 26:8; Isaiah 40:10, 51:9, 52:10. In Isaiah 53, the arm of the LORD is the saving work accomplished through the servant's suffering — and it goes unrecognized. The people look at the servant's affliction and assume he is "stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted" (53:4), when in reality "he was pierced through for our transgressions" (53:5).

The application to Jesus is direct. The signs were the arm of the LORD in action — the power of God displayed in healing, feeding, raising the dead. The message was the report — the teaching about the Father and the Son, the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd. And yet: who believed? The pattern of Isaiah 53 is replicated: God's saving power, enacted through a figure who will suffer and die, goes unrecognized by those who witness it.

"For this reason they could not believe, for Isaiah said again, 'He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes and perceive with their heart, and be converted and I heal them.'" The second quotation is from Isaiah 6:10, the prophet's commissioning vision. In Isaiah 6, the prophet sees the LORD seated on his throne, high and lifted up (hypselos kai eperemenon, Isaiah 6:1 LXX), attended by seraphim who cry "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory" (6:3). The prophet responds with confession of unworthiness (6:5), is cleansed by a coal from the altar (6:6-7), and is then commissioned: "Go, and tell this people: 'Keep on listening, but do not perceive; keep on looking, but do not understand.' Render the hearts of this people insensitive, their ears dull, and their eyes dim, otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and return and be healed" (Isaiah 6:9-10).

The passage is one of the most difficult in the prophetic corpus. Its language suggests that God deliberately prevents repentance. But the context in Isaiah 6 provides an explanation: the commission comes after the people's hearts have already been rendered insensitive by their own persistent refusal. The blinding and hardening described in Isaiah 6:10 is not an arbitrary act imposed on willing hearts but a judicial confirmation of a condition the people have chosen. Israel has been rejecting God's messengers for generations; God now announces that this rejection will continue and deepen. The hardening is judgment on prior refusal, not a cause of initial refusal.

This interpretation is consistent with what the author has shown throughout the document. The Pharisees rejected the evidence of the healed man in chapter 9 not because they were prevented from seeing but because they refused to see what contradicted their authority (9:24, 34, 40-41). Jesus told them: "If you were blind, you would have no sin; but since you say, 'We see,' your sin remains" (9:41). Their blindness is culpable, self-chosen — and then confirmed by divine judgment. The pattern is the same in 3:19-21: "This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their deeds were evil." The loving of darkness is the human act; the hardening is God's response to that act.

The author modifies the Isaiah 6:10 text slightly. Where Isaiah says "make the heart of this people fat" (pachynai, LXX), the author says "he hardened their heart" (eporosēn autōn tēn kardian). The verb poroo ("to harden, petrify") is used elsewhere for the disciples' own failure to understand (Mark 6:52, 8:17) and for Israel's hardening (Romans 11:7). The change to the active voice with God as subject ("he hardened") sharpens the agency: God is the one who acts, but the action is judicial, in response to the prior condition the people have cultivated through sustained refusal.

"These things Isaiah said because he saw his glory, and he spoke of him" (tauta eipen Esaias hoti eiden ten doxan autou, kai elalesen peri autou). This is an extraordinary statement. The author identifies the glory Isaiah saw in Isaiah 6:1-5 — "I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up" (LXX: eidon ton kyrion kathemenon epi thronou hypselou kai epermenou) — as Jesus's glory. The pronoun "his" (autou) refers to Jesus. Isaiah's vision in the temple was a vision of the pre-incarnate Word's glory. This is consistent with the prologue: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (1:1). If the Word was God, then the glory of God that Isaiah saw was the glory of the Word. The author does not flinch from the identification: the LORD seated on the throne in Isaiah's vision is the same person who now walks the streets of Jerusalem in flesh and will shortly be lifted up on a cross. The seraphim's "Holy, holy, holy" was spoken about the Word who became flesh and tabernacled among us (1:14).

This identification also means that the hardening described in Isaiah 6:10 — the hardening that occurred when Isaiah's people rejected the message about the glorious LORD — is the same hardening now occurring when Jesus's hearers reject the message about the one whose glory Isaiah saw. The pattern is consistent across centuries: the same glory provokes the same response, because the same human condition — the love of darkness rather than light — persists.

"Nevertheless many even of the rulers believed in him" (homos mentoi kai ek ton archonton polloi episteusan eis auton). The word homos ("nevertheless, all the same") introduces an important qualification. The hardening is not absolute. Even among the rulers (archontes — members of the Sanhedrin, the governing class), many believed. The hardening described in Isaiah 6:10 has not prevented all from seeing; it has confirmed the blindness of those who chose blindness. Others, even within the hostile establishment, have been able to perceive.

"But because of the Pharisees they were not confessing him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue" (alla dia tous Pharisaious ouch homologoun, hina me aposynagogoi genontai). The word aposynagogos ("expelled from the synagogue") appeared in 9:22, where the author explained that the Jews had agreed to excommunicate anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ. The same threat that shaped the behavior of the healed man's parents (9:22-23) now shapes the behavior of believing rulers. They believe but do not confess. Their belief is real (episteusan is aorist — they believed) but their confession is absent (ouch homologoun, imperfect — they continued not confessing).

This creates a significant tension with the document's own teaching about belief. In 1:12, the children of God are those who "received him" and "believed in his name." In 3:16-18, the one who believes has eternal life; the one who does not believe is condemned already. In 5:24, the one who hears and believes has passed from death to life. But in 8:31-32, Jesus told those "who had believed in him" that true discipleship requires continuing in his word. And in 6:60-66, many disciples who had been following withdrew and "were not walking with him anymore." The pattern throughout the document is that belief is not a single moment but an ongoing condition that can be genuine yet incomplete, or initial yet unsustained. These rulers represent a category the document does not celebrate: those whose belief does not issue in confession, whose faith is real but hidden, whose allegiance is privately held but publicly denied.

"For they loved the approval of men rather than the approval of God" (egapesan gar ten doxan ton anthropon mallon eper ten doxan tou theou). The word doxa here is translated "approval" or "glory" — the same word used for God's glory (1:14), the glory of the signs (2:11), and the glorification of the Son of Man (12:23). The rulers are confronted with a choice between two kinds of doxa: the doxa that comes from people (status, reputation, position within the ruling class) and the doxa that comes from God (the approval of the one who sent Jesus). They choose the former.

This diagnosis was anticipated in 5:44: "How can you believe, when you receive glory (doxan) from one another and you do not seek the glory (doxan) that is from the one and only God?" In chapter 5, the question was addressed to the same leadership class. The answer is now given: they cannot fully believe — or rather, their belief cannot produce confession — because they love human glory more than divine glory. The obstacle to confession is not intellectual but moral and social: they fear the loss of status more than they fear the loss of God's approval.

The verb egapesan ("they loved") uses the aorist tense of agapao, the same verb used for God's love in 3:16 ("God so loved the world"). The irony is sharp: God loved the world enough to give his Son; these rulers loved human approval enough to deny the Son. The same verb describes two loves moving in opposite directions.

div.title: Verses 44-50: Jesus's Final Public Declaration
div.p: "And Jesus cried out and said, 'He who believes in me, does not believe in me but in him who sent me. He who sees me sees the one who sent me. I have come as Light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me will not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my sayings and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world. He who rejects me and does not receive my sayings, has one who judges him; the word I spoke is what will judge him at the last day. For I did not speak on my own initiative, but the Father himself who sent me has given me a commandment as to what to say and what to speak. I know that his commandment is eternal life; therefore the things I speak, I speak just as the Father has told me.'"

"Jesus cried out" (Iesous ekraxen). The verb krazo ("to cry out, shout") indicates a public, forceful utterance. The same verb was used in 7:28 ("Then Jesus cried out in the temple, teaching") and 7:37 ("on the last day, the great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink'"). This is Jesus's final public cry. It functions as a summary and recapitulation of the themes of the entire public ministry, delivered at its conclusion with the urgency of a last appeal.

The placement is significant. After the note that Jesus "hid himself from them" (12:36b), the author has inserted the theological commentary on unbelief (12:37-43). Now Jesus speaks once more — a final, compressed declaration before the public voice falls silent. Whether this is temporally after the hiding or a summary statement the author places here as a thematic conclusion is debated; what matters is its function: it recapitulates the document's central arguments at the close of the public ministry.

"He who believes in me, does not believe in me but in him who sent me" (ho pisteuon eis eme ou pisteuei eis eme alla eis ton pempsanta me). The statement is paradoxical: believing in Jesus is believing in the Father. The relationship between Father and Son is so complete that faith directed toward Jesus reaches the Father who sent him. The claim has been made repeatedly: "I and the Father are one" (10:30); "the Father is in me, and I in the Father" (10:38); "I did not come of myself, but he who sent me is true" (7:28). The formulation here — "not in me but in him who sent me" — does not diminish Jesus but elevates the act of believing in him by identifying it with believing in God. To receive the sent one is to receive the sender (13:20: "he who receives whomever I send receives me; and he who receives me receives him who sent me").

"He who sees me sees the one who sent me" (ho theoron eme theorei ton pempsanta me). The verb theoreo ("to see, observe, perceive") is used for purposeful looking that leads to understanding (2:23, 6:40, 14:17, 19). Jesus is the visible form of the invisible God. The author stated this in the prologue: "No one has seen God at any time; the only begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father, he has explained him" (1:18). Jesus is the exegesis (exegesato) of the Father — the interpretation, the explanation, the visible display. To see Jesus is to see the Father because Jesus is the Father's self-revelation in flesh.

"I have come as Light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me will not remain in darkness" (ego phos eis ton kosmon eleltha, hina pas ho pisteuon eis eme en te skotia me meine). The light-darkness framework returns for the last time in the public ministry. The claim restates 8:12 ("I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in the darkness") and 9:5 ("While I am in the world, I am the light of the world"). The purpose clause — "so that everyone who believes in me will not remain (me meine) in darkness" — uses the verb meno ("to remain, abide, stay"). The word meno is one of the most important in this document (appearing over forty times), carrying the sense of permanent dwelling. The promise is that the one who believes will not remain in darkness — will not stay in the condition of not-seeing, not-knowing, not-perceiving that characterizes life apart from the light.

The phrase "everyone who believes" (pas ho pisteuon, present participle) describes an ongoing condition, not a past-tense achievement. The one who is believing does not remain in darkness. The active participation of believing is the condition under which the darkness is dispelled. This is consistent with the present-tense grammar of 3:16, 36; 6:35, 40, 47; 10:27-28.

"If anyone hears my sayings and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world." The conjunction of hearing (akouo) and keeping (phylasso, "to guard, keep, observe") recalls 8:51 ("If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death") and anticipates the farewell discourse's emphasis on keeping the commandments (14:15, 21, 23; 15:10, 20). To hear and not keep is the condition of the one who receives the message but does not act on it — a condition illustrated by the rulers of verses 42-43 who believed but did not confess.

Jesus's declaration that he did not come to judge but to save (ou gar elthon hina krino ton kosmon, all' hina soso ton kosmon) echoes 3:17: "God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him." The present mission is salvation, not condemnation. The judgment is real but it is not Jesus's primary purpose; it is the secondary consequence that falls on those who reject the salvation offered.

"He who rejects me and does not receive my sayings, has one who judges him; the word I spoke is what will judge him at the last day." The verb atheteo ("to reject, set aside, nullify") appears only here in this document. The one who rejects Jesus is not left without judgment; the word (logos) Jesus spoke becomes the judge. The word is not inert; it retains its force and its claim. On "the last day" (te eschate hemera) — the phrase used throughout the document for the final reckoning (6:39, 40, 44, 54; 11:24) — the word will serve as the standard of evaluation. Those who heard the word and rejected it will be judged by the word they rejected. The mechanism is self-condemnation: the light shone, and they preferred darkness (3:19). The word spoke, and they refused to receive it. The word itself testifies against them.

"For I did not speak on my own initiative, but the Father himself who sent me has given me a commandment as to what to say and what to speak" (hoti ego ex emautou ouk elalesa, all' ho pempsas me pater autos moi entolen dedoken ti eipo kai ti laleso). The claim of dependence on the Father has been made repeatedly: "I can do nothing on my own initiative" (5:30); "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me" (7:16); "I do nothing on my own initiative, but I speak these things as the Father taught me" (8:28); "I speak the things which I have seen with my Father" (8:38). The word entole ("commandment") appeared in 10:18 ("This commandment I received from my Father" — the commandment to lay down his life and take it up again). Now it extends to the content of Jesus's speech: everything he has said is under the Father's commandment. The words are authorized, not improvised.

"I know that his commandment is eternal life" (oida hoti he entole autou zoe aionios estin). The Father's commandment is identified with eternal life itself. This is not merely a commandment that leads to eternal life; it is (estin) eternal life. The identity between the commandment and the life it confers echoes the identity between the word and the life it bears: "In him was life" (1:4). The commandment the Father gave the Son — to speak, to act, to die, to rise — is the vehicle of eternal life for all who receive it.

"Therefore the things I speak, I speak just as the Father has told me" (ha oun ego lalo, kathos eireken moi ho pater, houtos lalo). The final sentence of the public ministry is a restatement of total alignment with the Father. Jesus speaks what the Father told him, exactly as the Father told him to speak it. The public voice that opened with "In the beginning was the Word" (1:1) closes with the declaration that every word spoken by Jesus in the flesh was the Father's word delivered through the Son. The ministry that began with the Word made flesh ends with the Word declaring that his speech was the Father's speech from beginning to end.

list.item: The chapter closes the public ministry that has occupied chapters 1-11 and opens the path to the cross. After verse 36b, Jesus hides himself from the public. After verse 50, the narrative transitions to the private setting of the Last Supper (chapter 13). Everything Jesus has said and done in public — every sign, every discourse, every confrontation — is finished. The chapter functions as both conclusion and transition: it gathers the themes of the public ministry into a final statement and sets in motion the events that will accomplish the ministry's purpose.

The anointing at Bethany (vv. 1-8) interprets Jesus's approaching death through the act of a woman who gives extravagantly. Mary's anointing of Jesus's feet with costly nard is described by Jesus himself as preparation for his burial. The anointing connects the household of Lazarus (the place where death was reversed) to the approaching death of Jesus (which will reverse death on a universal scale). Judas's objection exposes him as a kleptes — the same word used for the false shepherds of 10:1, 10. The contrast between Mary's lavish self-giving and Judas's self-serving theft anticipates the cross, where Jesus will give everything and Judas will betray him for a price.

The plot to kill Lazarus (vv. 9-11) reveals the authorities' response to the sign: suppress the evidence rather than receive its testimony. The chief priests' determination to kill the man Jesus raised from the dead is the definitive exposure of their posture toward God's works. They do not investigate the sign or inquire about its meaning; they eliminate the witness. The pattern matches Ezekiel 34's indictment of shepherds who harm the flock rather than tend it.

The entry into Jerusalem (vv. 12-19) presents the collision between the crowd's expectations and Jesus's self-presentation. The palm branches and the "Hosanna" shout cast Jesus as a Maccabean-style political liberator. Jesus's choice of a donkey reframes the kingship through Zechariah 9:9: the king who comes is peaceable, not military; his dominion extends to the ends of the earth, not through force but through the laying down of his life. The crowd and the king are speaking different languages. The Pharisees' frustrated observation that "the world has gone after him" is truer than they know, as the arrival of Greeks in the next scene immediately confirms.

The arrival of the Greeks (vv. 20-22) triggers the declaration that the hour has come (v. 23). Throughout the document, Jesus has said "my hour has not yet come" (2:4, 7:30, 8:20). The appearance of Gentile worshipers — the "other sheep" of 10:16, the first fruits of the "children of God scattered abroad" of 11:52 — signals that the moment for the shepherd's self-sacrifice has arrived. The scope of the mission has reached beyond Israel, and the grain of wheat must now fall into the earth so that it does not remain alone.

The grain-of-wheat teaching (vv. 24-26) provides the clearest explanation in the document for the necessity of Jesus's death. The single grain that remains unplanted produces nothing. The grain that falls and dies produces an abundant harvest. The shepherd's death is not a tragedy that the resurrection will later undo; it is the mechanism by which the harvest is produced. The pattern of dying-to-live is then extended to the disciples: the one who loves his life loses it; the one who hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life. The self-sacrificial principle is not unique to Jesus but defines the nature of discipleship for all who follow.

The troubling of Jesus's soul (vv. 27-28) reveals that the voluntary self-sacrifice is costly. Jesus considers and rejects the prayer "Father, save me from this hour." The hour is the very purpose of his coming. Instead he prays for the Father's name to be glorified, and the Father responds with a voice from heaven confirming that the name has been and will be glorified. The voice divides the crowd — some hear thunder, some hear an angel — enacting the pattern of division that has characterized the entire public ministry.

The declarations of judgment, the casting out of the ruler of this world, and the lifting up (vv. 31-33) describe what the cross accomplishes. The cross is the judgment (krisis) of the world-order that opposes God. It is the ejection of the ruler of this world — the power behind the murderous opposition to the light. And it is the universal drawing: "I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." The lifting up is simultaneously crucifixion (physical lifting onto the cross) and exaltation (the glorification of the Son of Man). The drawing is universal in scope (pantas), fulfilling the "other sheep" of 10:16, the "scattered children" of 11:52, and the Greeks of 12:20-22.

The author's commentary on unbelief (vv. 37-43) locates Israel's rejection of Jesus within the prophetic pattern described by Isaiah. Two Isaiah texts are cited: Isaiah 53:1 (the report and arm of the LORD unrecognized) and Isaiah 6:10 (the blinding and hardening of eyes and hearts). The author identifies Isaiah's vision of the LORD's glory (Isaiah 6:1-5) as a vision of Jesus's glory, stating that Isaiah "saw his glory and spoke of him." The hardening is judicial — a confirmation of the blindness the people have chosen — not an arbitrary prevention of belief, as the document has consistently shown that the resistance is rooted in the love of darkness (3:19), the refusal to hear (8:43, 47), and the preference for self-preservation over truth (9:22, 34).

The believing rulers who do not confess (vv. 42-43) represent a deficient form of faith that the document does not validate. They believe but do not confess because they love human glory more than divine glory. This echoes 5:44 ("How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another?") and stands as a warning: belief that does not produce public allegiance — that remains hidden for fear of social consequences — falls short of what this document means by believing. The contrast is between the man born blind, who confessed at the cost of expulsion (9:34-38), and these rulers, who suppress confession to retain their position.

Jesus's final public declaration (vv. 44-50) recapitulates the central themes of the entire public ministry in compressed form. Believing in Jesus is believing in the Father who sent him. Seeing Jesus is seeing the Father. Jesus has come as light so that believers do not remain in darkness. The word Jesus spoke will judge those who reject it on the last day. Jesus spoke nothing on his own initiative; every word was the Father's commandment, and that commandment is eternal life. The public voice closes with a reaffirmation of total unity between Father and Son — the unity that grounds every claim, every sign, and every invitation of the preceding eleven chapters.

The chapter brings the document's treatment of human agency and divine action into sharpest focus. On one hand, God hardens, God draws, God gives the commandment, God glorifies his name. On the other hand, humans choose: Mary gives extravagantly, Judas steals, the crowd waves palms with misguided expectations, the rulers suppress their own belief, the Greeks seek Jesus, the disciples fail to understand. The interplay between divine sovereignty and human responsibility is not resolved into a formula but held in tension, as it has been throughout: the Father draws (6:44), and the one who hears and learns from the Father comes (6:45); the hardening is real (12:40), and the love of darkness is the human act that precedes it (3:19). The chapter closes the public ministry with this tension intact, leaving the reader to reckon with both realities.

The light-darkness framework that began in the prologue (1:4-5) reaches its conclusion in the public ministry at verse 36. The light has come into the world (1:9, 3:19, 8:12, 9:5, 12:35, 46). The darkness has not comprehended it (1:5). Those who come to the light are exposed and transformed (3:21). Those who love darkness remain in it (3:19). The public ministry was the period when "the Light is among you" (12:35); now, as Jesus hides himself, the light withdraws from public availability. What remains is the word, which will judge on the last day (12:48), and the Spirit, which will come after Jesus's glorification (7:39, 14:16-17, 26; 16:7-15). The public shining of the light in the flesh is over. The chapter is the sunset of the incarnate ministry's public phase.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 12): Chapter 12 marks the end of Jesus's public ministry in this document. The chapter opens with the anointing at Bethany, where Mary anoints Jesus's feet with costly perfume — an act Jesus interprets as preparation for his burial (12:7). Judas objects on the pretense of concern for the poor, and the author interrupts to note that Judas "was a thief, and as he had the money box, he used to pilfer what was put into it" (12:6). The entry into Jerusalem follows (12:12-19), with the crowd waving palm branches and crying "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel" (12:13, citing Psalm 118:25-26). The Pharisees' exasperated remark — "You see that you can do nothing; look, the world has gone after him" (12:19) — is immediately confirmed by the arrival of Greeks who seek Jesus (12:20-22). Their arrival prompts Jesus to declare that "the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (12:23), the first time in the document that the "hour" is said to have arrived rather than "not yet come" (2:4, 7:30, 8:20). Jesus then speaks of the grain of wheat that must fall into the earth and die to bear fruit (12:24), of losing one's life to keep it (12:25), and of being "lifted up from the earth" to "draw all people" to himself (12:32). The author notes that the crowd cannot reconcile this talk of death with their understanding of the Messiah: "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever; how can you say, 'The Son of Man must be lifted up'?" (12:34). Jesus urges them to believe in the light while the light is among them (12:35-36a), and then "he departed and hid himself from them" (12:36b).

The author then provides a retrospective summary (12:37-43) explaining why, despite the signs, "they were not believing in him" (12:37). The explanation draws on two texts from Isaiah. First, Isaiah 53:1 (LXX): "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" — the Servant Song's acknowledgment that the message of God's saving work would not be universally received. Second, Isaiah 6:10 (LXX): "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes and perceive with their heart, and be converted and I heal them" — the prophetic commission of judicial hardening. The author then adds a remarkable gloss: "These things Isaiah said because he saw his glory, and he spoke of him" (12:41), identifying the glory Isaiah saw in the temple vision (Isaiah 6:1-3, "I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up") as the glory of Jesus. The section concludes with the observation that "many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they were not confessing him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the approval of men rather than the approval of God" (12:42-43). Finally, Jesus makes a last public declaration summarizing the themes of the entire public ministry: believing in him means believing in the one who sent him (12:44); seeing him means seeing the one who sent him (12:45); he has come as light so that those who believe will not remain in darkness (12:46); his word, not he himself, will judge on the last day (12:48); the Father who sent him gave him commandment regarding what to say and speak, and this commandment is eternal life (12:49-50).

Chapter 12 thus closes the public phase of the document. Every major theme has been stated: the relationship between Father and Son, the light-darkness division, the role of the signs, the judicial hardening of Israel's leaders, the hour of glorification through death, the drawing of all people through the "lifting up," and the cost of confession. The public ministry ends in a mixed verdict: many signs, widespread unbelief, some belief that remains hidden for fear of expulsion.

What the author argues immediately after (John 14): Chapter 14 opens with Jesus continuing to speak to the disciples in the same setting: "Do not let your heart be troubled; you believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you" (14:1-2). The chapter continues the private instruction that began in chapter 13, developing the themes of Jesus's departure and return, the relationship between the disciples and the Father, and the promise of the Spirit. Thomas asks "Lord, we do not know where you are going; how do we know the way?" and Jesus responds: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father but through me" (14:5-6). Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus replies: "He who has seen me has seen the Father" (14:9). The promise of "another Helper" (allon parakleton), the Spirit of truth, is given for the first time (14:16-17, 26). Jesus promises: "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you" (14:18). The mutual indwelling theme from 10:38 is extended to include the disciples: "In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you" (14:20). The chapter concludes with Jesus repeating his commandment of love (14:21, 23-24), promising peace (14:27), and announcing his departure: "I go away, and I will come to you... I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (14:28).

How chapter 13 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 12 ended with Jesus's withdrawal from public view ("he departed and hid himself from them," 12:36b) and a final public declaration that concluded the themes of the public ministry. Chapter 13 opens a fundamentally new section of the document. The audience shifts from the crowds, the religious authorities, and the public at large to the intimate circle of Jesus's own disciples. The setting shifts from the temple courts, the festival crowds, and the public spaces of Jerusalem to a private supper. The temporal horizon shifts from the ongoing work of signs and teaching to the immediate threshold of Jesus's death — "before the Feast of the Passover, Jesus knowing that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father" (13:1). The thematic focus shifts from the question "Who is Jesus?" (answered through signs, discourses, and confrontations) to the question "What must the disciples know and become before Jesus leaves?"

Chapter 13 is the hinge between these two phases. It performs three essential functions. First, it enacts the transition from public ministry to private instruction through a symbolic action — the washing of the disciples' feet — that embodies the meaning of Jesus's impending death and establishes the pattern for the community's life after his departure. Second, it identifies and removes the betrayer from the community, drawing a line between those who are "clean" and the one who is not, so that the teaching that follows in chapters 14-17 is addressed only to those who belong to Jesus. Third, it introduces the "new commandment" — to love one another as Jesus has loved them — which will be the defining mark of the community and the theme that pervades the remainder of Jesus's private instruction (14:15, 21, 23-24; 15:9-17; 17:26). The foot-washing, the departure of Judas, and the new commandment together establish the conditions under which the farewell discourse of chapters 14-17 takes place.

The chapter also fulfills and extends themes from the public ministry. The good shepherd who "lays down his life for the sheep" (10:11, 15, 17-18) now demonstrates what that laying-down looks like in practice: taking the form of a servant, washing feet, loving "to the end" (eis telos, 13:1). The grain of wheat that falls into the earth and dies (12:24) is about to fall. The "hour" that had "not yet come" throughout the first twelve chapters (2:4, 7:30, 8:20) has now arrived (12:23, 13:1). The light that shone in the public ministry is now concentrated on the small circle that will carry it forward, and the darkness is embodied not in the hostile authorities but in one of Jesus's own: "it was night" (13:30).

div.title: The Passover Setting and the Author's Theological Introduction (Verses 1-3)
div.p: "Now before the Feast of the Passover, Jesus knowing that his hour had come that he would depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going back to God..."

"Before the Feast of the Passover" (pro de tes heortes tou pascha). The temporal marker places the events of chapter 13 before the Passover meal itself. This creates a chronological tension with the Synoptic accounts, where the Last Supper is the Passover meal. In this document, the Passover has not yet occurred at the time of the supper described here; Jesus will be crucified on the day of preparation for the Passover, at the time the Passover lambs are being slaughtered in the temple (19:14, 31, 42). The author has structured the entire narrative so that Jesus dies as the Passover lamb — John the Baptist's identification of Jesus as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (1:29) and the notation that no bone of his body was broken (19:36, echoing the Passover instructions of Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12) converge in the timing: the true Passover lamb dies at the hour the temple lambs are killed. This chronological framing means the supper of chapter 13 is not the Passover meal but a meal that precedes it, and the foot-washing and the discourse that follows are set in the shadow of the approaching Passover.

The Passover itself is the foundational narrative of Israel's deliverance. Exodus 12 recounts how God brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt through the blood of the lamb applied to the doorposts, the angel of death passing over the marked houses, and the exodus itself — the departure "out of" (ek) Egypt into freedom. The Passover is therefore a narrative of departure, deliverance, and transition from bondage to a new identity as God's people. The author opens chapter 13 by describing Jesus's departure "out of this world to the Father" (ek tou kosmou toutou... pros ton patera) in language that echoes the exodus pattern: a departure from one condition to another, accomplished through the death of the lamb. Jesus is simultaneously the lamb whose death effects the deliverance and the leader who goes ahead, as Moses went ahead of Israel.

"Jesus knowing that his hour had come that he would depart out of this world to the Father" (eidos ho Iesous hoti elthen autou he hora hina metabe ek tou kosmou toutou pros ton patera). Three elements require attention.

First, "knowing" (eidos). The participle indicates Jesus's full awareness. He is not surprised by what is about to happen; he acts with complete knowledge. This continues the pattern of sovereign awareness the author has maintained: Jesus "knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was that would betray him" (6:64), "knew what he was going to do" before the feeding of the multitude (6:6), and declared that he lays down his life "on my own initiative" (10:18). Everything that follows in this chapter — the foot-washing, the identification of the betrayer, the new commandment — is performed by one who knows exactly where the evening will lead.

Second, "his hour had come" (elthen autou he hora). The "hour" (hora) has been the document's central temporal concept since 2:4, where Jesus told his mother at Cana, "My hour has not yet come." The same "not yet" appeared at the Feast of Tabernacles: "No one seized him, because his hour had not yet come" (7:30, 8:20). In 12:23, Jesus declared for the first time that "the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." Now the arrival of the hour is stated as accomplished fact (elthen, aorist: "has come"). The hour is the hour of his departure through death and return to the Father — it encompasses the cross, the resurrection, and the ascension as a single movement. In 12:27, Jesus had acknowledged the anguish of this hour ("Now my soul has become troubled; and what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I came to this hour") and then submitted to it. Now the hour is here, and Jesus acts within it with full purpose.

Third, "depart out of this world to the Father" (metabe ek tou kosmou toutou pros ton patera). The verb metabaino means "to pass over, to cross from one place to another, to make a transition." It appeared in 5:24: "He who hears my word, and believes him who sent me, has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life" (metabebeken ek tou thanatou eis ten zoen). The same verb now describes Jesus's own passage: he crosses from this world to the Father, just as the believer crosses from death to life. The death is not an end but a crossing — a passover, in the deepest sense of the word. The language frames the entire Passion not as tragedy but as transition: Jesus goes from here to the Father.

"Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end" (agapesas tous idious tous en to kosmo, eis telos egapesen autous). This is the author's summary statement, the interpretive key for everything that follows in chapters 13-17. Several elements are critical.

"His own" (tous idious): The phrase "his own" (ta idia / hoi idioi) has appeared before in this document with two different valences. In 1:11, "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him" — there "his own" referred to Israel, who rejected him. In 10:3-4, the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name and leads them out... he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice" — there "his own" meant the sheep who hear and follow. The usage here in 13:1 is the latter: those who belong to Jesus, who have heard his voice and followed. They are distinguished from "the world" (ton kosmon) in which they exist but to which they do not belong — a distinction that will be developed extensively in chapters 14-17 (especially 15:18-19: "If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, because of this the world hates you"; and 17:14-16).

"He loved them to the end" (eis telos egapesen autous): The phrase eis telos can mean "to the end" in two senses: temporally ("to the very last moment, until the end") and qualitatively ("to the uttermost, completely, to the fullest extent"). Both senses operate. Temporally, Jesus loves his own until the moment of his departure — he does not withdraw his love even as betrayal, denial, and abandonment approach. Qualitatively, the love reaches its ultimate expression in what is about to be performed: the foot-washing as enacted love, and the cross as love's full measure. The phrase signals that everything in the chapter — the basin, the towel, the warning about the betrayer, the new commandment — is an expression of this love carried to its completion.

"During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him" (deipnou ginomenou, tou diabolou ede beblekotos eis ten kardian hina paradoi auton Ioudas Simonos Iskariotes). The author interrupts the narrative to note that the devil has already placed the intention of betrayal into Judas's heart. The verb beblekotos (perfect participle of ballo, "to throw, put, cast") indicates a completed action: the decision has already been made, the die already cast. The devil (ho diabolos, "the slanderer, the accuser") appeared in 8:44, where Jesus told the unbelieving authorities: "You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth because there is no truth in him." The devil's work is murder and falsehood; Judas's betrayal will lead to murder, and the betrayal itself is an act of deception from within the circle of trust.

The identification of Judas by patronymic — "son of Simon" (Simonos) — distinguishes him from other figures named Judas (14:22: "Judas, not Iscariot") and anchors the betrayer as a specific, known individual. The author has already flagged Judas's character: he was a thief who pilfered from the common purse (12:6), and the earlier notation that "Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was that would betray him" (6:64) has been shadowing the narrative since the bread-of-life discourse. The betrayal is not a surprise but a known element in the drama, part of what Jesus acts within.

"Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going back to God" (eidos ho Iesous hoti panta edoken auto ho pater eis tas cheiras, kai hoti apo theou exelthen kai pros ton theon hypagei). This second "knowing" clause is extraordinary in its juxtaposition with what Jesus is about to do. The one who knows that all things are in his hands — all authority, all power, the cosmos itself (1:3, "all things came into being through him") — is about to kneel on the floor and wash feet. The one who knows his origin (he came forth from God) and his destination (he is going back to God) performs the act of a household slave. The author constructs the contrast deliberately: the greater the authority, the more astonishing the self-lowering. The claim is not that Jesus washes feet despite his authority but because his authority allows him to do what no one else's status permits. Only the one who holds all things in his hands can freely empty those hands to hold a basin and towel.

The phrase "the Father had given all things into his hands" (panta edoken auto ho pater eis tas cheiras) echoes 3:35 ("The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand") and 10:29 ("My Father, who has given them to me"). The "hands" into which all things have been given are the same hands that will wash the disciples' feet. The hand imagery from 10:28-29 — "no one will snatch them out of my hand... no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand" — is now enacted in a different register: the hand of power becomes the hand of service. The shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep first takes up a towel and serves them.

div.title: Verses 4-5: The Foot-Washing
div.p: "Got up from supper, and laid aside his garments; and taking a towel, he girded himself. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded."
"Got up from supper, and laid aside his garments" (egeiretai ek tou deipnou kai tithesi ta himatia). Two verbs carry symbolic weight beyond their literal meaning.

The verb "got up" (egeiretai) is a form of egeiro, which throughout this document and the broader apostolic literature is the verb used for resurrection — raising from the dead (2:19-22, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up"; 5:21, "For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life"; 12:1, 9, 17, of the raised Lazarus). While here it means simply "rose from the table," the reader who has been trained by this author's habit of layered language can hear a faint resonance with the resurrection: the one who rises from the supper to serve will rise from the tomb to live.

The verb "laid aside" (tithesi) is the same verb used in 10:11, 15, 17-18 for the shepherd laying down his life: "the good shepherd lays down (tithesi) his life for the sheep." In 10:18: "I lay it down (tithemi) on my own initiative." The deliberate use of the same verb for setting aside garments and laying down life creates a verbal link: this laying aside is a preview of that laying down. The garments stand for the life itself — the external covering, the visible identity that will be stripped away at the cross (19:23-24, where the soldiers divide his garments). Jesus's voluntary removal of his garments at the supper anticipates his voluntary submission to their removal at the crucifixion.

The word "garments" (himatia, the outer robe or cloak) is the same word used in 19:23 when the soldiers "took his outer garments" (ta himatia autou). The parallel is unmistakable for the reader of the complete document: the garments laid aside at the supper are the garments stripped at the cross. In both cases, the removal is Jesus's own act in the deeper sense — he lays them aside voluntarily (10:18).

"Taking a towel, he girded himself" (labon lention diezosen heauton). The lention ("towel, linen cloth") was the working garment of a slave. The verb diazonnymi ("to gird, to tie around the waist") describes the posture of a servant preparing to work. In the LXX, "girding" is associated with preparation for labor or battle (Exodus 12:11, "your loins girded" for the Passover meal; 1 Kings 18:46, Elijah girded his loins to run before Ahab). But the towel identifies the specific labor: not battle, not travel, but domestic service. The one who in the prologue was identified as the Word through whom all things were made, who was with God and was God (1:1-3), now wears the garment of a household slave.

"He poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel" (eita ballei hydor eis ton niptera, kai erxato niptein tous podas ton matheton kai ekmassein to lentio ho en diezomenos). The action is described with physical specificity: pouring water, washing feet, drying them. The verb nipto ("to wash" a part of the body, as opposed to louo, "to bathe the whole body" — a distinction that will become significant in verse 10) describes the cleansing of the feet, the lowest and dirtiest part of the body. In first-century Palestine, where roads were unpaved and sandals were the standard footwear, feet accumulated dust, mud, and filth. Foot-washing was performed upon entering a home and was universally regarded as the task of the lowest-ranking servant. In Jewish practice, the duty of washing a master's feet could be imposed on Gentile slaves or on the disciples of a rabbi, but it was considered too demeaning for a Jewish slave. The Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael on Exodus 21:2 (though codified later, reflecting earlier practice) distinguishes between duties a Hebrew slave must perform and duties that only a Canaanite slave can be required to perform, and foot-washing falls in the latter category. A rabbi might have his disciples carry his sandals, but to wash feet was beneath even a disciple's expected service.

Jesus, the teacher (13:13, "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am"), performs the act that was beneath the lowest disciple. The act is not merely humble; it violates the social hierarchy that defined teacher-student relationships in first-century Judaism. The teacher does not serve the student; the student serves the teacher. By reversing this, Jesus does not merely model humility as a virtue; he overturns the entire framework of honor and status that structured communal life.

The verb ekmasso ("to wipe off, dry") appeared in 11:2 and 12:3, where Mary wiped Jesus's feet with her hair after anointing them. The verbal connection links the two scenes: Mary served Jesus by anointing and wiping his feet; Jesus now serves the disciples by washing and wiping theirs. What Mary did for Jesus out of devotion, Jesus now does for his disciples out of love. The pattern of self-lowering service flows from Jesus and extends to all who follow him.

div.title: Verses 6-11: The Exchange with Peter
div.p: "So he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, 'Lord, do you wash my feet?' Jesus answered and said to him, 'What I do you do not realize now, but you will understand hereafter.' Peter said to him, 'Never shall you wash my feet!' Jesus answered him, 'If I do not wash you, you have no part with me.' Simon Peter said to him, 'Lord, then wash not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.' Jesus said to him, 'He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean; and you are clean, but not all of you.' For he knew the one who was betraying him; for this reason he said, 'Not all of you are clean.'"

"Lord, do you wash my feet?" (Kyrie, sy mou nipteis tous podas). Peter's question emphasizes the pronouns with force: "You — my feet?" The word order in Greek places the emphatic contrast on "you" (sy) and "my" (mou). Peter's objection is not about the act of foot-washing itself but about who is performing it and for whom. The Lord washes the servant's feet — this inverts everything Peter understands about the relationship between teacher and disciple, master and follower. Peter's resistance is not disobedience but a recognition of the scandal: the one Peter has confessed as Lord (6:68-69, "You are the Holy One of God") cannot be the one kneeling at his feet with a basin.

"What I do you do not realize now, but you will understand hereafter" (ho ego poio sy ouk oidas arti, gnose de meta tauta). The word arti ("now, at this present moment") is contrasted with meta tauta ("after these things, hereafter"). Jesus acknowledges that the meaning of the foot-washing is not transparent; it will be understood only in light of what comes after — the cross, the resurrection, the coming of the Spirit who "will teach you all things" (14:26) and "guide you into all the truth" (16:13). The foot-washing is a sign that requires future events to interpret it, just as the signs throughout the document required discourse to interpret them (the feeding required the bread-of-life discourse; the blind man's healing required the shepherd discourse). The full meaning of the foot-washing will become clear only when the disciples see the garments laid aside on the cross, the body broken for them, and the risen Lord who returns and breathes the Spirit upon them (20:22). The phrase meta tauta also echoes the author's frequent use of "after these things" as a narrative transition (2:12, 3:22, 5:1, 6:1, 7:1, 19:28, 21:1), connecting this moment to the larger sequence of events the document narrates.

"Never shall you wash my feet!" (ou me nipseis mou tous podas eis ton aiona). Peter uses the strongest possible negation: ou me ("by no means, never") plus eis ton aiona ("unto the age, forever"). The absoluteness of Peter's refusal mirrors the absoluteness of the promises throughout the document (6:35, "will never hunger"; 8:51, "will never see death"; 10:28, "will never perish"; 11:26, "will never die"). Peter uses the language of permanence and totality to refuse what Jesus is doing. The irony is that Peter's refusal, motivated by reverence, would place him outside the community: if Jesus does not wash him, he has no part with Jesus.

"If I do not wash you, you have no part with me" (ean me nipso se, ouk echeis meros met' emou). The word meros ("part, share, portion") carries deep significance in Israel's scriptures. The word is used in the LXX for the allocation of inheritance among the tribes. Deuteronomy 10:9: "Levi has no portion (meros) or inheritance with his brothers; the LORD is his inheritance." Deuteronomy 12:12: "the Levite... has no portion (meros) or inheritance with you." Psalm 73:26 (LXX 72:26): "God is... my portion (meris) forever." The meros is one's share in the covenant inheritance, one's place in the community of God's people. To have no meros with Jesus is to be excluded from the relationship, the community, and the inheritance that Jesus is establishing. Jesus's statement reframes the foot-washing from an optional act of humility to a necessary condition of belonging: the disciples must receive Jesus's service in order to have a part with him.

This is a reversal of the usual direction of service. Throughout the document, people have come to Jesus seeking what he can give — life, healing, bread, water, sight. Here Jesus tells Peter that he must receive something he does not want and does not think he needs. The act of receiving Jesus's lowly service is itself a condition of belonging. The disciple who refuses to be served by the master cannot be the master's disciple. The community Jesus is forming is one in which the leader serves and the followers must accept being served — a framework that directly challenges the honor-shame dynamics of the ancient world.

"Lord, then wash not only my feet, but also my hands and my head!" (Kyrie, me tous podas mou monon alla kai tas cheiras kai ten kephalen). Peter swings from absolute refusal to excessive demand. If washing confers belonging, Peter wants as much washing as possible. The response, while expressing devotion, reveals that Peter still does not understand the act. He treats it as a quantitative matter (more washing = more belonging) rather than grasping its qualitative significance.

"He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean" (ho leloumenos ouk echei chreian ei me tous podas nipsasthai, all' estin katharos holos). Jesus introduces a distinction between two kinds of washing. The verb louo ("to bathe the whole body") describes a complete cleansing already accomplished. The verb nipto ("to wash a part of the body") describes the removal of incidental defilement — the dust picked up on the journey from the bath to the house. The one who has bathed (ho leloumenos, perfect participle — indicating a completed action with ongoing results) is already wholly clean (katharos holos). Only the feet — the part that contacts the ground — need additional washing.

The language operates on two levels. On the literal level, it describes a common practice: a guest who had bathed at home before attending a banquet needed only to have the dust washed from his feet upon arrival. On the deeper level, the "bathing" represents the cleansing already accomplished through the disciples' relationship with Jesus — through hearing his word and believing. Jesus said in 15:3, "You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you." The cleansing "by the word" is the bath (louo); the foot-washing (nipto) addresses the ongoing defilement that contact with the world produces. The disciples do not need to be re-cleansed from the ground up; they need the continuous attention to the contamination that daily life in a hostile world produces. The foot-washing thus points to an ongoing practice of mutual care and renewal within the community, not a one-time initiation.

"And you are clean, but not all of you" (kai hymeis katharoi este, all' ouchi pantes). The pronouns shift from the singular "you" (addressed to Peter) to the plural "you" (hymeis, addressed to all the disciples). They are clean (katharoi) — the same word used in the Levitical purity system for ritual cleanness (Leviticus 11-15, where clean/unclean [katharos/akathartos] distinguished what was permitted from what was forbidden). But "not all" (ouchi pantes) introduces the exception.

"For he knew the one who was betraying him; for this reason he said, 'Not all of you are clean'" (edei gar ton paradidonta auton; dia touto eipen hoti ouchi pantes katharoi este). The author explains: the exception is Judas. The one who is "not clean" is the one whose heart the devil has already entered (13:2). The uncleanness is not ritual but moral — it is the uncleanness of betrayal, of treachery against the one who has served you. The present participle ton paradidonta ("the one betraying") indicates an ongoing condition: Judas is in the act of betrayal even now, at the table, as Jesus washes his feet. Jesus washes even the feet of the one he knows will hand him over. The foot-washing does not discriminate: the basin reaches Judas as well as Peter. But the washing does not change Judas's condition because cleanliness, in this document's framework, requires reception of Jesus's word and abiding in it (15:3, 8:31). The water touches Judas's feet, but the word has not entered his heart; the devil has occupied that space instead (13:2).

The statement "not all of you are clean" also establishes a theme that will recur throughout the farewell discourse: not everyone who appears to be in the community genuinely belongs to it. The vine metaphor of chapter 15 will develop this: "Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away" (15:2); "If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away as a branch and dries up" (15:6). Judas is the first and most dramatic instance of a branch that is "in" the vine in appearance but does not bear fruit and will be removed. His presence at the table, his receipt of the washing, and his departure into the night (13:30) enact what the vine metaphor will describe.

div.title: Verses 12-17: The Interpretation of the Foot-Washing
div.p: "So when he had washed their feet, and taken his garments and reclined at the table again, he said to them, 'Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord; and you are right, for so I am. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I gave you an example that you also should do as I did to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, you are blessed if you do them.'"

"Taken his garments and reclined at the table again" (elaben ta himatia autou kai anepesen palin). The verb "taken" (elaben, from lambano, "to take, take up, receive") reverses the earlier "laid aside" (tithesi). Jesus takes up what he set down. The verbal pattern — setting aside / taking up again — mirrors 10:17-18 precisely: "I lay down my life so that I may take it again (hina palin labo auten). No one has taken it from me, but I lay it down on my own initiative. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again (palin labein auten)." The garments laid aside and taken up enact in miniature the life laid down and taken up again. The foot-washing is a compressed dramatization of the entire movement from incarnation through death to resurrection: the divine one sets aside his glory, takes the form of a servant, performs the work of redemption, and resumes his place.

"You call me Teacher and Lord; and you are right, for so I am" (hymeis phoneite me ho didaskalos kai ho kyrios, kai kalos legete; eimi gar). Jesus accepts both titles without reservation. "Teacher" (didaskalos, equivalent to "Rabbi") was the standard address for a Jewish sage by his students. "Lord" (kyrios) carried a range of meanings from polite address ("sir") to the divine title used in the LXX to render the tetragrammaton YHWH. In this document, kyrios is used for Jesus with increasing weight: from the respectful address of the Samaritan woman (4:11, 15, 19) and the royal official (4:49) to Thomas's climactic confession, "My Lord and my God" (ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou, 20:28). Jesus affirms: the disciples are correct to call him Teacher and Lord. These titles are not courtesies; they describe what he is.

"If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet" (ei oun ego enipsa hymon tous podas ho kyrios kai ho didaskalos, kai hymeis opheilete alleton niptein tous podas). The argument is from the greater to the lesser (qal va-homer, the same reasoning pattern used in 7:23 and 10:34-36). If the one who holds the higher position has performed the act, those who hold the lower position are obligated (opheilete, "you ought, you owe it, you are indebted to") to perform it for one another. The word opheilete carries the sense of debt — something owed, not merely recommended. The foot-washing creates an obligation: the community of Jesus's disciples is bound to serve one another in the way Jesus has served them.

The phrase "one another" (allelon) is critical. Jesus does not say "you ought to wash the feet of those outside the community" or "you ought to wash my feet." The obligation is reciprocal within the community: "one another's feet." This establishes the pattern for the "one another" commands that will follow: "love one another" (13:34-35; 15:12, 17). The community's defining activity is mutual service and mutual love among its members.

"For I gave you an example that you also should do as I did to you" (hypodeigma gar edoka hymin hina kai hymeis poiete kathos ego epoiesa hymin).
