The word hypodeigma ("example, model, pattern") indicates that the foot-washing is not merely an isolated act but a paradigm — a pattern to be replicated. The conjunction kathos ("just as, in the same manner as") establishes correspondence: as Jesus did, so the disciples should do. The example is not restricted to the literal act of washing feet (though it includes that possibility); it extends to the entire posture of self-lowering service that the foot-washing embodies. The one who has received service from the Lord is obligated to extend the same kind of service to others within the community.

"Truly, truly, I say to you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the one who sent him" (amen amen lego hymin, ouk estin doulos meizon tou kyriou autou, oude apostolos meizon tou pempsantos auton). The double amen marks the statement as authoritative. The proverb about the slave and master appeared earlier in 15:20 (though later in narrative order), and a version appears in Matthew 10:24 and Luke 6:40. In this context, the proverb cuts in a specific direction: if the master has washed feet, the slave cannot claim to be above foot-washing. The slave is not greater than the master; if the master serves, the slave must serve. The claim to be "too important" for menial service is foreclosed by the master's own act.

The word apostolos ("one who is sent") appears only here in this document (the author typically uses the verb apostello or pempo rather than the noun). Its use here connects the disciples' mission to Jesus's own mission: as the Father sent Jesus (and Jesus served), so Jesus sends the disciples (and they must serve). The chain of sending — Father sends Son, Son sends disciples — carries with it the chain of service. The sent one is not greater than the sender, and the sender has established the paradigm by washing feet.

"If you know these things, you are blessed if you do them" (ei tauta oidate, makarioi este ean poiete auta). The word makarioi ("blessed, fortunate, happy") echoes the beatitude form found throughout Israel's wisdom literature and the Psalms (Psalm 1:1, "Blessed is the man"; Psalm 32:1, "Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven"; Psalm 119:1, "Blessed are those whose way is blameless"). The blessing is conditional on doing (poiete, present tense — ongoing practice), not merely knowing. Knowledge without practice does not produce blessedness. The distinction between knowing and doing is the same as the distinction between hearing and obeying that runs through the document: in 13:17, as in 8:31-32 ("if you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples"), the condition of blessedness is enacted faithfulness, not theoretical assent.

div.title: Verses 18-20: The Betrayer and the Fulfillment of Scripture
div.p: "'I do not speak of all of you. I know the ones I have chosen; but it is that the Scripture may be fulfilled, "He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me." From now on I am telling you before it comes to pass, so that when it does occur, you may believe that I am. Truly, truly, I say to you, he who receives whomever I send receives me; and he who receives me receives him who sent me.'"

"I do not speak of all of you" (ou peri panton hymon lego). The blessing of verse 17 — "you are blessed if you do them" — does not apply universally to those present at the table. One of those present will not do what Jesus has commanded; one is excluded from the blessing. The qualification echoes verse 10: "you are clean, but not all of you." The author repeatedly marks the distinction between the community as it appears and the community as it truly is.

"I know the ones I have chosen" (ego oida hous exelexamen). The verb exelexamen (aorist of eklegomai, "to choose, select, elect") indicates that Jesus's choice of the Twelve was deliberate, including the choice of Judas. This echoes 6:70: "Did I myself not choose you, the twelve, and yet one of you is a devil?" The choosing of Judas was not a mistake but part of the larger purpose, as the next clause makes explicit.

"But it is that the Scripture may be fulfilled, 'He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me'" (all' hina he graphe plerothe, ho trogon mou ton arton eperen ep' eme ten pternan autou). The quotation is from Psalm 41:9 (LXX 40:10). The psalm is attributed to David and describes a situation where a trusted intimate has turned against him: "Even my close friend, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted up his heel against me." The Hebrew reads: gam ish shelomi asher batachti bo okhel lachmi higdil alai aqev. The LXX renders this: kai gar ho anthropos tes eirenes mou, eph' hon elpisa, ho esthion artous mou, emegalynen ep' eme pternismon.

Several details are significant for the first-century hearer. First, the psalm describes betrayal by a table companion — one who shared the intimacy of eating together. In the ancient Near East, sharing a meal created a bond of trust and obligation. To eat someone's bread and then turn against them was among the most grievous violations of social covenant. The betrayal is not from an enemy but from a trusted friend, making it exponentially worse. Second, the phrase "lifted up his heel" (eperen pternan) is a gesture of contempt or violence — like an animal kicking, or the image of someone turning their back with a final act of disdain. The heel is the part of the body associated with the serpent's attack in Genesis 3:15 ("he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel"), though whether the author intends this connection is not certain.

In the psalm's original context, David speaks of his own experience of betrayal by a counselor or companion. The traditional identification connects this to Ahithophel, David's trusted advisor who sided with Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:12, 31; 16:20-17:3). Ahithophel ate at David's table, was David's intimate counselor, and betrayed him to his own son. Ahithophel's end was suicide by hanging (2 Samuel 17:23) — a detail that resonates with the tradition about Judas's death recorded in Matthew 27:5.

Jesus applies the psalm to Judas: the one who has been eating with him — sharing the most intimate fellowship of the teacher-disciple relationship — is about to raise his heel in betrayal. The word trogon ("eating, chewing, gnawing") is the same word used in 6:54, 56, 57, 58 for eating Jesus's flesh in the bread-of-life discourse. The verbal echo is striking: the one who "eats my bread" has been present at every meal, has shared in the fellowship, and yet will turn traitor. The betrayal comes from within, not from without — not from the Pharisees or the chief priests but from one of Jesus's own chosen.

"From now on I am telling you before it comes to pass, so that when it does occur, you may believe that I am" (ap' arti lego hymin pro tou genesthai, hina pisteusete hotan genetai hoti ego eimi). The phrase "that I am" (hoti ego eimi) is the absolute ego eimi — the divine self-identification that has appeared throughout the document (8:24, "unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins"; 8:28, "when you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am"; 8:58, "before Abraham was, I am"). Jesus tells the disciples in advance so that when the betrayal occurs, rather than destroying their faith, it will confirm it: the one who predicted the betrayal is the one who is — the one whose identity is disclosed by the divine name.

This establishes a pattern that the author will employ throughout the farewell discourse: Jesus tells the disciples what will happen before it happens so that the events, when they occur, will not devastate but confirm (14:29, "Now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens, you may believe"; 16:4, "These things I have spoken to you, so that when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you of them"). The disciples' faith will be tested by the coming events — betrayal, arrest, crucifixion — and Jesus's prior announcement transforms potential faith-destroyers into faith-confirming evidence.

"Truly, truly, I say to you, he who receives whomever I send receives me; and he who receives me receives him who sent me" (amen amen lego hymin, ho lambanon an tina pempso eme lambanei, ho de eme lambanon lambanei ton pempsanta me). This saying establishes the chain of authorization that will ground the disciples' future mission: the one who receives a sent disciple receives Jesus, and the one who receives Jesus receives the Father. The chain works in both directions: from the Father through Jesus to the disciples, and from the disciples back through Jesus to the Father. The saying assumes that the disciples will be sent (which Jesus will make explicit in 17:18, "As you sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world," and 20:21, "As the Father has sent me, I also send you"). Their authority derives not from themselves but from the one who sends them, just as Jesus's authority derives from the Father who sent him. The pattern of authorized representation — where the agent carries the authority of the sender — is well established in Jewish law (the concept of the shaliach, the authorized emissary whose words and acts carry the sender's authority).

div.title: Verses 21-30: The Identification and Departure of the Betrayer
div.p: "When Jesus had said this, he became troubled in spirit, and testified and said, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.' The disciples began looking at one another, at a loss to know of which one he was speaking. There was reclining on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved. So Simon Peter gestured to him, and said to him, 'Tell us who it is of whom he is speaking.' He, leaning back thus on Jesus' breast, said to him, 'Lord, who is it?' Jesus then answered, 'That is the one for whom I shall dip the morsel and give it to him.' So when he had dipped the morsel, he took and gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. After the morsel, Satan then entered into him. Therefore Jesus said to him, 'What you do, do quickly.' Now no one of those reclining at the table knew for what purpose he had said this to him. For some were supposing, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus was saying to him, 'Buy the things we have need of for the feast'; or else, that he should give something to the poor. So after receiving the morsel he went out immediately; and it was night."

"He became troubled in spirit" (etarachthe to pneumati). The verb tarasso ("to trouble, agitate, disturb, stir up") appeared in 11:33, where Jesus "was deeply moved in spirit and was troubled" (etaraxen heauton) at Lazarus's tomb, and in 12:27, "Now my soul has become troubled" (he psyche mou tetaraktai). The troubled spirit is not a sign of doubt or weakness but of the cost of what Jesus is about to do. He is about to identify the betrayer, which means he is about to set in motion the events that lead to the cross. The trouble is the trouble of one who loves and who faces the betrayal of love.

"Testified and said" (emartyrese kai eipen). The verb martyreo ("to testify, bear witness") is the author's technical term for authoritative testimony throughout the document (1:7, 8, 15, 32, 34; 3:11, 26, 32, 33; 5:31-37; 8:13-18; 15:27; 18:37; 19:35; 21:24). By using it here, the author marks Jesus's statement about the betrayal not as a mere prediction or emotional outburst but as formal testimony — a solemn declaration with the weight of a witness in court.

"One of you will betray me" (heis ex hymon paradosei me). The verb paradidomi ("to hand over, deliver up, betray") is used throughout the document for the act of betrayal (6:64, 71; 12:4; 13:2, 11, 21; 18:2, 5, 36; 19:11, 16, 30). The disciples' response — "looking at one another, at a loss" (eblepon eis allelous hoi mathetai aporoumenoi) — indicates that Judas's betrayal was not obvious to the group. The other disciples did not suspect him.

"There was reclining on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved" (en anakeimenos heis ek ton matheton autou en to kolpo tou Iesou, hon egapa ho Iesous). This is the first appearance of the figure the author identifies only as "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (also in 19:26, 20:2, 21:7, 21:20). The phrase en to kolpo ("in the bosom, on the chest") echoes 1:18, where the Son is described as being "in the bosom of the Father" (eis ton kolpon tou patros). The positional language creates a parallel: as the Son is in intimate relationship with the Father, so this disciple is in intimate relationship with Jesus. The disciple's proximity to Jesus gives him access to information the others do not have — he can ask privately what the group cannot determine publicly.

The reclining posture reflects Roman dining practice, which had been adopted in the Hellenized Jewish world for formal meals. Diners reclined on their left side, leaning on the left elbow, with the right hand free for eating. The person to the right of the host would recline with his back toward the host's chest, placing him "in the bosom" of the host. This was the position of honor and intimacy.

"Simon Peter gestured to him" (neuei oun touto Simon Petros). Peter, unable to ask directly, signals to the beloved disciple to inquire. This establishes a pattern that recurs: Peter acts through the beloved disciple as an intermediary (see also 20:2-8, where Peter and the beloved disciple run to the tomb; 21:7, where the beloved disciple identifies the risen Lord and Peter leaps into the sea). The two disciples function as a pair, with the beloved disciple having access to understanding or recognition that Peter lacks.

"That is the one for whom I shall dip the morsel and give it to him" (ekeinos estin ho ego bapso to psomion kai doso auto). The psomion ("morsel, piece of bread") dipped and given to a guest was an act of hospitality and honor at a meal. The host would dip bread into a common dish and hand it to a guest as a gesture of friendship and welcome. Jesus identifies the betrayer not by public accusation but by offering him an act of fellowship. Even the identification of the betrayer is performed through an act of service and honor. The irony is severe: the gesture of friendship singles out the one who will perform the ultimate act of betrayal.

"After the morsel, Satan then entered into him" (kai meta to psomion tote eiselthen eis ekeinon ho Satanas). The author escalates from "the devil" (diabolos) of verse 2 to "Satan" (Satanas). In verse 2, the devil "put into the heart" of Judas the intention to betray; now, after the morsel, Satan "enters into" Judas. The progression is from external temptation to full possession. The moment of the morsel — the moment of the host's act of honor — becomes the moment of Satan's entry. The one who receives Jesus's gesture of fellowship is simultaneously filled by the adversary of God. The juxtaposition is deliberate: at the very point where Jesus extends love, Judas receives something other than love. The morsel enters his mouth; Satan enters his being.

The name "Satan" (from the Hebrew satan, "adversary, accuser") appears in the LXX primarily in Job (1:6-12, 2:1-7), Zechariah 3:1-2, and 1 Chronicles 21:1. In Job, the Satan is a figure in the divine court who tests human loyalty; in Zechariah, the Satan stands to accuse the high priest Joshua. In the broader first-century Jewish context (reflected in the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Jubilees, and the Qumran literature), Satan/Belial was understood as the chief adversary of God, the leader of hostile spiritual forces. The author of this document uses "the devil" and "Satan" as synonymous designations for the same figure whose character was defined in 8:44: "a murderer from the beginning" who "does not stand in the truth."

"What you do, do quickly" (ho poieis poieson tacheion). Jesus's command to Judas is startling. He does not prevent the betrayal; he accelerates it. The imperative "do quickly" (poieson tacheion) is not permission but a sovereign direction of events. Jesus, who has declared that he lays down his life on his own initiative (10:18), now tells the instrument of his death to proceed without delay. The hour has come (13:1); the departure is underway; the shepherd is orchestrating the laying down of his own life. Judas is not the author of the plot but its tool; Jesus remains the agent even in his own handing over.

"No one of those reclining at the table knew for what purpose he had said this to him." The other disciples' ignorance confirms that Judas's role was not publicly known. Their guesses — that Jesus sent Judas to buy supplies for the feast or to give to the poor — are mundane and reveal how thoroughly Judas's treachery was concealed. That some supposed Judas should "buy the things we have need of for the feast" also confirms that the Passover meal has not yet occurred (the feast is still approaching), consistent with this document's chronology.

"So after receiving the morsel he went out immediately; and it was night" (labon oun to psomion ekeinos exelthen euthys; en de nyx). The three-word sentence "it was night" (en de nyx) is one of the most powerful statements in the document. The author has constructed an elaborate light-darkness framework from the prologue onward: "In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it" (1:4-5); "This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light" (3:19); "I am the light of the world" (8:12, 9:5); "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble" (11:9); "Walk while you have the light, so that darkness will not overtake you" (12:35). Throughout the document, light is the presence and activity of Jesus; darkness is the absence of Jesus and the domain of opposition to God.

When Judas goes out, he goes out from the presence of Jesus into the night. He leaves the light and enters the darkness. The statement is simultaneously literal (it is nighttime) and theological (he enters the realm of darkness, the domain of the one who has just entered him). Judas's departure from Jesus's presence is a departure from the light into the darkness — the same darkness that the prologue said "did not comprehend" the light (1:5). The brevity of the statement — en de nyx — gives it the force of a door slamming shut.

The departure of Judas also purifies the audience for what follows. From this point forward, everything Jesus says in chapters 14-17 is addressed to those who are "clean" (13:10) — the disciples who remain. The betrayer has been removed. The community is now composed of those who truly belong, and Jesus can speak to them without reserve about the Father's house, the vine and branches, the Spirit, the world's hatred, and his own return.

div.title: Verses 31-35: The New Commandment
div.p: "Therefore when he had gone out, Jesus said, 'Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him; if God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him immediately. Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, "Where I am going, you cannot come," now I also say to you. A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another, even as I have loved you, that you also love one another. By this all men will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.'"

"Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him" (nyn edoxasthe ho huios tou anthropou, kai ho theos edoxasthe en auto). The word "now" (nyn) is emphatic: at this moment, with Judas's departure, the glorification has begun. The verb doxazo ("to glorify") appears in the aorist (edoxasthe, "has been glorified, was glorified") — a past tense used for an event that is so certain it can be spoken of as already accomplished. This is the "hour" of glorification that Jesus announced in 12:23 ("The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified"). The glorification is not the opposite of the death but includes it: the cross is the means of glory, not the obstacle to it.

The title "Son of Man" (ho huios tou anthropou) has appeared throughout the document in connection with the "lifting up" (3:14, "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up"; 8:28, "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am"; 12:34). The double meaning of "lifted up" (hypsoo) — lifted on the cross and exalted to glory — is operative here. The Son of Man is glorified precisely in the act of being handed over, tried, and crucified. The glory is not post-death vindication but is present in the death itself. The background is Daniel 7:13-14 (LXX), where "one like a son of man" (hos huios anthropou) comes to the Ancient of Days and receives "dominion and glory (doxa) and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him." The son of man's glory in Daniel is a glory received from God; here the glorification is mutual: the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in him.

"God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him immediately" (kai ho theos doxasei auton en auto, kai euthys doxasei auton). The future tense (doxasei, "will glorify") points beyond the cross to the resurrection and exaltation. God will glorify the Son "in himself" (en auto, "in God's own presence/being") — which is to say, by receiving the Son back into the divine presence (17:5, "Now, Father, glorify me together with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was"). The word "immediately" (euthys) signals that the glorification will not be delayed: the cross leads directly to resurrection, and resurrection leads directly to exaltation. There is no interval of defeat between the death and the glory; the death is the glory.

"Little children" (teknia). This is the only time Jesus uses this form of address in the document (it is characteristic of the Johannine letters: 1 John 2:1, 12, 28; 3:7, 18; 4:4; 5:21). The diminutive teknia ("little children, dear children") conveys intimacy and tenderness. At the moment when the events of betrayal and death are set in motion, Jesus addresses his disciples with the language of a parent speaking to children. The relational warmth is heightened by the announcement that follows: he is about to leave them.

"Yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, 'Where I am going, you cannot come,' now I also say to you" (eti mikron meth' hymon eimi. zetesete me, kai kathos eipon tois Ioudaiois hoti hopou ego hypago hymeis ou dynasthe elthein, kai hymin lego arti). The phrase "a little while" (mikron) will recur in 14:19, 16:16-19, each time provoking confusion. Jesus had said to "the Jews" in 7:33-34 ("Yet a little while I am with you, and then I go to him who sent me. You will seek me, and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come") and 8:21 ("I go away, and you will seek me, and will die in your sin; where I am going, you cannot come"). Now he says the same thing to the disciples, but the meaning is different. For the hostile authorities, "you cannot come" was a statement of permanent exclusion — they would seek and not find because they had rejected the one who was going. For the disciples, "you cannot come" is a statement of temporal limitation — they cannot come now, but they will come later (14:3, "I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also"; 17:24, "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, be with me where I am"). Peter will make this distinction explicit in verse 36 by asking "Lord, where are you going?" and receiving the answer: "Where I go, you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later."

"A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another, even as I have loved you, that you also love one another" (entolen kainen didomi hymin, hina agapate allelous, kathos egapesa hymas hina kai hymeis agapate allelous). The word "new" (kainen) requires examination. The command to love is not new in itself — Leviticus 19:18 commands "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," and this was understood as a central obligation of the Torah. What is "new" is the standard of the love: not "as yourself" but "as I have loved you" (kathos egapesa hymas). The standard is not self-love projected onto others but the specific love Jesus has demonstrated — the love that washes feet, that lays down life, that loves "to the end" (eis telos, 13:1). The newness is in the measure: the love is to be patterned on Jesus's own self-giving love, which is qualitatively different from the Levitical command because it is modeled on a specific, concrete act of self-sacrifice.

The word entole ("commandment") echoes 10:18, where the Father gave Jesus a "commandment" (entolen) regarding the laying down and taking up of his life, and 12:49-50, where the Father's "commandment" (entole) is eternal life. The chain of commandment continues: the Father commanded the Son (10:18, 12:49-50); the Son now commands the disciples (13:34). The content of the commandment is love; the model of the love is Jesus's own; the scope is "one another" (allelous) — the members of the community.

The commandment is "new" also in the sense of Jeremiah 31:31-34 (LXX 38:31-34), where God promises "a new covenant" (diatheken kainen): "I will put my law within them, and on their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people... for they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest of them." The new commandment belongs to the new covenant. What was written on stone is now enacted in flesh — in the specific flesh of Jesus washing feet, and in the flesh of the community that follows his example.

"By this all men will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (en touto gnosontai pantes hoti emoi mathetai este, ean agapen echete en allelois). The identifying mark of Jesus's community is not doctrine, not ritual, not ethnic identity, not miraculous power, but mutual love. The verb gnosontai ("will know") indicates that this love will be visible — recognizable to those outside the community. The love among the members will function as testimony, as a sign that these people belong to the one who loved them to the end. In a first-century context where religious communities were identified by their observances (Sabbath, circumcision, dietary laws, temple worship, philosophical schools), Jesus identifies a radically different marker: the quality of their love for one another.

div.title: Verses 36-38: Peter's Boast and the Prediction of Denial
div.p: "Simon Peter said to him, 'Lord, where are you going?' Jesus answered, 'Where I go, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow later.' Peter said to him, 'Lord, why can I not follow you right now? I will lay down my life for you.' Jesus answered, 'Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, a rooster will not crow until you deny me three times.'"

"Lord, where are you going?" (Kyrie, pou hypageis). Peter asks the question that the farewell discourse will answer across four chapters. The question reveals that Peter has heard Jesus's announcement of departure but has not grasped its meaning. He thinks of a physical journey to a location. The answer — "where I go, you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later" (hopou hypago ou dynasai moi nyn akolouthesai, akoloutheseis de hysteron) — uses the verb akoloutheo ("to follow"), which has been the defining activity of discipleship throughout the document (1:37, 38, 40, 43; 8:12; 10:4, 5, 27; 12:26). Peter will follow — but not now. The "later" (hysteron) points beyond the immediate crisis to the time after the resurrection, when Peter's following will resume and ultimately lead to his own death (21:18-19, "when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will gird you, and bring you where you do not wish to go" — which the author glosses: "Now this he said, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God").

"I will lay down my life for you" (ten psychen mou hyper sou theso). Peter uses Jesus's own language. The verb tithemi ("to lay down") and the preposition hyper ("for, on behalf of") are the exact words Jesus used in 10:11, 15, 17-18 for the good shepherd laying down his life for the sheep. Peter claims to be willing to do for Jesus what Jesus has said he will do for the sheep. The claim is sincere but premature. Peter believes he can do what only the shepherd can do — lay down his life. But within hours, Peter will not lay down his life; he will deny three times that he even knows Jesus (18:17, 25, 27).

The irony is severe. The shepherd lays down his life for the sheep; the sheep cannot lay down its life for the shepherd. Peter's boast reverses the roles. In this document's framework, the act of laying down life belongs to the shepherd by unique authority and commandment from the Father (10:18). The sheep's role is to hear, follow, and receive — precisely what the foot-washing has just demonstrated. Peter's inability to accept the foot-washing (v. 8) and his claim to lay down his life (v. 37) are the same error in different forms: he resists receiving and insists on giving, when the entire evening has been structured to teach that the disciple must first receive from Jesus before doing anything.

"A rooster will not crow until you deny me three times" (ou me alektor phonesei heos hou arnesai me tris). The double negative ou me ("by no means, certainly not") makes the prediction absolute. The word phonesei ("will crow") is from phoneo ("to call out, to cry, to sound") — cognate with phone ("voice"), which has been the critical word in the shepherd discourse (10:3-5, 16, 27: the sheep hear the shepherd's voice). The cock's voice will mark the moment when Peter refuses to acknowledge that he has heard and followed the shepherd's voice. The verb arnesai ("you will deny") means "to say no, to disown, to refuse to acknowledge." Peter, who has just professed willingness to die for Jesus, will instead three times refuse to admit that he knows him.

The prediction does not end the relationship. Jesus has already said Peter "will follow later" (v. 36). The denial is real and devastating, but it is not final. The document will record Peter's restoration by the risen Lord at the Sea of Tiberias, where Jesus asks Peter three times, "Do you love me?" (21:15-17) — one question for each denial. The prediction of failure is given within the context of "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end" (13:1). The love does not stop at Peter's denial; it persists through it and beyond it.

list.item: The chapter marks the transition from public ministry to private instruction. The public phase of the document, in which Jesus performed signs, engaged in public debates, and confronted the religious authorities, ended in 12:36b ("he departed and hid himself from them"). Chapter 13 opens a new section addressed exclusively to "his own" (tous idious, 13:1) — the circle of disciples who have heard his voice and followed. The shift in audience corresponds to a shift in subject: from the question of Jesus's identity (answered through signs and discourses) to the question of how the community will live after Jesus's departure.

The foot-washing enacts in advance the meaning of Jesus's death. The sequence of actions — rising from the table, laying aside garments, taking the form of a servant, washing feet, then taking up garments again — mirrors the sequence of the incarnation, crucifixion, and resurrection that the document narrates. The verbal parallels are precise: "laid aside" (tithesi) in verse 4 uses the same verb as "lays down" (tithesi) his life in 10:11; "took" (elaben) his garments in verse 12 uses the same verb as "take it up again" (labein) in 10:18. The foot-washing is a compressed enactment of the gospel the document tells: the divine one descends, serves, dies, and rises.

The foot-washing establishes the pattern for the community's life. The "example" (hypodeigma, v. 15) Jesus gives is not merely about humility as an abstract virtue but about a specific practice: mutual service modeled on the self-lowering of the Lord. The community is defined not by hierarchy but by reciprocal service ("wash one another's feet," v. 14), and this service is not optional but obligatory (opheilete, "you ought," v. 14). The community's internal life is to replicate the pattern Jesus has enacted.

The chapter draws a line between those who are "clean" and the one who is not. The repeated qualification — "you are clean, but not all of you" (v. 10); "I do not speak of all of you" (v. 18) — identifies Judas as the exception within the group. Despite being chosen (v. 18), having eaten with Jesus (v. 18), and having his feet washed (v. 5), Judas remains "not clean." The author attributes this to the devil's entry into his heart (vv. 2, 27). The foot-washing touches Judas but does not transform him because cleanness in this document is a function of receiving Jesus's word and remaining in it (15:3, 8:31), and Judas has not done so. His departure into the night (v. 30) removes the unclean element from the community and prepares the audience for the intimate teaching of chapters 14-17.

The betrayal fulfills Scripture and confirms Jesus's identity. The quotation from Psalm 41:9 (v. 18) places the betrayal within the pattern of Israel's history — specifically, the experience of David, the anointed king, betrayed by a trusted companion. The betrayal does not disprove Jesus's messiahship; it follows the pattern of the Davidic king's own experience. Jesus tells the disciples in advance (v. 19) so that the betrayal, when it occurs, will confirm rather than undermine their belief that he is the "I am" (ego eimi). The events of the Passion are not evidence against Jesus's identity but evidence for it.

The "new commandment" establishes love as the defining mark of the community. The commandment to "love one another as I have loved you" (v. 34) takes the Levitical command to love one's neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) and transforms it by providing a new standard: not self-love but Jesus's own self-sacrificing love. The love that washes feet, that serves the betrayer, that loves "to the end" — this is the measure. The visibility of this love ("by this all men will know," v. 35) makes it the community's public testimony, replacing the signs and discourses of the public ministry as the means by which the world recognizes Jesus's disciples.

Peter's exchange with Jesus in verses 36-38 reveals the distance between intention and capacity. Peter claims willingness to lay down his life, using the shepherd's own language (cf. 10:11, 15, 17-18). But Jesus predicts denial, not death. The disciple's role at this stage is not to die for the master but to receive from the master — to accept the foot-washing, to hear the word, to abide in the vine. Peter's willingness is real but his capacity is not yet what it will become. The prediction of denial is given within the framework of ongoing love ("he loved them to the end," 13:1) and future restoration ("you will follow later," v. 36; cf. 21:15-19).

The temporal and symbolic markers unify the chapter around the theme of passage. The Passover setting (v. 1) evokes the exodus — the departure from bondage through the blood of the lamb. Jesus's own "departure out of this world to the Father" (metabaino, v. 1) is a personal exodus. The "hour" that has finally come (v. 1) is the hour toward which the entire document has been moving. Judas's departure into the "night" (v. 30) is the departure into darkness that the document's light-darkness framework has been describing since the prologue. The glorification that begins "now" (v. 31) is the fulfillment of the promise made in 12:23. Every temporal marker in the chapter points to the same reality: the decisive transition is underway. The lamb is about to be slain. The shepherd is about to lay down his life. The light is about to enter the darkness and overcome it (1:5).

The chapter's pronouns carefully delineate the boundaries of the community. "His own" (tous idious, v. 1) identifies those who belong to Jesus. "You are clean, but not all of you" (v. 10) distinguishes the truly belonging from the apparently belonging. "Not all of you" (v. 18) excludes the betrayer from the blessed. "Love one another" (vv. 34-35) defines the community's internal obligation. "All men will know" (v. 35) distinguishes the community from those outside it. The pronoun tracking reveals a community that is known, loved, served, and commanded — but that includes, until the moment of self-revelation, a member who does not truly belong. Judas's departure is the moment when the visible community and the true community become coextensive, and the teaching that follows is addressed to the true community alone.

The chapter's argument flows as a single unbroken movement. The author's sequence is: (a) the theological introduction establishing that Jesus acts with full knowledge and love (vv. 1-3); (b) the enacted parable of the foot-washing (vv. 4-5); (c) the exchange with Peter that interprets the washing as necessary for belonging (vv. 6-11); (d) the explicit teaching about the meaning of the washing as an example for mutual service (vv. 12-17); (e) the identification and departure of the betrayer, fulfilling Scripture and removing the one who does not belong (vv. 18-30); (f) the glorification announcement and new commandment, establishing the community's identity and mission (vv. 31-35); (g) Peter's premature claim and Jesus's prediction of denial, tempering the community's confidence with realism about their immediate capacity (vv. 36-38). There is no change of subject: every section flows from the one before it. The foot-washing leads to the teaching about cleanness, which leads to the betrayer's uncleanness, which leads to the betrayer's removal, which opens the space for the new commandment, which defines what the community will look like after Jesus departs. The entire chapter is a preparation for departure — Jesus preparing his disciples for his absence by showing them what his presence means and what their life together must become.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 13): Chapter 13 opened the private section of the document. The public ministry ended at 12:36b ("he departed and hid himself from them"), and from 13:1 onward Jesus speaks only to "his own" (tous idious) — the disciples who remain after Judas's departure into the night. The chapter performed three essential functions: (a) the foot-washing enacted in advance the meaning of Jesus's death, using verbal parallels to the good shepherd discourse (tithesi for "laid aside" garments / "lays down" life, 10:11; elaben for "took up" garments / "take up again" life, 10:18); (b) the identification and removal of the betrayer purified the audience, so that from 13:30 onward the teaching is addressed exclusively to those who truly belong; (c) the "new commandment" to "love one another as I have loved you" (13:34) established the defining mark of the post-departure community. The chapter ended with Peter's claim that he would lay down his life for Jesus — using the shepherd's own vocabulary (ten psychen mou hyper sou theso, echoing 10:11, 15) — and Jesus's prediction that Peter would instead deny him three times before the cock crowed. The chapter's final exchange established two realities simultaneously: the disciples' attachment to Jesus is genuine, and their capacity to follow him through the coming crisis is not yet what it will become.

What the author argues immediately after (John 15): Chapter 15 opens with the vine and branches metaphor: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser" (15:1). The metaphor develops the themes of abiding (meno) and fruit-bearing that chapter 14 has introduced. The Father removes (airei) every branch in Jesus that does not bear fruit and prunes (kathairei) every branch that does bear fruit so that it bears more fruit (15:2). The disciples are already "clean" (katharoi) "because of the word" (dia ton logon) Jesus has spoken to them (15:3) — connecting to the foot-washing's distinction between the bathed and the unbathed (13:10) and to the word-based cleansing that 14:23-24 describes. The condition for bearing fruit is abiding: "Abide in me, and I in you" (15:4). The branch that does not abide is thrown away, withers, and is burned (15:6). The love commandment from 13:34 is restated and expanded: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (15:13). The world's hatred of the community is introduced (15:18-25), and the parakletos is promised again (15:26-27), now described as "the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father" who "will bear witness about me."

How chapter 14 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 13 ended with the disciples in a state of disturbance. Jesus has announced his departure ("where I am going, you cannot come," 13:33), predicted Peter's denial (13:38), and removed the betrayer into the night. The small community that remains is troubled: the leader is leaving, the strongest among them will fail, and one of their own has just been revealed as a traitor. Chapter 14 opens by addressing this troubled state directly: "Let not your hearts be troubled" (me tarassestho hymon he kardia, 14:1). The chapter's entire argument is a response to the crisis of departure. It answers the questions that the announcement of departure has raised: Where is Jesus going? (14:2-4). How will the disciples find the way? (14:5-7). What will replace Jesus's physical presence? (14:16-18, 25-26). How will the disciples maintain their relationship with the Father and Son after Jesus is gone? (14:15, 21, 23-24). What will happen to the world? (14:17, 19, 22, 30-31).

Chapter 14 is thus the first extended response within the farewell discourse to the fact of Jesus's departure. Chapter 13 enacted the meaning of the departure (the foot-washing) and established the community's defining obligation (the love commandment). Chapter 14 now addresses the disciples' emotional and relational condition in light of that departure. The chapter moves from the promise of a destination (14:1-4) through the revelation of Jesus as the way to the Father (14:5-11) to the promise of continued divine presence through the Spirit (14:16-26) and concludes with the assurance of peace and the command to depart (14:27-31). Chapter 15 will then develop the conditions of remaining in relationship with Jesus (the vine and branches) and the consequences of the world's hostility. The movement is coherent: chapter 13 says "I am leaving and this is what it means"; chapter 14 says "here is where I am going, here is how you will still be connected to me, here is who will be with you"; chapter 15 says "here is how you must live in that connection and what you will face from the world."

div.title: Verses 1-4: The Troubled Heart and the Dwelling Places
div.p: "Let not your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."

"Let not your hearts be troubled" (me tarassestho hymon he kardia). The verb tarasso ("to trouble, agitate, disturb") appeared in 11:33 (Jesus "troubled himself" at Lazarus's tomb), 12:27 ("Now my soul has become troubled"), and 13:21 (Jesus "became troubled in spirit" when testifying about the betrayer). The same disturbance that Jesus felt in himself he now addresses in the disciples. The imperative me tarassestho (present passive, "do not let your hearts continue to be troubled" or "stop being troubled") indicates that the troubling is already occurring. The disciples are already disturbed by what they have heard: the departure, the prediction of denial, the exposure of betrayal. Jesus does not deny the grounds for their disturbance; he offers a different basis for their response.

The word kardia ("heart") in the LXX and first-century Jewish usage designates the center of the person — the seat of thought, will, and emotion. It is not merely the organ of feeling (as in modern usage) but the governing center of the whole person. When God searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10, LXX: "I the LORD search the heart"), he examines the entire inner life. When Jesus addresses the heart's trouble, he addresses the disciples' total orientation, not merely their emotional state.

"You believe in God; believe also in me" (pisteuete eis ton theon, kai eis eme pisteuete). The grammar of this sentence is ambiguous. The verb pisteuete can be either indicative ("you believe") or imperative ("believe!"). Four readings are possible: (1) "You believe in God, and you believe in me" (both indicative — a statement of fact); (2) "Believe in God, and believe in me" (both imperative — a double command); (3) "You believe in God; believe also in me" (indicative then imperative — an appeal that extends existing faith to include Jesus); (4) "Believe in God, and you will believe in me" (imperative then indicative — obedience to God leads to faith in Jesus). The context favors the third reading: the disciples already believe in God (this is assumed throughout the document); now, as Jesus announces his departure, they must extend that same trust to him — trust that his departure has a purpose, that his going is not abandonment.

The pairing of God and Jesus as parallel objects of trust is consistent with the document's claims throughout. In 5:23, the Son receives the same honor as the Father. In 10:30, "I and the Father are one." In 12:44, "He who believes in me, does not believe in me but in him who sent me." The call to believe in Jesus is not a departure from believing in God but an expression of it. The faith that trusts God must now trust the one God sent — especially when the one God sent is about to die.

"In my Father's house are many dwelling places" (en te oikia tou patros mou monai pollai eisin). The word mone ("dwelling place, room, abode") is rare. It appears only twice in the entire New Testament, both in this chapter: here in verse 2 and in verse 23. The noun derives from the verb meno ("to remain, abide, dwell"), which is one of the most important words in this document, appearing over forty times (1:38-39, 5:38, 6:27, 56, 8:31, 35, 12:46, 15:4-10, and frequently throughout). The mone is the place where one abides — the permanent residence, the settled dwelling, as opposed to transient quarters.

The phrase "my Father's house" (he oikia tou patros mou) appeared in 2:16, where Jesus cleansed the temple: "Do not make my Father's house a house of trade" (me poieite ton oikon tou patros mou oikon emporiou). In chapter 2, the Father's house was the Jerusalem temple — the place where God dwelt among his people. The temple in Israel's scriptures was the earthly counterpart of God's heavenly dwelling. Psalm 11:4 (LXX 10:4): "The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD — his throne is in heaven." Isaiah 66:1: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; where is the house you would build for me?" 1 Kings 8:27-30: Solomon acknowledges that even "heaven and the highest heaven" cannot contain God, yet prays that God's eyes will be open "toward this house night and day" and that he will hear from his "dwelling place in heaven." The earthly temple was understood as the meeting point between God's heavenly dwelling and his people on earth. When Jesus speaks of "my Father's house" now — on the eve of his death, when the temple he cleansed will become the house whose custodians kill him — the reference extends beyond the Jerusalem temple to the heavenly reality the temple signified: the presence of the Father himself.

The phrase "many dwelling places" (monai pollai) uses the adjective pollai ("many") to indicate sufficiency and abundance. There is room. The Father's house is not cramped or exclusive; it contains many permanent residences. The emphasis is reassurance: the disciples need not fear that there is no place for them. The anxiety produced by Jesus's departure — "where is he going? will there be room for us?" — is addressed by the declaration that the Father's house has abundant space.

In the LXX, the concept of a "dwelling place" (mone) for God's people in God's presence draws on the language of the tabernacle and temple. The Hebrew mishkan ("tabernacle, dwelling place") and its verb shakan ("to dwell, tabernacle") are the terms behind the prologue's statement that the Word "became flesh and dwelt among us" (eskennosen en hemin, 1:14 — the verb skenoo, "to pitch a tent, to tabernacle," is cognate with skene, the LXX rendering of the tabernacle). The movement from the Word tabernacling among the disciples in the flesh (1:14) to the Father's house having many permanent dwelling places (14:2) traces the trajectory of the relationship: what was temporary presence in the incarnation will become permanent dwelling in the Father's house.

"If it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you" (ei de me, eipon an hymin hoti poreuomai hetoimasai topon hymin). The clause "if it were not so, I would have told you" appeals to the pattern of truthfulness Jesus has established throughout the document. He has not concealed bad news from them — he told them about the betrayer (13:18-19), about Peter's denial (13:38), about the world's hatred (this will come in 15:18-25). If the Father's house had no room for them, he would not have hidden that either. The reassurance rests on Jesus's character as a trustworthy speaker.

The verb hetoimasai ("to prepare") is the aorist infinitive of hetoimazo ("to make ready, prepare"). In the LXX, the word is used for preparing a place of dwelling: Psalm 33:14 (LXX 32:14): "From where he sits he looks on all who dwell on the earth; he who fashions the hearts of them all, he who prepares their works" (though the usage varies). More directly relevant is Deuteronomy 1:33, where God "goes before you on the way to seek out a place for you to encamp" (LXX: proporeuomenos hymon en te hodo eklegomenos hymin topon). In Numbers 10:33, the ark of the covenant went before Israel "to seek out a resting place" (kataskepsasthai anapausin). The pattern is from Israel's wilderness experience: God goes ahead to prepare the place where his people will dwell. Jesus's going to "prepare a place" echoes the exodus pattern: the leader goes ahead, and the people follow to the place he has prepared. This connects to the Passover framework established in 13:1 — the departure from the world to the Father is a new exodus, and Jesus goes ahead to prepare the settlement.

"I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also" (palin erchomai kai paralempsomai hymas pros emauton, hina hopou eimi ego kai hymeis ete). The verb paralempsomai ("I will take to myself, receive, take along") is significant. The word paralambanno in first-century usage meant to receive someone into one's company, to take someone along. In the LXX, the word appears for gathering someone to oneself in fellowship. The promise is personal: Jesus will not merely send directions; he will come himself and take the disciples to be with him.

The phrase "where I am, you may be also" (hopou eimi ego kai hymeis ete) fulfills and answers the distressing words of 13:33: "Where I am going, you cannot come." In chapter 13, the disciples were told they cannot come now. Here the timeline is completed: Jesus goes, prepares, comes back, and takes them to be where he is. The "cannot come now" of chapter 13 becomes the "you may be also" of chapter 14. The temporal separation is real but not permanent.

The nature of the "coming again" (palin erchomai) is a question the text does not resolve into a single event. The present tense erchomai ("I am coming") rather than the future eleusomai ("I will come") may indicate an action already set in motion — a coming that begins with the resurrection, continues through the giving of the Spirit, and reaches its completion in the final return. The document uses "coming" language for multiple events: the resurrection appearances (20:19-29), the return of Jesus to the disciples through the Spirit (14:18, 23, 28), and the eschatological coming implied by "the last day" language (6:39-40, 44, 54). The chapter itself will offer at least two modes of Jesus's return: the coming through the Spirit (14:16-18, 23) and the eschatological coming that lies beyond the immediate horizon. The text does not force the reader to choose one referent; the "coming" is a single reality with multiple expressions.

"And you know the way to where I am going" (kai hopou ego hypago oidate ten hodon). This statement sets up Thomas's question in the next verse. Jesus assumes the disciples know both the destination (the Father) and the way (himself). They do, in fact, know these things, but they do not yet recognize what they know. The pattern is consistent with the document: the disciples possess knowledge that will become clear only "afterward" (meta tauta, 13:7) — after the resurrection and the Spirit's coming (cf. 2:22, 12:16).

div.title: Verses 5-7: Thomas's Question and the Declaration of the Way
div.p: "Thomas said to him, 'Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?' Jesus said to him, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him.'"

"Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" (Kyrie, ouk oidamen pou hypageis; pos dynametha ten hodon eidenai). Thomas's question is honest and concrete. He has heard Jesus say "you know the way" and responds with the direct admission that neither the destination nor the route is clear to him. Thomas is the disciple who appeared in 11:16, where he said "Let us also go, that we may die with him" — a statement of loyalty coupled with misunderstanding (he assumed the trip to Bethany would result in death). Thomas's pattern in this document is straightforward courage combined with incomplete comprehension. He does not pretend to understand what he does not. His question is not obstruction but the honest confusion that prompts revelation.
Thomas thinks of "way" (hodos) as a road — a path from here to there, a sequence of directions. Jesus's answer will redefine "way" from a route to a person.

"I am the way, and the truth, and the life" (ego eimi he hodos kai he aletheia kai he zoe). This is the sixth "I am" statement with a predicate in this document. The preceding five are: "I am the bread of life" (6:35, 48); "I am the light of the world" (8:12, 9:5); "I am the door of the sheep" (10:7, 9); "I am the good shepherd" (10:11, 14); "I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25). Each has reframed an abstract concept or religious symbol as the person of Jesus: the bread that sustains is not manna but Jesus; the light that illuminates is not the temple menorah but Jesus; the door to the sheepfold is not a gate but Jesus; the shepherd who tends is not a human leader but Jesus; the resurrection Israel awaits is not an event but a person.

Now "the way" (he hodos) is similarly reframed. Thomas asked for a road; Jesus offers himself. The "way" to the Father is not a set of instructions, a ritual pathway, or a moral program — it is a person. The way is not something Jesus teaches or points to; the way is what Jesus is.

The word hodos ("way, road, path") carries significant weight in Israel's scriptures. In the LXX, hodos frequently describes God's way of acting and the path God opens for his people. Isaiah 40:3: "Prepare the way (hodon) of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God." Isaiah 42:16: "I will lead the blind by a way (hodo) they do not know; in paths they do not know I will guide them." Isaiah 43:19: "Behold, I am doing a new thing... I will even make a way (hodon) in the wilderness and rivers in the desert." Psalm 25:4 (LXX 24:4): "Make me know your ways (hodous), O LORD; teach me your paths." Psalm 86:11 (LXX 85:11): "Teach me your way (hodon), O LORD, that I may walk in your truth." Proverbs 8:22: Wisdom says, "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his way (hodou), before his works of old." The "way" of the LORD in the Hebrew scriptures is both God's character (his pattern of action) and God's provision (the path he opens for his people to walk). Jesus identifies himself as both: he is the revelation of God's character (the truth) and the path God provides for access to himself (the way).

"The truth" (he aletheia). Truth (aletheia) has been a central concept in this document. In 1:14, the Word made flesh was "full of grace and truth" (pleres charitos kai aletheias). In 1:17, "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (he charis kai he aletheia dia Iesou Christou egeneto). In 8:32, "you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free." In 8:40, "I told you the truth (ten aletheian)." In 8:44, the devil "does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him." In 17:17, "Your word is truth" (ho logos ho sos aletheia estin). In 18:37, "For this I have been born, and for this I have come into the world, to testify to the truth." The word aletheia in this document consistently designates the reality of God as revealed through Jesus, in contrast to the falsehood, blindness, and deception that characterize the world's opposition to God. Jesus is not merely a truth-teller; he is the truth itself — the reality to which all of God's self-disclosure has pointed.

In the LXX, aletheia translates the Hebrew emet, which carries the sense of "faithfulness, reliability, trustworthiness" as well as "truth." God's emet is his dependability, his constancy, his keeping of promises: Psalm 25:5 (LXX 24:5), "Lead me in your truth (aletheia) and teach me"; Psalm 31:5 (LXX 30:6), "Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth (aletheia)"; Psalm 86:11 (LXX 85:11), "Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth (aletheia)." The prayer "teach me your way... that I may walk in your truth" from Psalm 86 is precisely what Thomas asks and what Jesus answers: the way and the truth converge in the person of Jesus.

"The life" (he zoe). Life (zoe) has been the document's first and deepest theme. The prologue declared: "In him was life (zoe), and the life was the light of men" (1:4). The phrase "eternal life" (zoe aionios) appeared in 3:15, 16, 36; 4:14, 36; 5:24, 26, 39; 6:27, 40, 47, 54, 68; 10:28; 12:25, 50. In 5:26, "As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself." In 11:25, "I am the resurrection and the life." The life that Jesus claims to be is not biological existence (bios) but the quality of existence that belongs to God and that God shares with those who believe — the life that death cannot extinguish, as Lazarus's raising demonstrated.

The three terms — way, truth, life — are not three separate attributes but three aspects of a single reality. Jesus is the way because he is the truth (the full revelation of God) and the life (the source of the life that God gives). The way to the Father is through the one who is the Father's truth and the Father's life. The three terms interpret one another: the way is truthful (it does not deceive), the way is living (it is not a dead road but a living person), the truth is the way (it leads somewhere — to the Father), the life is found only on this way and in this truth.

"No one comes to the Father except through me" (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei me di' emou). The statement is exclusive: the access to the Father is through Jesus alone. The preposition dia with the genitive (di' emou, "through me") indicates the mediating agent or channel. In the context of this document, where the entire argument has been that Jesus is the one sent by the Father, the revealer of the Father, the one in whom the Father is seen (1:18, 12:45), the exclusivity is not arbitrary but follows from the nature of the relationship. If Jesus is the only one who has seen the Father and come from the Father (1:18, 6:46), then he is the only avenue of access to the Father. The door of 10:7-9 is the same reality expressed in different imagery: "I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture."

The statement addresses the disciples' immediate situation. They are troubled because Jesus is leaving. Where is he going? To the Father. How will they reach him? Through the very one who stands before them. The way to the destination is not a set of coordinates but a relationship with the person who is both the path and the destination's inhabitant.

"If you had known me, you would have known my Father also" (ei egnokeite me, kai ton patera mou an edeite). The conditional is contrary to fact (second-class condition in Greek): "if you had known me (but you have not fully), you would have known my Father (but you have not fully)." The statement is a gentle reproof: despite three years of companionship, the disciples have not fully grasped who Jesus is and therefore have not fully grasped the Father he reveals. This is consistent with 1:10 ("He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him") and with the pattern throughout the document where even the disciples require further illumination.

"From now on you do know him and have seen him" (ap' arti ginoskete auton kai heorakate auton). The phrase ap' arti ("from now on, from this moment") marks a turning point. Despite the reproof, Jesus declares that from this moment the disciples do know and have seen the Father. The verbs are present tense: ginoskete ("you know") and heorakate ("you have seen," perfect tense — with ongoing results). Something has shifted. The announcement of Jesus's departure, paradoxically, is the beginning of deeper knowledge. The disciples will come to understand, through the events about to unfold — the cross, the resurrection, the Spirit — that in knowing Jesus they have been knowing the Father all along. The future understanding is so certain that Jesus speaks of it as already accomplished.

div.title: Verses 8-11: Philip's Request and the Mutual Indwelling of Father and Son
div.p: "Philip said to him, 'Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.' Jesus said to him, 'Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, "Show us the Father"? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works. Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves.'"

"Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us" (Kyrie, deixon hemin ton patera, kai arkei hemin). Philip's request echoes the great theophany requests of Israel's history. Moses asked God: "Show me your glory" (deixon moi ten doxan sou, Exodus 33:18, LXX). God replied that no one can see his face and live (Exodus 33:20), but he would place Moses in the cleft of the rock and let his glory pass by (33:22-23). Isaiah saw the Lord seated on his throne (Isaiah 6:1) — a vision this author has identified as a vision of Jesus's glory (12:41). Ezekiel saw the likeness of the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28). Philip stands in the line of these seekers. He wants a theophany — a direct, unmediated display of God's presence. He believes this would settle everything: "it is enough for us" (arkei hemin).

Philip appeared in the opening chapter as the one who found Nathanael and told him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote" (1:45). He was the disciple approached by the Greeks who wished to see Jesus (12:21-22). His request here reveals that despite his recognition of Jesus as the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, he has not yet grasped the full implication: that in looking at Jesus he has been looking at the Father.

"Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip?" (tosouton chronon meth' hymon eimi kai ouk egnokas me, Philippe). The question carries reproach but also pathos. The word tosouton ("so long, so much time") measures the duration of the relationship — three years of companionship, witnessing signs, hearing teaching — and finds that the knowledge remains incomplete. The verb egnokas (perfect tense of ginosko, "to know") indicates a settled state: Philip has not arrived at knowledge of Jesus despite the extended time. The reproach is not harsh but pained: the one who has been present has not been perceived.

"Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (ho heorakos eme heoraken ton patera). This is the most direct statement in the document of the identity between seeing Jesus and seeing the Father. The verb horao ("to see") in the perfect tense (heorakos, heoraken) indicates completed vision with permanent results: the one who has seen Jesus has, in that seeing, already seen the Father. The theophany Philip requests has already occurred. The glory Moses asked to see, the glory Isaiah saw in the temple — it has been walking beside Philip, eating with him, washing his feet. The incarnation is the theophany. The flesh of Jesus is not a barrier to seeing God but the medium through which God is seen.

This statement fulfills the prologue's declaration: "No one has seen God at any time; the only begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father, he has explained him" (1:18). The verb exegesato ("explained, exegeted, interpreted") in 1:18 presented Jesus as the interpretation of God. Now in 14:9, the language is visual: to see Jesus is to see the Father. The explanation is not a verbal commentary alongside the reality but the reality itself made visible. Jesus is not a messenger who describes the Father from a distance; he is the Father's self-presentation in human form.

"Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?" (ou pisteueis hoti ego en to patri kai ho pater en emoi estin). The mutual indwelling formula — "I in the Father and the Father in me" — appeared in 10:38: "the Father is in me, and I am in the Father." In chapter 10, the statement was made to hostile authorities who tried to stone him for blasphemy (10:31, 33, 39). Here the same formula is addressed to Philip — a disciple who believes but does not yet fully understand. The claim is the same in both contexts: the relationship between Father and Son is not one of parallel existence but of mutual interpenetration. The Father is not outside of Jesus, observing from heaven; the Father dwells in Jesus. Jesus is not separate from the Father, acting independently; he is in the Father.

"The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works" (ta remata ha ego lego hymin ap' emautou ou lalo; ho de pater ho en emoi menon poiei ta erga autou). The verb meno ("to dwell, abide, remain") appears here for the Father's presence in Jesus. The Father "dwelling in" (menon, present participle — continuously abiding in) Jesus is the source of both the words (remata) and the works (erga). The words and works are not Jesus's independent productions; they are the Father's activity performed through the Son. This reiterates 5:19 ("the Son can do nothing of himself, unless it is something he sees the Father doing") and 5:30 ("I can do nothing on my own initiative") and 12:49 ("I did not speak on my own initiative, but the Father himself who sent me has given me a commandment as to what to say and what to speak"). The consistency of the claim across the entire document establishes it as the fundamental structure of the Father-Son relationship: the Son is the visible agent of the invisible Father's action.

The shift from "words" (remata) to "works" (erga) in the same sentence is significant. Jesus begins by speaking of his words and then attributes to the Father the works. The words and the works are not separate categories; they are both expressions of the Father's presence. The signs (works) and the discourses (words) throughout the public ministry were equally the Father's activity through the Son.

"Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves" (pisteuete moi hoti ego en to patri kai ho pater en emoi; ei de me, dia ta erga auta pisteuete). Jesus offers two paths to belief. The first is direct: believe his word — his testimony about his relationship with the Father. The second is indirect: if the word alone is insufficient, let the works (erga — the signs, the healings, the raising of Lazarus) serve as evidence. This mirrors the argument of 10:37-38: "If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, though you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me, and I in the Father." The works are a lower but still valid pathway to the same destination. The works point to the same reality the words declare: the Father is present and active in Jesus.

div.title: Verses 12-14: Greater Works and Prayer in Jesus's Name
div.p: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father. Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."

"Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do" (ho pisteuon eis eme ta erga ha ego poio kakeinos poiesei). The double amen formula marks this as an authoritative declaration. The "works" (erga) that the believer will do are the same category of works Jesus has been performing — the works of the Father (14:10). The claim is extraordinary: the works are not confined to Jesus's physical presence but will extend through those who believe in him. The chain of authorized action — the Father works through the Son (14:10), and now the Son's works will continue through believers — extends the mission beyond Jesus's departure.

"And greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father" (kai meizona touton poiesei, hoti ego pros ton patera poreuomai). The word meizona ("greater") does not mean "more spectacular" or "more miraculous." The basis for the greater works is given in the causal clause: "because I am going to the Father." Jesus's departure to the Father — through death, resurrection, and ascension — will accomplish the glorification (12:23-24), the drawing of all people (12:32), the sending of the Spirit (7:39, 16:7), and the establishment of the community's mission to the world. The works will be "greater" in scope, not in kind. Jesus's ministry was confined to the geography of Palestine and the duration of roughly three years. The works performed through believers after the Spirit's coming will extend across the world and across centuries. The "greater" is a matter of reach and extent, made possible by Jesus's going to the Father and sending the Spirit.

The precedent in Israel's history is the relationship between a prophet's ministry and its aftermath. Elijah's ministry was powerful; Elisha asked for and received "a double portion" of his spirit (2 Kings 2:9) and performed more signs than Elijah. The pattern of the master's departure releasing greater capacity in the successors is established.

"Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son" (kai ho ti an aitesete en to onomati mou touto poieso, hina doxasthe ho pater en to huio). The phrase "in my name" (en to onomati mou) introduces a concept that will recur throughout the farewell discourse (14:14, 26; 15:16; 16:23, 24, 26). In first-century usage, to act "in the name of" someone meant to act as their authorized representative — with their authority, in accordance with their character, and for their purposes. The shaliach (authorized agent) in Jewish law acted "in the name of" the sender, and the sender was bound by the agent's actions within the scope of the commission. To ask "in Jesus's name" is therefore not a formula appended to prayers but a description of the nature of the asking: requests made in alignment with Jesus's character, mission, and purposes — requests that the authorized representative would make on behalf of the one who sent him.

The purpose clause — "that the Father may be glorified in the Son" (hina doxasthe ho pater en to huio) — defines the scope. The works and the prayers are directed toward the Father's glory. This is consistent with Jesus's own prayer in 12:28 ("Father, glorify your name") and will be repeated in 17:1 ("Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that the Son may glorify you"). The asking, the doing, and the works all serve a single end: the revelation and vindication of who the Father is.

"If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it" (ean ti aitesete me en to onomati mou ego poieso). The repetition reinforces the promise and identifies Jesus as the one who acts in response to prayer. The disciples are not left powerless by Jesus's departure; they have access to his continued action through prayer offered in his name. The one who goes to the Father remains accessible to those who ask.

div.title: Verses 15-17: The First Promise of the Parakletos
div.p: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you."

"If you love me, you will keep my commandments" (ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas teresete). The conditional clause (ean + subjunctive, a third-class condition indicating a genuine contingency) establishes the relationship between love and obedience. Love for Jesus is not a sentiment or an emotion; it expresses itself in keeping (tereo, "to keep, guard, observe, maintain") his commandments (entolas). The verb tereo appears throughout the document for faithful observance: 8:51 ("If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death"), 8:55 ("I know him and keep his word"), 15:10 ("If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love"), 17:6 ("they have kept your word"). The word entole ("commandment") in the plural here embraces all that Jesus has commanded, with the "new commandment" of 13:34 as the primary content: love one another as he has loved them.

The connection between love and obedience is not mechanical or legalistic. It is relational: the one who loves Jesus will naturally do what Jesus commands, just as Jesus himself, who loves the Father, does what the Father commands (14:31, "I do as the Father has commanded me"). The obedience flows from the love; the love is demonstrated through the obedience. Neither exists without the other.

The grammatical form of teresete is debated — it could be future indicative ("you will keep") or aorist subjunctive ("keep!"). If future indicative, it is a statement of fact: if you love me, the natural result is that you will keep my commandments. If imperative subjunctive, it is a command: if you love me, then keep my commandments. Both readings yield the same practical meaning: love and commandment-keeping are inseparable.

"And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper" (kago eroteso ton patera, kai allon parakleton dosei hymin). The word parakletos ("Helper, Advocate, Comforter") appears only in this document and in 1 John 2:1 in the entire New Testament. The word is derived from parakaleo ("to call alongside, to summon to one's aid") and in first-century Greek usage had legal connotations: a parakletos was one called to stand beside someone in a legal proceeding — an advocate, a defense counsel, an intercessor. In the Targums, the Aramaic equivalent peraqlita is used for an intercessor or defense advocate in the heavenly court. In 1 John 2:1, Jesus himself is called "a parakletos with the Father" (parakleton echomen pros ton patera, Iesoun Christon dikaion) — an advocate who stands before the Father on behalf of believers.

The word allon ("another") is critical. It means "another of the same kind" (as distinguished from heteron, "another of a different kind"). Jesus will ask the Father to send another parakletos — another advocate of the same kind as Jesus himself. The implication is that Jesus has been the first parakletos, the first advocate, the first one who stood alongside the disciples. The Spirit will be a second advocate of the same type, continuing in Jesus's absence the same kind of ministry Jesus performed during his presence. The Spirit does not replace Jesus with something different; the Spirit continues Jesus's presence in a different mode.

"To be with you forever" (hina meth' hymon eis ton aiona e). The phrase eis ton aiona ("forever, unto the age, into perpetuity") indicates that the parakletos's presence, unlike Jesus's bodily presence, will not be temporary. Jesus's physical presence with the disciples is ending ("yet a little while I am with you," 13:33). The Spirit's presence will have no such limit. The word "with" (meth' hymon, "with you") echoes the Emmanuel ("God with us") motif. In verse 17, the preposition will shift from "with" (para) to "in" (en), deepening the mode of presence from accompaniment to indwelling.

"Even the Spirit of truth" (to pneuma tes aletheias). The Spirit is defined by the genitive tes aletheias ("of truth"), which can be either a genitive of source (the Spirit who comes from the truth) or a genitive of characteristic (the Spirit whose nature is truth). Since Jesus has just identified himself as "the truth" (14:6), the "Spirit of truth" is the Spirit who belongs to Jesus, who communicates Jesus's reality, who continues Jesus's work of revealing the Father. The Spirit's function is truth — reality, disclosure, the opposite of the deception that characterizes the devil (8:44) and the world's blindness (12:40).

The phrase will recur in 15:26 ("the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father") and 16:13 ("when the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth"). The Spirit's work is consistently described as the continuation and completion of Jesus's revelatory mission.

"Whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him" (ho ho kosmos ou dynatai labein, hoti ou theorei auto oude ginoskei auto). The world (kosmos) — the order that opposes God, that loved darkness rather than light (3:19), that did not know him (1:10) — cannot receive the Spirit of truth because it lacks the capacity to perceive or know him. The verbs theorei ("sees, perceives") and ginoskei ("knows") are the same verbs used throughout the document for spiritual perception and understanding. The world's inability is not arbitrary exclusion but the consequence of its character: a world that has chosen darkness cannot perceive a Spirit whose nature is truth. The world that rejected the Word in the flesh will not receive the Spirit of truth.
