"You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you" (hymeis ginoskete auto, hoti par' hymin menei kai en hymin estai). The pronoun hymeis ("you") is emphatic, contrasting the disciples with the world. The disciples do know the Spirit — they have experienced his presence through their relationship with Jesus. The Spirit who will come as "another parakletos" has already been at work in and through Jesus's own ministry. The shift from par' hymin ("alongside you, with you") to en hymin ("in you") marks a transition: what has been external presence will become internal indwelling. The verb menei ("dwells, remains, abides") is the document's key verb for permanent, settled relationship. The Spirit's presence is not a visit but an abiding.

The preposition para ("alongside, beside, with") describes the Spirit's relationship with the disciples during Jesus's earthly ministry — the Spirit was present alongside them in the person of Jesus. The preposition en ("in") describes the Spirit's relationship after Jesus's departure — the Spirit will be within them. The transition from "with" to "in" is the transition from incarnational presence (God dwelling alongside his people in the flesh of Jesus) to pneumatic presence (God dwelling within his people through the Spirit). This fulfills and extends the tabernacle motif: the Word that "tabernacled among us" (1:14, eskenosen en hemin) will, through the Spirit, take up permanent residence within the community.

div.title: Verses 18-20: Not Orphans — The Promise of Jesus's Return and Mutual Indwelling
div.p: "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you. Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."

"I will not leave you as orphans" (ouk apheso hymas orphanous). The word orphanos ("orphan, fatherless, bereaved") describes children whose parent or guardian has died or departed. In the LXX, the orphan is one of the vulnerable classes whom God specially protects: "A father of the fatherless (orphanon) and a judge for the widows is God in his holy habitation" (Psalm 68:5, LXX 67:6). Deuteronomy 10:18: God "executes justice for the orphan and the widow." Lamentations 5:3: "We have become orphans (orphanoi), fatherless (apatroi)." The word carries the weight of abandonment, vulnerability, and loss of protection. Jesus's departure could leave the disciples as spiritual orphans — without their teacher, their protector, their shepherd. The promise is that this will not happen.

The address also echoes the "little children" (teknia) of 13:33, where Jesus used parental language for the first time. He called them children; now he promises not to leave them orphaned. The parental imagery frames the relationship: Jesus is not merely a teacher who moves on; he is a guardian whose charges must not be left unprotected.

"I will come to you" (erchomai pros hymas). The present tense erchomai ("I am coming") rather than eleusomai ("I will come") is the same form as verse 3: "I will come again" (palin erchomai). The coming is treated as already underway, already set in motion by the events of the hour. This coming has multiple referents within the chapter and the wider narrative: the resurrection appearances (20:19-29), the sending of the Spirit (14:16-17, 26), and the final return. The promise is that the separation is not permanent; Jesus is coming to them.

"Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me" (eti mikron kai ho kosmos me ouketi theorei, hymeis de theoreite me). The phrase "a little while" (mikron) will be developed extensively in 16:16-22, where the disciples are confused by the phrase and Jesus explains it through the image of a woman in labor. Here the statement is compressed: the world's ability to see Jesus will end with his death and burial. The world (kosmos) — the order that does not know God (1:10) and cannot receive the Spirit of truth (14:17) — will perceive the crucifixion as the end. Jesus will be dead and gone. But the disciples will see him — in the resurrection appearances, through the Spirit's presence, in the ongoing relationship that his return establishes.

The verb theoreo ("to see, observe, perceive") carries the sense of perception that leads to understanding. The world's theorein of Jesus will cease; the disciples' theorein will continue. This creates two classes of perception: those whose encounter with Jesus ended at the cross and those whose encounter continued beyond it.

"Because I live, you also will live" (hoti ego zo kai hymeis zesete). The statement is compressed and pregnant with meaning. The present tense ego zo ("I live") indicates an ongoing, permanent state — Jesus's life is not something that will resume after an interruption but is an uninterruptible reality. Even the death on the cross does not extinguish the life that is "in him" from the beginning (1:4). The future hymeis zesete ("you will live") ties the disciples' life to his: because he lives, they will live. Their life is not independent but derivative — it comes from his life, as the branch's life comes from the vine (15:4-5). The resurrection is the event that will demonstrate this: Jesus's life continues through death, and the disciples' life will be sustained by his.

"In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you" (en ekeine te hemera gnosesthe hymeis hoti ego en to patri mou kai hymeis en emoi kago en hymin). The phrase "in that day" (en ekeine te hemera) points to the day of understanding that will come after the resurrection and the giving of the Spirit. The knowledge (gnosesthe, future of ginosko, "to know by experience") is not theoretical but experiential: they will know by living within the relationship.

The mutual indwelling formula is now extended in a remarkable way. In verse 10, the mutual indwelling was between Father and Son: "I am in the Father and the Father is in me." Now the chain extends to include the disciples: "I am in the Father, and you in me, and I in you." The relationship between Father and Son is opened to include those who believe. The disciples are drawn into the same kind of mutual abiding that defines the Father-Son relationship. This is not absorption or dissolution of identity but interpenetration: as the Father is present in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Son is present in the believers and the believers in the Son. The chain is: Father in Son, Son in believers, believers in Son, Son in Father — a web of mutual indwelling that connects the disciples to the Father through the Son.

This fulfills the promise of verse 3: "where I am you may be also." The "where" is not merely a future location but a present relationship of mutual indwelling. To be "where Jesus is" is to be in the Father, because Jesus is in the Father. The spatial language of verse 2 (dwelling places in the Father's house) is now reinterpreted in relational terms: the dwelling place is the relationship itself.

div.title: Verses 21-24: Love, Obedience, and the Dwelling of Father and Son with the Believer
div.p: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him. Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, 'Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?' Jesus answered him, 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me.'"

"Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me" (ho echon tas entolas mou kai teron autas ekeinos estin ho agapon me). The verb echo ("to have, hold, possess") combined with tereo ("to keep, guard, observe") describes someone who both possesses Jesus's commandments and actively maintains them. The having is not passive ownership but informed holding — the person knows what Jesus has commanded. The keeping is not mechanical compliance but faithful observance. Together, they define love: the person who does this "is the one who loves me" (ekeinos estin ho agapon me). The definition is precise: love for Jesus is constituted by commandment-keeping, not by feeling, profession, or mystical experience alone.

This reverses the order of verse 15 (where love for Jesus was the condition, and commandment-keeping was the result). Here commandment-keeping is the evidence, and love is the conclusion. The two verses form a circle: love produces obedience (v. 15), and obedience identifies love (v. 21). Neither love without obedience nor obedience without love is the reality Jesus describes.

"And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him" (ho de agapon me agapethesetai hypo tou patros mou, kago agapeso auton kai emphaniso auto emauton). The chain of love extends: the disciple loves Jesus; the Father loves the disciple; Jesus loves the disciple; Jesus manifests himself (emphanizo, "to make visible, to disclose, to reveal") to the disciple. The verb emphanizo appeared in the LXX for divine self-disclosure: Exodus 33:13 (LXX), where Moses asks God to "manifest" (emphanison) himself; Wisdom of Solomon 1:2, "he is found by those who do not test him and manifests himself (emphanidzetai) to those who do not distrust him." The self-manifestation is not available to everyone indiscriminately but is conditioned on love-as-obedience. The one who keeps the commandments receives the revelation.

"Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?" (Kyrie, kai ti gegonen hoti hemin melleis emphanizein seauton kai ouchi to kosmo). Judas (not Iscariot) is identified by the parenthetical clarification — the author ensures the reader does not confuse this Judas with the betrayer who has already departed (13:30). This Judas appears only here in this document. His question reveals a common first-century Jewish expectation: the Messiah's manifestation should be to the world — a public, unmistakable, politically visible revelation of God's power. The expectation was shaped by texts like Zechariah 14:9 ("The LORD will be king over all the earth; in that day the LORD will be the only one, and his name the only one") and Isaiah 40:5 ("Then the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all flesh will see it together"). Why would the Messiah reveal himself privately to a small group and not publicly to the world?
Jesus's answer redirects the question entirely. The manifestation is not a spectacular event but a relational dwelling.

"If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (ean tis agapa me ton logon mou teresei, kai ho pater mou agapesei auton, kai pros auton eleusometha kai monen par' auto poiesometha). The word mone ("dwelling place, home, abode") now reappears — the same word used in verse 2 for the "dwelling places" in the Father's house. In verse 2, Jesus spoke of going to prepare dwelling places for the disciples in the Father's house. Now, in verse 23, the Father and Son come and make a dwelling place (monen) with the one who loves and obeys. The movement reverses: not the disciples traveling to the Father's house, but the Father and Son coming to dwell with the disciple.

This is one of the most significant reinterpretations in the chapter. The "dwelling places" are not merely future, heavenly rooms awaiting the disciples' arrival after death. They are present realities: the Father and Son make their home with the one who loves and keeps the word. The mone of verse 2 and the mone of verse 23 are the same word used in two directions: the disciple has a dwelling place in the Father (v. 2), and the Father and Son have a dwelling place in the disciple (v. 23). The relationship is mutual: the believer abides in God, and God abides in the believer. The spatial language of "my Father's house" is not contradicted but deepened: the Father's house is wherever the Father dwells, and the Father dwells in the one who loves the Son.

The background in Israel's scriptures is extensive. God's dwelling with his people is a central promise of the covenant. Exodus 25:8: "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst" (katoikeso en autois, LXX). Exodus 29:45: "I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God." Leviticus 26:11-12: "I will make my dwelling among you... I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people." Ezekiel 37:26-27: "I will set my sanctuary in their midst forevermore. My dwelling place (he kataskennosis mou) shall be with them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Zechariah 2:10 (LXX 2:14): "Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst (kataskennoso en meso sou), declares the LORD." The entire arc of Israel's covenant history moves toward God dwelling with his people. The tabernacle, the temple, and the prophetic promises all point to a time when God's presence will be fully and permanently with his people. Jesus's promise in 14:23 claims that this covenant goal is now realized — not in a building but in a person: the one who loves Jesus and keeps his word becomes the dwelling place of the Father and the Son.

The pronoun "we" (eleusometha, "we will come"; poiesometha, "we will make") is the first-person plural including both the Father and the Son as joint actors. Throughout the document, Jesus has spoken of the Father and himself in terms that maintain both unity and distinction: "I and the Father are one" (10:30), yet "the Father is greater than I" (14:28). Here the unity is expressed in shared action: "we will come" and "we will make our home." The Father and Son act together, as one, in taking up residence with the believing disciple.

"Whoever does not love me does not keep my words" (ho me agapon me tous logous mou ou terei). The negative statement completes the definition. Love and obedience are inseparable in both directions: the one who loves keeps the commandments (v. 15, 21, 23), and the one who does not love does not keep them (v. 24). There is no middle ground — no category of one who loves Jesus but disregards his words, and no category of one who meticulously follows instructions without loving the one who gave them.

"And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me" (kai ho logos hon akouete ouk estin emos alla tou pempsantos me patros). This reiterates 12:49 ("I did not speak on my own initiative, but the Father himself who sent me has given me a commandment") and 7:16 ("My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me"). To keep Jesus's words is to keep the Father's words, because they are the same words. To reject Jesus's words is to reject the Father's words. The chain of authorization is complete: the Father speaks through the Son, and the Son's words are the Father's words.

div.title: Verses 25-26: The Spirit's Teaching Ministry
div.p: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."

"These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you" (tauta lelaleka hymin par' hymin menon). The participle menon ("remaining, abiding") echoes the meno language that pervades the chapter. Jesus has spoken "while remaining alongside you" (par' hymin menon) — his physical presence with the disciples has been the context for all his teaching. The phrase acknowledges that this mode of communication is ending. He will not always be "remaining alongside" them in the flesh. A new mode of teaching is about to begin.

"But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name" (ho de parakletos, to pneuma to hagion, ho pempsei ho pater en to onomati mou). The parakletos of verse 16 is now identified as "the Holy Spirit" (to pneuma to hagion). The term "Holy Spirit" (pneuma hagion) appears in the LXX in Psalm 51:11 (LXX 50:13): "Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit (to pneuma to hagion sou) from me" — David's prayer after his sin with Bathsheba. Isaiah 63:10-11: "But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit (to pneuma to hagion autou)... Where is he who put his Holy Spirit (to pneuma to hagion) in their midst?" The Holy Spirit in these LXX texts is God's own presence active among his people. The parakletos is not an impersonal force but God's personal presence — the same presence that was in the midst of Israel, that David feared losing.

The sending is by the Father "in my name" (en to onomati mou). In verse 13, the disciples were told to ask "in Jesus's name." Now the Father sends the Spirit "in Jesus's name." The "name" functions as the sphere of authority and identity: the Spirit comes with Jesus's authorization, representing Jesus, continuing Jesus's work. The Spirit does not bring a new message or a different revelation; the Spirit carries the name — the identity and authority — of Jesus.

"He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you" (ekeinos hymas didaxei panta kai hypomnesei hymas panta ha eipon hymin ego). The Spirit's two functions are stated. First, "he will teach you all things" (didaxei hymas panta). The Spirit continues and completes the teaching that Jesus began during his physical presence. "All things" (panta) is comprehensive: the Spirit's teaching is not partial or supplementary but complete. The areas that remain unclear — what the foot-washing means (13:7, "you will understand hereafter"), what the death accomplishes, what the resurrection opens — will be illuminated by the Spirit's instruction.

Second, "he will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you" (hypomnesei hymas panta ha eipon hymin ego). The verb hypomimnesko ("to remind, bring to remembrance, cause to remember") indicates that the Spirit's work is not innovation but recollection. The Spirit does not bring new content independent of Jesus's words; the Spirit brings to mind what Jesus has already said. The disciples have heard Jesus's teaching for three years; the Spirit will activate that stored teaching, making its meaning accessible in situations that had not yet arisen when the words were first spoken.

This passage explains the phenomenon the author has already described. In 2:22, "When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered (emnesthesen) that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken." In 12:16, "These things his disciples did not understand at the first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered (emnesthesen) that these things were written of him." The remembering that occurred after the resurrection was the work of the Spirit bringing to mind what Jesus had said and enabling the disciples to understand it. The promise of 14:26 is the explanation of the process described in 2:22 and 12:16.

div.title: Verses 27-29: The Gift of Peace and the Going to the Father
div.p: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I. And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe."

"Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you" (eirenen aphiemi hymin, eirenen ten emen didomi hymin). The word eirene ("peace") translates the Hebrew shalom, which in the LXX and first-century Jewish usage is far more than the absence of conflict. Shalom encompasses wholeness, well-being, right relationship, prosperity, and the blessing of God. The standard Jewish greeting and farewell was shalom — "peace." Jesus uses the conventional departure formula but infuses it with new content: "my peace" (ten emen, emphatic — "the peace that is mine, my own kind of peace"). The peace Jesus gives is not generic well-wishing but something that belongs to him specifically — the peace of the one who is in the Father and who the Father is in, the peace of the shepherd who lays down his life voluntarily, the peace of the one who knows his origin and destination (13:3).

In the LXX, peace (eirene/shalom) is associated with God's covenant blessing. Numbers 6:26: "The LORD lift up his countenance on you and give you peace (eirenen)." Psalm 29:11 (LXX 28:11): "The LORD will bless his people with peace (en eirene)." Isaiah 9:6 (LXX 9:5): the coming ruler will be the "Prince of Peace" (archon eirenes). Isaiah 26:3: "You will keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you." Isaiah 54:10: "My steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace (diatheke eirenes) shall not be removed." Ezekiel 37:26: "I will make a covenant of peace with them." The peace Jesus bequeaths is the covenant peace — the shalom of God's fulfilled promise.

"Not as the world gives do I give to you" (ou kathos ho kosmos didosin ego didomi hymin). The world's giving is characterized by this document as transient, conditional, and self-serving. The world gives approval to those who belong to it (15:19) and withdraws it from those who do not. The world's peace is the absence of immediate conflict, contingent on circumstances. Jesus's peace is not contingent on circumstances — it is given to disciples on the eve of betrayal, arrest, and crucifixion. The peace exists in the midst of the very conditions that should destroy it.

"Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid" (me tarassestho hymon he kardia mede deilato). The command from verse 1 is repeated with an addition: mede deilato ("neither be afraid, neither be cowardly"). The verb deiliao ("to be afraid, to be cowardly") appears only here in this document. In the LXX, it appears in Deuteronomy 1:21 ("Do not fear or be dismayed," me phobou mede deiliasei), Joshua 1:9 ("Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened," me deilias), and Deuteronomy 31:6 ("Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or terrified," me phobou mede deiliasei). The language echoes the courage commands given to Israel before entering the promised land and before battle. The disciples are about to face their own wilderness — the chaos of the arrest, trial, and crucifixion — and Jesus addresses them with the same formula God used to address Israel at moments of transition and threat.

"You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you'" (ekousate hoti ego eipon hymin, hypago kai erchomai pros hymas). Jesus restates the dual movement: departure and return. The going and the coming are held together as a single plan. The departure is not an end but a pivot: the going enables the coming. This is the logic of 16:7: "It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you."

"If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father" (ei egapate me, echarete an, hoti poreuomai pros ton patera). The conditional is again contrary to fact (second-class): "if you loved me (but your love is not yet mature enough), you would have rejoiced." The statement is not a denial of their love but a diagnosis of its limitation. They love Jesus but they understand his departure only as loss. If they fully understood what his going to the Father accomplishes — the glorification, the sending of the Spirit, the preparation of dwelling places, the access to the Father — they would rejoice rather than grieve.

"For the Father is greater than I" (hoti ho pater meizon mou estin). The statement is significant and requires careful placement within the document's argument. Throughout the text, the author has maintained both the unity and the distinction between Father and Son. The unity: "I and the Father are one" (10:30); "the Father is in me and I am in the Father" (10:38, 14:10-11); "whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (14:9). The distinction: "I go to the Father" (14:12, 28) — one cannot go to oneself; "the Father who sent me" (4:34, 5:30, 37, 6:38-39, 7:16, 8:16, 12:49, 14:24) — the sender is distinct from the sent one; "the Father has given all things into his hands" (3:35, 13:3) — the giver is distinct from the receiver.

The statement "the Father is greater than I" maintains the distinction within the unity. In the context of this verse, the greatness of the Father is the reason for rejoicing: Jesus is going from the limitations of incarnate existence ("being with you" in the flesh, subject to suffering and death) to the Father, who is greater. The going to the Father is an ascent, not merely a departure. The disciples should rejoice because the one they love is going to a greater place. The word meizon ("greater") describes relational order — the sender is greater than the sent one, the Father who gives the commandment is greater than the Son who receives it — without diminishing the unity or the shared nature that the document has asserted.

The concept has precedent in the document's own framework. In 5:19-20, the Son does what he sees the Father doing — the Father shows, the Son does. In 5:26, the Father "has life in himself" and "has granted the Son also to have life in himself" — the Son's life-in-himself is granted by the Father, indicating an order of origin. In 10:29, "My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all" — the Father's greatness is asserted as the ultimate security of the sheep. The Father's greatness is not a rival claim to the Son's glory but the ground of the Son's mission and the goal of the Son's return.

"And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe" (kai nyn eireka hymin prin genesthai, hina hotan genetai pisteusete). This repeats the pattern established in 13:19: "From now on I am telling you before it comes to pass, so that when it does occur, you may believe that I am." The prior announcement transforms the events from faith-destroyers into faith-confirmers. The death, which will appear to be defeat, has been foretold by the one who claims to be the truth. When it occurs, the disciples will be able to recognize it as part of the plan rather than evidence of its failure.

div.title: Verses 30-31: The Ruler of This World and the Command to Depart
div.p: "I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me, but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."

"I will no longer talk much with you" (ouketi polla laleso meth' hymon). The time for extended teaching is running short. The arrest is approaching. The ruler of this world — the power behind Judas, behind the authorities, behind the entire structure of opposition — is on his way. The farewell discourse must come to its essential points quickly.

"For the ruler of this world is coming" (erchetai gar ho tou kosmou archon). The "ruler of this world" (ho archon tou kosmou) appeared in 12:31, where Jesus declared that "now the ruler of this world will be cast out" (ekblethesetai exo). The figure was identified there as the spiritual power behind the world's opposition to God — the devil of 8:44 who was "a murderer from the beginning." Now the ruler is "coming" (erchetai) — the arrest, orchestrated by Judas under Satan's entry (13:27), is the ruler's approach. The events of the Passion are not merely political or religious machinations; they are the ruler of this world's attempt to destroy the one who has been casting light into the darkness.

"He has no claim on me" (kai en emoi ouk echei ouden). The phrase literally reads "and in me he has nothing" (en emoi ouk echei ouden). The ruler of this world has no hold, no foothold, no authority, no part in Jesus. The word ouden ("nothing") is absolute. The devil, who entered Judas (13:27), has no corresponding entry point in Jesus. There is nothing in Jesus that belongs to the ruler's domain — no sin, no falsehood, no self-serving motive, no foothold for corruption. The contrast with Judas is stark: the devil found a place in Judas's heart (13:2); in Jesus, the devil finds nothing. The statement echoes the document's consistent presentation of Jesus's sinlessness: "Which one of you convicts me of sin?" (8:46).

The concept has scriptural precedent. In Job, the Satan tested Job's integrity and found, ultimately, that Job's faithfulness could not be overthrown (though Job's case was complex and involved suffering). In Zechariah 3:1-5, the Satan stood to accuse the high priest Joshua, but the LORD rebuked the Satan and clothed Joshua in clean garments. In Jesus's case, the Satan approaches not to accuse but to destroy, and finds not merely innocence but absolute emptiness of anything that belongs to his domain.

"But I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father" (all' hina gno ho kosmos hoti agapo ton patera, kai kathos eneteilato moi ho pater, houtos poio). Jesus's submission to the coming events — the arrest, trial, and crucifixion — is not defeat by the ruler of this world but obedience to the Father. The Father commanded (eneteilato, aorist of entellomai, "to command, give orders, charge") this course of action. The cross is not the ruler's victory but the Father's plan, and Jesus's obedience to it is the demonstration of his love for the Father. The phrase "so that the world may know that I love the Father" reveals the purpose: the crucifixion, rightly understood, is the visible evidence of the Son's love for the Father. The obedience that goes to death is the ultimate expression of the relationship the entire document has described: the Son does what the Father commands, says what the Father gives him to say, and now dies because the Father has commanded it (10:18).

"Rise, let us go from here" (egeiresthe, agomen enteuthen). The verb egeiresthe ("rise, get up") is the imperative of egeiro — the resurrection verb. As in 13:4, where the same verb described Jesus rising from the table before the foot-washing, the literal action (standing up to leave the room) carries a resonance with the resurrection. The command agomen ("let us go") is the same verb used in 11:7 ("Let us go to Judea again") and 11:15 ("Let us go to him" — to the dead Lazarus). Each previous use of agomen led to a confrontation with death: in chapter 11, the journey to Lazarus's tomb; now, the journey toward the cross.

The command "let us go from here" creates a textual problem: chapters 15-17 follow with additional discourse, and the actual departure does not occur until 18:1 ("When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples across the Kidron valley"). The simplest explanation is that the discourse of chapters 15-17 was spoken en route — during the walk from the upper room to the garden. The command to rise and go marks a transition within the farewell discourse: the intimate setting of the supper table gives way to the journey toward the garden of arrest.

list.item: The chapter is the farewell discourse's first sustained response to the crisis of Jesus's departure. Chapter 13 enacted the departure's meaning (foot-washing), identified the betrayer, and gave the community its defining commandment (love one another). Chapter 14 now addresses the questions the departure raises: where is Jesus going? how will the disciples follow? who will be with them after he leaves? The entire chapter moves from trouble (v. 1) to peace (v. 27), from anxiety about separation to assurance of continued presence.

The "dwelling places" language (monai, vv. 2, 23) operates in two directions simultaneously. In verse 2, Jesus goes to prepare dwelling places for the disciples in the Father's house — the disciples will have a home with God. In verse 23, the Father and Son come and make a dwelling place with the one who loves and keeps Jesus's word — God will have a home with the disciple. The same word mone is used for both movements. The language of Israel's covenant — God dwelling among his people (Exodus 25:8, Leviticus 26:11-12, Ezekiel 37:26-27) — is fulfilled not in a building but in a relationship. The dwelling is mutual: the believer abides in God, and God abides in the believer.

The declaration "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (v. 6) redefines the categories. Thomas asked for a road; Jesus offered himself. The "way" to the Father is not a set of instructions, a ritual, or a moral program but a person. The way, the truth, and the life are not three separate things but three aspects of a single reality: the access to the Father (way), the revelation of the Father (truth), and the life that the Father gives (life) are all located in Jesus. The exclusivity of "no one comes to the Father except through me" follows from the document's consistent claim that Jesus is the Father's only self-revelation in flesh (1:18, 12:45).

The Father-Son mutual indwelling, established in 10:38 and restated in 14:10-11, is extended in verse 20 to include the disciples. The formula "I am in the Father, and you in me, and I in you" draws the believers into the same relationship that defines the Father and Son. The "where I am, you may be also" of verse 3 is not merely a future spatial arrangement but a present relational reality: to be "where Jesus is" is to be in the web of mutual indwelling that connects disciple to Son to Father.

The relationship between love and obedience is stated with precision and without exception. Love for Jesus expresses itself in keeping his commandments (vv. 15, 21, 23). Absence of love results in failure to keep his words (v. 24). Keeping the commandments results in the Father's love, Jesus's love, and Jesus's self-manifestation to the believer (v. 21). The circle is closed: love produces obedience, obedience identifies love, and the reward of love-as-obedience is deeper relationship with the Father and Son.

The parakletos (Helper, Advocate) is introduced as "another" of the same kind as Jesus (v. 16). Jesus has been the first parakletos; the Spirit will be a second of the same kind. The Spirit is identified as the Holy Spirit (v. 26) and the Spirit of truth (v. 17). The Spirit's functions are threefold: to be with the disciples forever (v. 16), to teach them all things (v. 26), and to bring to their remembrance what Jesus has said (v. 26). The Spirit does not bring new revelation independent of Jesus but activates and illuminates what Jesus has already spoken. The Spirit's coming explains the "afterward" understanding pattern the author has described (2:22, 12:16, 13:7): the disciples did not understand at first, but after the Spirit came, they remembered and understood.

The promise "I will not leave you as orphans" (v. 18) addresses the pastoral crisis of the departure directly. The disciples are not being abandoned; they are being transitioned from one mode of Jesus's presence (physical, incarnational) to another (pneumatic, indwelling). The Spirit's presence within them (en hymin, v. 17) replaces Jesus's presence alongside them (par' hymin, v. 17). The transition is not loss but deepening: what was "with" becomes "in." The tabernacle motif of the prologue (the Word "dwelt among us," 1:14) evolves into permanent indwelling.

The chapter maintains the distinction between the disciples and the world at every point. The world cannot receive the Spirit of truth (v. 17). The world will see Jesus no more (v. 19). The self-manifestation is to the community, not to the world (vv. 21-22). The world's peace is different from Jesus's peace (v. 27). The ruler of this world is coming, but has nothing in Jesus (v. 30). The community is a distinct entity within but not of the world, sustained by a presence the world cannot perceive.

The statement "the Father is greater than I" (v. 28) maintains the relational order within the unity the document has asserted. The Father and Son are one (10:30), mutually indwelling (10:38, 14:10-11), jointly acting (14:23). Yet the Father sends and the Son is sent; the Father commands and the Son obeys; the Father is the destination and the Son goes to him. The "greater than" is the relational order of sender and sent, not a diminishment of the Son's nature or authority. In context, it is the reason the disciples should rejoice: Jesus goes to the one who is greater.

The ruler of this world "has nothing" in Jesus (v. 30). The devil who entered Judas (13:27) has no corresponding entry point in Jesus. The approaching death is not the ruler's conquest but the Father's command, obeyed by the Son in love. The cross, which the world will perceive as the ruler's triumph, is in reality the Son's act of loving obedience to the Father (v. 31), and it will result in the ruler's casting out (12:31).

The command "Rise, let us go from here" (v. 31) marks a transition within the farewell discourse. The supper-table conversation yields to the journey toward the garden of arrest. The verb egeiresthe carries the resonance of resurrection (the same verb used throughout the document for raising from death). The command agomen echoes the earlier journeys toward death (11:7, 15). The movement is toward the cross, but the vocabulary points beyond the cross to the rising.

The chapter's pronouns maintain careful distinctions. "You" (hymeis) throughout refers to the disciples who remain after Judas's departure — the "clean" ones (13:10), the community to whom the farewell discourse is addressed. "He" (ekeinos, v. 26) refers to the Spirit as a personal agent, not an impersonal force. "We" (v. 23) refers to the Father and Son acting in concert. "The world" (ho kosmos) refers to the order that opposes God, cannot receive the Spirit, and whose ruler approaches. The careful pronoun use delineates the relationships: the disciples are in Jesus, Jesus is in the Father, the Spirit is sent by the Father in Jesus's name, and the world stands outside this web of mutual indwelling.

The chapter's argument flows as a single unbroken movement from trouble to peace. The sequence is: (a) the troubled heart addressed by the promise of dwelling places and the going-to-prepare (vv. 1-4); (b) Thomas's question answered by the revelation of Jesus as the way to the Father (vv. 5-7); (c) Philip's request answered by the declaration that seeing Jesus is seeing the Father (vv. 8-11); (d) the promise of greater works and prayer in Jesus's name (vv. 12-14); (e) the link between love and obedience that opens the way for the Spirit's coming (vv. 15-17); (f) the assurance that Jesus is not abandoning them but coming to them in a new mode (vv. 18-20); (g) the mutual indwelling deepened to include the believer as the dwelling place of Father and Son (vv. 21-24); (h) the Spirit's teaching and reminding ministry that will sustain the community after Jesus's departure (vv. 25-26); (i) the gift of peace, the call to rejoice, and the prior announcement that transforms crisis into confirmation (vv. 27-29); (j) the approaching ruler who has nothing in Jesus, and the command to depart toward the cross (vv. 30-31). There is no change of subject: every section develops the response to Jesus's departure. The departure is not loss but transition — from physical presence to spiritual indwelling, from incarnational proximity to pneumatic intimacy, from the Word dwelling among them to the Father and Son dwelling within them.

div.title: Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (John 14): Chapter 14 opens the private instruction that began with the foot-washing and new commandment of chapter 13. The setting remains the evening before the Passover, after Judas's departure into the night (13:30). Jesus addresses the remaining disciples — those who are "clean" (13:10) — with the words "Do not let your heart be troubled; you believe in God, believe also in me" (14:1). He announces his departure to the Father: "In my Father's house are many dwelling places (monai); if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you. If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also" (14:2-3). Thomas asks about the way, and Jesus responds with the sixth "I am" statement with a predicate: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father but through me" (14:6). Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus declares the inseparability of Father and Son: "He who has seen me has seen the Father... Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me?" (14:9-10). The Father "abiding" (menon) in Jesus performs the works (14:10).

The chapter introduces the first promise of the Paraclete: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper (allon parakleton), that he may be with you forever; that is the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him, but you know him because he abides (menei) with you and will be in you" (14:16-17). Jesus promises: "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you" (14:18). The mutual indwelling is then extended to the disciples: "In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you" (14:20). This mutual indwelling is immediately conditioned: "He who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me; and he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will disclose myself to him" (14:21). Judas (not Iscariot) asks why Jesus will disclose himself to the disciples and not to the world, and Jesus responds: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode (monen) with him" (14:23) — using the noun from the same root as meno ("to abide"), the word that will dominate chapter 15. The counterpart is stated immediately: "He who does not love me does not keep my words" (14:24).

The second Paraclete promise follows: "The Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all that I said to you" (14:26). Jesus gives his peace — "not as the world gives" (14:27) — and announces again that he is going to the Father: "If you loved me, you would have rejoiced because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (14:28). He has told them before it happens so that they will believe when it occurs (14:29). Then: "The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me; but so that the world may know that I love the Father, I do exactly as the Father commanded me" (14:30-31a). The chapter concludes with the words: "Get up, let us go from here" (egeiresthe, agomen enteuthen, 14:31b).

What the author argues immediately after (John 16): Chapter 16 opens with a direct continuation of the warnings about persecution: "These things I have spoken to you so that you may be kept from stumbling" (16:1). The "these things" refers to the teaching about the world's hatred and the Spirit's testimony in 15:18-27. The persecution is specified: "They will make you outcasts from the synagogue (aposynagogous), and an hour is coming for everyone who kills you to think that he is offering service to God" (16:2) — the same synagogue expulsion that was threatened in 9:22 and 12:42, now extended to murder. The reason is stated: "These things they will do because they have not known the Father or me" (16:3), echoing 15:21 ("they do not know the one who sent me"). Jesus explains that he did not say these things from the beginning because he was with them, but now he is going to the one who sent him (16:4-5).

The chapter then develops the third Paraclete promise: "If I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you" (16:7). The Spirit's work is described in terms of the world: "He, when he comes, will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment" (16:8). The Spirit's work is then described in terms of the disciples: "When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own initiative, but whatever he hears, he will speak" (16:13). The chapter continues with the "a little while" sayings (16:16-22), the image of a woman's birth pangs transforming into joy, the promise of prayer in Jesus's name (16:23-24), and the announcement that Jesus will speak plainly about the Father (16:25). The disciples declare they now believe, and Jesus responds by predicting their scattering: "An hour is coming, and has already come, for you to be scattered, each to his own home, and to leave me alone" (16:32). The farewell discourse's second major section concludes: "These things I have spoken to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have tribulation, but take courage; I have overcome the world" (16:33).

How chapter 15 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 14 ended with "Get up, let us go from here" (14:31b), a statement that appears to conclude the supper setting. Whether the discourse of chapters 15-17 was spoken in a different location (perhaps on the way from the upper room to Gethsemane), or whether the author has arranged material without strict concern for physical movement, the content flows without interruption from what chapter 14 established. The subject matter is continuous; there is no change of audience, no shift in theme, and no new setting described. The disciples who were addressed in chapter 14 are the same "you" (hymeis) addressed in chapter 15. The argument proceeds without a seam.

The connection between chapter 14 and chapter 15 is organic and precise. Chapter 14 introduced the theme of mutual indwelling in abstract, relational terms: "I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you" (14:20); the Father and Son will "make our abode (monen) with him" who keeps Jesus's word (14:23). The noun mone ("abode, dwelling place") shares its root with the verb meno ("to abide, remain, dwell"), which appears in chapter 14 in connection with the Spirit who "abides (menei) with you" (14:17) and the Father "abiding (menon) in me" who does the works (14:10). Chapter 15 now gives this mutual indwelling a vivid, organic image: the vine and the branches. The abstract claim "you in me, and I in you" becomes the concrete reality of a branch drawing its life from the vine, and the vine bearing its fruit through the branches. The verb meno, which appeared five times in chapter 14, will appear eleven times in 15:4-10 alone — the highest concentration in the entire document. The concept that was introduced conceptually is now illustrated agriculturally.

Chapter 14 also linked the mutual indwelling to two conditions: keeping Jesus's commandments (14:15, 21, 23-24) and loving Jesus (14:15, 21, 23). Chapter 15 continues both threads: "If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love" (15:10); "This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you" (15:12). The new commandment of 13:34 — love one another as Jesus has loved — is now interwoven with the vine metaphor's demand for abiding, creating a single fabric: to abide in the vine is to keep the commandments, and the commandment is to love one another.

Chapter 14 promised the Spirit as Helper and described the Spirit's work as teaching and reminding (14:26). Chapter 15 will develop the Spirit's role as witness: "When the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, that is the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me" (15:26). The Spirit moves from teacher (chapter 14) to witness (chapter 15) to prosecutor/advocate (chapter 16, convicting the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment). Each chapter adds a new dimension to the Spirit's role.

Chapter 14 mentioned the world's inability to receive the Spirit (14:17) and the ruler of this world (14:30). Chapter 15 will develop this into a sustained description of the world's hostility: "If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you" (15:18). The world that cannot receive the Spirit will instead persecute those who have received the Spirit. The disciples' relationship with the world, hinted at in chapter 14, becomes the explicit subject of the second half of chapter 15.

Chapter 15 thus occupies a precise position in the farewell discourse's architecture. It answers three questions that chapters 13-14 have raised: (1) How do the disciples remain connected to Jesus after his departure? Answer: by abiding in him, as branches abide in the vine. (2) What does the community's life look like? Answer: mutual love, modeled on Jesus's self-sacrificing love, expressed in obedience to his commandments. (3) What does the community's relationship with the world look like? Answer: hatred and persecution, which the Spirit's testimony and the disciples' own witness will meet. Chapter 16 will then address what the disciples need to hear in order to endure: the Spirit's convicting work, the promise that sorrow will become joy, and the assurance that Jesus has overcome the world.

div.title: Verses 1-3: The True Vine
div.p: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away; and every branch that bears fruit, he prunes it so that it may bear more fruit. You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you."

"I am the true vine" (ego eimi he ampelos he alethine). This is the seventh and final "I am" statement with a predicate in this document (following "bread of life," 6:35; "light of the world," 8:12; "door of the sheep," 10:7; "good shepherd," 10:11; "resurrection and the life," 11:25; "the way, the truth, and the life," 14:6). Each of these statements has drawn on a central image from Israel's scriptures and claimed it for Jesus. The vine is no exception. It is one of the most deeply embedded images for Israel in the prophetic literature.

The vine as a figure for Israel is pervasive in the scriptures. Isaiah 5:1-7 contains the Song of the Vineyard, in which God describes planting Israel as a choice vineyard on a fertile hill: "He dug it all around, removed its stones, and planted it with the choicest vine (soreq). He built a tower in the middle of it and also hewed out a wine vat in it; then he expected it to produce good grapes (staphylen), but it produced worthless ones (agria)" (Isaiah 5:2, LXX). The parable is interpreted: "The vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his delightful plant. Thus he looked for justice (krisin), but behold, bloodshed (anomian); for righteousness, but behold, a cry of distress" (Isaiah 5:7). God planted, tended, and protected the vine — and the vine failed to produce the fruit God sought. The judgment follows: "I will remove its hedge and it will be consumed; I will break down its wall and it will become trampled ground. I will lay it waste" (Isaiah 5:5-6).

Psalm 80:8-16 (LXX 79:9-17) develops the same image in the form of a lament: "You removed a vine (ampelon) from Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You cleared the ground before it, and it took deep root and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow, and the cedars of God with its boughs... Why have you broken down its hedges, so that all who pass along the way pick its fruit? A boar from the forest ravages it, and whatever moves in the field feeds on it... It is burned with fire, it is cut down; they perish at the rebuke of your countenance" (Psalm 80:8-16, LXX 79:9-17). The vine is Israel, planted by God's hand, once flourishing, now ravaged. The psalmist pleads for restoration: "Turn again, O God of hosts; look down from heaven and see, and take care of this vine" (80:14).

Jeremiah 2:21 adds the element of degeneration: "I planted you a choice vine (ampelon), a completely faithful seed. How then have you turned yourself before me into the degenerate shoots of a foreign vine (ampelos allotria)?" The vine was planted faithful; it turned foreign. The fault lies with the vine, not the planter.

Ezekiel 15:1-8 addresses the uselessness of vine wood apart from fruit-bearing: "How is the wood of the vine (to xylon tes ampelou) better than any wood of a branch which is among the trees of the forest? Can wood be taken from it to make anything? Or can men take a peg from it on which to hang any vessel? Behold, it is put into the fire for fuel" (Ezekiel 15:2-4). The vine's wood is worthless for any purpose except burning. A vine that does not bear fruit has no value whatsoever — it cannot even serve as timber. The only destiny for a fruitless vine is fire.

Ezekiel 19:10-14 describes Israel as "a vine in your vineyard, planted by the waters; it was fruitful and full of branches by reason of abundant water. It had strong branches, fit for rulers' scepters... But it was uprooted in fury, cast down to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were torn off so that they withered; the fire consumed them" (Ezekiel 19:10-12). The vine's fruitfulness and its destruction are both narrated.

Hosea 10:1 adds the diagnosis: "Israel is a luxuriant vine (ampelos euklematousa); he produces fruit for himself." The vine is fruitful, but the fruit serves the vine's own purposes, not God's. The fruitfulness is selfish, not obedient.

A first-century hearer encountering the phrase "I am the true vine" would hear it against this entire tradition. Israel was God's vine — and Israel failed. The vine planted with the choicest stock produced worthless grapes (Isaiah 5). The vine brought out of Egypt was burned and ravaged (Psalm 80). The vine planted faithful degenerated into wild shoots (Jeremiah 2). The vine's wood was fit only for fire (Ezekiel 15). Now Jesus claims to be "the true vine" — he alethine ampelos. The adjective alethine ("true, genuine, real") is the same word the author has used consistently to distinguish the ultimate reality from the preliminary version: "the true light which, coming into the world, enlightens every man" (1:9) — as distinct from John the Baptist, who was "the lamp that was burning and shining" (5:35) but not the light itself; "the true bread out of heaven" (6:32) — as distinct from the manna Moses gave, which was real bread but not the ultimate bread; "true worshipers" (4:23) — as distinct from worship tied to a particular mountain or temple. In each case, the "true" entity is not a replacement of a false one but the fulfillment of what the earlier version anticipated. The manna was real but temporary; the true bread gives life permanently. The light of the lamp was real but limited; the true light enlightens everyone. So too: Israel as vine was real — genuinely planted by God, genuinely tended, genuinely called — but it did not produce the fruit God sought. Jesus is the vine that produces what God has always desired. He is the faithful vine that Israel was supposed to be.

The claim is not merely that Jesus is a vine, one among several possible vines. He is the vine — the true one, the one to which Israel's vine imagery always pointed, the one in which the fruitfulness God has sought since the planting will finally be produced.

"And my Father is the vinedresser" (kai ho pater mou ho georgos estin). The word georgos means "farmer, husbandman, one who works the land." In the LXX, the cognate verb georgeo appears in connection with agricultural labor (Genesis 2:5, 15; 4:2). In the parable of the vineyard in Isaiah 5, the LORD is the one who planted, dug, cleared, and tended the vineyard — the LORD is the georgos, the vinedresser. The identification of the Father as the vinedresser maintains the scriptural pattern: God is the one who tends the vine. But now the vine is not Israel as a nation; the vine is Jesus. The Father tends Jesus, and the branches that grow from Jesus are the disciples. The relationship between vinedresser and vine is the relationship between Father and Son that the document has described since the prologue: the Father acts through the Son, and the Son produces what the Father desires.
"Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he takes away" (pan klema en emoi me pheron karpon airei auto). Several elements require close attention.

First, the word klema ("branch, shoot") is the term for the vine's branches specifically, used for the extending parts of a grapevine that either bear or fail to bear grapes. In viticulture, the branches are wholly dependent on the vine for their life; a severed branch has no independent capacity to survive or produce.

Second, the phrase "in me" (en emoi) is attached to the fruitless branches, not only to the fruitful ones. The branches that do not bear fruit are described as being "in me." They are not outsiders, not strangers to the vine. They are connected — or at least they appear to be connected — to Jesus. This is consistent with the pattern the author has established throughout the document: Judas was chosen by Jesus (6:70, 13:18), ate at his table, had his feet washed by Jesus (13:5), and yet was "not clean" (13:10-11). The unfruitful branches in the vine correspond to the one who was "in" the community but did not truly belong. The vine metaphor extends the principle from a single individual (Judas) to a general category: every branch in Jesus that does not bear fruit.

Third, the verb airei ("he takes away, removes") is from airo, a word the author uses throughout the document. In 1:29, John the Baptist declares that the Lamb of God "takes away (airon) the sin of the world." In 11:39, 41, the stone is "removed" (arate, eran) from Lazarus's tomb. In 19:15, the crowd cries "Away with him, away with him (aron, aron), crucify him." In 19:38, Joseph of Arimathea asks to "take away (are) the body of Jesus." In 20:1-2, the stone "had been taken away (ermenon)" and Mary says "They have taken away (eran) the Lord." The predominant usage in this document is removal — to take something away from where it was. The vinedresser removes the fruitless branch from the vine. The action belongs to the Father (ho georgos, the vinedresser), not to the branch itself. The branch does not remove itself; it is removed.

"And every branch that bears fruit, he prunes it so that it may bear more fruit" (kai pan to karpon pheron kathairei auto hina karpon pleiona phere). The verb kathairei ("he prunes, he cleanses") creates a deliberate word-play with katharoi ("clean") in the next verse. Kathairei is from kathairo, meaning "to cleanse, purge, prune." In viticulture, pruning is the cutting back of living, productive branches — not to harm them but to redirect their energy from excessive foliage into greater fruit production. A branch that is not pruned will produce leaves and shoots but less fruit; a pruned branch, though temporarily diminished, produces abundantly. The pruning is not punishment but cultivation. The vinedresser cuts the fruitful branch not because it has failed but because it has succeeded, and he wants it to succeed even more.

The two actions of the vinedresser in verse 2 are therefore: removal of the fruitless (airei) and pruning of the fruitful (kathairei). These are the only two possibilities for a branch. Every branch either bears fruit or does not. There is no third category. The vinedresser acts on both, but the actions are opposite: one is eliminated, the other is cultivated.

"You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you" (ede hymeis katharoi este dia ton logon hon lelaleka hymin). The word katharoi ("clean") is the adjective that corresponds to the verb kathairei ("prunes/cleanses") in the preceding verse. The wordplay connects pruning to cleanness: the pruning the vinedresser performs is a form of cleansing, and the disciples have already been cleansed — by the word (logos) Jesus has spoken to them. The cleanness is not ritual but moral and relational: it comes through the word, not through washing (though the foot-washing of chapter 13 enacted it symbolically).

The statement echoes 13:10: "He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean (katharos holos); and you are clean (katharoi), but not all of you." In chapter 13, the qualification "not all of you" excluded Judas. Now Judas has departed (13:30), and the qualification is no longer needed. Jesus can say simply "you are clean" without exception. The audience has been purified by the departure of the one who was not clean. The disciples who remain are those whose relationship with Jesus is genuine, whose reception of the word has produced cleanness.

The word logos ("word") is the same word that opens the entire document: "In the beginning was the Word (logos), and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (1:1). The Word that created all things (1:3), that became flesh and dwelt among humanity (1:14), has spoken to the disciples, and that speech has cleansed them. In 8:31-32, Jesus said: "If you abide (meinate) in my word (logo), you are truly my disciples of mine; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free." In 17:17, he will pray: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word (logos) is truth." The word cleanses, sanctifies, and frees. The mechanism of cleanness is not a one-time event but the ongoing reception of what Jesus has spoken — a point that the following verses will develop through the imperative to "abide."

div.title: Verses 4-8: The Imperative to Abide and Its Consequences
div.p: "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches; he who abides in me and I in him, he bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away as a branch and dries up; and they gather them, and throw them into the fire, and they are burned. If you abide in me and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit, and so prove to be my disciples."

"Abide in me, and I in you" (meinate en emoi, kago en hymin). The verb meno ("to abide, remain, dwell, stay") is the most important word in this chapter and one of the most important in the entire document. It appears over forty times in the document as a whole, but its concentration in verses 4-10 is extraordinary: eleven occurrences in seven verses. The word carries a range of meanings that are all operative: to remain in a place (1:38-39, the disciples "stayed" with Jesus that day), to persist in a condition (3:36, the wrath of God "abides" on the one who does not obey the Son), to endure over time (12:34, "the Christ remains forever"), and to dwell relationally (6:56, "he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him"; 14:10, "the Father abiding in me does his works"; 14:17, the Spirit "abides with you").

The imperative meinate ("abide") is a command, not a description. The disciples are not told that they automatically abide or that their abiding is assured; they are told to abide. The command assumes the possibility of not abiding — otherwise the imperative would be meaningless. The form is aorist imperative, which in Greek typically denotes urgency or the initiation of an action: "Begin to abide and keep abiding." The "and I in you" (kago en hymin) is the reciprocal promise: if they abide in Jesus, he will abide in them. The mutual indwelling of 14:20 ("you in me, and I in you") is now expressed as a vine-and-branch relationship: the branch's life is in the vine, and the vine's fruitfulness is through the branch.

"As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me" (kathos to klema ou dynatai karpon pherein aph' heautou, ean me mene en te ampelo, houtos oude hymeis, ean me en emoi menete). The analogy is agricultural and absolute. A severed branch cannot produce grapes. The phrase "of itself" (aph' heautou, "from itself, on its own") describes the impossibility of independent productivity. The branch has no life source of its own; all its vitality comes from the vine's root system, through the trunk, into the branch. Cut the connection and the branch dies. The application is direct: "so neither can you" (houtos oude hymeis). The disciples can produce nothing of value apart from their connection to Jesus. The phrase "unless you abide in me" (ean me en emoi menete) is a conditional clause with a present subjunctive: the abiding must be ongoing, sustained, continuous.

The word "fruit" (karpon) carries the same resonance it held in the prophetic vine passages. In Isaiah 5, the fruit God expected was justice and righteousness (5:7). In Hosea 10:1, Israel produced fruit "for himself" — self-serving fruit. The fruit the Father-as-vinedresser seeks is not specified yet in the chapter, but the context of the new commandment (13:34, to be restated in 15:12, 17) and the pattern of the foot-washing suggest that the fruit is the visible expression of Jesus's love within the community: obedience, mutual service, and self-giving love modeled on Jesus's own.

"I am the vine, you are the branches" (ego eimi he ampelos, hymeis ta klemata). The identification is now made explicit. Jesus does not merely compare himself to a vine; he states that he is the vine and the disciples are the branches. The pronoun "you" (hymeis) is plural, addressed to the group of disciples present — the same group that was washed, instructed, and told to love one another. The relationship is organic: the branch is not attached to the vine by external fastening but grows out of it, shares its life, draws its sustenance from it. The identity of the branch is derived entirely from its connection to the vine. A branch that is separated from its vine is not a vine-branch anymore; it is dead wood.

"He who abides in me and I in him, he bears much fruit" (ho menon en emoi kago en auto, houtos pherei karpon polyn). The present participle ho menon ("the one who abides, the one who is abiding") describes an ongoing condition, not a past-tense achievement. The one who is presently, actively, continuously abiding in Jesus — and in whom Jesus is presently abiding — "bears much fruit" (pherei karpon polyn). The phrase "much fruit" (karpon polyn) echoes the grain-of-wheat saying of 12:24: "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (polyn karpon)." The much fruit of 12:24 resulted from the grain's death; the much fruit of 15:5 results from the branch's abiding. The connection between the two is the principle of dependence: the grain must die to itself (fall into the earth), and the branch must remain connected to something other than itself (the vine). Self-sufficiency produces nothing; dependence produces abundance.

"For apart from me you can do nothing" (hoti choris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden). The word choris ("apart from, without, separated from") indicates complete severance. The claim is absolute: without connection to Jesus, the disciples can produce nothing of value. The word ouden ("nothing") is unqualified. This echoes the document's sustained teaching about the Son's own dependence on the Father: "The Son can do nothing of himself, unless it is something he sees the Father doing" (5:19); "I can do nothing on my own initiative" (5:30). The same pattern of dependence that characterizes the Son's relationship with the Father now characterizes the disciples' relationship with the Son. The chain of dependence runs: Father to Son to disciples. The Father works through the Son (5:19-20, 14:10); the Son works through the disciples (15:5). Sever any link in the chain and the work ceases.

"If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away as a branch and dries up; and they gather them, and throw them into the fire, and they are burned" (ean me tis mene en emoi, eblethe exo hos to klema kai exeranthe, kai synagousin auta kai eis to pyr ballousin kai kaietai). This verse describes the fate of the branch that does not abide. Several elements require attention.

First, "if anyone does not abide in me" (ean me tis mene en emoi) — the conditional is third-class (ean + subjunctive), indicating a real possibility being contemplated. The "anyone" (tis) is indefinite: this is not addressed to a specific person but describes a general principle applicable to any branch. The possibility of not abiding is taken as genuine. The imperative of verse 4 ("abide in me") carries weight precisely because the alternative of verse 6 is real.

Second, "he is thrown away as a branch" (eblethe exo hos to klema). The verb eblethe is aorist passive of ballo ("to throw, cast"). The passive voice indicates that the person is acted upon — thrown out by someone else. The phrase exo ("outside, away") is the same word used for Judas's departure: after receiving the morsel, "he went out" (exelthen, 13:30). It is the same word used for the casting out of the man born blind from the synagogue (exebalon auton exo, 9:34-35). In 6:37, Jesus promised: "the one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out (ekbalo exo)." The verbal echo is significant: the one who comes to Jesus will not be cast out, but the one who does not abide is cast out. The difference is between the coming and the abiding — between initial approach and sustained connection.

Third, "dries up" (exeranthe, aorist passive of xeraino, "to dry up, wither"). The image is vivid: a severed branch, cut from its life-source, loses its moisture and becomes brittle. In the LXX, xeraino describes the drying up of water (Genesis 8:7, 14; Joshua 2:10; Psalm 74:15), the withering of plants (Isaiah 40:7-8: "The grass withers, the flower fades"; Ezekiel 17:9-10: the transplanted vine whose leaves "wither"), and metaphorically the desolation of nations and peoples under judgment (Isaiah 19:5-7; Ezekiel 37:11: "Our bones are dried up"). The withering of the severed branch is not gradual decline but terminal loss of life.

Fourth, "they gather them, and throw them into the fire, and they are burned" (synagousin auta kai eis to pyr ballousin kai kaietai). The impersonal "they gather" (synagousin, third person plural without a specified subject) is a common construction for general or indefinite agents. The gathering, throwing into fire, and burning reflect the standard practice of vine-dressing: dead branches were collected and burned, having no other use. Ezekiel 15:4-6 is the direct background: "Behold, it is put into the fire for fuel; the fire has consumed both of its ends, and its middle part has been charred... As I have given the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest to the fire for fuel, so I will give up the inhabitants of Jerusalem." The vine wood that does not bear fruit is fit only for burning. The image of fire (pyr) in Israel's scriptures is associated with divine judgment: "For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire" (Isaiah 66:15, LXX); "the day is coming, burning like a furnace; and all the arrogant and every evildoer will be chaff; and the day that is coming will set them ablaze" (Malachi 4:1, LXX 3:19).

The sequence — thrown out, dried up, gathered, burned — describes a complete process of removal and destruction. There is no indication that the branch can be reattached after being thrown out. The imagery moves in one direction: from vine to ground to fire. The verse is a warning addressed to the disciples: the one who does not abide in Jesus faces this fate. The warning is real and specific, not hypothetical decoration. The author who has already shown one of Jesus's own chosen twelve departing into the night (13:30) does not treat the possibility of a disciple's departure as merely theoretical.

"If you abide in me and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (ean meinte en emoi kai ta rhemata mou en hymin meine, ho ean thelete aitesasthe, kai genetai hymin). The positive counterpart to verse 6. The conditional has two parts: "if you abide in me" and "my words abide in you." The first describes the disciples' sustained connection to Jesus; the second describes the internalization of Jesus's teaching. The two are inseparable: to abide in Jesus is to have his words dwelling within. The word rhemata ("words, sayings, utterances") is distinct from logos ("word" in the singular, as a comprehensive term for Jesus's message). The plural rhemata refers to the specific things Jesus has said — the particular instructions, promises, and commands that the disciples have heard throughout the document. When these words are internalized, the disciples' will aligns with the Father's will, and their prayers are answered because their desires have been shaped by Jesus's words. The promise is not a blank check for any wish; it is the assurance that those who are formed by Jesus's words will ask for what the Father wants to give.

The connection between abiding and prayer echoes 14:13-14: "Whatever you ask in my name, that will I do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it." The condition in chapter 14 was "in my name" (en to onomati mou); here the condition is abiding and having Jesus's words abide within. The two conditions are complementary: to ask "in my name" is to ask as one who abides in Jesus and is shaped by his words. Prayer that emerges from genuine abiding is prayer aligned with the vine's purposes, and such prayer is effective.

"My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit, and so prove to be my disciples" (en touto edoxasthe ho pater mou, hina karpon polyn pherete kai genesthe emoi mathetai). The verb edoxasthe ("is glorified") is aorist passive: the Father's glorification is accomplished through the disciples' fruit-bearing. The word doxa ("glory") has been central to the document since the prologue ("we saw his glory," 1:14) and has been connected to the signs (2:11), to the hour of Jesus's death and resurrection (12:23, 28; 13:31-32), and to the mutual glorification of Father and Son (17:1, 4-5). Now the disciples' fruit-bearing is added as a means of the Father's glorification. The Father is glorified when the vine produces what it was planted to produce. Isaiah 5 described the vineyard that did not glorify the owner because it produced worthless grapes. This vine — the true vine — produces much fruit, and the Father receives glory through it.

The phrase "and so prove to be my disciples" (kai genesthe emoi mathetai) uses the verb ginomai ("become, prove to be, show yourselves to be"). The verb suggests process and demonstration: by bearing much fruit, the disciples become — or are shown to be — what they claim to be. Discipleship is not merely a label but a condition demonstrated by fruit. This echoes 8:31: "If you abide (meinate) in my word, you are truly my disciples." The word meno appears in both passages as the condition of genuine discipleship. In 13:35, the mark of discipleship was love for one another: "By this all men will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Now the mark is fruit-bearing, which the following verses will define as love carried out in obedience.

div.title: Verses 9-11: The Chain of Love and Abiding in Love
div.p: "Just as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you; abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love; just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love. These things I have spoken to you so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be made full."

"Just as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you" (kathos egapesen me ho pater, kago hymas egapesa). The conjunction kathos ("just as, in the same way as") establishes correspondence: the love Jesus has for the disciples is patterned on the Father's love for Jesus. The chain of love runs: Father loves Son; Son loves disciples. This chain has been established since 3:35 ("The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand") and 5:20 ("For the Father loves the Son, and shows him all things that he himself is doing"). In 17:23, the chain will be stated explicitly: "You loved them, even as you loved me." The love is not a general benevolence but the specific, active, self-giving love that the document has described: the Father gave the Son (3:16), and the Son gave himself (10:11, 15, 17-18). The aorist tense of both verbs — egapesen ("loved") and egapesa ("I loved") — describes love as a completed, historical act: the Father's love for the Son has been demonstrated; Jesus's love for the disciples has been demonstrated (through the foot-washing, the teaching, the care he has given them throughout his ministry).

"Abide in my love" (meinate en te agape te eme). The imperative meinate ("abide") reappears, now with a new object: not "in me" (as in verse 4) but "in my love." The love of Jesus is a space, a reality, a domain in which the disciples are commanded to remain. The love is not an emotion they produce but a condition they inhabit — a relationship they maintain by remaining within its sphere. To "abide in my love" is not identical to "abide in me," but the two are inseparable: the love is the defining quality of the vine-branch relationship, and to remain in the vine is to remain in the love.

"If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love" (ean tas entolas mou teresete, meneite en te agape mou). The mechanism of abiding in love is now specified: keeping Jesus's commandments (entolas). The conditional ean ("if") with the aorist subjunctive (teresete, "keep, observe, guard") describes a condition that must be fulfilled. The result — "you will abide in my love" (meneite, future indicative) — follows from the condition. The abiding is not unconditional; it depends on keeping the commandments. The word tereo ("to keep, guard, observe") is the same word used in 8:51 ("If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death"), 8:52 ("Abraham died, and the prophets; yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste of death'"), 14:15 ("If you love me, you will keep my commandments"), 14:21 ("He who has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me"), 14:23 ("If anyone loves me, he will keep my word"), and 14:24 ("He who does not love me does not keep my words"). Throughout the farewell discourse, keeping and loving are intertwined: love produces obedience, and obedience sustains the relationship. The relationship is not static; it is maintained through active, ongoing responsiveness to what Jesus has commanded.

"Just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love" (kathos ego tas entolas tou patros mou tetereka kai meno autou en te agape). Jesus offers himself as the model. His own relationship with the Father operates on the same principle: he keeps the Father's commandments and therefore abides in the Father's love. The verb tetereka (perfect tense of tereo, "I have kept and continue to keep") describes a sustained, completed-with-ongoing-effect condition. Jesus has kept the Father's commandments throughout his entire ministry — "I do exactly as the Father commanded me" (14:31) — and this obedience is the basis of his abiding in the Father's love.
