Someone other than the beloved disciple — a community, a group of associates, those who received his testimony — vouches for its truthfulness. The word alethes ("true, truthful, reliable") is the same adjective used in 19:35 ("his testimony is true," alethine) and 5:31-32 ("If I alone testify about myself, my testimony is not true [alethes]; there is another who testifies of me, and I know that the testimony which he gives about me is true [alethes]"). The truth of testimony in this document is always verified by corroboration — by multiple witnesses (5:31-39), by the works themselves (10:25), by the Father's confirmation (8:18). Here, the "we" of the community confirms the beloved disciple's testimony. His witness is not self-authenticating; it is received and affirmed by those who know him and know what he has reported.

The verse also completes the document's witness structure. The chain of testimony runs: the Father testifies about the Son (5:37; 8:18); the Son testifies about the Father (1:18; 14:9); the works/signs testify about the Son (5:36; 10:25); the Spirit testifies about the Son (15:26); the disciples testify (15:27); the beloved disciple testifies as the primary eyewitness (19:35; 21:24); and the community confirms the testimony ("we know that his testimony is true"). The document is itself testimony — written so that "you may believe" (20:31).

"And there are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they were written in detail, I suppose that even the world itself would not contain the books that would be written." The closing statement echoes the note in 20:30 that "many other signs Jesus also performed... which are not written in this book." But the final verse goes further than 20:30 with deliberate hyperbole: the world itself could not contain the books. The verb oiomai ("I suppose, I think") introduces the author's personal estimation, a rare first-person intrusion. The hyperbole is not a failure of literary judgment but a declaration of scope: the document has been selective, and the selection has been driven by purpose (20:31). What was included was included for a reason; what was omitted was not omitted because it was unimportant but because no document could capture the fullness of what Jesus did.

list.item: The chapter resolves the narrative of Peter's failure. The threefold denial beside a charcoal fire (18:17, 25, 27) is answered by a threefold restoration beside a charcoal fire (21:15-17). The restoration is not a word of forgiveness spoken in passing but a structured reversal that matches the denial point for point: three questions for three denials, the rare word anthrakia linking the two fires, and a commission issued with each affirmation. Peter's status is not merely restored but transformed: the disciple who failed as a follower is now commissioned as a shepherd. The one who could not stand beside a slave-girl's question is now charged with feeding and tending the flock of the good shepherd.

The shepherd commission transfers pastoral responsibility to Peter while maintaining Jesus's ownership of the flock. Each commission is framed with the possessive "my" — "my lambs," "my sheep," "my sheep." Peter does not become the owner of the flock; he becomes its caretaker under the authority of the one who laid down his life for it (10:11, 15). The vocabulary of feeding (bosko) and shepherding (poimaino) draws directly on the shepherd discourse of chapter 10 and on the Ezekiel 34 background that stands behind it. Jesus, the good shepherd who fulfills God's promise to shepherd Israel through "my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:23-24), now delegates the day-to-day care of the flock to Peter. The delegation does not diminish Jesus's role as shepherd; it extends it through a commissioned agent.

Peter's predicted death fulfills his earlier boast and completes the pattern of the good shepherd. In 13:37, Peter declared "I will lay down my life for you." The declaration failed at the moment of testing (18:17, 25, 27). But the prediction of 21:18-19 announces that Peter will, in fact, lay down his life — not in his own strength but in the weakness of old age, not on his own terms but led where he does not wish to go. The language "signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God" (21:19) deliberately echoes the identical phrase used for Jesus's own death (12:33; 18:32). Peter's death is patterned after Jesus's: both are described as glorifying God, both involve being taken by others, both are forms of the cross. The promise of 13:36 — "you will follow later" — finds its definitive meaning: Peter will follow Jesus all the way to death.

The command "Follow me" frames the entire chapter and closes Peter's narrative arc. Peter was called to follow at the beginning of the document (1:42-43; and the verb akoloutheo describes his discipleship throughout). He attempted to follow on his own terms (13:37; 18:10-11) and failed (18:15-27). He is now called again — the same command, the same verb, the same shepherd's voice. But the following now has a specific destination: a death that glorifies God. Discipleship in this document has never been abstract; it has always been a response to the shepherd's voice (10:27), a walking in the light (8:12), an abiding in the vine (15:4-10). Now, for Peter, it is also a walk toward the cross. The following that began at the Jordan ends at a place Peter does not choose, led by hands that are not his own.

The beloved disciple's role as witness is distinguished from Peter's role as shepherd. The chapter assigns distinct functions to the two central figures. Peter feeds, shepherds, and follows to death. The beloved disciple testifies: he sees and bears witness (19:35; 20:8; 21:24). The two roles are complementary, not competitive. The beloved disciple recognized the Lord from the boat (21:7) — perception is his gift. Peter threw himself into the sea (21:7) — action is his gift. The beloved disciple provides the testimony on which the document rests; Peter provides the pastoral care through which the community is fed. Jesus's rebuke — "What is that to you? You follow me!" (21:22) — prevents the comparison of the two callings. Each disciple has a calling from the same shepherd, and neither calling diminishes the other.

The return to the Sea of Tiberias connects the ending of the document to its beginning. The first disciples were called near the Jordan (1:35-51). The first sign was performed in Galilee (2:1-11). The feeding of the five thousand and the bread-of-life discourse occurred at the Sea of Tiberias (6:1-71). Now the final manifestation occurs at the same sea. The geographic return creates a literary inclusio: the story ends where it started, in Galilee, by the water, with fishermen, in the presence of Jesus. The movement from Galilee to Jerusalem for the Passover, the crucifixion, and the resurrection is now followed by a return to Galilee — not as retreat but as the site of restoration and commission. The risen Lord meets his followers in the place of their daily labor, not in the temple courts. The shepherd calls from the shore of the sea, as he called from the banks of the Jordan.

The fruitless night and the abundant morning enact the document's central principle about dependence on Jesus. The disciples' failure to catch anything during the night and the overwhelming catch at Jesus's word in the morning are the narrative illustration of 15:5: "Apart from me you can do nothing." The vine-and-branch metaphor of chapter 15 is here enacted in the fishermen's experience. Without Jesus's direction, the labor produces nothing. At his word, the labor produces more than the net can hold. The principle governs the commissioned life that follows: Peter will shepherd not in his own capacity but under the authority of the one who has called him. The feeding that Peter is commanded to do is sustained by the same word that filled the net.

The unbroken net and the number 153 point toward the scope and unity of the gathered community. Whether or not the number 153 carries specific symbolic meaning, the text emphasizes two features: the catch is very large, and the net is not torn. In a document that has prayed for unity — "that they may all be one" (17:21) — and that has identified the "other sheep that are not of this fold" who will hear the shepherd's voice and become "one flock, one shepherd" (10:16), the image of a single net holding an enormous and diverse catch without breaking carries resonance. The gathering will be vast, but the community will hold. The unity the shepherd prayed for will be maintained.

The chapter identifies the beloved disciple as the document's authoritative witness and attributes the written testimony to him. The verse "This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and wrote these things, and we know that his testimony is true" (21:24) anchors the entire document in eyewitness testimony. The testimony theme that runs from 1:7 (John the Baptist's witness) through 19:35 (the eyewitness at the cross) to 20:30-31 (the purpose statement) now receives its final identification: the beloved disciple is the testifier. The "we" who vouch for his testimony represent the community that received, preserved, and transmitted his witness. The document is not anonymous reflection but sourced testimony, and the source is the disciple who reclined on Jesus's breast, stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb, recognized the Lord from the boat, and is now named as the one who wrote.

The chapter's closing hyperbole — that the world itself could not contain the books — asserts both the selectivity of the document and the inexhaustibility of Jesus's significance. The author has chosen what to include based on a stated purpose: "that you may believe" (20:31). What was not included was not irrelevant but simply beyond the capacity of any written record to contain. The statement places the document within its proper limits: it is a true and sufficient testimony for its stated purpose, but it does not pretend to be exhaustive. The reality of what Jesus did and who Jesus is exceeds what can be written, and the final word of the document is an acknowledgment of that excess.
